line: IPO Hov, no need for reverse merger
vault_lines: IPO Hov, no need for reverse merger
meaning:
An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a company (called the issuer) issues common stock or shares to the public for the first time. It is done as a way for companies to raise money. Jay is saying that he doesn’t need the help, and has that kind of money on his own

A reverse merger is exactly the opposite, and is sometimes called a “reverse IPO”. It is the acquisition of a public company by a private company to bypass the lengthy and complex process of going public. It’s no accident that a reverse merger is more typically called a reverse takeover.

Jay seems to be saying that he is ready to “go public” as a titan of industry on his own – no need to disguise his intentions or try to play it low-key.

Interestingly, Jay’s business partner-turned-enemy Dame Dash has a cousin (Darien Dash) who was the first African-American to own a company to go through a reverse merger in 2000.

vault_lines: In a hurricane of emotions
meaning:
Just as he was before recording “Minority Report” in 2006, Jay is inspired by the pain and suffering of his race. “Hurricane” implies power, confusion, and raw energy.

“Smack dab” calls back to the wrestling imagery; it means to smack someone, and to be “in the middle.”

A quote from Decoded, originally in regards to Hurricane Katrina, is appropriate here:

…in America, we process that sort of thing as a tragedy. When it happens to black people, it feels like something else, like history rerunning its favorite loop… I got angry. But more than that, I just felt hurt. In moments like that, it all starts coming back to you: slavery, images of black people in suits and dresses getting beaten on the bridge to Selma, the whole ugly story you sometimes want to think is over. And then it’s back, like it never left. I felt hurt in a personal way.. Maybe I felt some sense of shame that we’d let this happen to our brothers and sisters."

“The Hurricane” was also a popular wrestler.

line: Pray your little cousin ain’t fall from the place that you fall asleep
vault_lines: Pray your little cousin ain't fall from the place that you fall asleep
meaning:
Shortly after the disappearance of his father Adnes Reeves when he was 11 or 12 years old, Jay Z suffered another traumatic loss when one of his cousins died after falling out of a broken window in a neighboring Marcy Projects apartment. Jay spoke about the impact the episode had on him at an early age in Decoded:

My cousin fell out of a project window. The bars on the window weren’t on right. It’s the kind of tragedy that makes you question God about the disparities in the way people live. When niggas in the game get shot, it’s tragic in its way, but you can maybe argue that they knew what was up when they got into that life. But when it happens to a kid, you realize that there’s something even more  troubling going on in the universe, and you start wanting an answer. Or worse, you get used to it.

He also detailed the event on “Young, Black and Gifted.”

The expression “the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree” means that sons and daughters are like their parents; Jay prays those close to him aren’t forced to endure what he had to as a youth.

The Brooklyn neighborhood where he grew up was, and still is, severely impoverished and incredibly difficult to exit successfully, let alone alive. Losing family members to violent acts, especially those perpetrated by the police, is a real fear existing in the projects around America—statistics would have Jay, his family, and his friends creating wills at just age 18.

Hov told Oprah in 2009 that he was only 9 years old when he witnessed his first murder in the Marcy Projects:

I saw a guy get shot when I was 9. And he wasn’t even a bad guy. His name was Benny. He was the guy who would take us to play baseball. We always believed he could have made it to the majors. He was that good. Some guy was chasing him – and then I heard a shot and saw him on the floor.

line: I acted out, my life a stage, ten thousand people watchin’ Where’s the little boy I knew? I must have forgot him Stuntin’, of course we never grew But we’re alone now and I’m singing this song for you Stuntin’, of course we never grew But we’re alone now and I’m singing this song...you
vault_lines: I acted out, my life a stage, ten thousand people watchin'
meaning:
This is a direct reference to Donny Hathaway’s “A Song For You”:


I’ve acted out my life on stages
With ten thousand people watching

But we’re alone now
And I’m singing this song to you


Though Jay has lived a successful life in the public eye for the world to see, deep down he’s still a kid from the projects. Chasing his dreams and living a lavish lifestyle may have made him superficially happy, but deep down he’s still struggling with the insecurities of being a fatherless kid from the ghetto.

Before his father left their family, Jay was a happy person, although still quiet and soft-spoken as he is now. But after experiencing the trauma of his “superhero” leaving him behind, he became very angry, withdrawing from his studies and isolating himself from his family. That young boy closed himself off so he wouldn’t be hurt again that deeply.

Jay came to terms with his father’s absence on 2003’s “Moment of Clarity,” but he realizes that he never really dealt with some of that pain head on, only covered it up with material possessions. Jay plays off the double meaning of “stuntin'” to make the point, referring both to showing off and preventing one’s growth. Money’s allowed Jay to live the carefree life of a boy, meanwhile stunting his own personal development.

In his book Decoded, Jay spoke a bit about this journey:

There’s a line in Fade to Black, the concert film we did for The Black Album, where I say, ‘I sometimes step back and see myself from the outside and say, who is that guy?’ Over time I’ve worked to get more clarity about my past and present and to unify my outside shell and soul, but it’s ongoing.

line: (All this work can pay off) I just want all this work to pay off (Just don’t calculate us) Don’t calculate us
vault_lines: I just want all this work to pay off
meaning:
Black people have fought for their right to be treated equally ever since the 1600s. With the Civil Rights Movement nearly 60 years in the past, they’re still fighting every day to be treated equally. The work didn’t end in 1968.

Jay wrote extensively in his book Decoded about the influence and role hip-hop played in continuing the battle for equality:

There’s a knee-jerk fear in America that someone – especially someone young and black – is coming to take your shit. But in hip-hop, the truth is, we don’t want your shit. We came out of the generation of black people who finally got the point: No one’s going to help us. So we went for self, for family, for block, for crew… It’s just a rational response to the reality we faced.

Progress has been made: Barack Obama is president, and artists like Jay himself, as well as Puff Daddy, Birdman, Drake and especially Oprah Winfrey offer something to aspire to for young black people.

And yet despite these incredibly hard-fought gains, innocent black kids are seen as “less innocent.” Incarceration rates are hugely skewed. Black people are seemingly judged, or “calculated,” as more dangerous than any other race, for no other reason than the colour of their skin.

line: Sick of hiding in holes and behind hyperbole
vault_lines: Sick of hiding in holes and behind hyperbole
meaning:
“Hyperbole” is an exaggerated statement. In the case of hip-hop, this means lyrics that aren’t designed to be taken seriously, they’re written and rapped to entertain listeners.

Because of his drug dealing past, his misogynistic lyrics, and his brushes with the law, he’s been labelled a certain way, even recently being cast as a negative influence by conservative media.

Jay could mean both himself and his detractors are  sitting comfortably behind hyperbole and using it to justify their position. Jay’s excuse: It’s just entertainment. Others claim it’s a bad influence on young black people.

Also, notice the assonance and alliteration: hiding in holes and behind hyperbole.

Whose daughter couldn’t escape the reach of the preacher’s hand

Jay comments on a grandfather abusing an aunt. The effects of sexual assault permeate the daily lives of survivors, which makes it difficult to heal. That struggle can then ripple down, and be felt throughout a family or an entire community.

Inappropriate responses by non-perpetrator family members towards a sexual assault survivor can have many profound negative effects on the survivor, and can lead to the shattering of familial relationships. One repulsive act can destroy a community for generations to come.

line: This is the real me unfold Gangster is love, I’m thuggin’, I’m huggin’ This is tougher than any gun that I raised Any crack that I blazed, that was nothin’ Peeling back the layers, uncovering Scars that never healed, I never kept it this real

meaning:
“Jay Z” is a pseudonym for the man behind the persona, Shawn Carter. As he said in Decoded:

Rappers are just crafting a character that the listener can relate to.

Jay addresses us as Shawn, a Black man in America with a Black wife and a Black daughter. In this raw and revealing state, he realizes he has scars from his own personal traumas: his dad leaving, his nephew dying, his cousin falling out a window to his death in the Marcy Projects, watching his brother Eric fall into a deep drug addiction and then Jay having to shoot him at the age of 12 when he stole his jewelry to pay for crack cocaine, losing his close friend Biggie in 1997, three separate relationships, including a miscarriage, losing close friend Aaliyah in 2001, losing close friend Bobalob who was shot dead in 2003, and his dad dying just a month after they had reconnected.

 The emotional pain from selling drugs and using weapons pales in comparison. Over his entire rap career, he hasn’t been this explicit about his own thoughts and feelings.

His “angel” may be Blue, Beyoncé, or both. Beyoncé has an impeccable voice, and Blue loves singing his music:

She plays a song and she goes, ‘More, Daddy, more … Daddy song.’ She’s my biggest fan. If no one bought the Magna Carta, the fact that she loves it so much, it gives me the greatest joy. […] She’s genuine, she’s honest, because she doesn’t know it makes me happy. She just wants to hear it.

Although this song was created long before LEMONADE dropped, it now has stronger emotional links to the imagery in the “Sandcastles” video.

Jay implores society not to make racial judgments about Black people.

When this song was released, he spoke about the song’s relation to recent incidents of police brutality committed against Alton Sterling and Philando Castile:

I trust God and know everything that happens is for our greatest good, but man … it’s tough right now.

Another meaning of spirituality is “relating to the soul as opposed to material things.” Jay’s 2013 album was criticised for being too materialistic. He makes it clear this has nothing to do with material goods or even his rap persona. He’s removing the layers so he can speak directly to the people as one of them.

Jay also incorporates wordplay here—he uses alcohol to overcome his fears and anxieties, and “spirits” are a type of alcohol. Alcohol is also a type of poison, not only is Jay not poisonous, he’s using dangerous substances to cope with the injustice black people are facing.

Putting one’s hands in the air has become a cultural symbol for protest against unnecessary police brutality, specifically towards Black people. Following the shooting of Michael Brown, the “hands up, don’t shoot” gesture became widely recognized for this purpose.

Jay compares Garner’s conceding pleas to tapping out in WWE wrestling matches. The officer didn’t stop, and Garner was killed.

The other side of the narrative relates to Jay’s authenticity, especially compared to his contemporary competition. Since violence in wrestling is staged, the reference to WWE implies others spit fake bars, while Jay raps from the heart. He’s been wrestling on the streets with the barriers young black men face.

Jay’s version of “tapping out” is when he left the streets and created Roc-a-fella Records,

meaning:
Tension and fear amongst the Black community cause Jay to lose sleep. They’re targeted by police, and he likens the experience to his days hustling in the streets, and sleepless nights born of anxiety and fear.

It also relates to the popular saying “stay woke,” which means to keep informed.

“Change Clothes” was the first single off 2003’s The Black Album, a track that was deemed influential in changing the style of hip-hop, moving away from over-sized jerseys and do-rags (symbols of the ghetto), to button up suits and high fashion.

Jay was 34 when The Black Album came out, and while people say he’s since lost touch with the hood, he provides evidence here to the contrary. He’s still very much in tune and in touch.

Hov is in an unhealthy mental state for fear of lacking the fathering skills to raise his daughter and the world she must grow up in. He suggests drinking alcohol or having a psychiatric intervention may help him cope.

Jay has long said he uses music as his therapy, and doesn’t see a benefit) in traditional methods of psychiatric help:

We were raised to hold a lot in, so for me making music is like therapy. It gives me a chance to express my emotions and the things I have going on, so yeah, I’m exposed.

To suggest he visits a therapist is a big step for Hov, alluding to the severity of the pain he is feeling from the atrocities being committed against his race in America.

I don’t wanna have to just repeat another leave another
Baby with no daddy want no momma drama

Add to this the difficulties being Black, and Jay’s reaching for the alcohol. to numb the pain. He’s shattered as a person, and it’s possible he means the country itself is shattered by this epidemic it is embroiled in. His own attempts to combat systemic and violent racism aren’t enough.

meaning:
These lines introduce the song’s structure. Every two lines form a couplet, comparing life in affluent parts of America with the harsh realities of the ghetto.

These disparities, and Jay-Z’s own experience of living in these two different worlds, is a constant theme throughout his music. In 2018’s “SUMMER,” he talks about how music has changed his life from ducking bullets to his children being sound asleep.

In his memoir, Decoded, Jay-Z explains this real life tragedy:

My cousin fell out of a project window. The bars on the window weren’t on right. It’s the kind of tragedy that makes you question…the disparities in the way people live. When niggas in the game get shot, it’s tragic in its way, but you can maybe argue that they knew what was up when they got into that life. But when it happens to a kid, you realize that there’s something even more troubling going on in the universe, and you start wanting an answer. Or worse, you get used to it."

line: All the screams from the ghetto, all the teens ducking metal here So they steam like a kettle here
vault_lines: All the screams from the ghetto, all the teens ducking metal here
meaning:
“Steam” is a double entendre. First, he references drugs and the smoke (or “steam”) that comes from smoking drugs like heroin. He is referencing the idea that many people get high to dull the pain and struggled associated with poverty. This imagery also calls back to the line about China White heroin, and how it allows its users to “take flight.”

“Steam” is also a reference to the anger those in poverty feel toward people who are more affluent. When someone is mad, they’re often described as “steaming hot.”



Finally, he transitions to the next couplet with a reference to the Devil, who lives in a place consumed by fire. Thus being “close to the Devil” would make a kettle “steam.”

song: Young Gifted and Black Freestyle [Mariah Carey Skit]
line: Right in front of my sight, like “here”, yeah “There’s your ticket out the ghetto, take flight right here
vault_lines: Right in front of my sight, like “here”, yeah
meaning:
In this line, heroin is personified. Like a devil on his shoulder, it’s encouraging Jay to sell drugs in order to earn money and escape the ghetto.

The phrase “take flight” is also a double entendre: the drug gives its users a chemical high, but would also allow Jay-Z to lift himself out of his circumstances.

Jay-Z has rapped about his past as a heroin dealer throughout his career. You can find examples in his early work, like his 1996 collaboration with B.I.G., “Brooklyn’s Finest”, and later years like 2007’s “Roc Boys (And The Winner Is…).”

Did you sell crack to your mother?
When I said that, I meant [it as] a metaphor for, like, the mothers of our nation.

Continuing the theme of this verse, this is both ironically heartbreaking but also ambiguous.  He suggests his mom motivated him to do better for himself and not let oppressive social forces hold him back, but he betrayed his “mother”, metaphorically, all of the mothers he sold crack to, by turning around and getting them addicted to drugs. This is complex because though selling to his mom is heinous, these crimes allowed Jay to gain the money to start his rap career. Jay accused Rivera of making and selling counterfeit copies of his fourth studio album, then stabbed him with a five-inch knife at least twice, according to a police account.

On December 10, 1999 Hov’s defense attorney Michael Richman (an infamous attorney used by hip-hop artists, also known in the Bronx as ‘Don’t Worry Murray’) claimed that video footage shot at the time of the event exonerates the rapper. But after being given the tape by Richman, Manhattan’s District Attorney Robert M. Morgenthau and the case’s presiding Supreme Court judge decided to still press on with the case. According to Richman, and Hov himself in this freestyle, this just shows how set the D.A. was on convicting Jay-Z.

A year later, after Hov’s case was settled in December 2001, many in the industry would say they believed that the District Attorney’s office pursued cases against Jay-Z so ruthlessly because they had embarrassingly lost the case against Puff Daddy in March 2001; with Puff being acquitted on all five charges of possessing guns and bribery in relation to a nightclub shooting.

This also connects to the Noah line above; in Genesis 9:20-9:27 Noah curses his son Ham for seeing him naked. The curse was that all of Ham’s descendants would be servants, a biblical verse which was cited in the 18th and 19th centuries as a justification for black slavery – African-Americans were called “the children of Ham.” So Jay embracing his identity as Ham/H.A.M. is not just trendy slang-jacking, but a deep statement on the strides made by blacks in a society that still works to subjugate them.

It’s no accident that James Baldwin’s searing meditation on civil rights, The Fire Next Time (1963), took its title from  this episode of Genesis.

line: And I got a question: Are you forgiving guys who live just like me?
vault_lines: And I got a question:
meaning:
Here Jay is interrogating God, just as he does on songs such as in 1996’s “D’Evils,” 2003’s “Lucifer,” and 2006’s “Beach Chair.” Depending on the song and his mood sometimes this questioning is in a confrontational way, sometimes in a more plaintive way.

But these lines aren’t about God in the traditional sense, they’re almost questions back to myself. Do I forgive guys who live just like me? It’s a question that haunts a lot of us—and the song is a defense, a case that in some ways we’re just products of our environment. But I’m not convinced that it’s that simple.

line: And government? Fuck government! Niggas politick theyselves

meaning:
I wrote this at a time when I felt the government was irrelevant to the ways we organized, resolved conflict, and took care of ourselves. ‘Politic’ is slang for the kind of talk that works things out.

Positive government intervention in the dire situation in the projects is nowhere to be seen, so the residents are on their own and have to make their own rules. Because they feel ignored by the rest of society, a community often agrees to ignore the laws associated with illegal activities. This creates a shared law of ethics in the hood, wherein the “niggas are politic[ing] theyselves.”

line: Where you can’t put your vest away And say you’ll wear it tomorrow ’Cause the day after we’ll be saying “Damn, I was just with him yesterday”

It was a very intense and stressful situation. There was playing in the johnny pump and the ice-cream man coming around and all of these games that we’d play; then suddenly it would turn just violent and there would be shootings at 12 in the afternoon on any given day.

line: I’m from where they ball and breed rhyme stars
vault_lines: I'm from where they ball and breed rhyme stars
meaning: ‘Ball’ has three meanings: to fuck, to spend money, and to play basketball. I’m talking about playing ball here, but I’m nodding to the other meanings, too. ‘Breeding’ rhyme stars connects back directly to the rest of this verse: The drugs and guns, the fun and the risk, and, most of all, the survival-of-the-fittest competition, is enough pressure to crush coal into diamonds. It’s an idealized, almost romantic, way to look at this life, a sudden reverse after the song’s bleak beginning.

line: Where the drugs czars evolve,
vault_lines: Where the drugs czars evolve,
meaning:
The ‘drug czar’ here obviously isn’t the one that works for the government.

The violent environment in the Marcy Houses breeds deadly competitors. The kingpins at the top of the food chain are constantly changing their tactics to keep control of the borough.

Hov also gives a criminal flip to the term “drug czar”—an informal name for the person who directs drug-control policies in the United States. The title was first used during the Reagan administration—President Reagan himself was arguably the first crack cocaine kingpin.

The Coup’s “I Love Boosters!” is the greatest song ever written about these hood heroes.

line: I’m from where the beef is inevitable, summertime’s unforgettable

The Summer seasons living in the Marcy Houses were unforgettable—for both positive and negative reasons:

It was a very intense and stressful situation. There was playing in the johnny pump and the ice-cream man coming around and all of these games that we’d play; then suddenly it would turn just violent and there would be shootings at 12 in the afternoon on any given day. It was a weird mix of emotions. One day, your best friend could be killed. The day before, you could be celebrating him getting a brand-new bike.

The girls that ignored Jay and his Marcy Houses crew because of their seemingly talkative demeanor would head over to the Tompkins Housing Projects, hoping to meet some honest guys. Jay sees this as foolish, knowing that the dudes in Tompkins were just as shady as Jay and his crew.

Tompkins niggas might’ve seemed somehow different from Marcy niggas, but we were all in the same game, after the same shit, using the same techniques.

line: I’m from the other side where the other guys don’t walk too much
vault_lines: I'm from the other side where the other guys don't walk too much

Hov delves into Ernest Crawley’s thesis that each individual is separated from others by a narcissism of minor differences. Sigmund Freud coined the phrase “der Narzissmus der kleinen Differenzen” to describe this phenomenon.

There’s a saying, ‘the narcissism of small differences,’ that applies exactly to the way we divvied up the hood: It was projects versus projects, and then building versus building, clique versus clique, brother versus brother.

line: News cameras never come

meaning:
When composing this track Jay remembered an article he has read on a horrific crime in Brooklyn, in the October 2, 1990 edition of the New York Times:

Two young men who admitted that they had raped and sodomized a 39-year-old woman and then thrown her from the roof of a four-story building in Brooklyn last year were sentenced yesterday to terms of 6 to 18 years in prison … Her case, whose shocking brutality was comparable to that of the Central Park jogger, which occurred only a few days earlier, prompted some harsh criticism of the news media, which did not devote comparable attention to it, in part, critics said, because the Central Park jogger was white and the Brooklyn victim was black.

Hov is lamenting how news cameras—and by extension, mainstream society—pay no attention to the dire effects of poverty in the projects.

Ice Cube’s “Doughboy” made a famous observation about this at the conclusion of 1991’s Boyz n the Hood:

Being a 4'4" tall adult would also mean you are minute in stature—therefore the ever-witty Hov is delivering a homophone here on Manute’s name and an adjective for small.

A “crossover" dribble is a basketball maneuver in which a player dribbling switches the ball rapidly from one hand to the other, marking a change in direction.



“Clap boards” is also basketball speak—the image Jay paints finds a player in the air, slapping the backboard while they either are dunking the ball, or grabbing a rebound. The slapping sound ricochets through the project courtyards like a gunclap.

vault_lines: I'm from where niggas pull your card, and argue all day about
meaning:
This is one of the age-old barbershop arguments in rap fan circles, especially in New York. Hov, The Notorious B.I.G. and Nas are all New York rappers that are often considered three of the greatest of all-time. Trust me when I say their fans can talk for hours on who is a better MC.

Hov explained in his biography Decoded just how emotive hip hop music can be:


When I was a kid the debate was LL versus Run-DMC, or, later, Kane versus Rakim. Next year it might be Drake versus J. Cole. It’s a tribute to how deeply felt hip-hop is that people don’t just sit back and listen to the music – they have to break it down, pick the lyrics apart, and debate the shit with other fans who are doing the same thing.

When people talk about forms of media, sometimes they compare lean-forward media (which are interactive, like video games or the
Internet) and lean-back media (which are passive, like television or magazines). Music can be lean-back sort of media, it can just wash over you or play in the background – but hip-hop is different. It forces people to lean forward – lean right out of their chairs – and take a position.

line: An ounce away from a triple beam Still using a hand-held weight scale

meaning:
The drug dealers in the neighborhood have not yet even made enough money to afford an expensive triple-beam scale to measure their product, and thus must use the lesser hand-held one.

Hov explained these lines in Decoded in 2010:


I’m triangulating my location. The block from hell is a double entendre: my block is in close proximity to the worst of the worst, but it’s also ‘the block from hell,’ like it emerged from a flaming pit. ‘Not enough shots from stray shells,’ means that where I’m from no one is really safe from a stray bullet.

The last line ‘an ounce away from a triple beam’ – is a drug-game detail that niggas in the streets picked up on immediately. That ounce away is the difference between struggling and making real money, and a lot of hustlers stay an ounce away and never graduate. But the aspiration to move up to the triple-beam is real, and the handheld weight scale is symbolic of that street-level hustler’s hunger – you can hold his weight in your hand, but his hunger is enormous.

line: Niggas thought they deuce was live, then I hit ’em with trips And I reached down for their money, pa, forget about this

Lucky Lefty is describing the dice game of “Cee-lo,” religiously played by corner drug hustlers with three dice. While rolling two fives (shoot the five) is good, three of the same number (trips) will beat two of the same number (deuce). Hov then bends down and picks up his winnings off the pavement.

Hov is describing the life of the drug addicts and crackheads he has witnessed—and most likely dealt drugs to—in the Marcy Projects. They have lost their way in life chasing the illegal high, forced to now live on the streets in squalor.

This idea of people literally losing their religion due to unanswered prayers and tough times is a recurring idea in Hov’s catalog, most fully addressed on the 2011 song “No Church in the Wild” in lines such as this one

The words “church is the flakiest” may be a reference to the Rev. Floyd Flake , pastor of Allen African Methodist Episcopal Church in Queens, who was indicted on embezzlement and tax evasion charges in the early 1990s, only to have the charges dismissed. Now that’s teflon…

The churches really were the flakiest, whether they were storefronts or big old-school churches with vaulted ceilings and steeples. When your prayers aren’t answered, you start to think that maybe there’s no one there to answer them. line: Where cats catch cases, hoping the judge R-and-R’s
vault_lines: Where cats catch cases, hoping the judge R-and-R's
meaning:
‘R-and-R’ stands for ‘reverse and remand,’ an order from a court to reverse a decision or refer it back to a lower court.

In legal terms Jay may also be referring to being “released on own recognizance.” In other words, the aforementioned “cats” hope that the judge will release them from custody prior to trial without them having to post bail or a bond, allowing them to remain free until their trial date. Of course, if they do not receive an “R-on-R” decision bail is normally set or they are remanded to custody without bail.

Furthermore, “R and R” is another term for rest and relaxation, meaning perpetrators get caught, but hope that the judge “takes it easy” on them due to their situations.

“Wet” refers to cocaine sold quickly, before the crack’s even dried up. The weight of the crack is also heavier with this water content—therefore if you sell it you’ll get more money for giving up less product.

Selling weight ‘wet’ meant to sell the crack so fast it didn’t even have time to dry from the cooking. It’s cheating, but I justify it in the next line.

line: We’ll never know

His question remains hauntingly unanswered. Jay has been fairly closed-mouthed about his spirituality, except for one post-9/11 freestyle:

And no, I’m not a Christian, though I believe in God
But I don’t believe in the Devil, my beliefs are odd
If we the people was given free will from God

This also circles back to the 2nd line of the verse, “And niggas is praying to God so long that they athiest”.  The assumption is that with very few prayers answered, Jay’s question will likely see the same result, i.e. we’ll never know.  Also, there’s no real way (outside of blind faith) of physically knowing the answer until death.  Likewise, athiests do not believe in religion so based on their beliefs, they will literally “never know” the answer to that question.

Another triple entendre from a rapper that uses them often.

Yet, as he has grown older and experienced the uncertainty that surrounds streaming numbers, he no longer sees the Billboard charts as a true sign of success.

line: Three-fifths of a man, I believe’s the phrase
vault_lines: Three-fifths of a man, I believe's the phrase
meaning:
This is a reference to the 3/5th’s compromise of the US Constitution, proposed by James Wilson and Roger Sherman at the Constitutional Convention in 1787. While counting American censuses prior to the end of slavery, each slave was counted as 3/5 of a person. In other words, for every five slaves, three people were counted in the population.

This satisfied the larger, southern states, who could use large slave population to boost national representation, while not having to pay as much in taxes (issues proportionally to the population). At the same time, it somewhat appeased opponents of slavery in the Northern states, who believed that slaves should not be counted.

This compromise, which had major benefits for state power, was at the expense of African-Americans. It dehumanized African-Americans (remember, most blacks in the United States were slaves) and set the tone for their legal disenfranchisement for nearly 2 centuries.

This continues JAY-Z’s statement of irony in the previous line: America may be the land of the free, but since its inception, African-Americans have been treated differently based on the color of their skin.

line: One-time know I got a knack to get that change Leader of the black gang, R-O-C, mane
vault_lines: One-time know I got a knack to get that change
meaning: “One-time” is an idiom commonly used in urban areas to refer to the police. Here, Jay-Z’s reference of the police’s knowledge regarding his “knack to get that change” is an allusion to his prominence in the underworld of drug dealing. Further, they are cognizant of his status as the “Leader of the black gang, R-O-C mang,” and thus know that he is the head of a an organization with purportedly criminal motives – that is, the police investigating him (in his past) were well aware that he is in charge of a criminal conspiracy in a manner that parallel’s his then-status as Owner/CEO of Roc-a-fella Records.

Throw away the key is an idiom used to say, “never release from jail.” Not only do the police want to throw hustlers in prison, they want to keep them there.

Also, “key” or “ki” is slang for a kilogram of drugs (more specifically, cocaine). The cops might find drugs on you and they want to destroy or get rid of it (throw it away). In Freeway’s eyes, this is just law enforcement trying to prevent him from feeding his children.

vault_lines: Crossover, slam dunk, Rucker Park with the flow, Young
meaning:
This is an interesting finish to the verse. Jay shouts out Rucker Park which is the scene of the Entertainer’s Basketball Classic, a basketball tournament that see’s celebrity owners coaching a team of amateur street basketballers mixed with the occasional professional ringer. This ties in heavily with Jay’s earlier Pro-Am imagery and his basketball links from the first verse.

Jay famously waded in to battle in this scene in 2003, and the story is one steeped in mystery and history. The full story can be read here and it is well worth the time.

The tournament is famed for its showcase of dirty, silky skill, so Jay shouts out a couple of basketball moves and explains that his flow is everything that makes the Rucker Park games great: Professionals shooting it out with amateurs, and the highest level of untouched skill on display in the game.

meaning:
106 & Park during this period was a rap and R&B video countdown show, in the same vein as TRL. Whilst Jay has appeared on the show since these lyrics were written, and his videos featured prominently on it, he is referring more to the fans in the crowd, and the basic nature of the majority of the music that was making it on at the time. “D'Evils”, for instance, would never have appeared on that show.

His flow, then, is so advanced that when he puts the effort in, such as on this songs, he is “off the charts”, meaning not only is he a statistical anomaly who can’t be matched, he isn’t even featured on the charts, because the flow is too complex for the children of 106 & Park to understand.

line: Niggas taking it lightly, had to darken the flow Way I put it together, tear ’em apart with the flow

meaning:
He throws in two sets of antonyms here: light/dark and put it together/tear'em apart to enhance the depth of his lyrics, highlighting that it isn’t just his flow that is versatile.

He used a similar couplet on Kanye’s “Never Let Me Down”, and it’s indicative again of his status in the game.

During the early part of his career, when he was involved in The Originators, his flow was double and triple time, stacking syllables and focusing on speed. This was not attracting the mainstream attention he craved, and on Reasonable Doubt, specifically on tracks like “Regrets” and “Can I Live” his flow was dramatically different, but much darker, to appeal to those who weren’t feeling his lyrical ability.

The way he raps is so smooth, so artistic, so beautiful, that even if his rhymes are occasionally descriptions of crimes, you have to pardon them.

As Jay was the President of Rocafella records, he also has the ability to “pardon” illegal activities. He also had a song entitled “Guilty Until Proven Innocent”, in which he lamented the way rappers were treated by the police and the justice system. But placing this subtle line in this song, 2 years later, he’s shown how he has grown from a thug to a boss with the ability to influence legal proceedings.

line: With no deal, who you gonna rap to now? Start your own record company, that’s profound
vault_lines: With no deal, who you gonna rap to now?
meaning:
When he joined the music game Jay-Z couldn’t find himself a label to sign him. Eventually he conquered this obstacle by setting up his own label, the infamous Roc-A-Fella Records with Dame Dash and Kareem ‘Biggs’ Burke.

Since 1993 Jay and Dash had been driving around New York selling singles out the back of their car trying to build hype. They had been taking meetings with labels all over town, including Def Jam and Polygram, but no one was willing to sign Young Hov. So he signed a deal with PDR in 1995, and was given around $30,000 in return for a few singles and an album. Straight away Hov and Dash had many frustrations with the label, including royalties disagreements and the label’s lack of promotion for the single ‘I Can’t Get With That’. On one visit to the PDR offices they noticed that the entire marketing campaign the label had planned for the official release of ‘In My Lifetime’ consisted of just one box of flyers for street distribution. The label was unwilling to meet their promotional expectations, so Hov and Dash split from the label and handled the radio promotion and video shoot themselves. Using the buyout money they officially formed Roc-A-Fella Records, rented a small office space on John Street in Manhattan, and the rest is history…

It came up that Jay was working on his last album and we might be able to get him some music. I sent him one record with the hook, intro, and everything in it already. They called back like, “Yo, send the files.” Then Jay called like, “Tell your peoples I think I bodied this beat. Tell them to come to the studio.” It was surreal. We just sent one beat. That was our first placement ever. I wasn’t even really a producer, I was in a rap crew. The kid that sang on the hook lived across the street from me in the projects. We recorded the hook in my house. The beat was maybe a year or two old before I even sent it to him. I had played it for a couple people and they didn’t get it. Certain tracks are just meant for certain artists.

For the 10th anniversary of the album, they broke down the production of the track for Jay Z’s Life + Times site:

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tIk6hHsUEOQ

line: But the real shit you get when you bust down my lines
vault_lines: But the real shit you get when you bust down my lines

Many of Jay-Z’s lines require exegesis to be understood fully. For this reason, Jay-Z even wrote a book called Decoded to explain many of his own iconic lyrics.



However, Jay-Z should get with the times and just get a Rap Genius Verified account.

line: [Intro: JAŸ-Z] Are you not entertained? Are you not entertained? Is this not why you are here?
vault_lines: Are you not entertained? Are you not entertained?
meaning:
A soundbyte from this clip from Gladiator, perhaps the meme guys' college dorm room movie,
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uzt6vlpdZWM

Jay starts the track like this to analogize his experience in rap to the blood sport of a gladiator, implying that he sacrifices himself or aspects of his life for the sake of entertaining others (e.g. not being able to live normally due to his fame or obligations to his fans).

It could also be interpreted as a shot at Jay’s detractors. The soundbyte comes from a scene after Crowe completely dominates the other gladiators and still the crowd does not applaud or accept him, much as Jay had completely dominated the rap game up to this point and yet still was not fully loved by rap fans leaving him to wonder Is this not why you are here?

Jay would go on to win another gauntlet with the The Black Album debuting at #1, going up against G-Unit’s Beg for Mercy in first week sales.

meaning: I haven’t even really started yet – this is just me warming up.  “EQ'ing” a track is adjusting the levels of the audio frequencies, which you do before you really start listening

line: In fact, I’m just previewin’ it
vault_lines: In fact, I'm just previewin' it
meaning:
This song was the “street single” for the album, and thus most listeners heard it before the album was released

This has a deeper meaning too, as the preceeding lines talk about how Jay got to where he is today. But what’s happened up to this point is just a preview; HOV has a lot more to accomplish.

line: And I’m back for more, New York’s ambassador Prime Minister, back to finish my business up
vault_lines: And I'm back for more, New York's ambassador
meaning:
Jay has always seen himself as someone who brings the gritty realities of NYC’s street life, in particular his native Marcy projects, to a wide audience.  As he rapped in 1999’s “Come and Get Me,”

I made it so you could say Marcy and it was all good
I didn’t cross over, I brought the suburbs to the hood

His fame increased year by year and so did the importance of his lyrics, from just a kid from the ghetto he turned into one of New York City’s ambassador and now he can be considered as important as a Prime Minister.



The Black Album, which contains this song, was supposed to mark Jay’s retirement from rap and it’d have marked the end of his career.

Jay-Z has a habit of using “Jewish” to mean “good or conservative with money” (cf. “This Can’t Be Life”, where he raps: “flow tight like I was born Jewish”)

This was written before Ms. Stewart’s arrest and imprisonment

Busta apparently responded. From Vibe:

On the 2003 mixtape track ‘You’re A Memory,’ Busta picked a beef with Jay-Z, who had merely called Busta ‘animated’ on ‘What More Can I Say.’ The problem was, the average dude in the hood ‘might not have a clear understanding of what the word animated means,’ DJ Kay Slay explains. Busta Rhymes is animated, but he was like, ‘Yo man, Jay went subliminal at me, what should I do?’ Busta lashed back at Jay: ‘If you ain’t know, I keep it in the stash of the wagon,’ he rapped, ‘the wrath of the dragon is felt when I’m cocking the cannon.’

Busta also literally did animation, in that he voiced Reptar in The Rugrats Movie, as this clip shows

Hov, a pun on Jehovah, is another of Jay-Z’s rap handles, a brag that he is the God MC. Just like he said in the previous lines, no other rapper can back up his lyrics with facts as much as Hova can.

Noah Callahan-Bever of Vibe was with 50 when he heard this line, and details 50’s reaction:

50’s eyes reveal something between confusion and anger. “Did you hear what he just said!?” he questions, to no one in particular. It’s quickly explained that, while certainly a reference to 50, it’s not necessarily a dis, and that Jay actually bigged him up on the radio before debuting the song. 50 sinks into his seat thinking, brooding, his fingers folded together. Even when no one else has drugs (“a drought”), he can still rely on the dealing of potent marijuana (“purple”). In addition to the precipitation puns, purple rain has other connotations

line: I’m not a biter, I’m a writer for myself and others
vault_lines: I'm not a biter, I'm a writer for myself and others
meaning:
“Biting” is basically rap plagiarism: it means to use another rapper’s line without giving credit. Jay has often been accused of “recycling” the Notorious B.I.G.’s raps, such as here.

On the other hand, Jay has ghostwritten raps for numerous other rappers from Dr. Dre to Bugs Bunny (no joke).

During the height of their disagreement, Cam'ron used this line in an audio collage to point out Jay’s homages to other artists.

line: These fucks, too lazy to make up shit, they crazy They don’t, paint pictures, they just, trace me

Jay has actually used this very comparison to assert that other rappers just copy his lines before, in his verse on Sauce Money’s “Pre-Game”

Also, the big punchline-they don’t “paint,” they “trace:” since you “trace” lines (in this case rap lyrics) around something you’re trying to copy

The second line here was sampled by Tyler The Creator on Jack and the Beanstalk from Bastard.

For those that think Hov’s thing is bling-blinging
Either haven’t heard the album or they don’t know English
They only know what the single is and single that out
To be the meaning of what he’s about

line: There’s never been a nigga this good for this long
vault_lines: There's never been a nigga this good for this long
meaning:
Not only is Jay being a good rapper, he’s breaking records putting himself on a level above everyone else. Prior to the release of The Black Album, Jay dropped a platinum album for 7 years in a row:



Reasonable Doubt (1996)

In My Lifetime, Vol. 1 (1997)

Vol. 2… Hard Knock Life (1998)

Vol. 3… Life and Times of S. Carter (1999)

The Dynasty: Roc La Familia (2000)

The Blueprint (2001)

The Blueprint 2: The Gift & The Curse (2002)



As it stands today, all of Jay-Z’s 14 albums (including 3 collabos) have gone at least platinum. No one in hip hop (or music, period) history comes close to having this combination of success and longevity.

line: I’m just looking for love, I know somebody got it

line: I look in the mirror, my only opponent

He repeats this sentiment again in the album during “Who Gon Stop Me?” with the line: “only thing can stop me is me” which answers the main question posed by that song.

At one point they were hosting Swizz, Pharrell Williams, Rihanna and famed shoe designer Christian Louboutin in their suite.

line: Goddammit

line: Mama, look at your son, what happened to my smile?
vault_lines: Mama, look at your son, what happened to my smile?
meaning:
Jay alludes to “Smile” by 2Pac and Scarface, where the two encouraged everyone to keep a smile on during tough times.

Jay admits that fame has taken its toll on him and made it difficult for him to enjoy himself anymore. While fame sure put a smile on his face after it took him from the Marcy projects to superstardom, close to 20 years in that limelight took can take that smile away in a hurry.



This is not a phenomenon exclusive to rappers, as WWE wrestler Shawn Michael retired from the game when he felt he had “lost his smile” after experiencing success.

line: Riskin’ my life, I’m already dying, so fuck it, well
vault_lines: Riskin' my life, I'm already dying, so fuck it, well
meaning: Jay feels he has been in the game too long to reverse his fate. The fame may or may not take his life, but that outcome is no longer in his hands. So while Jay does reveal vulnerability on songs such as this one, most of Watch The Throne is he and Ye boasting about and embracing fame, rather than pointing out its pitfalls. Jay’s smart enough to realize that success isn’t all it’s cracked up to be, but will still continue to live his lavish life until the day he dies – he just wanted to let us know he’s not entirely pleased about it.

meaning:
Here, Jay-Z makes reference to his long-held claim that he doesn’t write any of his rhymes down, instead opting to compose the lyrics in his head and recite them straight from memory.

Bay area producer Rick Rock is on record as saying that he witnessed the process first hand whilst collaborating with Hov on several tracks from his 2000 album Dynasty: Roc La Familia.

Similarly, in an in-studio scene from Fade to Black, the accompanying movie to Jay’s then-retirement record The Black Album, Hip-Hop legend Rick Rubin can be seen telling Beastie Boy’s member Mike D that he has “never seen anything like” Jay’s recording process, after witnessing him spitting his verses straight from memory during the making of “99 Problems”.

line: The judge said, “Is this that thug from the Kit-Kat club?” But I got enough chips stacked up to make the bitch back up
vault_lines: The judge said, "Is this that thug from the Kit-Kat club?"
meaning:
Here, Jay-Z makes reference to the much-publicised 1999 incident in which, during an album release party for Q-Tip’s debut solo album Amplified at New York’s Kit Kat Club, he stabbed record producer Lance “Un” Rivera. Jay had suspected Rivera of being responsible for leaking his then-recent album Vol. 3… The Life and Times of S. Carter.



Hov plead guilty to the charges and, the year prior to the release of this song, was sentenced to three years of probation for the attack, avoiding the very real possibly of jail time. He understandably views this as something of a win, and attributes the favourable outcome of the case to his ability to bankroll himself with a solid legal defence.

Interestingly, given that he is collaborating with Cam'ron on this track, Cam would later offer up an alternate explanation for Jay’s assault on Rivera that night, claiming it actually stemmed from a disagreement over his relationship with female rapper Charli Baltimore.

line: Rucker game attender with the Bent parked On the sidewalk with the temp plates on the fender
vault_lines: Rucker game attender with the Bent parked
meaning:
Jay likes to remind people that, despite what they might have heard to the contrary, his status in the hood is still firmly intact, which he does here with with a couple of basketball references.

Rucker Park is a basketball court in Harlem, famous as a streetball venue. Over the years it has served as both a breeding ground for and sideline attraction to a host of NBA talent.



Despite his wealth and fame, you’re perfectly likely to find Hov there, taking in a game. The fact that he’s in attendance will be easily evidenced by the brand new Bentley (identifiable by the temporary dealership plates still hanging from it) that he’s left outside, parked right there on the curb!

The implication here is that he’s so confident in the level of respect he commands in the streets that he thinks nothing of leaving a car worth several hundreds of thousands of dollars parked up in Harlem, the notion that it might get stolen doesn’t even occur to him.

Similarly, you’re just as likely to catch him front and centre at a Knicks game, jewellery on display for all to see. Whilst courtside at the Garden is a decidedly more upscale setting than Rucker Park his point remains the same; he’s right there in clear view, not hiding from anyone.

Interestingly, the year following this songs release Jay would actually enter his own, star-studded team into Rucker Park’s Entertainer’s Basketball Classic tournament,  counting a just-drafted prospect by the name of Lebron James amongst his ranks.



He came tantalisingly close to unseating fellow New York emcee, and one-time rival, Fat Joe’s Terror Squad team for the title, but was ultimately derailed when the 2003 New York blackout coincided with his sides final, potentially championship winning game.

Jay would reprise his “rock'n'roll” persona on 2008’s “Jockin' Jay-Z,” in which he raps:

That bloke from Oasis said I couldn’t play guitar
Somebody shoulda told him I’m a fucking rock star

This was in response to Jay’s Glastonbury performance in 2008.

The “rock star” stereotype is someone who is incredibly famous, and sometimes disliked due to indulgent behaviour.

“Lo-Lo’s” means both low profile tyres  (Jay is keeping a low profile around the police) and “lowrider,” a type of vehicle with an after-market suspension kit designed to lower it. They’re often illegal, so Jay isn’t too keen on any police attention.

This “low profile” has him froze; he’s keeping still to avoid drawing attention to himself. “So cold” also means to be kitted in expensive jewellery, as Kelly was in the first verse, and to be unfeeling or unemotional. meaning:
Jay is either referencing Tony Montana, Tony Soprano, or both, in his classic double entendre fashion. The case for Soprano, the protagonist of the HBO Series The Sopranos, is that the final scene of the series shows Tony and his family at a restaurant and ends with the screen fading into darkness, heavily implying that Tony is killed.

This could also be a reference to the classic “Is this what its all about/Say goodbye to the bad guy” restaurant scene in the 1983 crime drama Scarface as “Tony Montana” (Al Pacino) started to crack under the pressure of when his marriage and drug dealing business took a turn toward the worst.

line: The Lord is my rock, I speed dial through salat
vault_lines: The Lord is my rock, I speed dial through salat
meaning:
Speed dial is a function on mobile phones that allows users to dial a number through a limited amount of keys (typically only 1 key).

Salah (or salat) is the Arabic word for prayer. Salah is the second of the Five Pillars of Islam, and is performed in a routined, cyclical manner. There are five obligatory prayers that are spread across different times of the day (sunrise, midday, afternoon, sunset, night).

Electronica is saying prayer is his shortcut for reaching and communicating with God.

line: Back when Emory Jones was catchin’ a fed charge I knew less about Chesimard, all about Pablo Escobar
vault_lines: Back when Emory Jones was catchin' a fed charge
meaning:
Anyone familiar with the origin story of Shawn “Jay Z” Carter has heard of his drug-dealing past.  In this line, Jay refers to his friend and former partner-in-crime Emory Jones, who was sentenced in January 2000 to nearly 16 years in prison.  Jay dedicated his 2006 song “Do U Wanna Ride” to Jones.

In this line, Jay reflects on the frame of mind he held during his drug-dealing days and contrasts that mind-state with his current frame of mind.  As a drug dealer, Jay was acutely aware of the life and legacy of Colombian drug kingpin Pablo Escobar.  Today, Jay acknowledges the life and legacy of Assata Shakur (born JoAnne Deborah Bryan and sometimes referred to by her married surname, Chesimard), who was a freedom fighter, former member of the Black Liberation Army and godmother to rap legend Tupac Shakur (2Pac).



Joanne Chesimard, a.k.a. Assata Shakur, and 2Pac.

line: Some of the cons, I suffered for prose

Playing on the homophones “pros & prose” and pros’s antonym “cons”, Jay explains that some of the people who defraud or trick him, do so with language i.e. contracts, novels, textbooks and newspaper articles; all examples of prose.

Jay Elect continues his wordplay by opening the next line with “poetry,” which is the antonym of prose.

He’d hammer home this imagery on 2013’s “La Familia,” a song about his position as the “head of the family”, the family being both his own (wife and children) and his group of associates.

Jay’s first two albums, Reasonable Doubt and Vol. 1 also carried deep lyrical ties and references to the Mafia.

line: [Produced by Just Blaze]
vault_lines: Turn my music high, high, high, higher
meaning:
This beat is one of the best examples of the Roc-a-Fella sound of the early 00’s, defined by sound bank drums mixed with pitched up and distorted soul samples.

This production style, spearheaded in part by the album this track came from, provided a stark, raw sea change from the slippery, synthesized Trackmasters/Puff Daddy sound that had defined the previous epoch, the so-called “Jiggy Era”, of shiny suits, Cristal and recognizable ‘80’s samples. It provides an epically aggressive backing to Jay’s swaggering rhymes.

It samples James Brown’s compatriot Bobby Byrd’s song “I’m Not To Blame”, who’s normally deep, gruff voice is rendered almost unrecognizable by the mixing.

line: We The Best Music
vault_lines: And all that shit real too, ah
meaning: We The Best Music Group is the name of the label that DJ Khaled founded in 2008.

line: My body, my ice, my cash, all real, I’m a triple threat
vault_lines: My body, my ice, my cash, all real, I'm a triple threat
meaning:
Beyonce’s mention of having a “real” body after her “Break The Internet” verse could also be a jab at Kim Kardashian, whom she reportedly dislikes.

Kim’s 2014 “Break The Internet” Paper Magazine Cover went viral at the time of release and sparked controversy as to whether her butt was “real”.

“Real” cash could also refer to JAY-Z and Beyonce’s complicated relationship with the Kardashian-Wests. On JAY-Z’s 4:44 album he raps about how he regrets loaning 20 million dollars to Kanye West. JAY-Z told Time Magazine that he’s since repaired his relationship with Kanye but it’s unclear whether​ Beyonce still has beef.

line: Top off the coupe and it look like Freaknik
vault_lines: Top off the coupe and it look like Freaknik
meaning:
In the late ‘80s and early '90s, Freaknik was initially a picnic organized by students from Historically Black Colleges to celebrate spring break. The event quickly grew into a large festival and celebration of life in Atlanta, which drew over 100,000 people in 1993.

In an oral history by Atlanta Magazine: Freaknik: The rise and fall of Atlanta’s most infamous street party, Jermaine Dupri describes the significance of Freaknik:

I had to have a convertible during Freaknik. I wanted to be seen, but I wanted to see everybody at the same time. It was the beginning of “flexing,” in every kind of way. The birth of riding around with your system blasting, with TVs in your car. All of that stuff came from people wanting to be seen at Freaknik.

line: I break the internet, top two and I ain’t number two
vault_lines: I break the internet, top two and I ain't number two
meaning:
Bey' interpolates a bar from Drake’s “Gyalchester”:

I know I said top five, but I’m top two
And I’m not two and I got one
Thought you had one, but it’s not one, nigga, Nah​"

While fans and media outlets have pointed out that this lyric could be directed at Kim Kardashian (see more in the following annotation), this lyric is probably a reference to Beyoncé internet-breaking album Lemonade and relationship with JAY-Z.

Beyoncé and JAY-Z are arguably music’s “top two” and contrary to outdated gender stereotypes, Beyoncé isn’t her man’s “number two"—she’s a boss in her own right. This ties into the previous line about being a lady but also being the "realest nigga in the room.”

line: Dujac by the mag, that’s how we do wine
vault_lines: Dujac by the mag, that's how we do wine
meaning:
In 2018, JAY-Z started hosting DJ Khaled at his Bel-Air estate for business meetings where they drank $3,500 magnum-sized bottles of Domaine Dujac pinot noir. Their first “Dujac Meeting” came on January 2, and the second was on January 22.

Khaled has since shouted out Hov for introducing him to the winemaker ​and has made sure to save his Weight Watchers points so he can have a glass with dinner.

line: Meanwhile Georgie Porgie Cinnamon sendin’ me threats Save your breath, you couldn’t beat a flight of steps Try that shit with a grown man I’ll kill that fuckboy with my own hand And hop back in the coupe (Woo, woo)
vault_lines: Meanwhile Georgie Porgie Cinnamon sendin' me threats
meaning:
On February 26, 2012 George Zimmerman fatally shot Trayvon Martin, a 17-year old high school student, in a gated community in Sanford, Florida. In a widely reported trial, Zimmerman was charged with murder for Martin’s death, but was acquitted at trial due to the state’s controversial “stand-your-ground” laws.

JAY-Z is executive producing a six-part documentary series about the murder for a July 2018 release on the Paramount Network. The network has said Rest in Power: The Trayvon Martin Story is more than a tragic narrative about a young man’s life cut short—it’s a story about race, politics, power, money, and the bias of the U.S. criminal justice system.

In December 2017, George Zimmerman responded to Hov’s impending documentary, telling interviewers:

I know how to handle people who fuck with me, I have since February 2012. […] [JAY-Z] would find himself coming out of the south side of a gator if he comes to Florida and bothers my family.

Zimmerman has claimed that a private investigator and film crew had been at his parents' and uncle’s homes seeking interviews.

“Georgie Porgie” is an English nursery rhyme from the mid-19th century about a cowardly boy, which Hov flips to call  Zimmerman out for his cowardice in shooting an unarmed teenager.

line: That’s a raspberry beret The kind you find in a second-hand store That’s a vintage piece Kind that make haters kiss their teeth, you can’t buy this new
vault_lines: That's a raspberry beret
meaning:
This is a reference  to the chorus of Prince’s 1985 song “Raspberry Beret”:

Raspberry beret
The kind you find in a second-hand​ store
Raspberry beret
And if it was warm she wouldn’t wear much more
Raspberry beret
I think I love her

Most associated with the French, a beret is a soft, round, flat-crowned hat. The rap mogul’s vintage ‘61 Chevrolet Corvette convertible has a removable red roof—that is, a “raspberry beret.” While you can’t buy a “new” '61 Corvette, you could buy a second-hand vehicle for upwards of $80,000.

line: If they’re tryna party with the queen They gon’ have to sign a non-disclosure, ayy
vault_lines: If they're tryna party with the queen
meaning:
A non-disclosure agreement is a legal document that prevents parties from disclosing information that goes on in certain scenarios, events, or transactions. B is so exclusive and private that if you even want the chance to party with her you have to sign one of these.

Additionally, it’s a snipe at Tiffany Haddish who told the press about an incident where an actress got too close to JAY-Z. Haddish told the press:

The actress touched JAY-Z’s chest and Beyoncé came walking up like…’Biitttchhh!’ But, she didn’t say that,” Haddish clarified. “But her demeanor, her body from the way she walked up on them said, “Get your hand off my man’s chest.”

Haddish then goes on to say that she’s not at liberty to say exactly what happened.

Furthermore, if you slow the song down at 2:50, you can here Beyonce’s background vocals after “They gon' have to sign a non-disclosure, ayy” say “Tiffany.”

line: No jewels in this Patek Philippe It’s complicated, three million apiece Sheesh, that’s how we do time
vault_lines: No jewels in this Patek Philippe
meaning:
A known watch aficionado, JAY-Z is seemingly boasting of his latest acquisition: a 2017 Patek Philippe “Grand Complications” timepiece that comes with a $3 million price tag.



Unlike the flashy, diamond-embellished timepieces worn by other rappers, Hov lives by a particular mantra when it comes to his purchases:

I don’t got the bright watch, I got the right watch

Also, note the subtle social commentary and wordplay with “how we do time”—a clever way of letting the listener know that he’s too rich to “do time” in prison. African American men have long outnumbered their white counterparts within the US prison population; but, as of 2019, that statistical gap appears to be less glaring.

line: ’61 with the thing off Me and Blue havin’ a sing-off
vault_lines: '61 with the thing off
meaning:
On February 18, 2018, ​JAY-Z was photographed as he drove his daughter Blue Ivy around Los Angeles in his drop-top ‘61 Chevrolet Corvette.



This is the same convertible seen in his and Beyoncé’s “‘03 Bonnie & Clyde” video back in 2002.

line: One-point-five for the Landaulet
vault_lines: One-point-five for the Landaulet
meaning: Jigga is referencing the Mercedes-Maybach Landaulet droptop model which was put out from 2008-2012 by the Mercedes-Maybach brand. The car came fully equipped with a semi-automatic folding soft top for the vehicle’s rear seats.

line: 91 thousand for a wine bill Keep it real with you, that was Juan’s bill
vault_lines: 91 thousand for a wine bill
meaning:
JAY-Z is referring to the $91,135 champagne bill incurred at his business partner OG Juan Perez’s 50th birthday celebration on February 18, 2018. A bill from Playroom NYC in Uptown New York shows the party purchased 40 bottles of JAY-Z’s Armand de Brignac brand during their time at the club. On “Top Off” Hov keeps it real and admits the bill was mistakenly declared his by media outlets when it was, in fact,​ Juan who picked up the tab.



“Juan” sounds like “one,” referencing how it was only one of the bills they held that night—the group had earlier spent $13,000 on dinner at the Japanese restaurant Zuma, and $9,000 at Made in Mexico in Inwood, Upper Manhattan.

line: Screamin’, “Free my nigga Meek Mill” Niggas can’t wheelie in this free world
vault_lines: Screamin', "Free my nigga Meek Mill"
meaning:
Rapper Meek Mill was incarcerated in 2017 for two to four years due to a probation violation as a result of an incident that involved Meek popping a “wheelie” on a dirt bike in NYC for a music video shoot. Meek is from Philadelphia where there’s a rich biking culture, which JAY-Z shouted out on his 2017 collaboration with Frank Ocean “Biking.”

“Can’t wheelie in this free world” is a play on the 1993 movie Free Willy. It was about an orca whale who was trapped in the wild and was later freed by compassionate amusement park workers. Jay’s calling for similar compassion for Meek.

Jay has been quite vocal in advocating for Meek’s freedom from saying “Free Meek Mill” at his concerts to penning an article for the NY Times about wrongdoings in the criminal justice system in which he described the sentence as “unjust and heavy-handed.”



A poster calling for Meek’s freedom paid for by JAY-Z's​ Roc Nation.

line: This ain’t no mothafuckin’ ’91
vault_lines: This ain't no mothafuckin' '91
meaning: UGK first came up in 1991 but they’d been around since 1987, so Pimp C’s literally saying “I’m not a beginner”.

meaning:
Jay has held on to this unreleased verse from the late, but great, Chad Butler (Pimp C). Partnered with Bun B, he was half of the rap duo UGK. He was one of the most influential rapper/producers to date. Sadly, he died of a codeine (cough syrup) overdose on Jay’s birthday (December 4th) in 2007.
RIP



This verse is sampled on Drake’s “Faithful,” which leaked April 1st 2016.

line: Just ’cause you born in Port Arthur, don’t make a nigga trill
vault_lines: Just 'cause you born in Port Arthur, don't make a nigga trill
meaning:
Represent for Port Arthur

Port Arthur, Texas is the birthplace of Pimp C and Bun B.  Being trill is to be 100% real; standing up for what you believe in and having loyalty to those who have your back. Pimp C is stating that you aren’t trill simply because you are from Port Arthur – it is a title you must earn.

Trill has been an ever-present term for the UGK members – Bun B has named his solo studio albums (up to this point) Trill, II Trill, Trill OG and Trill OG: The Epilogue.

line: I don’t fuck with nobody in this shit but Bun Deal give me a million, you gotta give that nigga one
vault_lines: I don't fuck with nobody in this shit but Bun
meaning: Pimp C wasn’t one to hold his tongue – if he had a problem, he’d come out and say it so they could hear. That said, he was fiercely loyal to his UGK brethren Bun B; he refused to take money from a label unless Beeda got the same.

line: ‘Keep your foot off in they ass’ is what Ken told me
vault_lines: 'Keep your foot off in they ass' is what Ken told me
meaning: Pimp C was good friends with a pimp named Pimpin' Ken.  He has performed interludes on UGK albums in the past, as well as featuring on tracks such as “Two Type of Bitches”. Ken gave Pimp C some good advice – don’t take no shit from people, and don’t back down.

Why would Ja Rule tell Irv Gotti to “be easy on the cut?”

Well, before he became a platinum producer and top rap CEO, Irv Gotti was known as DJ Irv. And he would cut up and scratch records at local parties.
