vault_lines: Recognize, understand (It's— It's— It's time to build
meaning:
For the song’s hook, producer Irv Gotti samples Rakim’s lyric from Eric B. & Rakim’s 1986 debut single “Eric B. Is President.”

No tricks in ‘86 it’s time to build.

The term “build” originated with members of the Five Percent nation and became popular slang in East Coast rap songs during the 1980s and 1990s. It means to get together, share knowledge and build bridges of positivity.

line: So flame on, I turn my game on to Expert Niggas get chills when you hear my name on the network
vault_lines: So flame on, I turn my game on to Expert
meaning:
The Human Torch from Marvel Comics' Fantastic Four would shout out “flame on” before igniting his body with fire.



By using the same line in his rhyme, Jay is telling us how hot he is when he turns the difficulty level of his rap game up to expert, like gamers do when they’re playing on their favorite gaming console.

Hov believes it’s all enough to give his competition chills at the mere mention of his name.

line: Google dangled around a crazy check
vault_lines: Google dangled around a crazy check
meaning: As the owners of YouTube, Google have a say in deciding the royalty rates artists are paid for the video views they gain on the site. Jay is implying Google dangled a sizeable royalty cheque in front of him.

line: You know niggas die for equal pay right? You know when I work I ain’t your slave right?
vault_lines: You know niggas die for equal pay right?
meaning:
Jay compares his fight for equal rights in music to that of equal pay for black people during the Civil Rights Movement. It’s surprising to note just how many people died during this period.

As Jay says on “We Made it (Freestyle)”:

I own my own masters

line: Oh niggas is skeptical when it’s their own shit
vault_lines: Oh niggas is skeptical when it's their own shit
meaning:
A similar sentiment to that expressed on “Murder To Excellence”,

If you put crabs in a barrel to ensure your survival
You’re gon' end up pulling down niggas that look just like you

Black culture is willing to stand behind Apple or Steve Jobs, but not their own people.

line: The only one they hating on look the same as you
vault_lines: The only one they hating on look the same as you
meaning:
This is another flip on the racial theme of the freestyle, but also positions Jay as an “every man”, immune from the corporate machine.

he claims that because he is from the bottom, because he came from the struggle and the streets, he is the same as all the people in the crowd, and all the people in the twittersphere who are attacking TiDal.

Essentially, when the media turns on TiDal, they are turning on the very artists that made the music industry. They believe they are ratting out a tyrant who’s only interest is making money out of music, but in truth that was never Jay’s intention.

They’re trying to keep us in a crabs in a barrel situation.

line: Pharrell even told me go with the safest bet
vault_lines: Pharrell even told me go with the safest bet
meaning:
Pharrell is an established entrepreneur in his own right, and a frequent collaborator with Jay. His opinion holds weight, and it must be remembered that Jay is a huge figure in the industry, so if Pharrell is telling Jay Z to play it safe, he must have a very good reason to be doing that..

That reason is probably his association with Apple Music, including being a guest DJ for the service.

line: Jimmy Iovine offered a safety net
vault_lines: Jimmy Iovine offered a safety net
meaning:
There was a rumor floating around that Jimmy Iovine tried to lure artists away from Tidal, and on to Beats.

Jay told Billboard in March 2015 that Jimmy was actively poaching the artists he knew Hov had been talking to about joining Tidal, including Drake and Pharrell Williams. He was offering them more money upfront, as opposed to the Tidal shares Jay was offering.
He was disappointed in Jimmy’s behaviour, saying:

I think that’s just his competitive nature, and I don’t know if he’s looking at the bigger picture: That it’s not about me and it’s not about him; it’s about the future of the music business.

line: I don’t take no checks I take my respect
vault_lines: I don’t take no checks I take my respect
meaning:
This is a slight misstep. Jay certainly took a check when he signed with Live Nation for a huge amount of money. However, that deal did allow him to maintain creative control over every single aspect of his career, something he has never once given up to anyone else.

He owns his own masters. And while some rappers may claim they’d rather be paid in respect than money, Jay Z is one of the few artists in the world who has managed to achieve both revenue streams.

In 2018 when his deal with Live Nation is completed Hov will own his own music label, streaming service, management group, sports agency, and every single one of his master recordings.

line: I understand if you don’t understand, I figure I’m Jigga That’s where we differ I take what’s mine, you accept what they give you, I get you
vault_lines: I understand if you don’t understand, I figure I’m Jigga
meaning:
One of Jay’s main concerns is that the public don’t understand his vision with Tidal. While he aims to to shake up the industry, more established structures want to do things their way. This links back to record companies, who’ve profited from artists without ever really contributing anything outside of money.

On the other end of the spectrum, Jay mentions artists criticizing him. He understands that those who are stuck in poor contracts, or are comfortable accepting what labels give them don’t know any better.

line: And I don’t need no middle man to talk to my niggas
vault_lines: And I don’t need no middle man to talk to my niggas
meaning:
Instead of a press-release, Jay would rather take to Twitter and defend his business dealings. This is a very unique situation in the business world.

Also note – Tidal is a company owned by the artists, unlike other streaming services like Spotify. So at Tidal there literally is no middle man.

line: So I’m the bad guy now I hear, because I don’t go with the flow Don’t ever go with the flow, be the flow
vault_lines: So I’m the bad guy now I hear, because I don’t go with the flow
meaning:
While Hov’s king of the flow, Tidal has endured endless criticism since launching. Jay’s investment in Tidal has caused headaches for more established players in the streaming business. It’s also not the first time Jay’s been labelled as the bad guy.

Most of what Jay’s done in his career has gone against the grain – he’s never settled for mediocrity or copied the format of artists and business people before him.

This is also a play on words to Jay’s new streaming service, “Tidal” as in the flow of a tidal wave.

line: That’s cool, I know they trying to bamboozle you
vault_lines: That's cool, I know they trying to bamboozle you
meaning:
Carrying on from his earlier line, Jay now postures that the true shucking and jiving is going on via the major players in the streaming game.

What is interesting is that Spotify has endured very similar criticism, yet Apple and Beats, despite making Dr. Dre incredibly rich, has not endured any criticism.

The corporate machine is well oiled when two almost identical services are perceived in totally opposite ways.

This is also a reference to the 2000 satirical film Bamboozled, directed by Spike Lee. The main characters in the film are tricked into disgracing the entire African American race by performing on a popular racist TV show. They were “bamboozled.”

line: TIDAL, my own label, same difference
vault_lines: TIDAL, my own label, same difference
meaning:
Jay already has his own label, Roc Nation, but this has a deeper meaning. Tidal isn’t something he bought in to to turn a profit. He is moving Tidal in to the Hov Lane, which means that it is now an integral part of his business model and the structure of his organisation.

He is making the point that this isn’t something he buys in to, to make quick money off. He believes in Tidal and stands behind it, success or failure. It also functions as a record label of sorts, as artists can upload their own music onto the site, with Jay saying:

I’m on Tidal. I don’t have a record deal

line: Lucy you got some ’splaining to do
vault_lines: Lucy you got some 'splaining to do
meaning:
A reference to I Love Lucy, and possibly Kendrick’s use of “Lucy” during “For Sale (Interlude)” off To Pimp A Butterfly, which came out 2 months before this freestyle dropped.

Lucy is the “star” of the show, or Spotify. Whenever Lucy did something wrong on the show, Rick would use the word “splainin”, to claim she had to explain herself. Spotify is making mistakes, as are Youtube, so Jay plays the role of Rick, calling them out for the trouble they have caused the industry and claiming they now need to explain exactly what is going on behind closed doors.

Spotify is also positioned as Lucifer.

line: We gon’ turn style, I ain’t your token nigga
vault_lines: We gon' turn style, I ain't your token nigga
meaning:
The whole idea of Tidal is to “turn the tide” in the music streaming industry.

Jay and his associates believe that currently, the system is unfair for artists and everyone involved in writing and producing music. Too much of the profit goes to corporate entities and people who have no creative input.

Rather than take market share away from the big companies, the plan is for Tidal to spark a conversation amongst industry insiders and music fans, and to prompt them to seek a more equitable solution.

Jay claims he isn’t just the figurehead of this company by using the powerful image of a “token nigga”. He is in it from the ground floor, and this is part of his legacy now.

In typical Hov fashion, he slips a double entendre in to the mix, with the “turn-style” “token” play referring to the way in which a subway works.

line: Let them continue choking niggas
vault_lines: Let them continue choking niggas
meaning:
Continuing from the previous lines, Jay is referencing Eric Garner, an African American male who died after being strangled by the NYPD.

Again, he isn’t trying to be disrespectful, or diminish the impact that those events had on those involved, but rather to highlight that injustice exists at all levels.

line: Spotify is nine billion they ain’t say shit
vault_lines: Spotify is nine billion they ain't say shit
meaning:
Jay is alluding to the current value of Spotify, believed to be around $8.4 billion as of April 2015. This is a huge figure and comes in part due to the low royalty fees they pay the artists. Some artists, most notably Taylor Swift took her music down from Spotify after a row over royalty fees.

Since Tidal’s emergence, Spotify have kept quiet and  continued to operate the same way. Jay implies that their silence indicates guilt, and that they recognise that Tidal is a fairer system but are sitting on their hands so as not to stir the pot and break up the situation they currently have.

line: Spending millions on media trying to confuse you
vault_lines: Spending millions on media trying to confuse you
meaning:
Referring to his belief that “Many big companies” have a smear campaign against Tidal, including Apple.



As Emory Jones, one of Hov’s closest confidants said:

They say we have a lot of nerve to even think that we can step in the same space with them. They really are spending millions to smear #tidal because they know that we are not afraid to jump in that ring.

line: You know I came in this game independent right?
vault_lines: You know I came in this game independent right?
meaning:
Jay’s very first deal, with Priority Records was merely a distribution deal. In his own words, Priority was a trip for him. They had a box full of flyers to promote Reasonable Doubt and that was the extent of their marketing budget.

Jay and Dame shopped their demo to many labels, but in the end no-one wanted to sign him on a major label deal for a multi-album contract, so Jay created Rocafella, hence his independence, which he has maintained throughout his entire career.

line: I had to talk to myself, Hov you used to it It’s politics as usual
vault_lines: I had to talk to myself, Hov you used to it
meaning:
This was a freestyle done live and this would seamlessly enter “Politics as Usual”, a classic track off Reasonable Doubt!

The self-talk is instructive, as it shows the plight of the entire industry. If Jay-Z is still facing the same struggles after 20 years, after all his success, after all his fame and influence, it’s a slightly pessimistic message. Is it all worth it? Is it even possible?

line: You know this ain’t back in the days right? But I can’t tell, how the way they killed Freddie Gray right Shot down Mike Brown how they did Tray right?
vault_lines: You know this ain't back in the days right?
meaning:
A blatant reference to the shocking violence perpetuated by white policeman against black Americans that has been in the news recently.

Jay is challenging the perception that Tidal can’t work by juxtaposing it with the way in which Black people were marginalised “back in the day”. People are saying it will fail and cannot be successful, and by referencing the way in which Black people are still marginalised in modern society, Jay shows that racism is still abundant and a cancer that has yet to be eradicated.

The men were killed without due process. They were shot down because of prejudice. Jay is saying the same thing is happening to Tidal. People are shooting it down without giving it a chance.

line: You know I ain’t shucking and jiving and high fiving
vault_lines: You know I ain't shucking and jiving and high fiving
meaning:
Shucking and jiving is the act of joking and acting evasively in the face of authority. The term was used during slavery to describe situations where slaves were accused of mischief and deceiving their slave masters. The context that Hov is using the term is: he won’t pander to the corporations and become their black court jester. he will not modify his behaviour in order to fit in better with the views of the upper echelon of business.



By the end of the freestyle he has flipped this line on its ear, claiming that whilst the more illustrious streaming services have accused him of deceiving, and have discredited his Tidal Facts campaign, the truth is it is the Youtube’s, the Spotify’s and the Apple’s who are doing the “shucking and jiving”.

line: You bought nine iPhones and Steve Jobs is rich Phil Knight worth trillions you still bought those kicks
vault_lines: You bought nine iPhones and Steve Jobs is rich
meaning:
It’s hypocritical to come at HOV saying his service isn’t going to last. Yet, many people buy Iphones, making the late Steve Jobs rich from his design but not the individuals who compose the phone or assisted the design. The royalties are skewed.

The same can be done for Phil Knight, the man who created Nike and the designs. He made so much money and people pay exorbitant amounts for Jordans. The shoes are made in china and worth twenty or so dollars yet its sold for hundreds.

line: Now it’s a duet, and you wet, when you check out The technique from the two TECs ,and I don’t need two lips To blow this like a trumpet, you dumb shit
vault_lines: Now it's a duet, and you wet, when you check out
meaning:
An impressively dense and underappreciated series of lines that continue the gun/music wordplay.

To begin, the listener initially takes the line, “you wet, when you check out,” to refer to the blood in which Jay’s victim would be drenched when he kills him.

However, he goes on to use “check out” to imply that the person he describes is checking out Jay’s lyrical skills, or “technique,” as described in the next line. “Wet” can then be interpreted as either:
1) sweat from fear when they check out his skills
2) wet from “sweating” – slang for copying – his style.

This latter interpretation is an elegant nod to Eric B. & Rakim’s legendary “Don’t Sweat the Technique,” which essentially means “don’t copy the style.”



These two interpretations of “wet,” along with the aforementioned “blood” interpretation when reading “check out” to refer to murder, set up “wet, when you check out” as a bona fide triple entendre.

But wait, there’s more! The wordplay is only built upon in the ensuing lines. Firstly, when he adds that the technique is from the “2 Tecs” (e.g., two 9-Tec guns), this makes the “technique” refer to shooting. Thus, “technique” becomes yet another word that serves both a gun-based and music-based (lyrical skills) interpretation.



One final gun/music play is made in these lines, as he talks about making his gun blow just like a trumpet, although he doesn’t need two lips – just a trigger.

line: Now they ‘bout to free me up, what you think I’m gon’ be, what? Rehabilitated? Man, I still feel hatred
vault_lines: Now they 'bout to free me up, what you think I'm gon' be, what?
meaning:
The debate on the failure of the rehabilitative function of prisons and whether sentencing should take into account the rehabilitation of criminals (or if prisons should even be tasked with rehabilitation) is long-standing and ongoing.  Nonetheless, public perception is precisely that prison should rehabilitate or at least that upon emerging from prison, a former inmate should be rehabilitated.  In Jay’s lyrics, this is foregrounded, as is the other long-standing problem of differential sentencing, and the terrible impact it had in exacerbating recidivism rates (caused by the generational resentment) of black men in America (crack dealers often being black, the laws were effectively racial; a situation improved in 2010 by The Fair Sentencing Act).  Before the Fair Sentencing Act,

…under a 1986 law, 50 grams of crack (the weight of a candy bar) led to a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years — the same sentence that applied to 5,000 grams of powdered cocaine (enough to fill a brief case). A street dealer of crack cocaine often got a longer sentence than the major trafficker who sold the powdered cocaine made into crack.

In the article, “The Debate on Rehabilitating Criminals: Is It True that Nothing Works?”, it is noted that,

On January 18, 1989, the abandonment of rehabilitation in corrections was confirmed by the U.S. Supreme Court. In Mistretta v. United States, the Court upheld federal “sentencing guidelines” which remove rehabilitation from serious consideration when sentencing offenders. Defendants will henceforth be sentenced strictly for the crime, with no recognition given to such factors as amenability to treatment, personal and family history, previous efforts to rehabilitate oneself, or possible alternatives to prison. The Court outlined the history of the debate: “Rehabilitation as a sound penological theory came to be questioned and, in any event, was regarded by some as an unattainable goal for most cases.” The Court cited a Senate Report which “referred to the ‘outmoded rehabilitation model’ for federal criminal sentencing, and recognized that the efforts of the criminal justice system to achieve rehabilitation of offenders had failed.”

Jay is using his trademark gifts of lyrical compression and literary concision to distill the essence of these vitally important issues, examining through the lense of his personal history (“the streets gave me all I write in this song”).  It is a debate that is well discussed in Charles R. Tittle’s 1974 paper on “Prisons and Rehabilitation”, where he posits that,

The only way to in which prisons can escape the onus of failure [to rehabilitate] is by abandoning the rehabilitative mission.

A similar theme was covered in a traditional English nursery rhyme, “Jack and Jill.” That Jill had the homie Jack whipped, and he’s going up hills and fetching pails of water for her – next thing you know he is falling off the top and his “crown” is broke:

line: To that project in D.C. where my man caught his death at Over my years, I’ve seen Rooks get tooken by the Knight

meaning:
There were a lot of Brooklyn kids heading down to Maryland, Virginia, and D.C. in the mid-nineties, chasing new markets for crack. And a lot of them died.

Rooks and Knights are chess pieces. Rooks are the more valuable pieces, so for a Knight to take a Rook is, in Jay’s metaphor, an up-and-coming hustler knocking off a more established dealer.

Alternatively, rooks can stand for rookies. And knight/night is a homophone. So, the line could mean that the young hustler is actually getting knocked off by the night-time, which symbolizes the danger of working and living on the streets.

The crack game
The rap game (as in: “Somehow the rap game remind me of the crack game”)
Ordinary games such as chess, on which Jay relies to design his metaphors in this verse.
The game of life. Refer to the hook and see that Jay says that he’s “stuck in this life forever” and that he cannot change the rules of that game



Think of “game” as Jay’s pivot foot, on which his multiple lyrical moves originate

 Jay also pronounces “conduit” like “con do it”, which means Jay used the streets like a criminal, which he discusses in the next few lines.

In ‘94 he was dating his ex-girlfriend Stephanie, who he met in Virginia when he was in the state moving drugs. They dated for five years from 1991-1996, with Hov living between her home in Virginia and his apartment at 560 State Street in Brooklyn.



This refers to something that happened to me around that time, 1994, when my girl of five years got pregnant and lost the baby in a miscarriage. Now, obviously, miscarriages happen everywhere, to anyone, but the point is that on top of the especially acute paranoia and disappointment and exhaustion I’m feeling from the street life, friends getting shot, your family being broke, I have to deal with the everyday tragedies that stalk everyone. A drug dealer operates in a market, just like a legitimate business. Jay claims a 100% mark-up, meaning he’s selling the drugs for double what he paid. This is quite standard according to anecdotal evidence.

To “duck flip” is to someone them until he requires something of them. Flipping refers back to stealing women. He sells the contract on to another pimp, hence earning extra cash.

During the early 2000s there was a move towards pimping in song. Most of the artists never actually engaged in the practice, and Jay Z in Decoded addressed the pimping narrative, claiming it wasn’t meant to be true to life.

The man became extremely rich, but now that he’s behind bars, things aren’t looking so good for him in terms of money. Meanwhile, Jay-Z is the first rapper to become a billionaire.

line: Married to the streets, no date of annulment It seems every time it comes up, they postpone it

To “annul” something is to render it invalid. It’s a term usually used in the US relating to marriage. It is retroactive, hence it differs from divorce. An annulled marriage is viewed as having never been valid, meaning it never existed in a legal sense.

Jay may have divorced himself from the streets, but the relationship still exists in his music. In 2016 he was still dropping knowledge from his addiction to the street life. He continued to promote his street origins on 2001’s “Takeover,” and his 2003 mixtape S. Carter Collection was filled with rhymes pertaining to gun violence.

line: All I try to do is try to get up out the dirt Guess he’s tryin’ to do the same, told me get up out his turf I wanted to talk to him, but that shit’d never work
vault_lines: All I try to do is try to get up out the dirt
meaning:
All Jay is trying to do is carve out a life for himself that doesn’t involve the street and the dangers of dealing. His would-be assailant is doing the same.

The parallels between these lyrics and Jay’s dispute with Lance Rivera are quite clear. The story goes that Jay’s fourth album, Vol. 3… Life and Times of S. Carter, was leaked a full month before it’s eventual release date. Jay was passionate about it in Decoded:

I was flipping out on Def Jam staff, accusing people of having something to do with the bootleg copies on the street. I just couldn’t believe how flagrant it was… People kept giving me the same name as the source of the bootlegging. It was someone I knew, someone I never would have suspected.

Lance was a record producer and a record executive, and a close friend of Jay’s until the incident. He explained in Decoded he walked up to Lance and tried to speak to him about it, but Lance “got real loud with me right in the middle of the club.” Jay then blacked out, and ended up being charged with assault.

Lance was probably trying to make a quick buck off the bootleg, but it may have cost him credibility in the industry. Jay lost even more, put on probation for 3 years and trotted out in front of the media as a dangerous criminal.

line: It’s a cold cold world but I blew my hand
vault_lines: It's a cold cold world but I blew my hand
meaning:
Winter is a recurring theme in Jay’s music Just as he did in the first verse he employs some wordplay surrounding the season. When your hand is cold, you blow on it to warm it up. “Blow” is also another term for cocaine, so when the world was cold Jay sold cocaine to make it through.

To “blow” your hand is card-playing lingo, and means don’t over-stretch yourself or do something you will regret later.

It’s likely these words, and the rest of the verse, is related to his stabbing of Lance Rivera, which occurred in 1999 but wasn’t resolved until mid-2001, around the time Jay would have been working on this record.

meaning: Kells may not be your traditional thug singer, but he was shot in the shoulder at the age of 11, and was charged with battery in 1996. Despite these incidents he’s likely employing some poetic licence here.

line: You either, stand or fall, I chose to stand The hawk outside, so I blow my hand It’s a cold cold world but I overstand Tryin’ to stay focused but I feel hopeless damn Can’t cope with bein’ broke, I’m a man - c’mon
vault_lines: You either, stand or fall, I chose to stand
meaning:
One of Jay’s most popular and prolific themes: he’d rather “die enormous than live dormant.” The seasons are also a regular theme in his music, and the “hawk” means a bitterly cold wind. He uses that metaphorically to also mean the world is cold, so he has to “blow” his hand: both to warm it up, and to sell cocaine to overcome the cold.

“Overstand” is related to the word “understand,” and it means to be fully enlightened about a situation, and be in control of it. You may understand how the crack game works, but can you control it’s trajectory?

line: Police in the background, screamin’ put the thing down That’s how hard I was tryin’ to put my thing down Si-rens ringin’ out, old ladies screamin’ out All this attention for me and I’m barely sixteen now .. it’s feelin’ like a dream now Handcuffed, roughed up, I’m tossed in the bing now I’m lyin’ next to fiends now, that’s the end of the story Let me bring y’all niggas back to the very first scene now (Come on)
vault_lines: Police in the background, screamin' put the thing down
meaning:
Jay takes a non-linear approach to telling this story, beginning at the conclusion, then going back to the start to explain how he arrived there.

Ironically, Jay was never arrested for firearm possession during his days as a drug dealer. It wasn’t until he became a rapper he ran into trouble, catching a gun charge in 2001. The charges against him were dropped, unlike in this narrative, where he is “tossed in the bing,” or prison.

He did shoot his brother when he was just 12 years old. He may be using some of that experience to deepen the meaning behind these bars.

line: We was cut from the same cloth and what was under his shirt was his Momma’s rent, his young brother’s clothes My nephew’s food, and with that I sqooze .. and with that I froze Now my life is frozen in time behind these iron poles And this story is told, for young soldiers Who never choose the life we chose
vault_lines: We was cut from the same cloth and what was under his shirt was his
meaning:
Jay was facing someone in the exact same position as him. “Under his clothes” he may have been carrying a weapon, used to procure these items for his family, drugs for sale, or the actual items. “Cut from the same cloth” means they’re of the same background, or of the same mindset.

Jay had the drop on this kid, so he shot him. And he was caught, now living a life behind bars for the life he chose.

And it’s nobody’s fault I made the decisions I made
This is the life I chose, or rather, the life that chose me

It also echoes another song recorded around this time, “Ballad for the Fallen Soldier,” a track that equates hustling with a young soldier going to war. This is presented as a cautionary tale: Learn from the mistakes of these two kids.

line: And you got a couple of beans and you don’t have a clue? Your situation is bleek, I’ma keep it real ’cause Fuckin’ with me, you gotta drop a mil’ ’Cause if you gonna cop somethin’, you gotta cop for real
vault_lines: And you got a couple of beans and you don't have a clue?
meaning:
This section puns on the names of Jay-affiliated artists, most of whom were signed to Roc-A-Fella at the time – Beanie Sigel, DJ Clue, Memphis Bleek, Rell, Amil, and Pharrell Williams of the The Neptunes. The pun on Amil’s name is particularly notable, since Amil was dropped from the Roc-A-Fella label recently prior to the release of The Blueprint.

This section is a direct answer to Nas, who used this same device to insult Jay on a then-current freestyle. The relevant lines are

Rip the Freeway, shoot through Memphis with Moneybags
Go to Philly, order cheese steak, and eat Beans fast

The “Amil/a mill” pun works further as a response to Nas to show a million dollars before trying to mess with Jay.

A great line – he insults the would-be litigants by saying that even if they won, it wouldn’t faze him at all.

Lance Un Rivera did sue Jay Z over the stabbing but later settled out of court to an undisclosed amount. Around that same time, there was a lady that sued jay Z for her vocals on Izzo(H.O.V.A).

This is most likely a direct shot at those two incidents since he’s known to address any grievances he has or incidents that are reported in the media through his music releases.

line: I’m not guilty, now give me back my bread Mr. District Attorney, I’m not sure if they told you I’m on TV every day, where the fuck could I go to?
vault_lines: I'm not guilty, now give me back my bread
meaning:
A reference to Jay’s real-life legal case (he was accused of stabbing Lance “Un” Rivera). Incidentally, despite his protestations, Jay actually plead guilty in that case. He would reference this case in his music numerous times, most humorously in “Dear Summer”.

In this case Jay wants the D.A. to set a bail for him in order to avoid jail, his fame prevents him from being a flight risk so there’s no reason why he shouldn’t have the chance to stay out of prison. Bread refers to bail money, which would be returned to him after being found not guilty.

line: Charges don’t stick to dude, he’s Teflon

meaning:
Teflon, or polytetrafluoroethylene, is used as a non-stick coating for cookware. Thus, charges will not “stick” to Jay, just like food will not stick to Teflon. This appellation was originally put on Mafia head John “The Teflon Don” Gotti, because the majority of attempts to convict him resulted in either a hung jury or an acquittal.

Also note that teflon is an almost ‘perfect’ electrical insulator (like glass) and therefore his use of the word ‘charges’ is correct in this context as well

line: Since this is a New Era, got a fresh, new hat
vault_lines: Since this is a New Era, got a fresh, new hat
meaning:
In November 2006 Jay-Z was returning to the rap game after a short-lived retirement; but the scene was a lot different from when he left in 2003. 50 Cent was taking over the world, Nas began lamenting the death of hip-hop, and Lil Wayne was now ruling the mixtape circuit.

Wearing many hats during his illustrious career, Jay had transformed too. At the time of Kingdom Come’s release he was the President of Def Jam Recordings and had been focused on success in business and the boardroom. His return to music, or his “new era,” was partially because of his lack of faith in the new rappers, and needing to save his label’s financial position.

New Era is the headwear company that makes the official on-field hats for Major League Baseball, including Hov’s world famous Yankees cap, which featured on the album’s cover.

line: Fresh like Mannie be, chain like anti-freeze Shoebox full of cash, dealer-man hand me keys Pantries full of Arm & Hammer Don’t take Nancy Drew to see what it do, I’m a damn G (Ugh)
vault_lines: Fresh like Mannie be, chain like anti-freeze
meaning:
Jay drops a bunch of references to describe just how fly he is, as well as how deeply he is entrenched in the cocaine slinging game.

Mannie Fresh is a Southern producer, his name provides Jay with his fresh to death tag.

Anti-Freeze is used in cars in the middle of winter so their cooling system doesn’t freeze solid. “Cold” is another way of saying “incredible”, “diamond studded”.

His shoebox of cash shows he’s living outside of the law in his money making ways. He can’t keep it in a bank because it would arouse suspicion. Rather than the dealer handing him keys to a car, he’s actually handing him “ki’s” of cocaine, which is a kilogram, a huge amount with a staggering street value.

Arm & Hammer make baking soda, a key ingredient in the cooking up of crack cocaine for sale.

Nancy Drew is a fictional detective, who was incredibly good at her job. It doesn’t take a professional to realise Jay sits atop the Gangster totem pole.

line: Back when rappers wouldn’t dare play lyrical roulette With a automatic weapon I was rappin’ with a TEC
vault_lines: I was a real star
meaning:
In the early part of Jay’s career, he faced little lyrical opposition. He allegedly washed Busta Rhymes during a school yard battle, Dame Dash claims he beat Big L in a battle in Harlem, and his rap battle with DMX is legendary.

Around the year 2000, and the unsavoury incident with Nas, Jay’s competition began to come for him. By the time 2006 rolled around, he really did have beef with like 100 children.

He plays their insubordination off with Russian Roulette, the art of loading a gun with a solitary bullet and pulling the trigger until that bullet releases. Jay’s rapid rhyme schemes mimmick the effects of an automatic Tec 9 handgun. Dangerous and fast.

This bleeds in to the shade he throws at this new school. A “video car” is one that is rented solely for the purpose of flexing on camera.

He asked me about my Maybach, think he had the same
Except mine tinted and his might have been rented

Jay’s famous off-white Lexus was just one of a fleet of cars he comandeered during this period.

Countless times he’s described himself as a hustler first.

It’s only fair that I warn ya, rap’s my new hustle
I’m treating it like the corner, fuck with me if you wanna

He plays on the term “wrapper”, a way for hustlers and fiends to conceal their drugs. He’s made much more money slinging raps than he ever did on the street.

During this retirement he went on a world tour, created Unfinished Business with R. Kelly, Collision Course with Linkin Park, and held down a number of guest spots…

In the first example, we can cite his exit from the drug world to set the rap game on its ear. By doing this, he starts a new hustle, this time making hits instead of selling them.

After The Black Album, Jay temporarily retired from music to pursue the presidency of Def Jam Records.

Hov alluded to his new boardroom hustle in a freestyle around this time:

line: That’s why they call him Hov, ’cause he came before all this shit Bought a six, quarter seven, skipped on them quarter eights Bought a nine for nonstop Glock work all the time (Woo!)
vault_lines: That's why they call him Hov, 'cause he came before all this shit
meaning:
Hov is a shortening of Jay Hova, itself a play on Jehova, a religious term meaning God. God created all, hence he came before everything we see.

Jay was introduced to the game young, beginning his hustling career during the 80s, a time well before the memories of most internet critics or current rappers.

As a result, he throws some drug terms at us and equates then with vehicles and accessories from that point in time.

The 6 is a reference to the Mercedes Benz S600.

“Quarter 7” is the BMW 645i from the 1980s.

“Quarter 8’s” is the BMW 7 series, specifically the 745, a car Jay rarely references due to his Maybach obsession.

A quarter is also an ounce of cocaine, and an “8 ball” is one eighth of an ounce (half a quarter). A small amount for a small time hustler, something Jay didn’t concern himself with.

The 9 Glock is a reference to a 9mm pistol. It completes the time metaphor, and links in with his 10 year veteran finale.

VVS = Very Very Slightly included, a grade of diamond clarity



VVS boulders is alluding to not only how big his diamonds are, but how high-quality they are too. He also plays with the word set here which can have two meanings:


His diamonds which are real are ‘set’ visibly out in the open in his day to day life, not just on camera.
‘Setting’ is when you place a diamond in jewelry. They are ‘set’ in a bezel, therefore continue with his comment that his jewelry has real diamonds in them.

“Wood” is in comparison to platinum or gold status records. Selling “wood” means you sold nada. Not enough.

This frustrates Jay. He expressed this on “Moment of Clarity”, and his “If I Can’t (Freestyle)” verse.

I tried to be modest on Blueprint 2
But ya’ll don’t respect modest, ya’ll respect ma dollars
You got to believe I think like a artist
But my bills through the roof can’t do numbers like The Roots

He claims the blogs and the critics are upset with him for not delivering more intellectual music, but these kinds of fans aren’t the ones buying his records in bulk. He’s forced to dumb down and pander to the lowest common denominator in order to make money off his art.

These lines are also an example of criticism of the rap game from within its borders. Hov is reflecting on the events of the rap game during his “retirement” stint. To him, the music being released was sup-par: all beat and hook, no substantial lyrics.

line: Saint Hov, story takes place in ancient Egypt They’ll cut off the nose to spite their face, they’ll steal ya Jesus I can’t tell Hattie White that blue-eyed version is make believe stuff She throw me out the house, say, “Ye deliver us from this heathen” I say that to Ms. Tina, she’ll sneeze at sun, her photic reflex
vault_lines: Saint Hov, story takes place in ancient Egypt
meaning:
Hov starts off the passage with the idiom “cut off the nose to spite the face,” which warns the listener of doing something that will damage themselves more than the object of their anger. Hov previously used this idiom on his June 2017 track “4:44” while addressing his infidelity with spouse Beyoncé:

Like the men before me, I cut off my nose to spite my face

Relating back to Hov’s African roots and his story beginning in Egypt, the Great Sphinx of Giza had its nose defaced by an unknown person or group. The destroyer of the Sphinx remains unknown as of this track’s release. Hov previously related his roots to the Sphinx on his March 2014 track “We Made It Freestyle”:

Face all on the Sphinx
Story all in the wall of the pyramids

Hov then discusses the long-standing debate of the race of Jesus and how his most popular depiction in the Western has become a light-skinned, blue-eyed, and seemingly appropriated version:



While Jesus' actual race is unknown, it has been studied by many academics and it is theorized that the spiritual figure would have more of a dark or olive complexion with darker eyes rather than the popular white depiction that is most frequently seen. This is based off models and depictions of other Galilean Semites that were from the same time that Jesus is written to be have been alive.

He then introduces the controversy of his issue in relation to family members – Hattie White, Jay’s grandmother, and Ms. Tina Knowles-Lawson, Jay’s mother-in-law – representative of two followers of Christianity. He reveals that they would be unreceptive to the thought of Jesus being unlike the Western model they know the spiritual figure as, showing how followers of the faith would not want to embrace Jesus' true darker complexion on a massive scale.

Relating back to Knowles' distrust in a truer form of Jesus, photic sneeze reflex is a condition that causes sneezing in response to stimuli such as looking at bright lights, including the Sun. Hov makes a double entendre with the word “Sun,” meaning that she will sneeze at the bright light of the Sun but would also figuratively “sneeze,” or exude disbelief, at the true appearance of God’s son, Jesus, when shown a figure different that the traditional one she knows.

line: I’m a page turner, sage burner, Santeria Chongón, December baby, my Orishas
vault_lines: I'm a page turner, sage burner, Santeria
meaning:
Chango is an Orisha, or a higher divinity in the Afro-Cuban religion Santeria. The deity one of the most feared in the faith, as characteristics associated with it include power, strength, fire, and other elemental forces. Jay has referenced the religion before in his verse on Drake’s September 2013 hit “Pound Cake / Paris Morton Music 2”:

My saint’s Changó, light a candle
El Gran Santo on the mantle

The “December baby” Hov talks about is himself – his birthday is December 4, 1969. Hov shares this day with the designated feast day of Chango, which is December 4, allowing Hov to compare himself to the deity in the next line with “Saint Hov.”

It’s also worth noting that before JAY-Z’s verse starts you can hear the sound of a page turning, hence the line “I’m a page turner.”

line: They both had straightening combs, little did they know I hold the heat next Neither tool can be used to fix our defects P.S. we born perfect, fuck all the B.S

In reference to the “combs” and “heat,” Jay explains that “neither tool"—meaning both a literal tool and a gun (slang definition of tool)—will ever truly fix the problems or perceived imperfections one has. Be it poverty or pressure to conform to Eurocentric features (e.g., using straightening combs on Afro-textured hair), these are "our defects.”

“P.S.” operates as double entendre as well.

P.S. is a common abbreviation used at the end of letters—in this case, the track—to indicate an additional thought or postscript.

Adobe Photoshop, a popular photo editing software, is often abbreviated as PS as well. This is yet another “tool” Jay Z evokes.

line: As God as my witness, timin’ was my mistress
vault_lines: As God as my witness, timin' was my mistress
meaning:
This metaphor is significant to this song, in terms of presenting the origins of their problems.
- “As God my witness” has similar meanings to the one of a wedding vow. The use of God here also reassures his woman that Z would never break his trust.
- “Timin' was my mistress” indicates that he fooled around with time, hence the use of the word mistress, with seductive connotations. He says that time is distracting and is a vital component in his life, as he was too busied managing his time to pay attention to his woman. This may also be indicative of his busy lifestyle, as he cannot find the time for her. He was having an affair with time, and cheating with it on his woman, as he had no other choice to do so. The indication of time (an abstract idea) as a mistress is also symbolic of the insignificant things that people pursue in life, rather than spending time with their loved ones.
- Lastly, the mentioning of  God and the concept of having a mistress in one sentence indicates how holy, sweet yet bitter their relationship is, as these ideas are almost oxymoronic in nature in terms of religion.




He also mentions the stars and their power above to connect with Sade’s first lines in the song, which emphasizes their relationship’s value to Jay Z.

In the first verse’s introductory lines, Jay borrows some Jamaican patois and common roots reggae tropes to ground his story in an historical perspective.

Lions are often used to represent royalty and African pride.  Rastafari’s association of Haile Selassie with the Lion of Judah, symbol of the Israelite tribe of Judah, made the lion a recurring motif in roots reggae music.  The Rastafari interpretation of Zion as a utopian Promised Land at odds with the corrupt, oppressive machinations of Babylon is another common reggae theme.  Rhyming “lion” with “Zion” is also familiar, with Bob Marley’s “Iron Lion Zion” being a notable example.

“Likkle yout” is patois for “little youth,” and here refers to the Black people unjustly denied their noble birthright when they were stolen from Africa (Zion) and bound into slavery in the New World.

Releasing in 40 days

However, the number also has deep symbolic meaning in Islam, a culture in which Jay is deeply rooted and at many occasions on this record. Jay uses the phrase most similarly to Islam’s sacred text, the Quran, to the story of the prophet Moses at Mount Sinai, who was ordered by his Lord to fast for 40 days on top of Mount Sinai before god bestowed him with the Ten Commandments:

And We made an appointment with Moses for thirty nights and perfected them by [the addition of] ten; so the term of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron, “Take my place among my people, do right [by them], and do not follow the way of the corrupters. (Surah Al-A'raf [7:142-143])

Jay plays off of the story to make a literary device in comparison to the recording time for his all-important album. Jay’s studio session was Moses' fasting, as he was prepping to give his people, or his fans, his all-important, long-awaited debut record, while Moses waited to give his people, the Israelites, their all important message from the Lord, the Ten Commandments.

Interestingly enough, the record itself draws even further similarities to the story, with A Written Testimony, the record that Jay came out with after 40 days, having ten tracks similarly to the Ten Commandments' ten clauses.

line: Niggas thought they was ill, found out they was ill And it’s like you knew exactly how I wanted you to feel
vault_lines: Niggas thought they was ill, found out they was ill
meaning:
Hov is saying “People thought they were on my level, thought they were ‘ill’ like me but they found out they were really sick in a bad way, outmatched and overwhelmed. I set the tone so perfectly, it’s like I controlled how they felt. I played the game so well, they reacted exactly how I intended.”

Jay-Z is using a play on the word ill, which in hip hop slang can mean cool, dope, or skilled, but also literally means sick or weak. He’s saying they thought they were dope, but they were actually in over their heads. And the second line shows his calculated dominance, his ability to not just outperform, but manipulate perception and emotion.

Also this works as a triple entendre:


“Ill” as in dope: They thought they were raw, talented, on his level.
“Ill” as in sick: They were actually messed up, weak, not built for the game.
“Eel” which ties to the “eww” as in a slimy, spineless creature: A metaphor for suckers, snakes, or fake people, slippery and untrustworthy. He’s saying they’re not just not ill, they’re bottom-feeders.



That subtle pronunciation flip from ill to eel creates that extra diss, not just that they were wrong about themselves, but that they’re lowlife types trying to swim with sharks.

Jay’s genius is that he never says “eel” outright, but he makes you hear it. That’s wordplay at its finest.

vault_lines: So stop with that childish shit, nigga, I'm grown
meaning:
This may seem like a paradoxical line in a song where he calls someone garbage and lame, but it indicates two things.

Firstly, don’t forget Jay sonning Prodigy in the first verse. Verse 4 is about his position in the rap game. It’s testament to the power of Nas that he even has Jay defending himself, considering the first song on the album is entitled “The Ruler’s Back”. His maturity will ultimately fail him, but for now he claims the higher road.

Secondly, he was about to embark on a campaign to “upgrade” his style and image. On The Black Album his track “Change Clothes” was pivotal in a culture shift in hip hop. At the time, he was saying “I am dismissing you and moving on to bigger and better things”. It didn’t quite pan out that way.

Jay would embrace his Ruler status on Watch The Throne in 2011 with Kanye.

line: Y’all niggas gon’ learn to respect the king
vault_lines: Y'all niggas gon' learn to respect the king
meaning:
After the death of Biggie, who was regarded as the best MC in the New York area, a tussle to attain that crown began, most notably and famously between Nas and Jay Z.

Jay acknowledged this battle during his track “Where I’m From”:

Who’s the best MCs, Biggie, Jay-Z, or Nas?

In live performances around the time, notably during his Fade to Black concert DVD, he would refuse to use Nas' name during the song, replying “Nah” when the crowd filled it in for him.

He’s not only throwing shade at Nas on this line, but every other rapper from New York. He crowns himself the King, meaning everyone else is underneath him.

line: But along with celebrity comes ’bout seventy shots to your frame
vault_lines: But along with celebrity comes 'bout seventy shots to your frame
meaning:
Jay would reference Big’s classic track more explicitly later in the album, but here he uses it as an aggressive statement.

More Money More Problems. Jay is famous for his subliminal disses, and his ability to remain calm and collected when being attacked from all sides. He only explicitly goes after the big fish.

It’s hard to do when you’ve got nothing to prove
Everybody know you better, you in a lose lose
Cause even when you win, ultimately you lose
Real n—s like, “Why Hov talking to Dude?”

His claim here is that by going at Nas hard on wax in this verse, he is bringing him in to the spotlight. During his Breakfast Club interview Charlemagne remarked that the beef “helped Nas”. Jay is sending a warning though: with great fame comes great danger.

line: I know you miss it, Nas, the (Fame)
vault_lines: I know you miss it, Nas, the (Fame)
meaning:
Fame is pronounced to sound like it does in David Bowie’s song “Fame”.

At the time, Nas' fame, not quite at the fever pitch of post-Illmatic, was nonetheless incredibly high. It Was Written ended up selling 5 million copies, and by 2001 Nas was still being spoken of as the possible and probable King of New York.

One could argue Jay had crossed over, and brought the suburbs to the hood in a more effective manner. One could also argue that Nas was on a downward spiral until Stillmatic, buoyed by the track “Ether”, was released. There’s no doubt the beef helped both their careers, but Nas was still incredibly famous when “Takeover” dropped.

line: Don’t let ’em gas you like Jigga is ass and won’t clap you Trust me on this one, I’ll detach you Mind from spirit, body from soul They’ll have to hold a mass, put your body in a hole
vault_lines: Don't let 'em gas you like Jigga is ass and won't clap you
meaning:
To “gas” someone up is to fire them up, to pump them up, to convince them to act in a certain manner.

Jay explained that his own crew was gassing him up to go at Prodigy.

Notice the figurative similarity between the words “ass” and “clap.”

Everybody wanted it to happen, like they did! There was a time like everybody was like ‘please, please let this guy go away’

He re-ups on the final line from the first verse. This isn’t just rap music, this is Jay’s life and livelihood. He will kill you.

line: Roc-A-Fella students of the game, we passed the class ’Cause nobody can read you dudes like we do
vault_lines: Roc-A-Fella students of the game, we passed the class
meaning:
Jay’s young-uns came up under one of the greatest teachers. Jay himself was an avid student of hip hop as a youth, calling his time on the road with Big Daddy Kane his “college days”.

He also resurrects his earlier shot about bringing a pen to a test. Jay and his crew, when tested, present their full arsenal, and pass with flying colours.

He’s seen this before, he’ll see it again. He knows.

I know when you’re schemin, I feel when you plottin
I got, mental vision, intuition
I know where you goin I read your mind’s navigational system

line: Well, we don’t believe you, you need more people
vault_lines: Well, we don't believe you, you need more people
meaning:
Playing again on Mobb Deep’s name, Jay explains that he doesn’t believe their crew rolls deep and that to take on the Roc crew they’ll need heavy reinforcements.

Prodigy’s verse on “Shook Ones Pt. II” was a shuddering dismissal of other rappers and street personalities.

You all alone in these streets, cousin

Jay dismisses it in one line.

line: You was a ballerina, I got the pictures, I seen ya
vault_lines: You was a ballerina, I got the pictures, I seen ya
meaning:
“Pushing weight” means to be selling drugs in large quantities. In 1988 Jay-Z was selling lots of drugs and made a lot of money from it which he claimed he was still spending money from about 8 years later in his 1996 song “Dead Presidents II”:

I dabbled in crazy weight without rap, I was crazy straight
Partner, I’m still spendin' money from ‘88, what?

So while Jay-Z was dealing drugs, Prodigy was dressing up in a Michael Jackson outfit while he attended his grandmother’s concert program.



Although funnily enough in 1989, Jay-Z featured on his mentor Jaz-O’s song “Hawaiian Sophie” where he wasn’t looking tough or gangsta either.



Prodigy responded in Mobb Deep’s song “Crawlin”:

‘88, is you crazy?
That’s when I was fuckin’ Sophie and you was pumpin' for poison
My nigga Killa Dang woulda spit in your face

Nas would also mention this year  in his diss track “Ether” where he would say that Jay-Z was not a gangsta during this time:

In ‘88 you was gettin’ chased through your building
Callin' my crib and I ain’t even give you my numbers
All I did was give you a style for you to run with
Smilin' in my face, glad to break bread with the God
Wearin' Jaz' chains, no TECs, no cash, no cars
No jail bars, Jigga, no pies, no case
Just Hawaiian shirts, hangin' with little Chase

The next year, he would mention 1988 again, in his song “Made You Look”:

Rooftop, like we bringin' ‘88 back

At 2001’s Summer Jam, when Jay-Z performed this part of the song he put the pictures of Prodigy as kid in a Michael Jackson outfit, up on the big screen. Many people thought that Jay-Z ended Mobb Deep’s career by doing this but in Prodigy’s 2011 audio book The Autobiography Of Mobb Deep’s Prodigy My Infamous Life, he stated that it didn’t ruin Mobb Deep or hurt their album sales.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2jHTFioFCew&t=497s

Prodigy responded in Mobb Deep’s song “Burn”:

And that shit that you pulled ain’t do me no damage
You don’t know me, nigga, but we ‘bout to change that shit

And he responded again in Mobb Deep’s song “Crawlin”:

And your retaliation was weak, baby pictures?

In Jay-Z’s 2002 interview with Angie Martinez on Hot97, he said Prodigy deserved to be put up on the screen as Prodigy was dissing him harshly on mixtapes so it was either that or to try to beat Prodigy up or something.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RZoezvNJetM&t=2434s

About 7 years later, Jay-Z would again mention dissing Prodigy at Summer Jam in Young Jeezy’s song “Put On Remix”:

I put Prodigy in his place on that Summer Jam screen

In Prodigy’s audio book The Autobiography Of Mobb Deep’s Prodigy My Infamous Life, he said that after Murder Inc. artist Vita had told him that her label’s boss Irv Gotti wouldn’t allow her to be in the music video of Mobb Deep’s song “Burn”, he figured that Jay-Z must’ve gotten the pictures from Irv Gotti and that Irv Gotti had gotten the pictures from his other Murder Inc. artist Ashanti who had went to Prodigy’s grandmother’s concert program when they were kids.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZQdQ3qyblfQ&t=4298s

In July 2012, Prodigy was on Power 105’s The Breakfast Club where he said that the pictures came from when he was at his grandmother’s concert program:

That came from my grandmother’s program. Every year, she did a concert at Carnegie Hall in Lincoln Center and she would do this program booklet for the families and kids that were in the school, of course, she had her grandson in there and I thought I was Michael Jackson back in the day, so I had my Mike getup on and all of that. That’s where that picture came from.

line: The Broad Street Bully, we runnin’ this rap shit
vault_lines: The Broad Street Bully, we runnin' this rap shit
meaning:
Beanie Sigel refers to himself as the Broad Street Bully. It was also the title of his 2009 record. It’s a reference to the 1970s Philadelphia Hockey team that was commonly referred to as the Broad Street Bullies.

Nas would play on this chorus during his “Ether” diss record.

line: M Easy, we runnin’ this rap shit
vault_lines: M Easy, we runnin' this rap shit
meaning: This is a reference to Memphis Bleek, whose name is an acronym for “Making Easy Money Pimpin’ Hoes In Style.”

line: So you won’t confuse it with just rap music
vault_lines: So you won't confuse it with just rap music
meaning:
He tells Prodigy that if he wants then their beef can get serious for real and that it won’t just stay on records.

In Prodigy’s 2011 audio book The Autobiography Of Mobb Deep’s Prodigy My Infamous Life, Prodigy says that the next month in October 2001 he along with some of his boys went to Puff Daddy aka P. Diddy’s restaurant Justin’s on 21st Street in Manhattan which Jay-Z also happened to be at. Prodigy found out and him and his boys covered the entrance of the restaurant and when Jay-Z saw Prodigy and his boys, Jay-Z extended his hand to shake Prodigy’s and then he contradicted his line here as he told Prodigy:

It ain’t no beef. It’s just music, man, no drama

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZQdQ3qyblfQ&t=3224s

Prodigy then responded in Mobb Deep’s song “Burn” as he said in his 2011 audio book The Autobiography Of Mobb Deep’s Prodigy My Infamous Life that Jay-Z told him it ain’t no beef just music so he gave Jay-Z some just music to listen to on “Burn”:

Just pain, just sufferin' and worst than that
You let me get my hands on you so I’m takin' advantage

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZQdQ3qyblfQ&t=4186s

line: [Chorus]
vault_lines: R-O-C, we runnin' this rap shit
meaning:
Kanye’s epic use of classic rockers The Doors “Five to One” made for one monumental beat. This instrumental stands completely on its own. The bass is thunderous, the Jim Morrison vocal samples are eerie. The haunting guitar riffs take Hov’s lines from tough to truly sinister. The track contains 3 samples.

The first sample you hear is at the start of the song, its vocals and instrumentals from “5 to One” by The Doors.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6dI0rwRGdVs
Then he samples the line:

We run New York

http://youtu.be/1VRZq3J0uz4?t=36s
From “Sound Of The Police” by KRS-ONE multiple times spread out througout the record to further emphazies his point with the song.

The third and final sample is the word “Fame” from the David Bowie song “Fame”. Fame was then flipped to make it sound like “lame” to further diminish Nas status. That sample was popular back when it came out as in whole clubs “sang” with it.
http://youtu.be/J-_30HA7rec?t=1m

With guitar riffs and keyboards from time to time to further add to atmosphere of a freight train comming through. The hard-hitting instrumental compliments Jay’s delivery as well as lyrical intent as in taking over the game with it.

line: Nigga, switch up your flow, your shit is garbage
vault_lines: Nigga, switch up your flow, your shit is garbage
meaning:
Compare Nas' Illmatic to his then recent album Nastradamus, it was clearly evident that Nas changed his flow to suit a more mainstream appeal. But by doing so, it impacted Nas to the point where his lyrics had to follow a similar suit as well.

Ironically, Jay-Z’s flow actually changed over time. Prior to his acclaimed debut, Reasonable Doubt, Jay came with a chopped and speedy flow that can be heard in a classic Big L 7 minute freestyle, and on another Big L track, as well as all of Jay’s early work including “I Can’t Get Wid Dat”.



Over time, Jay-Z’s flow developed and changed greatly. He is now regarded as having one of the best and most diverse flows in the game, a fact he trumpeted on “Hovi Baby” which is a dizzying display of linguistic manipulation.

line: [Verse 3]
vault_lines: R-O-C, we runnin' this rap shit
meaning:
Verse 3 was added for the album version of The Blueprint. Here, we see Hov’s first real shots on wax toward Nas, attacking his discography, personal life, character and more. What’s notable about this verse is that while the first two are only 16 bars, and aimed mostly at Mobb Deep, Jay doubled the recording to make it 32 bars. Notice that even the 3rd verse on Nas’ response, “Ether”, also has 32 bars.

This would begin hip-hop’s most talked about beef.

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fu1d9r59UI8

line: That’s why your (Lame), career’s come to an end It’s only so long fake thugs can pretend
vault_lines: That's why your (Lame), career's come to an end
meaning:
Sooner or later, someone will test Nas’s mettle as a thug and he’ll have to show if he’s really the thug he’s rapped about being or not. This could also be a clever play on Nas’s opening line in his song “The Message”:

Fake thug, no love, you get the slug
CB4 Gusto

Jay-Z planned on ending Nas’s career with this diss track but ironically enough he ended up doing the opposite as this track actually gave Nas new motivation and passion that he used to make his album Stillmatic which featured his response diss track “Ether”. The album was critically acclaimed, went platinum and revitalized Nas’s career.

line: I showed you your first TEC on tour with Large Professor (Me, that’s who)
vault_lines: I showed you your first TEC on tour with Large Professor (Me, that's who)
meaning:
Large Professor has confirmed this story in various interviews. The incident took place in Washington DC in the early 90s (back when DC was the murder capital of the US).

Nas and Jay-Z were on the same tour, Nas with Large Pro’s group Main Source and Jay with The Jaz. After the show was cut short by promoters, angry fans followed the rappers back to the tour bus. Taking no chances with the rowdy D.C. crowd, young Hov pulled a TEC-9 semi-automatic from a duffel bag:

We were figuring we were gonna have to knuckle down. Jay came outta nowhere, reaching in his gym bag like, ‘Don’t even sweat these niggas. I got that.’

Akinyele was also featured on this tour in 1991, and has confirmed the validity of Hov’s claim.

Was this the first time Nas saw a TEC? Possibly not, but the line is definitely based on an actual event.

Note: The “Me! That’s who!” you hear in the background is sampled from the bathtub scene in Scarface.
https://youtu.be/cs8I_mlOG2Q?t=207

line: But I know, the sun don’t shine if son don’t shine
vault_lines: But I know, the sun don't shine if son don't shine
meaning:
Nas insisted on adding a verse to “Oochie Wally”; Jay Z accuses him of trying to steal attention (“shine”) from his friend; Nas also calls himself God’s son.



Also note the use of the homophone “sun” and “son”.

In 1994, Mobb Deep released a song featuring Nas called “An Eye for an Eye”, which featured the lines:

As time goes by, an eye for an eye
We in this together son your beef is mines
So long as the sun shines to light up the sky
We in this together son your beef is mines

As Jay said on “Dig A Hole”,

Why not wait to catch them all together?
That’s why you dig one big hole, one time

He collects both Mobb Deep and Nas in his hole. Nas, being God’s Son, proved on “Oochie Wally” he wasn’t shining. Hence, Jay has removed their “sun”, destroying the bond they shared on that song.

line: No, you’re not on my level, get your brakes tweaked
vault_lines: No, you're not on my level, get your brakes tweaked
meaning:
Jay means both  literally (aka another short joke) as well as in the slang sense of the phrase, meaning “on par”.

Brakes as in on a car, and “breaks” as in choose better breaks (the short section of a song, usually a drumbeat, that is sampled and repeated to create the backing track of a rap song) to make music for your songs, which are not very good. A standard Jay homophone.

This goes along with the car theme since he already said that he was gassed up. “So, Prodigy, get your brakes fixed because you need to stop”.

line: And all you other cats throwin’ shots at Jigga You only get half a bar, fuck y’all niggas
vault_lines: And all you other cats throwin' shots at Jigga
meaning:
Wordplay off of shots and bar as you would take shots of alcohol at a bar or pub. So everyone else that’s taking shots at Jay-Z is only getting half of the bar to get shots from so they won’t have as many shots to take.

He dismisses everyone else that’s dissing him but he refuses to mention them by name as they’re so insignificant to him. This is directed towards Jadakiss and the rest of his group The LOX with whom Jay-Z’s artist and right hand man Beanie Sigel, as well as Beanie Sigel’s group State Property, were beefing with at the time. The Lox member Styles P had even threw a shot at Jay-Z in The Lox’s diss tracks “Breakin’ The Rules Freestyle” and “White Label / Jigga That Nigga Freestyle”.

This diss also refers to Jayo Felony who was beefing with Jay-Z over a line that Jay-Z had said in his song “Change The Game” to which Jayo Felony had then dissed Jay-Z in his song “True’d Up”.

This diss is also directed towards Fat Joe who was also beefing with Jay-Z. In a 2022 interview with Math Hoffa, Fat Joe would even say that Jay-Z dissed him in his song “U Don’t Know” which is from this same album The Blueprint.

This line is also directed at Outlawz member Napoleon who had dissed Jay-Z in the redone version of 2Pac’s song “All Out” from his posthumous album, Until The End Of Time that was released a few months prior in March.

It’s also directed at 50 Cent who disses Jay-Z throughout his song “Be A Gentleman” which is a response to Jay-Z’s line dissing 50 Cent in his song “It’s Hot (Some Like It Hot)” which itself is a response to 50 Cent’s line about Jay-Z in his song “How To Rob”.

Seeing as how Jay-Z is unwilling to name the last few people and only addresses them with half a bar, this shows that Jay-Z notes both Prodigy and Nas as worthy adversaries as he mainly disses them in this song especially Nas who he even calls out by name which he didn’t do for Prodigy.

line: Nigga, I know you well, all the stolen jewels
vault_lines: Nigga, I know you well, all the stolen jewels
meaning:
“Jew-el” is a reference to a Nas line from It Ain’t Hard To Tell:

Nas, I analyze, drop a jew-el, inhale from the L

Getting your jewels stolen is one of the biggest insults imaginable among rappers. This line implies that it has happened to Nas, a claim which Jay furthered on “Super Ugly” with the lines

This nigga never sold asprin, how you Escobar?
Had to buy your chain back the last time you got robbed



Also, Prodigy was robbed for his chain during the first HNIC “Keep It Thoro” video, and again at the Y.B.E. videoshoot.

line: You are not deep, you made your bed, now sleep
vault_lines: You are not deep, you made your bed, now sleep
meaning:
You may call your group Mobb Deep, but you are in fact not “deep” at all – i.e. you do not have many people behind you in the streets. In addition, he is mocking Nas' image as a “deep” or “conscious” rapper – something he would do to even greater effect on his song “The Blueprint 2”:

‘Cause a nigga wear a kufi, it don’t mean that he bright
'Cause you don’t understand him, it don’t mean that he nice
It just means you don’t understand all the bullshit that he write

Sleep here is a metaphor for death, which is somewhat derivative of Nas’s classic line on “New York State of Mind”

I never sleep, cause sleep is the cousin of death.

Jay is killing Nas’s career and Nas brought it on himself by coming after him.

line: Do not bark up that tree, that tree will fall on you I don’t know why your advisers ain’t forewarn you Please, not Jay, he’s not for play
vault_lines: Do not bark up that tree, that tree will fall on you
meaning:
If you attack me (verbally or physically), it will backfire and you will be hurt instead. People close to Nas (and Jay) should have told him not to mess with Hova.

Also, a play on the word “bark”, which is the rough exterior of a tree and the idiom “Barking up the wrong tree” can mean for one to take the wrong course of action.

Years later, 50 Cent would advise The Game against beefing with Jay, proof that he is feared by even the most battle-hardened rappers.

line: A wise man told me don’t argue with fools ‘Cause people from a distance can’t tell who is who
vault_lines: A wise man told me don't argue with fools
meaning:
Literally a person from a distance just sees two people arguing, and not who is right or wrong. The wise man Jay is referring to is probably Mark Twain.

Never argue with a fool, onlookers may not be able to tell the difference.

Jay might also be referencing the wise Solomon who wrote many proverbs about answering fools, such as these ones in Proverbs 26:4-5:

Do not answer a fool according to his folly,
Or you will also be like him.
5 Answer a fool as his folly deserves,
That he not be wise in his own eyes.

This ties in with Jay’s theory on his lesser foes, and the high esteem he holds Nas in. The final 2 bars in this song are:

And all you other cats throwing shots at Jigga
You only get half a bar – fuck y'all niggas

He doesn’t even bother to directly address them. Even in 2013 he was being lauded for keeping his cool when being attacked.

line: Because you-know-who (Who) Did you-know-what (What?), with you-know-who (Yeah) But just keep that between me and you for now
vault_lines: Did you-know-what (What?), with you-know-who (Yeah)
meaning:
Jay-Z refers to the affair he had with Carmen Bryan who’s the mother of Nas’s first child Destiny Jones.



Their affair was not known publicly at the time so Jay-Z threatens to reveal this publicly if Nas responds. Which Nas did with his diss track “Ether”. Jay-Z would then in his diss track “Super Ugly [I Got Myself A Gun]”, talk about having slept with Carmen Bryan while she was still with Nas. To which Carmen responded to with her diss track “Carmen’s Got A Gun”.

line: What, you tryna kick knowledge? (Fuck outta here)
vault_lines: What, you tryna kick knowledge? (Fuck outta here)
meaning:
This line got a direct response from Nas in his reply song “Ether”:

Ask me if I’m trying to kick knowledge?
Nah, I’m trying to kick the shit you need to learn, though
The Ether, the shit that make your soul burn slow

Jay is making fun of Nas’s attempts to portray himself as a prophet or conscious rapper;  Jay elaborated on this critque on “Blueprint 2”:

And y'all buy the shit, caught up in the hype
Cause the nigga wear a kufi, it don’t mean that he bright
Cause you don’t understand him, it don’t mean that he nice
It just means you don’t understand all the bullshit that he write

In the movie Belly, Nas played the character “Sincere”, whilst Oliver Grant played the character “Knowledge.”

line: Two of them shits was doo One was nah, the other was Illmatic That’s a one hot album every ten year average And that’s so (Lame)
vault_lines: That's one every, let's say two,
meaning:
Two of Nas' albums were subpar (I Am and Nastradamus). For dramatic effect, Hov is underrating It Was Written which is a very good record that doesn’t quite match Illmatic (“that’s one hot album”).

This line can also read “Two of them shits was DUE,” as in “expected” or “doo” as in shitty.

The ‘lame’ ‘fame’ and ‘brain’ are a play on words sampled from the David Bowie song ‘Fame’.

line: That’s one every, let’s say two,
vault_lines: That's one every, let's say two,
meaning:
4 albums in 10 years works out to one every 2.5 years, but Jay rounds down to 2, which was still quite a distance between releases back then (and today even).

The source of Jay’s mockery is his own prolific output. During “Heart of the City” off this record, he states:

But the only thing running is numbers fam
Jigga held you down 6 summers; damn, where’s the love?

The Blueprint was his 6th album since 1996, all of them (eventually) going platinum. He would go on to release 2 more in the next two years, both platinum, totaling 8 in 8 years, an unrivaled run.

line: Four albums in ten years, nigga? I could divide
vault_lines: Four albums in ten years, nigga? I could divide
meaning:
Those would be Illmatic, It Was Written, I Am…, and Nastradamus

Despite Illmatic dropping in 1994, Nas’s rap debut was in 1991 on “Live At The Barbecue” by Main Source and he went on tour with Large Professor (a member of Main Source) before Illmatic dropped. “Takeover” was recorded in 2001 so that was about 10 years.

line: Use your (Brain) You said you’ve been in this ten, I’ve been in it five, smarten up, Nas
vault_lines: You said you've been in this ten, I've been in it five, smarten up, Nas
meaning:
Jay claims to be richer, more successful, and more critically acclaimed than Nas even though Nas has been rapping for twice as long.

To be fair to Nas, Jay is fudging the numbers a bit. He counts Nas’s entire career right from his debut on “Live at the Barbeque” but completely ignores his own output prior to Reasonable Doubt. That leaves out Jay’s work with The Jaz (which began way back in 1986) and early 90s features like “Can I Get Open” and “Show And Prove” which came out around the same time as Nas’s first solo material.

Count both artists' careers from their debut albums and there’s really only two years between them. Technically, if you go by their first features, Jay has a good 5 years on Nas.

line: And you ain’t get a coin, nigga, you was gettin’ fucked then I know who I paid, God, Serchlite Publishing
vault_lines: Nigga, you a (Lame)
meaning:
Another response to Nas’s line in his diss track “Stillmatic Freestyle”:

You show off, I count dough off when you sample my voice

He claims that Nas actually didn’t make any money off of him sampling Nas’s voice in his songs “Dead President$” and “Rap Game/Crack Game” because Nas had signed his publishing rights over to his A&R executive Michael “MC Serch” Berrin who is the head of Serchlite Publishing so that’s where the money that Jay-Z paid to use the Nas sample went to. MC Serch had spoke about this:

I never really paid that line much mind. It was a way of Jay getting underneath Nas' skin. The truth of the matter is we don’t own Nas' publishing, never have. We administer Nas' publishing, but Nas owns his own publishing. So when Jay said he paid Serchlite Publishing, it’s not necessarily true. It’s just a way of getting under Nas' skin.

He also spoke about this in a 2018 interview with Vladtv where he said that Nas actually owns Jay-Z’s publishing for the song Dead President$:

I was the national director of cross over promotion for Def Jam…I was working Jay-Z’s records with Dame Dash. They came to me and said “Hey we need to clear the sample for Dead Presidents…Can you give us, like, a fair deal?” I said “Well, the publishing’s the publishing” I said “but yeah, I mean your my man, like, you know, cut a check for two-thousand dollars, we’ll, we’ll clear the clear the sample, no problem. Done. He’s like "You’ll have a check in twenty minutes”, “Fine” called Zomba, I said “Hey, we’re still gonna take twenty-five percent of publishing on this record, Nas is gonna get twenty-five percent because, twenty-five percent of the record is Nas is, is shit but they’re gonna give us two-thousand dollars”…That’s it that’s the whole story. I took a small advance but I made sure Nas got twenty-five percent so Jay can say whatever he wants, Jay doesn’t own any Nas publishing but Nas owns Jay publishing. So he can say whatever he wants on the Ether record to kinda make Nas and get under Nas skin but Nas even knows the truth, because Nas after that, on three other records gave me, showed me love for, you know,  for helping his career.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jvTbFRp9GR4&t=42s

He once again spoke about this in a 2021 interview on Drink Champs:

The true story about that, that’s really crazy. So I’m the head of CHR at Def Jam, and, uh, they’re about to put out Reasonable Doubt. line: ”Oh, this my jam! This my shit! We don’t know a word to a verse, all we know is the chorus ’Cause the chorus repeats the same four words for us”
vault_lines: We don't know a word to a verse, all we know is the chorus
meaning:
This section further elaborates on the idea presented before it. That we as the listeners are to blame for this trend of simple, dumbed down music, and the market will keep producing it as long as we keep listening.

Eminem emphasizes this point clear as day in this section. He describes the relationship between a hit Pop song and the average music listener. In these three lines, we are able to see both cause and effect in the vicious cycle of music production and success.

These three lines can be viewed as somewhat of a circle. With no particular start and end point, and that is the point. We as a people listen to the chorus, not the verses, the Chorus now center stage repeats itself so we can remember it, and finally, we love the song. Each of these three lines could be placed in any order that is what makes this section so powerful. Eminem is describing a circle, a circle that will never stop unless it is broken.

While we can argue for days over the philosophy of a changing human race towards sound bites, constant stimulation and the overall effect these have on our psychology. I believe the message is simpler than that. I think that the message Eminem is trying to convey in this section and throughout this entire song is that we as the listener must overcome this circle ourselves.  While it may take time or even some work to find someone we enjoy listening too, if we give up and accept low effort cash-grab songs we will kill real music with no one else to blame but ourselves.

While I realize this song specifically deals with the effect of this low effort trend on Hip Hop. I believe that it pertains to the entire music industry. For more information and another interesting take on this very same idea, I would highly recommend the song Repeat Stuff, by comic/musician Bo Burnham. The talks about the effects of corporate built Pop/Love songs designed to appeal to young people, be catchy and be memorable. The song itself is a satirical interpretation of a corporate built love song and is both very funny and dark at the same time. I cannot recommend it enough even if you just want to laugh.
