Here we see Eminem further explore the themes of simplicity in music and ignorance in audience first defined in the section above this one. These two themes remain predominant both throughout the entire song and the changing artist interpretations.

Even though these two themes will be a predominant focus for the entire song, this section primarily fixates on the second theme, complacency, and ignorance of the audience. Eminem (as per his style) wastes no time in presenting his feelings on the matter, describing the average music consumer who is more interested in getting drunk, hearing simple beats from pop songs and picking up chicks than actually listening to the music.

This is not the first time that Eminem has voiced his anger at current music trends, but perhaps this song is his most direct stance on the subject. Hip Hop artists and fans often voice similar concerns, condemning music that follows this beat-heavy trend. Few, however, are able to fully summarize, label and demonstrate this trend as comic/musician Bo Burnham. In his “Make Happy” tour Bo Burnham labels this changing genre as “Beat Fetishism”, where words and songwriting are traded in for a “sick beat.” He then continues on to satirize the practice by rapping Little Teapot and Baa Baa Blacksheep over a “sick beat.” Video below.

Perhaps the most important thing to take away from this section is not an anger at the music industry or frustration at artists who use these techniques but to realize that the problem stems from us, the listener. This is elaborated further in the next section in the song directly below this one.

meaning:
During American Gangster Frank’s circle begins to expose him. Huey’s expensive suit is small change compared to the eventual wiring of one of Frank’s brother’s drivers, which eventually brings his entire empire down.

These occurrences signal a spiral in Frank’s demeanor. His success begins to become a burden. He is pictured in his mansion with his beautiful wife, refusing to give in, frustrated by the circumstances.

In an interview in 2007, with the now-defunct Blender magazine, Hov explained these gangster film-inspired lines, saying being rich isn’t exactly what he had come to expect:

In the context of the album, it was that Scarface moment when Tony Montana sits in the restaurant and looks around and says, ‘This is all it’s about?’ You get to that point where it’s like, ‘Okay, I drove the Rolls Phantom around the corner and… nothing happened.’ And you ask yourself, ‘That’s it? I thought blondes was gonna be jumping on my hood!’

Jay never expressed these emotions before on wax. Tracks like “Can I Live” were defiant statements of intent, and even “A Week Ago” refused to show remorse or resentment for his current predicament.

Ski said in the same interview,

“I never even noticed [it was edited on the album version.] Not at all. When I do songs, I don’t go back and listen to them. I just do them, and I keep doing them. That’s one weird thing about me. I heard people saying I’m the luckiest man on the planet. I like to think I stay ready. A wise man once told me luck is a sub-mystical energy that dances around the universe randomly bestowing people with satisfaction and joy. As he eloquently described in Decoded:

I was on the streets for more than half of my life from the time I was thirteen years old… I lost people I loved, was betrayed by people I trusted, felt the breeze of bullets flying by my head… I went dead broke and got hood rich on those streets. I hated it. I was addicted to it. It nearly killed me. But no matter what, it is the place where I learned not just who I was, but who we were, who all of us are. It was the site of my moral education.

JFK’s early life was nothing like Jay’s. His family was well off, and he was well educated.

Whilst JFK was assassinated, no such threat has been offered against Jay’s life since he left the streets.

JFK was, of course, the President of the United States. Jay Z, just a year after this record was released, was named president of Def Jam records.

It’s probable Jay knew of the deal well before the rest of us, and decided to slip a sneaky preview in to his hot new single…

The real reason for the mention of JFK’s name here is his famous lineage. Jay is planning to create a Dynasty, which he is head of, in the manner of the Kennedy’s. He would later go on to mention the family in “Pray” and “100$ Bill.”

line: ”I can’t believe the mouth of this prick He said, ‘put his mouth on his dick’” I know we gotta talk ’bout that, I know you salt ’bout that You on the tip like I don’t like you I got four kids, three baby mothers - I’m just like you
vault_lines: He said, 'put his mouth on his dick'"
meaning:
In a memorable and emotional verse on the prequel to this track Sigel had some very harsh words for his father.

He went as far as alluding to, but not quite specifically stating, the idea that his old man could suck his dick.

Obviously this is an incredibly disrespectful thing to say to anybody, let alone your own father, and Beans addresses the people who thought it was over the line, conceding the lyric was born out of anger, and perhaps doesn’t reflect his true feelings.

He admits that, whilst he still has serious issues with his Dad, he recognises the similarities between the two of them. He has had multiple children with different women, perhaps resulting in him not becoming quite the father he himself had hoped to become.

This could be taken a couple of ways, either he is sympathising with his Dad to some extent now that knows how difficult fatherhood can be, or he is blaming him failing to give him a blueprint for how a good father should act, dooming him to repeat the same mistakes.

Regardless, Sigel would continue to have family woes throughout his career, going as far as to end up in jail in 2005 due to a failure to keep up with his child support payments.

line: Soon we come together like man and man and build
vault_lines: Soon we come together like man and man and build
meaning:
Jay’s father left him and his family when he was only 11 years old, and it’s something that he has carried with him throughout life, being open about it in his music and in the media.

He states here that, despite his anger, he would like to reconcile with his Dad, man to man, and hopefully make some progress towards bettering their relationship.

“Build” is a term that’s rooted in the teachings of the Five Percent Nation, essentially meaning to create something positive and be productive.

Although Hov himself, as far as we’re aware, isn’t a member of the Nation it’s not uncommon for their teachings and lingo to spring up in Hip-Hop, as the religion has long been intertwined with rap culture.

Jay would ultimately get his wish and end up back on speaking terms with his old man, but not until the age of 33, after this record was released. Unfortunately, in a bittersweet ending to the tale his Dad died a few months after the two of them reconnected, although Jay has stated he was happy to have had the chance to reconcile with him and felt a weight lifted from him when he did.

line: Hope you didn’t think success would make me less mad
vault_lines: Hope you didn't think success would make me less mad
meaning:
All of Jay-Z’s successes and ever-increasing fame doesn’t distract him from the pain he holds inside him due to his disrupted upbringing; or make him any less upset at his father for leaving him. Hov explained this feeling to Oprah in 2009 when he took her back to his childhood home in the Marcy Projects:

Anger. At the whole situation. Because when you’re growing up, your dad is your superhero. line: Nigga this the payback, I know you bitch niggas from way back Niggas wanna clown, but the pound, it don’t play that Get yourself found drowned where the lake at
vault_lines: Nigga this the payback, I know you bitch niggas from way back
meaning:
More 2Pac references. The song “Unchained” was a re-working of the James Brown song “The Payback”, a song whose theme is occasionally borrowed in making this track.

Last chance, fancy pants
Oh very well gunshot.

The “pound” is gun, usually a Desert Eagle, which is referred to as the “4 Pound”.

line: Bring your rides out, bring your buggy eyes out Turn your six, I laid back in the Maybach
vault_lines: Bring your rides out, bring your buggy eyes out
meaning:
Jay name checks 3 of his favourite vehicles here.

“Buggy eyes” refers to a Porsche, either a 911 or a Boxster.

You can’t fight me, in the Porsche I’ll box you out.

Jay owns a 911, but he shouts out the Boxster more often.



The second car mention is the Mercedes Benz S600, the top model in the S-Class range.

600 drops, Hercedes Benz.

The final car is the most famous car in hip hop history: the Maybach.

This is one of Jay’s gold-standard subject matter cars. His music is littered with references to the car, and his video’s feature it prominently.

First one to cop, I’m the Maybach muse
First one in the coupe, I’m on my third six-deuce.

line: We bring them knives out or we let them burners spit I bring them pies out if niggas wanna burn the strip
vault_lines: We bring then knives out or we let them burners spit
meaning:
More food wordplay. Knives signify the weapons, lyrical in this instance, that are drawn in response to the threat issued by people hating. Burners are guns, but also part of a barbecue, hence the word “spit”, which is an apparatus used to cook meat. The burners “spit” because Jay unloads his weapon.



A “pie” is a kilo of cocaine, and “burning the strip” has a triple meaning. Firstly, it relates to riding out; a fast or expensive car would burn up the strip of road outside a popular club. It’s also an expression used when someone burns the strip of meat they are cooking. And because a burner is a gun, and the strip is where dealers sell cocaine, to “burn the strip” means to shoot up the block or corner that Jay is working on.

line: (Some people hate) Gyeah, uh, yeah (Some people hate) Uh, uh, uh (Some people hate) Yeah! You know what I think? (I think they’ve lost their minds) They say success breeds envy
vault_lines: (Some people hate) Uhh, nah, you know what I think?
meaning:
The content of the hook is almost contradictory to the overall feel of the song. The explanation is that some people are just haters. Jay would later utilise sarcasm to claim he really doesn’t care about people hating on him, but the fact he even created this song, and spent 3 verses attempting to justify his standing in the game and his skills on a technical level is testament to there being a kernel of truth in his lines.

It hurts when you say that I ain’t the one
You haters
How do I gain your favor
I need to know cause I care
I need you to love me, I swear, look here!

line: Please we ain’t afraid of none of ya’s; who want it with us? Ain’t nuttin changed since the ninety-six summer, c’mon
vault_lines: Since ninety-six, every year
meaning:
With the addition of M.O.P. to the Roc crew, beef holds no threat, as Jay is now surrounded by shooters on all sides.

Funnily enough, not many crews did want it with The Roc at the time. 50’s beef with Jay didn’t translate to his Shady Records stable, and it was really only Nas who was systematically targeting the entire crew.

He ends the verse with the obligatory shout out to his shuddering debut Reasonable Doubt which birthed Roc-A-Fella Records.

line: Til I’m deceased in a coffin I’ma be a beast on these beats releasing early and often
vault_lines: Til I'm deceased in a coffin
meaning:
Funnily enough, it was around this time that the term “camel” came to be used when describing or referencing Jay. He’s still using similar imagery.

One technique he utilised in his career was releasing a slew of records in quick succession (His first 7 albums were all released between 1996 and 2002), right at the beginning of the cold weather. He’s always been infatuated with winter, and how winter can be a commentary on both life and work.



He’s also a “shoot first” type of personality.

line: A payment for brushes with police officers A peace offering from the Gods for the streets I was tossed in
vault_lines: A payment for brushes with police officers
meaning:
One of the biggest themes of Jay Z interviews that focus on his beginnings in the street is survivor’s guilt. While he made it out of the maelstrom of death and destruction that gangbanging and drugs caused, 99% of his cohorts and associates didn’t.

Countering that, he recognises that his was a preordained circumstance, and that he was placed in that situation for a real reason. His rap sheet was nowhere near as long as some contemporaries, whether by skill or luck, yet he certainly had police brushes.

He also compares himself to an artist. In the same way his most favoured Basquiat was paid for painting (brushes), Jay is paid for his art works.

line: Got a chip on my shoulder the size of the Golden Nugget in Vegas And fuck being famous, I came to get the butters
vault_lines: Got a chip on my shoulder the size of the Golden Nugget in Vegas
meaning:
The Golden Nugget is a huge hotel in the middle of Las Vegas, and although it doesn’t actually have a large golden nugget in it’s vicinity, it’s size is adequate enough for Jay’s “chip” to be quite large.



He plays on the word “chip”, referencing the casino’s in Vegas and betting chips. To have a chip on one’s shoulder means they are confident, even cocky.

“Butters” has two meanings. Firstly, butter is money. Courting fame is seen as something quite uncool in hip hop music, and Jay’s main reason for rapping, and always has been, is to make money.

“Butter” also mean skills, or that something is very good, and silky smooth. Jay’s constantly evolving flow is a testament to the hard work and effort he has put in to his craft, chasing the technical acclaim more so than Grammy’s or other awards.

line: That old fashioned word It’s a word called love Called looooove Called looo-oooo-oooo-oooo-oooo-ove
vault_lines: That old fashioned word
meaning: The wonderfully spun sample, “Word Called Love” by Brian and Brenda Russell, serves as a jumping point for this song. Playing up to the “Gift & The Curse” theme of the record, we have two seemingly polar opposites: hate and love. Jay melds them in to a coherent statement, but explains that at the core of any action or activity is a desire to be liked or loved.

line: Something must be seriously wrong with the world I know y’all ain’t hating [Chorus] (Some people hate) Don’t tell me niggas is hating (Some people hate) Uhh, nah, you know what I think? (Some people hate) I think... (I think they’ve lost their minds) Think y’all lost your mind Y’all got me on my shit
vault_lines: Something must be seriously wrong with the world
meaning:
“Got me on my shit” means Jay’s feelings have been hurt, and as a result, he is bringing out his more lyrical side in an attempt to convert the haters.

During his early career, hate was not something he acknowledged or spoke about. A change was effected on the song “Renegade”:

Motherfuckers say that I’m foolish I only talk about jewels
Do you fools listen to music or do you just skim through it?

Whilst he also addressed it on “Money, Cash, Hoes”, his attitude was a little more dismissive:

Fuck all y'all haters, blow dick

As his career progressed, and his successes mounted, it was with a sick perversion that Jay viewed his hate. On The Blueprint 3 he even dedicated an entire song to it.

line: Please, your disdain for the brothers ain’t gon’ change the numbers It’s the strengthening of chain among us
vault_lines: Please, your disdain for the brothers ain't gon change the numbers
meaning:
Roc-A-Fella became quite an inflammatory record label during the early 2000s. Jay’s beef with Nas involved the entire crew. Freeway was beefing with Jadakiss, Jay had initiated beef with 50 Cent and Cam'Ron wasn’t keeping his nose clean either.

Roc-A-Fella was a dynasty under threat from outside sources, yet they were selling huge amounts of records. Beanie Sigel went gold twice with The Truth and The Reason, Memphis Bleek had done the same with The Understanding and Coming Of Age, and Cam'Ron actually went platinum with Come Home With Me.

They kept signing artists, and those artists kept selling records, despite criticism.

line: Or niggas just bored, wanna be in shit ’Fore they get to rappin’, start believing it, think they Ali and shit
vault_lines: Or niggas just bored wanna be in shit
meaning:
During the movie Streets Is Watching, Jay was being shot at, and he mused that his assailants were possibly just “bored”, and that their motive was no more malicious than a desire to inject some excitement in to their day. His competition has no material, which he made blatantly clear in the first verse. There’s no reason to go at Roc-A-Fella, until you get in the booth.

Once you’re in the booth, the studio gangsters toughen up, and start believing they’ve got the skills of Muhammad Ali, the greatest boxer to ever have lived.

line: I guess it’s just the penalty of leadership I guess I’m what niggas wanna be and shit
vault_lines: I guess it's just the penalty of leadership
meaning:
Referring to The Penalty of Leadership, a famous advertisement by the vehicle company Cadillac.



Jay is, of course, the head of his record label, and with great power comes great responsibility. Certainly, there’s a few throwing rocks at the throne.

line: You bastards know me, the one and only Big homie from the Roc, I think you pastors lonely You need Jesus in your life It’s either that or y’all gon’ make me Put the double Desert Eagles in your life, nigga
vault_lines: I know y'all ain't hating
meaning:
Jay’s relationship with the Lord is a complex one. He can wind a religious tale incredibly well if required, and he always thanks God in the credits on his CD packaging. Yet he calls himself “Jay Hova”, the God MC.

It can be difficult to sort through his intention, but during this period in his career, he was the God. His rap persona is The One and Only, and the pastors (a sly shot at Ma$e who was undergoing his religious conversion at the time) are losing their flock, as fans now worship at the altar of Jay Z.

It’s a slightly more audacious take on the bible. Join this congregation, or Jay will shoot at you with not one, but two Desert Eagles.

line: Shoot faster than Kobe, nigga
vault_lines: shoot faster than Kobe, nigga
meaning:
Kobe Bryant is known for his shoot-first mindset



Jay also used Kobe’s scoring prolificness for a pun on his 1998 Sauce Money collaboration, “Pre-Game”:

As a youth explosively, clappin' off the roof
Shootin' guard like Kobe

line: They try to take me out the game but I’s alive It’s like a old Negro spiritual, but I mastered Tobey With a splash of Monster Kody,
vault_lines: They try to take me out the game but I's alive
meaning:
“Toby” is a character from the Roots series.

His original name was Kunta Kentae but being that he was a slave, he was forced to have a Slave (White) name.  In the movie, they whipped him until he accepted the name change.

An “Old Negro Spiritual” is a song/chant slaves used to perform as a way of communication.

Jay-Z says “I’s Alive” to show solidarity with those enslaved spoke to each other.

During this period it must be remembered Jay was still facing racism in his day to day life, white people who believed he shouldn’t be as well off as them. “Mastered Toby” shows Jay mastered the slave masters. “Toby” is the white name that they attempt to give Kunta Kentae in Roots, and so by “mastering” Toby Jay has mastered his enemies.

Hop off the slave ship
Popped off my chain and took it to Jacob, I got it gold plated
Walked in that bitch like “Nigga we made it!”
I own my own masters
You know I ain’t missin' no royalty statements.

line: I’m back, stronger than ever, surprise, surprise
vault_lines: I'm back, stronger than ever, surprise, surprise
meaning:
Muhammad Ali went through some legal struggles during his career, yet he was famously victorious in them. When he came back to the sport for the Fight of the Century, and won, he completed one of the greatest comebacks in sporting history.

Jay’s legal problems pale in comparison, yet he certainly came back strongly, releasing The Blueprint to widespread critical acclaim in 2001.

He is also referring to his feud with Nas, and the damaging track “Ether”. Nas may have won that battle, but as he would later say:

I became stronger after Ether.

Ironically, on yet another diss track, this time aimed at Jim Jones. He was still taking heavy shots at Nas on this record, with the song “Blueprint 2” a shuddering diss.

line: I roll with the punches so I survive I bob and weave, move my feet from side to side
vault_lines: I roll with the punches so I survive
meaning:
Borrowing some lines from Public Enemy’s “Prophets of Rage”, Jay explains that he takes the criticism and the hate on board and keeps moving, reacting to it when it occurs rather than preempting it or premeditating his responses.

It’s also yet another punchline after his mention of Ali in the previous line. Jay “rolls with the punches”, meaning he raps using punchlines, and his are greater than those of his competition, which is why he always comes out victorious.

line: Au contraire, nigga, I am here ’cause I earned this shit By riding out when niggas had learners’ permit
vault_lines: Au contraire, nigga, I am here 'cause I earned this shit
meaning:
“Au Contraire” Is French For “On The Contrary”. It’s not quite “international HOV” but it’s close when coupled with the globetrotting exploits elsewhere on the record.

Another sly shot at Nas, whom Jay admonished in “Takeover” for not putting in the work in the streets before rapping about it.

When rappers were 15 or 16, on their learners permits, Jay was driving back and forth to Trenton with drugs in his car, living the life he was rapping about.

line: Being that I’m flesh of your flesh, blood of your blood Come from the same hood you come from We share basically the same stories
vault_lines: Being that I'm flesh of your flesh, blood of your blood
meaning:
Referencing DMX’s album Flesh of My Flesh, Blood of My Blood he notes that he feels he is the same as his fans/haters. He is fron the projects and therefore identifies with them and respects them, he expects the same in return.



In “Hail Mary” Pac also uttered the words:

Eat my flesh, flesh of my flesh.

line: Raw, rough and rugged, when addressing the mass public My attitude is fuck it ’cause motherfuckers love it
vault_lines: Raw, rough and rugged, when addressing the mass public
meaning: Continuing on with the 2Pac references, these lines are from “Ambitionz Az A Ridah”.

line: I came from the gutter, my success in this game Is sort of like Pro-jectic Justice
vault_lines: I came from the gutter, my success in this game
meaning:
Jay’s start in the game, and his early life, is legendary. A true rags to riches story. His “poetic justice”, a literary device used to bestow rewards upon people who deserve them and dole out punishment to those acting wrong, is played on, calling it “projectic justice”, combining his start in the projects with the popular literary term. He was born and raised in Marcy Projects.

Poetic Justice is also a film that starred 2Pac, so Jay continues that reference.

line: Thought niggas would appreciate what I came and did Since ninety-six, every year
vault_lines: Thought niggas would appreciate what I came and did
meaning: Jay-Z released an album every year since his 1996 debut Reasonable Doubt.  The year of this album was 2002, so Jay is saying you would think people would appreciate seven albums in seven years.

line: That can’t leave and how the chinks gotta feed ’em For the rest of they life Fucking wings, fried vegetable rice
vault_lines: That can't leave and how the chinks gotta feed 'em
meaning:
Beanie is referring to Asians who run the  carryouts (popular name for in and out Chinese restaurants) in inner-city neighborhoods. 3 piece chicken wings with fried rice was and still is to this day a staple in poverty stricken areas. It was fast and cheap. Less than $5 dollars back in 90s-00s and could be ready in less than 7 minutes.

A half ice tea half lemonade was usually added for a $1.

I used to personally order it with fries instead of rice. In DC we have mumbo sauce. IYKYK.

line: [Outro]
vault_lines: Please believe that, some how, some way
meaning: Note this is the same whistling melody from the original collaboration between these 3 artists.

line: The Lord be a-willing and the creek don’t rise I’ma be a nigga and these streets gon’ rise (Some how, some way, some how, some way) I’ma be a nigga and these streets gon’ rise (Some how, some way)
vault_lines: Some how, some way
meaning:
“Lord willing and the creek don’t rise” is a popular English saying. It’s been around for centuries, and is essentially a subtle variation on “come hell or high water”. Whatever will be, will be, and all that is left after the hard work is hope.

Scarface remains adamant he is on the path out of the ghetto, yet for it to lead to success he will need divine intervention. “I’m a be a nigga and these streets gonna rise” is a powerful message. He embraces his lifestyle, and, rather than climbing out alone, he wants to raise the entire hood up with him, pull them over the precipice and in to prosperity.

line: Serving these niggas flippers, quarter-ounces and jippers Agents snapping your picture, neighbors plotting to get ya
vault_lines: Serving these niggas flippers, quarter-ounces and jippers
meaning:
A flipper is ecstasy, or as it is commonly known today, molly.

I started small time, dope game, pushin on the corner
Twenty cent cook-up, fifty flippers if you want ‘em.

A quarter ounce is usually a term associated with marijuana, but as it is a unit of measurement, it can describe cocaine as well. Zip can be both crystal meth, or a way of saying “an ounce” of any illegal drug.

When I was talking Instagram
Last thing you wanted was your picture snapped.

This is the flip side of the drug trade: the anxiety. Federal agents are on your case, and your neighbours are after you, whether because they are your competition on the strip, or they’re just plain fed up with all the crime associated with their street.

line: Fuck sitting in the living room, guarding the steps Working inside a smoke house, starving to death
vault_lines: Fuck sitting in the living room, guarding the steps
meaning:
Slum housing is a derogatory term for very low income, low cost, mass-produced living area’s that can become a breeding ground for crime and violence. Similar in a sense the Projects in Marcy that Jay himself came from. This is the reality of the ghetto for some: working in the kitchen, cooking crack.

These mothafuckas fucking talking that comeback shit like they cooking crack. Shit, I ain’t fronting, all I want my pockets green like slum change, you know what I’m saying?

Everyone want’s to get out of the hood, to lace their pockets, to go legal and straight.

line: Another chapter based on how I get that game Just hanging round my neighborhood, bang my street Sit and watch the passerbys play my sweep
vault_lines: Another chapter based on how I get that game
meaning:
“Game” refers to both his floss/stunt game, as well as the drugs he sells. Both of these are connected, as the way he gets “game” is by selling work.

He’s from Houston, and tracks like “Crack” show just how deep you can fall when drugs are entered in to the equation.

When he bangs his street, he is both gangbanging and running it solo, selling drugs to addicts and base heads. Sitting on the stoop and shrewdly judging those who walk past; is that the police, or a potential customer?

line: Right here’s another lil’ story ’bout this clique I claimed
vault_lines: Right here's another lil' story 'bout this clique I claimed
meaning:
Scarface is well known as being an incredibly vivid ghetto story teller. His verse on the original “This Can’t Be Life” is steeped in praise and folklore.

As both Jay and Face tell it, they were kicking around in Baseline, shooting pool, about to do their verses, when Face recieved the fateful phone call. Jay offered the chance for him to go home and re-write his verse. Instead, Scarface went away for a few minutes, wrote a new verse, came back in the booth, and spit it in one take.

He’s one of the best.

line: We gotta grip of shorties on the block All they do is smoke weed and drink 40s, cop they lil quarties Enough to get the latest Roc, newest Glock, old Jordies
vault_lines: We gotta grip of shorties on the block
meaning:
A “grip of shorties” refers to a group of younger kids who have now made the transition from child to street personality. This could be due to the seductive characteristics of the drug dealing game, or simply, as Beanie has made perfectly clear, out of necessity.

“Quarties” refers to 7 grams of Marijuana, meaning these kids are incredibly low level drug dealers. The motivation at first might be to hit the block and make some money for their family. Once that cash starts coming in though, they spend it on themselves, purchasing Rocawear (shameless cross-promotion, although Beans never got a cheque for his part in the franchise), a new weapon, or a retro pair of Air Jordans.

The cycle then repeats itself, and the truth of the matter is until you’re making serious bank, there’s no simple way out of the hood.

line: In they beds all bunched in tight, no less than three or four You know how it go, two by the foot, two by the headboard Man I’m getting scared for them (Yeah I know) That’s how I feel for them
vault_lines: In they beds all bunched in tight, no less than three or four
meaning:
Kanye would mirror this sentiment on “Family Business”, but it was the legendary Ghostface Killah way back in 1996 who first uttered lines similar to this:

Roaches everywhere, cousins and aunts was there
Four in the bed, two at the foot, two at the head
I didn’t like to sleep with Jon-Jon he peed the bed
Seven o'clock, pluckin' roaches out the cereal box
Some shared the same spoon, watchin' Saturday cartoons.

Space is so limited, and family’s keep multiplying.

line: No breakfast, Cap’n Crunch at night How the kids eating lunch at night?
vault_lines: Gotta be kidding, no breakfast, Cap'n Crunch at night
meaning:
Such a potent image, of kids waking up excited to start a new day, running around outside playing, with no food in their stomach’s, either because they are poor, or their mom smoked or drank her paycheck away.

The father isn’t around, so it’s a single mother trying to get by.

Nigga you was an abusive pops
Fuck you left me out to dry, stuck.

line: All the petty ass wars fuck the night scene up ‘Member Lil’ Eddie draw, man, how he light Mean up? Then they wonder why we light green up
vault_lines: All the petty ass wars fuck the night scene up
meaning:
2Pac said it in 1996:

And still I see no changes, can’t a brother get a little peace
It’s war on the streets and a war in the Middle East.

It still rings true. Black on black crime is so wasteful when viewed objectively from an outsiders perspective, and Beans shows maturity to be able to take himself out of that situation and view it from a different angle.

Even the man who seems to be on top of every situation, Jay Z, occasionally smokes to calm his nerves.

okay I’m getting weeded now
I know I contradicted myself, look, I don’t need that now
It’s just once in a blue when there’s nothing to do
And the tension gets too thick for my sober mind to cut through.

Sigel was still on this train of thought in 2009 when he was arrested for marijuana possession.

line: Moms smoke, kids can’t chase the ice cream truck Girls fighting over rope, the young boys hype things up Niggas fighting over coke, the young boys light things up
vault_lines: Moms smoke, kids can't chase the ice cream truck
meaning:
The sad state of affairs were such that mothers were so stressed from being stuck in the hood, they smoked crack to ease the pain. Beans presents 3 separate narratives in the space of 5 bars; introducing the dealers servicing the addicts, and the children who are also suffering.

All you did was motivate me; “Don’t let ‘em hold you back”
What I do? I turned around and I sold you crack.

Stunting in the hood now becomes paramount, as young boys lie about their wealth (Rollies are imagined). At the higher level, the dealers are stuck out in the snow, hustling to survive, and those same young boys are shooting, lighting up weapons, to gain an advantage.

line: Twenty niggas on the block tryna chase that buck Nosey neighbors and haters keep they face on stuck Cops roll up on the pavement, break the dice games up
vault_lines: Twenty niggas on the block tryna chase that buck
meaning:
Sigel Street is notorious for it’s drug trade, but this could be equally true for hundreds of blocks throughout the country.

As Ja Rule explained in his book Unruly, selling drugs was a competitive sport. There’d be multiple dealers on each block trying to coerce the junkies in to take their product over that of their competition.

“Chase that buck” is what these dealers did, day in day out. But it wasn’t always a violent pursuit. This is a career for some, and they played dice games together, enduring neighbours who’d rather call the cops than connect with “dangerous” youth’s.

line: To Lil’ Nell, Sigel Street, I ain’t forget you
vault_lines: To Lil' Nell, Sigel Street, I ain't forget you
meaning:
Beans was born and raised on Sigel Street in Philadelphia, known as one of the top drug corners in the city.

It inspired his name, and in 2009 he was arrested there for aggravated assault.

line: And, still I grew Some how I knew that the sun’ll shine through and Touch my soul, take hold of my hand Look man, a tree grows in Brooklyn
vault_lines: I, seen the worst of the worst
meaning:
Jay was born in to the struggle, and it never as clear, honest, and raw as in Marcy Projects. The seed he planted on infertile land grows, inexplicably, in to a tree.

It’s a reference to the 1943 novel of the same name, a typical rags to riches story which was more potent due to the fact the main character was a woman.

Jay’s aspirations have always come with a tinge of confidence,

Put me anywhere on God’s green earth, I’ll triple my worth.

line: Some day the cops’ll kill a muh’fucker
vault_lines: Some day the cops'll kill a muh'fucker
meaning: Still a potent message, and one he continues to preaching. Even back in 2002, Police were known to use excessive force against Black people, more so than they did against White people.

line: Please believe that, some how, some way We gotta make it up out the hood some day Some how, some way We gotta make it up out this life, c’mon Some how, some way We gotta make it up out the hood some day Some way We gotta make it up out this life
vault_lines: Please believe that, some how, some way
meaning:
The original song, “This Can’t Be Life,” dealt with the pain and suffering that people stuck in the hood, stuck in a life of crime, or just genuinely stuck in a bad situation, experience on a daily basis.

To all my street niggas, project niggas
Real niggas, worldwide
Let’s reflect, everybody got a story
We all ghetto B. Here’s mine.

It’s such a potent message. While a lot of Jay’s music glamourises the street, the hustle, and the spoils, he’s always tinged his music with the knowledge that, eventually, he would have to withdraw.

From Decoded:

… Acute paranoia and disappointment I’m feeling from the street life, friends getting shot, your family being broke, I have to deal with the everyday struggles that stalk everyone. And when that hits you, sometimes it becomes clear that you have to get out, that this really can’t be life, it has to be more.

line: Southside, Sunnyside is the blocks I run South Acres, South Park, niggas all got guns Over here we got this code Charlie, get that there We know tomorrow ain’t a promise so we get that now
vault_lines: Southside, Sunnyside is the blocks I run
meaning:
Scarface is from South Acres and also shouts out South Park in other songs, such as “Money and the Power”

Deep in the heart of South Park lurks a stalker
S.A. fool, native Houston South Parker
Born and brought up to be a heartless motherfucker

Sunnyside is a predominantly African-American community in Houston. It is known as one of the most dangerous areas in the state, so it’s not a stretch that everyone around him is carrying a weapon. That escalates the danger, and breeds a culture of living in the moment. It also breeds a desperation that see’s residents much more careless about death and the consequences of illegal actions.

line: Wish I could take us all On this magic carpet ride through the sky
vault_lines: Wish I could take us all
meaning:
Jay wishes all the people he used to hustle with could experience the unusual success he’s experiencing now and uses a magic carpet as a metaphor.



He’s often expressed similar sentiments, for example:

In the name of those who ain’t make it my progress is your success, please live through me

Survivor’s guilt is a common theme in his music.

line: Back to back steam up, try to relax but I can’t, I lean up Ain’t the L or the reefer that steam up (That steam up) It’s my head and I’m stressed to the point I get a fever
vault_lines: Back to back steam up, try to relax but I can't, I lean up
meaning:
Chain smoking marijuana is not improving the situation, even mixing it with Lean is not taking the edge off the pain.

Imagine being stuck in such a situation that the best pharmaceuticals you have at your disposal cannot induce a safe mindset?

In these lines Sigel introduces his connection with the addicts he is serving. He understands their pain and their desire to remove the stress from their lives. The only difference is they are willing to seek a stronger substance than marijuana or cough syrup.

Y'all dont even know every day I’m living with stress.

This sense of hopelessness is a common thread in Sigel’s work. The stunning “I Can’t Go On This Way” was in a similar vein to his message on this song.

line: I, used to play the hall and fifth floor Me and my boys, we all poor, getting high I, seen the worst of the worst I deserve every blessing I receive, I’m from the dirt I, planted my seed on unfertile land Myrtle Park, Marcy, Flushing and Nostrand
vault_lines: I, used to play the hall and fifth floor

line: Wednesdays, I’m up in Shine; Cheetah’s, Monday night I’m fucking with the model chicks Friday night at Life

meaning:
Shine, Cheetah, and Life were three popular nightclubs in the late ’90s. Mark Ronson was a DJ at all three. When asked about Ronson’s DJing in 2000, Jay told New York Magazine, “Nigga is nice.”

Shine—later known as The Canal Room—was known for its live musical performances. Jay hosted a showcase for his new artists there in 2005. The club was located in Chinatown at 285 West Broadway.

The Cheetah Club was located in the Flatiron District at 12 W. 21st Street. A 1999 New York Times article described the club’s Monday night party:

Most of the violations took place at hip-hop parties the club gave on Monday and Wednesday nights, the police said, when the sidewalks sometimes filled up with hundreds of young people…In August, one patron pulled a handgun and critically wounded another, Captain Levine said…In September, a fight outside led to two fatal shootings near Gramercy Park.

Life was located in the West Village at 158 Bleecker Street. Promoter Steve Lewis remembers seeing Jay at his club:

For a long time Life was the last great club. Life’s Hip Hop Room was super hot with DJ Mark Ronson coming into his own. I saw Puffy and Jay-Z get up to give a newly arriving Stevie Wonder their table. It was Titanic-era Leo and there were live shows from Siouxsie and Isaac Hayes and Grace Jones. Pretty crowd, always mixed, always fun.

line: Niggas see me in the streets with no bodyguards Just two big guns that’ll body your squad
vault_lines: Niggas see me in the streets with no bodyguards
meaning:
Jay protects himself from stick-up kids by carrying guns that will kill (“body”) a whole crew.

Ten months after releasing this song, Jay had changed his tune on the subject of bodyguards. On 2000’s “Streets Is Talking,” he spits:

You see me with a bodyguard
That means police is watching
And I only use his waist to keep my Glock in
But when shit goes down
You know who’s doing the popping

What made Jay start rolling with bodyguards? It’s likely that his 1999 arrest for the stabbing of Lance “Un” Rivera raised Jay’s profile in the law enforcement community to the point where he became a target of the so-called “hip-hop police.” Carrying his own guns suddenly became too risky, so hiring armed bodyguards became a smarter way to protect himself while avoiding arrest.

In 2001, Jay was arrested for gun possession alongside his bodyguard Hamzah Hewitt. Jay was cleared of this charge, but his bodyguard pled guilty and was sentenced to one year in prison.

vault_lines: I got 'em Iceberg shit they thought I knew Snoopy
meaning:
Hov is referencing two brands of clothing he frequently wore and would buy for the women he was having relations with: first Iceberg, and then later his own Rocawear brand.

Iceberg clothing is an Italian knitwear company that had branched into sportswear in the ‘90s. The company would cover their pieces in cartoon characters—with Snoopy of Peanuts fame being the one most utilized.



Hov wore a lot of their pieces, and he, Dame Dash, and Kareem “Biggs” Burke believed that they were largely responsible for Iceberg’s record sales. In 1998 they set up a meeting with the brand’s board to explore a partnership—but as Dash later revealed:

The vibe with the company was that they weren’t sure if they wanted to touch hip-hop. Or have us represent [them]. I said ‘Yo, I feel we’ve tripled your sales. Help us to do our own clothing company, or at least pay us to represent it.’ I walked out there like ‘[We’re] definitely doing Rocawear.’

Rocawear was officially launched in 1999, starting in the label’s first offices on John Street with three employees stitching the logo onto shirts. As part of their cross-branding, the Roc family’s outfits soon became 98% Rocawear, and the stock began flying out the door. The company grossed $80 million in sales in just eighteen months.

“Living in the shadow feels like the safe place to be” suggests that hiding one’s true identity or living in the shadows can provide a sense of safety or protection. It may refer to the struggle of keeping one’s true self hidden due to societal expectations or fear of judgment.

“No harm for them, no harm for me” implies that by conforming to societal norms or expectations, one may avoid harm or criticism from others. It reflects the notion of blending in or playing it safe to avoid potential negative consequences.

“But life is short, and it’s time to be free” signifies a realization that life is finite and time should not be wasted in suppressing one’s true identity or desires. It suggests a call to break free from societal constraints and live authentically.

“Love who you love because life isn’t guaranteed” emphasizes the importance of embracing love and relationships without restrictions or fear. It conveys the idea that life is unpredictable and uncertain, and one should cherish and express love for whomever they choose, regardless of societal norms or expectations.

Overall, these lyrics encapsulate the theme of self-acceptance, the courage to be true to oneself, and the pursuit of love and freedom in the face of societal pressures. The inclusion of JAY-Z’s mother’s spoken outro about her own homosexuality adds a personal touch and reinforces the message of embracing one’s true identity.

The lyrics “Living in the shadow, can you imagine what kind of life it is to live?” express the experience of living a double life or hiding one’s true self from others. The lines “In the shadows, people see you as happy and free, because that’s what you want them to see” suggest that the person intentionally projects an image of contentment and liberation, perhaps to avoid judgment or maintain certain expectations from others. They create an illusion of happiness and freedom, concealing their internal struggles and the constraints they feel.

The lyrics further highlight the internal conflict faced by the individual: “Living two lives, happy, but not free.” This line implies that although they may appear happy in the public eye, they are not truly free to express their authentic self or live their life as they desire. It reflects the burden of hiding a significant aspect of their identity or personal truth, which restricts their sense of genuine happiness and freedom.

Overall, these lyrics convey the challenges and complexities of living in secrecy or inauthenticity, showcasing the toll it takes on a person’s emotional well-being and their longing for genuine acceptance and liberation.

line: This was meant to be a haiku, huh
vault_lines: This was meant to be a haiku, huh
meaning:
Haiku is a traditional form of Japanese poetry. Haiku poems consist of 3 lines. The first and last lines of a Haiku have 5 syllables and the middle line has 7 syllables. The lines rarely rhyme.

Jay is saying that he was going to keep this short and punchy, likely limiting the message to three bars and doing a clever rhyme switch, but instead he went on for whole seven bars (including this one), all because he has so much to say from experience. Indeed, as he raps on “Marcy Me,” it’s incredible that he managed to make it out of the hood. As a drug dealer his life was expected to be short, but ended up being an long story. Similarly, Reasonable Doubt was originally intended to be his first and only album. Instead he ditched his original style, dumbed down for the masses and extended his career.

Also, notice the pattern of the three bars which conclude with this one:

Dump ‘em all in the bayou, uh
Everybody wave bye to the guy you thought you could lie to
This was meant to be a haiku, huh

The first and the last bar of the three are short bars which only take up three of the four beats, leaving some air for ‘huh’ and are accented into three segments each — two parts for the bar and one for ‘uh’. The second bar is a long complex bar which Jay flows with five definite accents:

Everybody | wave bye  | to the guy | you thought | you could lie to

Thus Jay expertly imitates the structure of Haiku, landing three consecutive bars in the 3 – 5 – 3 pattern.

line: But my story’s too wide to fit inside a line or two
vault_lines: But my story's too wide to fit inside a line or two
meaning:
Here Jay gives a nod to the 1986 track “Eric B. Is President” by Eric B. & Rakim where Rakim showed off with a novelty flow, overflowing a line into the next bar:
“The party is live, the rhyme can’t be kept in-
Side, it needs erupting just like a volcano”

By 1986 Jay had already been immersed in the street life for a few years, so even back then his story was wider than your average. With the success and achievements he’s had since, you can barely embrace what he’s been through.

In the previous bar Jay says that he meant to rhyme the above as a Haiku, keeping it three short lines, but he has so much to tell that he can’t even fit in into the bars.

Oddly enough, Jay doesn’t overflow here, and ‘line’ lands almost exactly of the fourth beat of the bar, although he manages to quickly squeeze in ‘or two’, before landing the next bar.

Further still, this is a reference to Jay’s drug dealing past and a warning to not try to reduce his character and success to his past illegal activities. His story is much more than just drugs (a line or two).

All in all, this could be a triple entendre: giving an overflowing nod to Rakim and Nas, telling of not being able to fit his story into just two bars of the verse, and letting everyone know that he’s much more than his drug-dealing past.

line: Oh y’all thought I was washed? I’m at the cleaners Launderin’ dirty money like the Teamsters, huh
vault_lines: Oh y'all thought I was washed? I'm at the cleaners
meaning:
The Teamsters was a labor union for truck drivers and warehouse workers. The union rose to its greatest prominence under the leadership of Jimmy Hoffa from the 1930s to 1950s.

With most trucking and manufacturing company’s strong ties to the mob, the Teamsters felt the need to make “certain accommodations” for the ruling crime organizations in order to unify all the laborers under a single branch. Such acts included the aforementioned money laundering and racketeering.

With the newly elected President John F. Kennedy’s appointment of his younger brother, Robert, as the Attorney General, Hoffa and the Teamsters were put under the legal system’s bright lights. After only a few years of a heavy pursuit, AG Kennedy and his “Get Hoffa” squads were able to convict Hoffa for attempted bribery and fraud in 1963. Hoffa’s sentence was commuted by President Nixon in Dec 1971, just five years into his thirteen year sentence.

Jimmy Hoffa was last seen at 2:45pm on July 30, 1975, at a restaurant in the Bloomfield Terrace of Detroit. He was reported missing by his wife after Hoffa did not return “back home.”

The suspected killers were thought to be tied to the Italian Mafia as well as the fledgling Teamsters union. Hoffa’s body was never found, leading to one of the world’s most notable conspiracy theory topics.

Hov is not “washed” as some have suspected as he’s aged of the years.  He’s in the studio (cleaners) making himself more relevant and important than he’s been since Watch the Throne dropped 6 years prior.

The line also refers to Jay laundering dirty money from his extracurricular activities. He’s using the money to further the footprint himself and other black Americans have in the legitimate business world. As referred to in “Family Feud”:

Interestingly, Jay actually attended therapy prior to the release of 4:44. In a 2017 interview with Dean Baquet of The New York Times, he spoke on the insights therapy provided him:

I grew so much from the experience. But I think the most important thing I got is everything is connected. Every emotion is connected and it comes from somewhere.

JAY-Z only wants happiness for his mother, and is therefore encouraging her to disregard any vitriol or hate thrown her way based on her sexuality.

Biggs first put me on to Cristal in the early days of Roc-A-Fella. We were drinking it in the video for “In My Lifetime” in 1994. We didn’t have a record deal yet, but back then we’d show up at clubs in Lexuses and buy bottles of Cristal, while most people in the clubs were buying Moët. It was symbolic of our whole game — it was the next shit. It told people that we were elevating our game, not by throwing on a bigger chain, but by showing more refined, and even slightly obscure, taste. We weren’t going to stick to whatever everyone else was drinking or what everyone expected us to drink. We were going to impose our sense of what was hot on the world around us. When people all over started drinking Cristal at clubs — when Cristal became a household name among young consumers — it wasn’t because of anything Cristal had done. It was because of what we’d done. If Cristal had understood this dynamic, they never would’ve been so dismissive. The truth is, we didn’t need them to tolerate us with “curiosity and serenity.” In fact, we didn’t need them at all.

It turns out Jay really didn’t need them. In 2014, he purchased the Armand de Brignac (also known as “Ace of Spades”) champagne brand, following racist remarks from Cristal manager Frederic Rouzaud. Now, Hov is frequently drinking and talking about the brand—almost at the frequency which rising artists mention drinking codeine.



Chris Paul, nicknamed CP3, has worn the number 3 throughout his entire NBA career—hence the “tray/trey” homophone. He also hails from the “Tre-4”, another name for Winston-Salem, NC. Paul was also featured in Jay’s “Footnotes for 4:44” video.

It is no coincidence that these explicit reveals coincided with the birth of Blue Ivy—a child certainly gives purpose.

Jay and Bey want to impart certain values onto their twins so, along with Blue, they can continue the truth-seeking work of their parents. Hov discloses his hope that they have a boy and girl to carry on their legacy, as it is a longtime dream of his to re-write his father’s wrongs with a son.

If taken as subliminal jabs at Drake, these lines are Hov’s continued explanation of why the Canadian rapper simply isn’t at his level. He sets his points as rhetorical questions, acting confused as to why Drake continues to come for his throne when his position doesn’t match his braggadocios attitude.

Jay Z owns his master recordings and a thriving entertainment company, Roc Nation,, while Drake is signed to at least three different companies, which his masters are locked into. As Hov previously explained, that is a lot of people with their hands in his bag.

Hov also owns his own streaming service, TIDAL, while Drake is locked into a deal with rival service Apple Music. Jay offered ownership of TIDAL to Drake, but at the very last minute he switched sides. He suggests Drake is nothing but a “runner” for Apple and his labels, while Hov is the “boss” of his musical destiny.

Hov also references his own drug-dealing past with the imagery of him as a firm-handed boss, controlling his drug-runners on the street.

And we always knew we were gonna do something together besides making records together; we just had to find out what it was. 2016 was a banner year for Khaled. He achieved worldwide fame through his Snapchat account, landed numerous endorsement deals, and displayed a continued penchant for bringing high-tier artists together to create #1 bangers. line: I’ve been playin’ cards with the house money
vault_lines: I've been playin' cards with the house money
meaning:
“Playing with house money” is a gambling expression referring to the act of betting with money that you’ve already won from a casino. There is a lowered risk when betting with house money, and it’s possible to earn huge rewards.

Jay Z has been playing with house money for much of his career. When Roc-A-Fella Records sold 49% of their company to Def Jam Recordings in 1997, it opened Jay and his artists up to major label budgets. For example, he spent $1 million of Def Jam’s money on his “Big Pimpin'” video. The success of the video and track ensured Vol 3… Life and Times of S. Carter went 3x Multi-Platinum, earning him a big return.

When he left Def Jam in 2008, he signed one of the biggest music contracts ever with Live Nation, earning him $150 million upfront. The touring giant financed the formation of his entertainment company Roc Nation, giving him $5 million a year for overheads, $25 million to invest in Roc Naion ventures, and $10 million per album he records. In 2013, he signed a publishing deal with Universal Music Group, ensuring that the costs of distributing music produced by his Roc artists would fall on Universal.

Hov also sold a 33% stake in his TIDAL streaming service to Sprint for $200 million. As part of their deal, Sprint agreed to finance a $75 million marketing and development fund for TIDAL artists and projects.

line: And a fella can’t make me fancy (make me fancy)
vault_lines: And a fella can't make me fancy (make me fancy)
meaning:
Throughout her career Beyoncé has always encouraged female empowerment. This has been true since her early days in Destiny’s Child, with songs like 2000’s “Independent Woman, Pt. 1” becoming an anthem for young women. On her 2016 album LEMONADE, she took a stand against male infidelity and worked to empower Black women.

The “fella” here is her husband Jay Z. On Bey’s 2013 track “Flawless,” she expressed how her marriage does not define her, but is a partnership that provides mutual support. Bey is a firm believer in self-admiration before looking to others for love.

line: Shinin’, shinin’, shinin’, shinin’, yeah (shinin’, yeah) All of this winnin’, I’ve been losin’ my mind, yeah (losin’ my mind)
vault_lines: Petty, petty, petty, I've been winnin' steady
meaning:
Individually, and as a couple, Beyoncé and Jay Z have been extremely successful throughout their 20 year careers.

Jay Z kicked off his 2017 by selling 33% of his TIDAL streaming service to Sprint for $200 million, making its current value 11-times his original purchase price; his Roc Nation Sports management company was named as the exclusive agency of record for MLS soccer’s Houston Dynamo; and his plans for a new venture capital fund with Roc Nation partner Jay Brown were released.

On February 22, Jay Z was inducted into the prestigious Songwriters Hall of Fame, becoming the first rapper ever to earn this acclaim. He is currently working on his 13th solo studio album.

Beyoncé ran 2016 by surprise-releasing the empowering single “FORMATION” and performing at the Super Bowl 50 halftime show in February. This was followed with the critically-acclaimed visual album LEMONADE in April. Her accompanying “Formation World Tour,” which featured Khaled as her opening act, sold over 2.42 million tickets and grossed $256 million from 49 sold out shows.  The tour stands as one of the top 20 highest grossing tours of all time.

“Shining” was released directly following the 59th Grammy Awards, where Bey took home “Best Music Video” for “Formation” and “Best Urban Contemporary Album” for LEMONADE. Hov’s two-bar effort on Drake’s original version of “Pop Style” was nominated for “Best Rap Performance,” but lost to “No Problem.”

meaning:
After pleading guilty to a September 1997 drug distribution charge, Emory “Clash” Jones was sentenced in January 2000 to nearly 16 years in prison. Along with Jay and his childhood friend and business partner DeHaven Irby, Jones had run a large [illegal] business headquartered on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. In 2010’s Decoded Hov spoke openly of “doing work” in Maryland, but revealed that period “ended badly—shootouts in clubs, major police investigations, whole crews arrested. I got out of there just in time. Some of my best friends weren’t so lucky. It was tragic.”

After he recorded the “Do U Wanna Ride” dedication to his friend in 2006, Hov would write a letter to Baltimore’s Judge Benson Legg detailing the $50,000 position at the Roc Apparel Group being held for Emory upon his release. Jay’s letter was included as part of a sentence reduction motion filed in August 2009. Emory’s motion was accepted and he was released in April 2010—37 months earlier than expected.

In the early-90’s Jay-Z and DeHaven Irby expanded their drug business, which had initially started in Brooklyn then moved to Trenton, New Jersey, down to Maryland. There they met Emory “Vegas” Jones, whose house in Cambridge would become the cooking spot for them when travelling along the I-95.



Jones was later convicted of cocaine trafficking and was sentenced to 16 years in jail. In 2009 Jay wrote to the judge handling Emory’s release asking for leniency on his sentence, explaining he had a legit job at Rocawear waiting for him.

The line also connects with the previous one about a meth lab, tying up a pop cultural reference to the famed television show Breaking Bad, in which former teacher Walter White and his ex-student Jesse Pinkman turn an old RV caravan into a meth lab.

Just as the forty acres and a mule were supposed to help the black man get his place in society, Jay suggests the modern black man is entitled to use violence (represented by the Glock, a gun) as a tool to achieve social justice. By referencing “forty acres and a mule” he also reminds the listener that the supposed good intentions of the government rarely pan out, in his experience and also throughout history. Nas in Hennessy’s 2021 “Dear Destiny” campaign.

They gave him a little look. We got to do that more. Like the drug dealer awards. But like they do in the Grammy’s, all the technical awards. Like all that shit. That’s hot!

line: Rich niggas, black Bar Mitzvahs Mazel tov – it’s a celebration, bitches! “L’chaim!”
vault_lines: Rich niggas, black Bar Mitzvahs
meaning:
Hov drops a few references to Jewish culture here, using them as a symbol of success. He is, in some way, re-enforcing the stereotype often placed on Jewish people that they are all overtly-wealthy. But in 2003 he was honored by the Foundation for Ethnic Understanding for his work improving Black-Jewish relations, so we can assume he is positive in his intent.

He begins by painting the picture of a “Bar Mitzvah,” which is a coming-of-age ceremony for a young boy. It is custom to give money to the celebrant; this is done in multiples of $18 which is symbolic of giving “chai” or life. So much money is brought to the “Roc Boys” party that Hov feels like it is his Bar Mitzvah.

“Mazel tov” is a Jewish phrase meaning “good luck” or “congratulations;” while “l'chaim” is a Jewish toast literally meaning “to life.” They are both phrases you would say at a Bar Mitzvah when wishing for continued success for the party in question.

“It’s a celebration, bitches!” is a line Dave Chappelle delivered during one of his infamous impersonations of musician Rick James:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9tN1Leiu7tQ

line: Sweet! Let that ride out! Bring the horns back in, yeah This is black superhero music right here, baby American Gangster Taking flight, coming to a town near you Soon as I touch down, I just want y’all to start playing the horns like... Hovi’s home! Lukey, baby! Hahahahaha... oww!
vault_lines: Let your hair down, baby, I just hit a score
meaning: “Lukey” is simply Frank Lucas, the character Jay is emulating on this record. Jay’s obsession with the black superhero peaked on 2006’s “Kingdom Come”, where he compares himself to a number of famous comic book characters.

line: Number one D-boy, shame he could rhyme
vault_lines: Number one D-boy, shame he could rhyme
meaning:
A D-Boy is a dope dealer. Jay was, by his account, one of the best, but rap kept tugging him back in to the legitimate world.

Jay calls himself a reluctant rapper. He was making great money in the streets, and saw his partner Jaz-O get hurt by record labels. During Decoded, Jay explained that the experience with Jaz hurt him, and caused him to double his efforts in the streets.

N—s wanna kidnap wifey
Good luck with that bruh
You must gonna hide your whole family
What you think we wearing black for

vault_lines: Rare Porsches, rare portraits

This can be seen as a bridge between two periods of Jay’s job. The first involves cars, copious amounts of expensive cars that litter his lyrical back catalogue before 2007. Red is pronounced as a near homophone of rare, and a rare red Porsche of the time of the movie was the 959.



Transition forward in to the art world, a place Jay is very comfortable in, even calling himself the modern day Pablo Picasso. His current music is littered with references to famous artists and paintings.

“Hit a lick” means to partake in a robbery, whatever form that may take. “Things get across” refers to a successful drug smuggle, something that was paramount in Frank Lucas' story.

The feeling of a plane landing with kilo’s of drugs is euphoric, the kind of feeling this song mimics.

line: Take what the Forbes figured, then figure more ’Cause they forgot to account what I did with the raw
vault_lines: Take what the Forbes figured, then figure more
meaning:
During “Dead Presidents II” Jay uttered the immortal lines:

Partner, I’m still spending money from ‘88

His drug money is naturally off the books of entities like Forbes. They estimated that he made around $34 million in 2006. If we’re being realistic, with Jay’s penchant for expensive things, there’d be very little of that drug dealing money left over, save possibly for a couple of stacks in his 504 Streets stash box for sentimental reasons.

line: Let your hair down, baby, I just hit a score Pick any place on the planet, pick a shore
vault_lines: Let your hair down, baby, I just hit a score

Jay has been lacing his girls with expensive vacations for decades.

We used to use umbrellas to face the bad weather
So now we travel first class to change the forecast
Never in bunches, just me and you

line: Look at how I’m chilling, I’m killing this ice
vault_lines: Look at how I'm chilling, I'm killing this ice
meaning:
Ice means both diamond encrusted jewelry and actual ice for him to lay his expensive bottles of Champagne on.



It can also be interpreted in the context of enemies “ice grilling” Jay, or giving him an eyeful of hatred. He plays on the word chill to show how relaxed he is about competition.

line: Yeah, thanks to all the hustlers
vault_lines: Yeah, thanks to all the hustlers
meaning:
For the sake of the narrative, Jay has upgraded. Despite his back catalogue being littered with references to his hustling prowess, he’s taking on a much more acclaimed and important role: Kingpin.

These days, a brother gotta admire me from four fiends away

The hustlers are the young kids who actually sell the drugs. They flip, re-up, then get back on their shift.

line: Thanks to a little change, I tore you out the game Bullet wounds will stop your buffoonery Thanks to the pastor, rapping at your eulogy
vault_lines: Thanks to a little change, I tore you out the game
meaning:
A snide shot at Cam'ron latter who Jay had very active beef with at the time.

Notably, Cam'Ron was shot in 2005, claiming that the assailant “threw up the Roc sign” after the incident. This was the culmination of a short but vicious beef between the two surrounding the break up of Roc-A-Fella Records.



After the incident Cam’s record sales were never the same, nor did his career ever reach the heights that he attained while signed to Roc-A-Fella.

Jay shouts out 50 Cent, one time beef recipient, who released the Cam'Ron dissing “Funeral Music” on Buck The World this same year.

line: First of all, I wanna thank my connect The most important person, with all due respect
vault_lines: First of all, I wanna thank my connect
meaning:
The “Connect” is the person who supplies a dealer with drugs. Without the connect there can be no drug kingpin.

In the movie, Frank Lucas' connect is his cousin in Asia who is able to supply cheap, high quality heroin, which Frank re-brands “Blue Magic” and sells for a fraction of the cost of his competition. During his book Decoded Jay explains that as a dealer in Trenton, he and DeHaven were able to undercut their competition in a similar manner.


‘Roc Boys’ is the hustler at his height. It’s a celebration. [So first I thank the connect.] Like, how you put him so high that you had to tell God, chill out, right?

When I heard the horns, the first thing I said was that cause that’s what I do when I listen to music. I’m just giving all my secrets out, that’s what I’m supposed to do, right? Feed it back into the game and hopefully people will pick up on the things.

meaning: The track is wickedly similar to the treatment for the video for “Who You Wit II,” originally off the Sprung Soundtrack and re-done for Jay’s second LP In My Lifetime, Vol. 1 as “Who You Wit II.” In that video, Jay competes in the “International Players Ball.” During this track, he is celebrating his victory as the leading dealer in the city.

line: The Roc Boys in the building tonight (Hey!) Oh, what a feeling, I’m feeling life
vault_lines: Oh, what a feeling, I'm feeling life
meaning:
“Roc Boys” is an umbrella term used to describe Rocafella records cohorts. State Property had an album entitled The Roc Boys, while Beanie Sigel and Freeway regularly referred to themselves as Roc Boys. Kanye West is one of the key members of the Roc crew.

They’re celebrating Jay’s successes, as both friends and associates would.

line: Cheers – toast to crime
vault_lines: Cheers – toast to crime
meaning:
A toast to where all of his success started, and somewhat ironic, considering he has discussed the trials and tribulations of dealing drugs in Brooklyn already in this song, for him to blow it off so nonchalantly with a mere ‘cheers’ seems insincere, but the setting that Jay-Z paints in this song (lavish party) makes the negatives seem almost impossible.

Jay still credits his success to crack dealing. If he hadn’t learnt the ways of the world on the street, he may never have made it as a rapper.

line: Put your hand out the window, feel the force Feel the Porsche,
vault_lines: Put your hand out the window, feel the force
meaning: We know Jay is a Porsche enthusiast, and they are incredibly powerful cars. Throwing your hands out the window is a sign of joy, and the force signifies that Jay and his girl are living life in the fast lane.

A constant saying used by Denzel’s character in the movie.

vault_lines: Which means I get it from the ground

During American Gangster Frank takes a trip to Vietnam, directly to the source of the heroin, and places an order with the actual grower. He’s at the very top of the dealing tree, cultivating relationships with suppliers.

In an ensuing scene, he introduces his cousins to the business, allowing them an opportunity to sample the product.

line: This apple sauce is from the apple orchard This kinda talk is only reserved for the bosses
vault_lines: This apple sauce is from the apple orchard
meaning:
His “apple sauce” (crack) is from the “apple orchard” (tip-top source).

Jay is also the Boss of the Big Apple, New York.



Apple sauce from the actual orchard also implies it is pure and fresh, rather than the cut down, manufactured apple sauce peddled by some companies.

What I’m talking about is when you chop my dope down
to one, two, three, four, five percent and then you call it Blue Magic,
that is trademark infringement.

Britney Spears has no “steps,” meaning that she is an incompetent dancer. She’s also tried and failed rehab multiple times.



A video of Jay-Z breaking it down

meaning:
Jay-Z is “getting away with murder” figuratively when he “slings” (sells) “yay(o)” (cocaine). The drugs he sells are literally killing people.

Just like OJ Simpson got away with murdering his  wife  Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman.



Also, a more tongue in cheek invocation of some of the acts he signed to the Roc. People don’t hold (Uncle) Murda (who gave us maybe RapGenius' favorite awesomely terrible line ) against Jay because he also blessed us with (Kan)Ye.

“OJ” also means “Orange Juice”, and is a play off his line “Pink Rose”, another, more adult beverage.

line: Hit defrost Ice cold, jewels got no flaws Drop got no top, you on the top floor
vault_lines: Ice cold, jewels got no flaws
meaning:
Jay weaves some wordplay around the interior feature of most cars: the defrost button.

His girl’s finger is icy, a term used to describe an abundance of diamonds or jewels.

Jewel means both the woman (she is flawless) and her jewelry. The 4 C’s of judging the quality of a diamond are Carat Weight, Cut, Colour and Clarity. Clearly this girl is in the highest echelon.

To enhance that imagery, Jay explains that she is the top floor. Not only that, Jay’s car is roofless, and he resides in the penthouse suite at the top of the building.



His final layer of meaning harks back to 2001, when he rapped:

We used to use umbrellas to face the bad weather
So now we travel first class to change the forecast

Hitting defrost is a way of saying they will escape the cold winter and vacation in a different hemisphere.

My chick burning down Bergdorf’s
Comin' back with Birkin bags
Your chick is like, what type of purse is that

Beyoncé certainly seems to enjoy it…

vault_lines: Boys in blue, who put greed before the badge
meaning:
Hov is thankful to the cops who are willing to accept his bribes instead of arresting him.
Notice the green/blue color juxtaposition. Similar to his line in Go Crazy:

Attract money, my worst color is light green
My favorite hue is Jay-Z blue

Notice too the very ambiguous ‘greed’/‘green’ homophone. It’s a circuitous homophone, given that the meaning is the same either way, but Jay can afford to coast given that he’s DBOTY (Dope Boy of the Year).

During the movie, there is a scene where Frank is caught with drugs in the trunk of his car. The result is he is forced to bribe the officer who caught him, starting a vicious cycle that admittedly keeps Frank on the street and at the head of his criminal enterprise.
