Drug dealers putting cash in each of these containers is a rap meme.

Placing a lot of cash in a brown paper bag comes up with particular emphasis.

In Decoded, Jay-z also explains how he used to write rhymes on a brown paper bag.

line: Illest since the Row had it, nigga now the Roc got it
vault_lines: Illest since the Row had it, nigga now the Roc got it
meaning:
Jay-Z is recalling the dominance of Death Row Records in the 1990s, which was established after the success of their first release—Dr. Dre’s The Chronic—in 1992. At their peak, the West Coast label released several multi-platinum albums from a roster that included arguably the greatest producer in hip-hop (Dr. Dre), two superstars (Snoop Dogg and 2Pac), and a solid supporting cast (Tha Dogg Pound, Nate Dogg, The Lady of Rage)—all led by the most feared executive in the music business (Suge Knight).

On his 1998 single, “Money, Cash, Hoes,” Jay received backlash from other New York rappers after he appeared to rebuke them while respecting the duality of “illness” for one particular Death Row move displayed in Tha Dogg Pound’s controversial music video for their 1995 single “New York, New York”:

It’s like New York’s been soft ever since Snoop came through and crushed the buildings

Death Row’s dynasty was crushed in 1996 with the departure of Dr. Dre and the death of 2Pac, two major events that caused the remaining artists to eventually escape the Row. Their rivals in the East, Bad Boy Entertainment, suffered a similar downfall after the death of The Notorious B.I.G. in 1997.

Jay-Z filled the void left by Biggie and 2Pac with the success of his third album—1998’s Vol 2… Hard Knock Life—and that success led to him building a bridge between the East Coast and West Coast by writing the 1999 Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg single “Still D.R.E.” Jay was arguably the biggest star in hip-hop after the success of his critically acclaimed 2001 album, The Blueprint, and while his Roc-A-Fella Records roster might not have reached the heights of Death Row’s dominance, the success of Cam’ron and Kanye West ensured the Roc wouldn’t be seen as just a one-man army.

line: My road to glory was Road To Perdition
vault_lines: My road to glory was Road To Perdition
meaning:
Perdition refers to “the state of being in hell forever as punishment after death.”

Similar to the previous line, Jay parallels his own rise to fame with that of a film plot. Road to Perdition stars Tom Hanks as a mob enforcer who takes revenge on those who killed his family. While the killings seem easy in the moment, the consequences of his actions lead to darker outcomes than he ever imagined. Jay’s no killer, but succeeding in the music industry comes with it’s fair share of vices.



Jay is a film buff who frequently features movies in his work. His first offering Act I: Eternal Sunshine (The Pledge) was built from Jon Brion’s soundtrack to the film Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, and featured samples from Charlie and The Chocolate Factory and “Abracadabra” is titled after a quote from The Prestige and samples dialogue from the movie. The three Act structure of his projects is also patterned after the format for magic tricks in the movie.

line: [Intro: JAY-Z]
vault_lines: I got these niggas, Breezy!
meaning: Hov’s additions to the track are from his song “Success” featuring Nas. The track appeared on his album American Gangster, which was inspired by the film of the same name.

line: You pay a cost to be a boss, nigga, I paid the wager
vault_lines: You pay a cost to be a boss, nigga, I paid the wager
meaning:
Jay feels you have to pay your dues until you “make it”. Jay goes a step further, not only has he paid his dues but he “paid the wager” by gambling his whole career on attaining success.

This is similar to Jay Z’s line:

I paid the cost to be the boss to floss this hard

line: Yes sir, I’m a soldier of love
vault_lines: Yes sir, I'm a soldier of love
meaning:
You can lead from the front without violence. Ghandi was a great, if not the greatest modern purveyor of this ideal.

Also a reference to Sade’s song “Soldier of Love”.

line: A thousand wishes from a million slaves could raise a savior
vault_lines: A thousand wishes from a million slaves could raise a savior
meaning:
We did the math – that’s one billion wishes.

Jay believes together the human race is stronger, and a mass collective of consciousness cannot be stopped – the saviour is what is born from that consciousness.

The line also reflects Jay’s recurring references to black people enduring enslavement.

From “We Made It (Remix)”:

they can’t relate to our struggle, my nigga
We came up from slavery

line: Hardcore Thriller pop, Michael Jackson nigga rock
vault_lines: Hardcore Thriller pop, Michael Jackson nigga rock
meaning:
Jay refers to the famous song and album title by the King of Pop Michael Jackson. Jay’s music is like a harder, updated version of Mike’s.

Jay’s usage of the phrase “nigga rock” reminds us once again that it was Black artists who originated rock and the other music today’s artists draw inspiration from.

line: And even though I walk in the narrow valley of death All I see is green pastures, bitches screaming from the rafters
vault_lines: And even though I walk in the narrow valley of death
meaning:
Jay’s lyricism is infused with Biblical allusions. He uses two verses from Psalm 23 to describe himself.

Psalm 23:4:

Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.

Psalm 23:2:

He makes me lie down in green pastures and leads me beside still waters.

Also, bitches screaming from the rafters is a nice touch – Jay has women all over the world.

line: This is lightning striking, feel how the Zeitgeist feel Get a slight chill
vault_lines: This is lightning striking, feel how the Zeitgeist feel
meaning:
Jay’s music has the gravity of the film trilogy Zeitgeist. His comparison implies his music challenges the corrupt powers-that-be and can enlighten, and empower its audience.

The documentaries explore religion, creation of the universe, mythology and the economical system. According the films website, the goal of the series is:

To explore what makes us who we are, how we relate, what we are doing and what we should be doing if we wish to live in a peaceful, humane, sustainable and healthy global society.

line: A thousand visits to these dickheads at these major labels From Big Daddy Kane, to big daddy Cain and Abel
vault_lines: A thousand visits to these dickheads at these major labels
meaning:
Jay credits the major label “dickheads” for the current division in hip-hop. 1980s legend Big Daddy Kane represents the state of hip-hop before A&Rs became heavily involved, and Cain’s fratricidal attack on Abel is akin to what the labels are doing to hip-hop.



Alternatively, Jay could be touching on his own story where he front from a rap icon like BDK to a Biblical legend thanks to his prioritization of spirituality.

line: Drowning all my sorrows and woes in the club
vault_lines: Drowning all my sorrows and woes in the club
meaning: Jay’s openly admitted he’s had problems with drugs and alcohol. Many believe this is what initially delayed new music being released.

line: All hail the lyrical, Grand Wizard Imperial
vault_lines: All hail the lyrical, Grand Wizard Imperial
meaning:
The Grand Wizard, or Imperial Wizard is the national leader of the KKK.

Jay re-appropriating “Grand Wizard Imperial” fits into a long history of oppressed people re-appropriating and stigmatizing labels to transcend oppression.

line: Google me, baby, understand where I’m coming from
vault_lines: Google me, baby, understand where I'm coming from
meaning:
No, Jay, it’s “Genius me, baby…”

Jay has a similar line on “Minutes of Moog” where he asks a female to find out who he is.

line: Mastered both sides of The Force
vault_lines: Mastered both sides of The Force
meaning:
Jay alludes to the Star Wars films – the “Force” is a metaphysical, universal power in the Star Wars universe that can be used for both good (the Light side of the Force) and evil (the Dark side of the Force).

Jay has mastered both sides of the Force and created his own lightsabre – requisites of a Jedi.



Jay has dropped similar lines on “Not A Disturbance” and  “Shuckin' & Jivin'”.

line: Okay, it’s a Slumdog opera The tale of a king whose name wasn’t on the roster

Jay draws parallels between Slumdog Millionaire and his own rise to fortune. Jay has a similar story: he was living as a homeless nomadic, but is now signed to Jay Z’s label Roc Nation.

line: I call it as it happen, the art of quality rapping One autobiographical chapter could start up the rapture
vault_lines: I call it as it happen, the art of quality rapping

Jay’s ability to spit the truth is the hallmark of a great rapper. Like Kanye West, he could raise hell by enlightening others of the truth.

This sentiment has been echoed in numerous rap songs, notably Jay Z’s “Imaginary Player”, and Ab-Soul’s “I’m A G”.

line: And “Act II: The Turn” is just the memoirs with no omissions
vault_lines: And "Act II: The Turn" is just the memoirs with no omissions
meaning:
Act II: The Turn is supposedly Jay’s second record, the follow-up to the one-track event that was “Eternal Sunshine: The Pledge”. Those familiar with The Prestige know of his love for its mythos; in the three-step process:

The second act is called “The Turn”. The magician takes the ordinary something and makes it do something extraordinary. Now you’re looking for the secret… but you won’t find it, because of course you’re not really looking. You don’t really want to know. You want to be fooled. But you wouldn’t clap yet. Because making something disappear isn’t enough; you have to bring it back

In the context of his music, we both want new music from him and to keep him as the elusive figure that captured the world’s attention years ago.

line: Beware, but prepare for the polarization, it’s the globalization Warn all the clergymen and notify Satan I been waiting, this the notarization I been patient
vault_lines: Beware, but prepare for the polarization, it's the globalization
meaning:
Jay’s been fighting against both clergymen and Satan for a long time, planning for the best time to strike.

He’s ready to wage war, and the whole globe will be split in two – into those with him and those against him. This is his official word, and evidence that he’s prepared.

line: My life feel like a highlight reel
vault_lines: My life feel like a highlight reel
meaning:
Jay tips his cap to Dr. Dre line, borrowing a line from his song “Die Hard”:

My life is like a highlight reel

So many extravagant and stunning things are happening in Jay’s life that every moment of it is exciting and interesting.

line: And I ain’t leave the thugs alone The humble and the meek will surely inherit the mud we on
vault_lines: And I ain't leave the thugs alone
meaning:
As Jesus said in Matthew 5:5:

Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.

Jay’s remained humble and stayed true to the same people he grew up with, even though he has plenty opportunity to move permanently into a higher class.

Jay Z also referred to the bible verse on his song “Lucifer”.

line: We came a mighty long way from standing near the stove In the cold, the greatest story ever told The realest niggas see the pain in my story boards The true believers say, “Wallahi, I support the boy”
vault_lines: We came a mighty long way from standing near the stove
meaning:
Jay Elec was once poor and homeless, and couldn’t afford a place to live, let alone heating bills.

While he’s taken the hip-hop world by storm and become a public advocate of his faith – it’s his story that lives in the music, appealing to people from all walks of life. Those from the streets sympathize with his struggles, and those that share his faith say they “swear to Allah” (“Wallahi”) that they support him.

Note that he pronounces “boy” using the Philadelphia slang “bul” of the same meaning. It is a well known fact Jay spent time in Philly. The slang coincides with “Wallahi”, considering the huge Islamic population among the African American community in Philadelphia.

line: Actual-fact syndrome That’s why I dropped the jewel on every verse you heard me shit on
vault_lines: That's why I dropped the jewel on every verse you heard me shit on
meaning: Actual facts are the 7th lesson in the Nation of Islam’s 120 Lessons. This explains why we hear new Jay Electronica music so infrequently: he isn’t just picky, he claims to have a syndrome that forces him to ensure nothing he releases is less than actual facts.

line: My swag is on 1.21 jiggawatts, 10 trillion kilowatts
vault_lines: My swag is on 1.21 jiggawatts, 10 trillion kilowatts
meaning:

vault_lines: This is the number one rule for your set
meaning:
REGRETS EQUALS REDEMPTION

JUSTICE.Reasonable Doubt, Jay-Z’s first album, came out in 1996. I was just graduating and heading to Los Angeles to begin the post-college chapter of my life. I was grown – or at least I thought I was – and ready to see what life had to offer me. I remember listening to “Regrets” on a cassette tape I made to listen to while on the 4-hour plane ride. I remember rewinding the song over and over because this rule of learning to live with regrets kept challenging me to think about a life that was ahead of me that I knew deep down could go one of two ways: south, and heading back home to momma to try it again, or north, and heading back home to momma having achieved something worthwhile while living on my own in the City of Angels. I was afraid. And on that plane I contemplated coming back to Atlanta where my comfort zone was safe. Two things stuck with me. Just before I boarded that plane for LA, my mom told me “don’t take no wooden nickels because you can’t buy anything with them”, and Jay-Z rapping over and over about this rule of learning to “live with regrets.” Learn to live with regrets. Don’t take no wooden nickels. Don’t take no wooden nickels. Learn to live with regrets. Huh? In my twenty-something year old mind, I didn’t want regrets. And I damn sure didn’t want money made outta wood. I just wanted rewards. All this wisdom was scaring me!! Eventually it hit me. Paired together, my mom’s words with Jay-Z’s brought me some piece of mind. (At least enough to not hop back on the plane heading home to Georgia.)

“To get ahead in life mistakes are inevitable. And oftentimes mistakes become regrets. But remember to take care of yourself, and if you try as best as possible to make careful decisions then the regrets stay at bay.” This is how I rationalized it. I carried this with me then, and I carry it with me now. Mistakes I’ve made. Plenty of them. However, I’ve learned that out of the mistakes come redemption and forgiveness. Therein lies the justice of regrets

The Daily Dose of Realness: In Decoded (2010), Jay-Z says that “Regrets” was the last song on the album because “It’s the last feeling you have before you go to sleep or feel when you wake up and look at yourself in the bathroom mirror” (265). Mistakes bring about regrets, and regrets can be a heavy burden. That’s life though. The silver lining is that regrets create a space for forgiveness and personal redemption, both of which neutralize any heaviness. Both of which are necessary on the road to success. That’s the number one rule to survival a la Shawn Carter. The number two rule is don’t take no wooden nickels a la my mommy dearest. Take care of yourself. Take care of others. Godspeed

line: If you do then, how would you explain? I’m ten years removed, still the vibe is in my veins I got a hustler spirit, nigga, period Check out my hat yo, peep the way I wear it
vault_lines: If you do then, how would you explain?
meaning:
Referring back to the previous line, Jay continues to ruminate on the addictive nature of the drug game, not only for the fiends being served the product but for the hustlers doing the selling.

To anyone who doubts this he asks them to explain why even now, ten years, eight albums and many millions of dollars removed from his time in the streets, he still craves the buzz that he experienced during that time of his life.

He puts this down to upbringing. Essentially, “you can take the boy out of Marcy, but you can’t take Marcy out of the boy”. He’s sees hustling as something that is ingrained in his very being, which is a common, often re-occuring lyrical motif in Jay’s music.

He points towards the style in which he still wears his hat, slanted to one side in the fashion which he became accustomed to on the streets, as evidence that he’s still the same old Shawn.



Hov dedicates an entire track later on in this album’s running order, the wistful, Neptunes produced “Allure”, to further elaborate on the point he’s making here.

line: Now, back to our regularly scheduled program, L’Album Noir: The Black Album
vault_lines: Now, back to our regularly scheduled program, L'Album Noir: The Black Album
meaning:
The PSA concludes and we are returned to L'Album Noir (French for “The Black Album”).

“Public Service Announcement” wasn’t on The Black Album (or even recorded) until the 11th hour before the album went to production, and this same outro was used on the track it replaced, “Looking at My S Dots.”

Rather than a PSA, “Looking at My S Dots” had been framed as commercial, as it was a short song designed to promote Jay-Z’s new S Dots shoe brand.



Anyone know why they chose French, or who’s speaking here?

line: I just rolled the dice, trying to get some change And I’d do it twice, ain’t no sense in me Lying as if I am a different man And I could blame my environment but There ain’t no reason why I be buying expensive chains
vault_lines: I just rolled the dice, trying to get some change
meaning:
Here’s where life gets “complex.” I’m innocent because I didn’t invent the game, the game came to the hood via a bunch of people from the outside: the big drug suppliers, the gun worst, were actively involved. And we – the hustlers at the street level – definitely didn’t invent the poverty and hopelessness that drove a generation of desperate kids to start selling drugs. But when I “do it twice.” The second time is not out of desperation to survive or to resist the status quo, but out of greed for the spoils of the game.“
                                 - Jay-Z "Decoded”

Note the dual meaning of “change” here as well.

Also, “lyin' as if I am a different man” contains some lion wordplay: “Lion as if I am a different mane.”

line: [Produced by Just Blaze]
vault_lines: Sponsored by Just Blaze and the good folks at Roc-A-Fella Records
meaning:
Just added this song to the album at “the eleventh hour”:

The album was finished, cases were already made. Then, while I was mixing something else, at the last-minute, I made the beat for “PSA.” Jay was doing press at a studio around the corner. All the different outlets were coming to listenings. In the midst of that, I ran back to the studio where Jay was and was like, Dude, listen to this. He liked it but he was like, “We’re already done.” I’m like, “We’re not done until this song is finished.” So before each press listening session, he’d run back into my room, write four bars down, go back and do another round of press, come back to me. We did that all night…To get “PSA” on the album, we literally stopped the CDs and records from being manufactured, stopped all the artwork from being printed. We ended up pulling a song called “Looking at My S Dots” from the album to put “PSA” on, literally in the eleventh hour. Just two or three weeks later, we were at the Madison Square Garden show and when “PSA” came on everybody already knew every word of the song and the place exploded. It was an amazing feeling.

Just Blaze also talks about it in this Revolt TV video:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iXbhQCJkszw

line: Ving ain’t lie

Actor Ving Rhames narrated the 2003 hip-hop documentary Beef which featured the highly publicized feud between Jay-Z and Nas.

Jay has explained that this second verse is his response to an essay highly critical of him by Elizabeth Mendez Berry.

Jay is acknowledging that the critiques of the essay are all valid.

Phrasing it as he did makes the line a reference to the Notorious B.I.G. line:

Revenge I’m tastin' at the tip of my lips
I can’t wait to fill my clip in his hips
‘Pass the chocolate, Thai!’
Sing ain’t lie
There’s Jason with his back to me
Talkin' to his faculty

Sing was a character in Biggie’s “Somebody’s Gotta Die” who gave Biggie accurate info on where the killer of Big’s friend was chilling so that Big could kill him.

line: I walk like a ballplayer
vault_lines: Check out my swag' yo, I walk like a ballplayer
meaning:
Double entendre:


In baseball, if a pitcher misses the strike zone 4 times, the batter gets to go to first base. This is called a walk. (Also, Jay could be saying now that he is rich and famous, he gets to do what he wants to, with free passes for high profile things. A walk in baseball could be considered a free pass.)
Nowadays in baseball, and other sports, athletes are getting paid enormous amounts of money. It’s understandable that a ball player would walk with a little swagger in his step. Jay walks with swagger, too.





This all ties to Jay’s love of the New York Yankees.

line: Either love me, or leave me alone
vault_lines: Either love me, or leave me alone
meaning:
Either appreciate his craft or don’t take the time to check it out because it is only a waste of time and will do you no good.

“Love Me or Leave Me Alone” is a song by Brand Nubian.

Elizabeth Mendez Berry wrote in her essay: “Squint and you see a revolutionary. But open your eyes to the platinum chain around his neck: Jay-Z is a hustler.” No doubt. It’s a simple truth, but complex too. Identity isn’t a prison you can never escape but the way to redeem your past is not to run from it, but to try to understand it, and use it as a foundation to grow.“ (Carter 2010, p31)

line: Fellow Americans, it is with the utmost pride and sincerity that I present this recording as a living testament and recollection of history in the making during our generation

line: My homie Strict told me, “Dude, finish your breakfast”
vault_lines: My homie Strict told me, "Dude, finish your breakfast"
meaning:
“Strick” is John “Franchise” Strickland, a NYC street ball legend. During a 2003 tournament at Rucker Park in Harlem, Strickland (who played for a team managed by Jay) told a teammate who didn’t follow through on an easy lay-up, “dude you have to finish your breakfast”.

Jay took the advice as well, and plans to apply it to his career by not phoning it in on his last album before retirement (The Black Album was one of his many “final albums”).

line: Nigga, I get my “By any means” on whenever there’s a drought
vault_lines: Nigga, I get my "By any means" on whenever there's a drought
meaning:
Whenever there’s a “drought” – i.e., drugs are in short supply, Jay does whatever is needed to get his.

This references the famous 1965 speech by Malcolm X:

We declare our right on this earth to be a man, to be a human being, to be respected as a human being, to be given the rights of a human being in this society, on this earth, in this day, which we intend to bring into existence by any means necessary.

“Just to amplify the connection I’m trying to make between revolutionaries and hustlers, I invoke Malcom’s famous By Any Means Necessary” slogan"   - Jay-Z “Decoded”

It could also be applied to when theres a drought in the rap game – no good music for a while. Jay-Z’s music means people will need the umbrellas in the next line.

line: Hov, oh, not D.O.C. But similar to them letters, “No One Can Do It Better”
vault_lines: Hov, oh, not D.O.C.
meaning:
Jay goes old school here and references N.W.A affiliate The D.O.C. and his classic 1989 album No One Can Do It Better, or perhaps the song of the same name off that album.

If you listen super close, you can actually hear a snippet of “No One Can Do It Better” playing in the background as Hov delivers this line.

line: Hope you don’t think users are the only abusers Niggas getting high within the game
vault_lines: Hope you don't think users are the only abusers
meaning:
And it’s not just the material spoils that keep you going: You start getting addicted to the thrill of it, the adrenaline rush of going to see your connect in a small building in Harlem in a lobby that you’ve never been in, where you go in with a bag of money and come out with a bag of work. Or the feeling when you come around the corner back home and all eyes turn to you because everyone knows who you are — you represent something successful and free and dangerous, all at once. You have the best car, the best jewelry, the whole package. You taste a strange kind of fame. It’s as addictive as the shit you’re selling, and just as deadly.

—Jay-Z, Decoded (p31)

Wordplay on high. Referring to the feeling of intoxication and moving up the ladder.

line: This is a public service announcement Sponsored by Just Blaze and the good folks at Roc-A-Fella Records
vault_lines: This is a public service announcement
meaning:
As Just Blaze told Fader:

We ended up pulling a song called “Looking at My S Dots” from the album to put “PSA” on, literally in the eleventh hour.

“Looking at My S Dots” was a roughly minute-long interlude that Jay introduced as a “commercial break” to promote his new shoe line.

But they opted to go with a public service announcement instead, where they do us the favor of reminding us that Jay-Z is the best.

line: Get your umbrellas out because that’s when I brainstorm
vault_lines: Get your umbrellas out because that's when I brainstorm
meaning: A drought in the game is when the supply or demand starts to dry up — and that’s when resourceful hustlers have to start getting creative. If that means getting violent, the “brainstorming” might just lead to someone getting wet, as in bloody, which is why you need to get your umbrella out, for protection. It’s a dramatic, violent image to convey the way desperation and hunger can explode. (Carter 2010, p31) from Decoded.

line: I’m like Che Guevara with bling on, I’m complex
vault_lines: I'm like Che Guevara with bling on, I'm complex
meaning:
In the critical essay that inspired this verse, Elizabeth Mendez Berry wrote:

When he rocks his Guevara shirt and a do-rag, squint and you see a revolutionary. But open your eyes to the platinum chain around his neck: Jay-Z is a hustler.

Jay publicly sported the look during the making of his MTV Unplugged special, and had previously referred to himself on record as “Jay Guevara.”
The chain was a Jesus piece that Biggie used to wear, according to Jay.



Jay is like Che Guevara in that they are both revolutionaries, in a way. Jay started a “revolution” in the rap world/pop culture, and Che, a noted revolutionary, was essential to the movement that overthrew Fulgencio Batista, a U.S. backed dictator in Cuba. Needless to say, Jay doesn’t share Che’s economic opinions; he’s clearly showing off his wealth by wearing “bling” (jewelry).

The contradiction in the symbols shows the contradictions in Jay-Z’s character, which make him complex. Perhaps Jay is suggesting something about the duality of man.

In Decoded Jay mentioned how him becoming a millionaire in a white man’s society is just as revolutionary as Che’s ventures.

In these four lines I use five different variations on “do” and “dude” (plus “jewels” whose hard “j” sounds almost like a “d”) to create a percussive rhythm within the beat"
 - Jay-Z in “Decoded”

line: So that’s what I’ma do, take you back to the dude with the Lexus Fast-forward the jewels and the necklace

Jay is stating he is as tough as ever, but with more luxuries. He has been “ridin' Lexus since ‘94”, so the “dude with the Lexus” is his young self.

Jay wants you to “fast-forward” from his young self to his current self, drenched with jewels and necklaces.

So he’s effectively going to give you the best of his young self, all the way to the best of his current self.

line: I check cheddar like a food inspector
vault_lines: I check cheddar like a food inspector
meaning:
This line combines two separate pieces of slang – “check” means to collect, “cheddar” means money – to create a third piece of new slang – “a food inspector” – that only makes sense if you decode the first two phrases.

“Check cheddar” is an alliteration that adds force to the image.

—Jay-Z, Decoded

line: Got the hottest chick in the game wearin’ my chain, that’s right
vault_lines: Got the hottest chick in the game wearin' my chain, that's right
meaning:
Beyoncé, arguably the biggest female star in music, was Jay’s girlfriend at the time (now wife).



This verse appears as an interlude in the “Dirt Off Your Shoulder” music video, and Beyoncé makes a cameo (albeit obscured by the IR camera effect) wearing a Roc-A-Fella chain as this line is delivered.

They were (and still are in many respects) very private about their relationship, hence the image distortion and the indirect reference to her here. They’d been privately dating since at least 2001, but weren’t public about it for years.

line: Flyer than a piece of paper bearin’ my name
vault_lines: Flyer than a piece of paper bearin' my name
meaning: A deceptively deep line.  The use of flyer as a pun for flier conveys two meanings.  The first that Jay-Z is “fly,” i.e. cool.  The second that he himself is a better advertisement than an actual flier.  After all, he’s a business, man.

line: Fresh out the fryin’ pan into the fire
vault_lines: Fresh out the fryin' pan into the fire
meaning:
This is an idiom from a 15th-century fable meaning “to go from a bad situation to a worse situation.”

The “frying pan” is used to cook crack – the “fire” is the heat of the entertainment industry lifestyle. Jay thinks music is more pressure than selling crack! (Jay has stated that “the hustle” – for him – refers to music.. but, hey, you can’t knock the hustle..)

line: I guess even back then you can call me CEO of the R-O-C, Hov
vault_lines: I guess even back then you can call me
meaning:
A simple double entendre of “Roc-A-Fella,” our company, which we call the Roc, and “rock,” common slang for crack because of the way the coke crystallizes when you cook it. I drop the “frying pan” into the next line to keep the comparison going. In the line after that I complete the connection between selling rock and selling the Roc, applying the streets and supplying the music biz. Both take ruthlessness. In fact, the music industry is the fire to the crack game’s frying pan.“

- (Carter: 2010 p28) from Decoded

line: I used to move snowflakes by the O-Z
vault_lines: I used to move snowflakes by the O-Z
meaning: He used to deal cocaine, which is white and fine like snowflakes by ounces (oz).

meaning:
Hov seemingly plays off a line from Digital Underground’s “Humpty Dance”:

So just let me introduce myself
My name is Humpty, pronounced with a “umpty”

This line also echoes the Rolling Stones' “Sympathy for the Devil,” which beings:

Please allow me to introduce myself
I’m a man of wealth and taste

But as a veteran MC, Hov is re-introducing himself.

Hov is one of his nicknames, short for “Jay-Hova” (a pun on “Jehovah”, the Hebrew name for God), the “God MC.”

Kanye originally composed this verse for an unreleased track called We Are Young, which was later scrapped from Watch The Throne and given to fun.
When We Are Young was not included in the final project, Kanye reused some of his verse and adapted it for Primetime.

vault_lines: I told her run a bubble bath
meaning: A hovercraft is a vehicle suitable for both land and water. Yeezy is telling his wife to float in the bubble bath like a hovercraft would float effortlessly on water.

line: My fifteen minutes of fame has stretched beyond
vault_lines: My fifteen minutes of fame has stretched beyond
meaning:
Jay alludes to the famous Andy Warhol quote

In the future, everyone will be world-famous for 15 minutes

In 2011 Jay had been in the rap game for 15 years.

Jay already referenced Warhol in “Already Home”, Lupe Fiasco’s “Pressure” and later on he will drop his name in “Picasso Baby”.

Moreover, his book Decoded is covered by the artist’s 1984 painting entitled Rorschach.

line: New money, I found the fountain of youth
vault_lines: New money, I found the fountain of youth
meaning: For a lot of artists the money income is a Gaussian curve: they start off with basically nothing, they have a big hit album and then eventually fall off. Jay on the other hand always finds way to expand his business ventures, whether it’s buying Nets stocks, founding a clothing line (Rocawear), opening a sports agency (RocNation Sports) or being an ambassador for a high end brand like D'Usse or Armand de Brignac.

line: Our third eon, that’s what the fuck we on
vault_lines: Our third eon, that's what the fuck we on
meaning:
A eon is a word used to indicate an era or a long period of time; Watch The Throne marks the beginning of Ye and Hova’s third era.

The first was in 2000-2001: Kanye was just putting his name out there and Hova was at the top of his game; Ye helped Jay produce Blueprint and The Dynasty: Roc La Familia which gave him his first gold plaque with “Izzo (H.O.V.A.)” and a big reputation as a producer.

The second era starts in 2003, with the release of Jay Z’s farewell project The Black Album and Kanye’s debut LP The College Dropout which would be followed by two more classics in Late Registration and Graduation.

The third one started in 2010 with the release of My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy and Watch The Throne in 2011 which would then be followed by Magna Carta… Holy Grail by Jay Z and Yeezus by Kanye, two extremely polarizing albums respectively for their marketing strategy and their sound.

line: [Produced by No I.D.]
vault_lines: Still wearing my 23s, they can't fuck with the boy
meaning:
A mix of pianos and strings in the intro of Primetime set the tone for one of the best tracks on the record. No I.D. delivers a really deep and soft paced beat that is in complete juxtaposition with the previous track, H.A.M..

The sample used on the track is from Orange Krush’s “Action”:

http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sl1gKNzNywo

line: Niggas gon’ kill me, I swear they better be lying I never live in fear, I’m too out of my mind
vault_lines: Niggas gon' kill me, I swear they better be lying
meaning:
West interrupted Taylor Swift’s speech at the MTV’s 2009 Video Music Awards, who had just won the award for best video, saying that Beyoncé should have won the award:

Im sorry, but Beyoncé had one of the best videos of all time.

Ye received several death threats after the incident, but he wasn’t afraid since he was out of his mind at the time and couldn’t feel the chemical reaction in the brain that cause fear.

line: We in the time of our lives, baby Turn the music up, prime time
vault_lines: We in the time of our lives, baby
meaning: Primetime is when most television viewers watch TV, and the most popular programs are broadcasted. As this relates to The Throne, they Jay claims both are still in the prime of their careers despite being older than the average rap star.

line: Nigga, we rollin’, beat the deuce
vault_lines: Nigga, we rollin', beat the deuce
meaning:
Continuing with the gambling metaphor suggested by “Aces”, Jay compares life to a game of craps, promising that he won’t roll a 2 and crap out of the game.

It could also be a nod to old school legend Masta Ace’s most notable song is 1990’s “Born to Roll”.

line: I started in ’88, got warm in ’92 I landed in ’96, that’s the year I came through
vault_lines: I started in '88, got warm in '92
meaning:
Jay started off his rap career by jumping on tracks by his mentor Jaz-O such as “Hawaiian Sophie” and then started to build a little buzz for himself in the early 90’s when he rap battled with LL Cool J and served as a hype man for Big Daddy Kane.

In 1996 he’d eventually release his classic debut album Reasonable Doubt, which cemented him as one of the greats in hip hop history.

line: The night is young, what the fuck we gon’ do? Ooh
vault_lines: The night is young, what the fuck we gon' do? Ooh
meaning: Jay and Ye are both in the “primetimes” of their lives, meaning they have a lot to look forward to. In television, primetime is between 8-9 PM, meaning that if this night is a metaphor for the rest of their lives/careers, there are plenty hours of partying left to do.

line: Champagne, I’m sipping on it, shit tastes different, don’t it? You know what? You right It’s like the best damn champagne I had in my life
vault_lines: Champagne, I'm sipping on it, shit tastes different, don't it?

This continues what Ye has been saying for the last few lines – even though Ye has had enough money to buy first-class flights and expensive champagne for years, these material items weren’t as satisfying when he was still struggling to get to where he wanted to be.

Now that he has dropped his magnum opus, became equals with his big brother, and been catapulted to a level of success rarely ever seen by a black man in America, he can finally enjoy them.

line: More money, forty-year-old phenom
vault_lines: More money, forty-year-old phenom
meaning:
He has more money now than when he was younger meaning he has great longevity while other one-hit wonders fall out of the scene after 1 or 2 albums. Unlike them, Jay gets mo' money but not mo' problems, as his homie Biggie would say.

Hova also plays on the word “phenom” that usually describes a young sensation; even though he is 40 and has been in the rap game for 15 years at the time of release, his music is still super fresh.

line: Prime time, never hit these heights I mean it’s like, it’s like our first first-class flight
vault_lines: Prime time, never hit these heights
meaning:
Can we get much higher?

Kanye suggests that despite the incredible success he has experienced in the past, he has never been “higher” than he is right now. While he had already dropped 5 classic platinum albums and won a boatload of Grammy’s, none of it compares to this album, where Kanye transforms from Jay’s protege to his equal.

Yeezy compares this experience to the first time he flew first-class and realized how much better it is than coach.

line: Still wearing my 23s, they can’t fuck with the boy Far as them sixteens, I’m 23 of it all
vault_lines: Still wearing my 23s, they can't fuck with the boy

Showed up at the last supper in some brand new Js

When it comes to verses – composed of 16 bars – Jay is the Michael Jordan of the rap game.

At age 42, Jay is still better than 24 year old rappers (cough Drake cough). If he had to pick a jersey number it’d be 45, just like Jordan did when he came out of retirement.

When I come back like Jordan, wearing the 4-5
It ain’t to play games with you, it’s to aim at you, probably maim you

24 also sounds like “20 foes”, which is probably why Jay carries a .45 with him (or at least on his bodyguard!).

line: Cassius in his prime, coloring out of the line ’Cause they don’t want nobody that’s colored out of the lines
vault_lines: Cassius in his prime, coloring out of the line
meaning:
A reiteration of Kanye’s blog post in February, 2010:

If we don’t do what you feel is the shit, you beat us up verbally and mentally, like a catholic school teacher beating a creative student into submission. I can hear you screaming ‘color inside the lines!!!‘ Well fuck your coloring book, color by numbers approach to life.

The white community did not like how Cassius Clay acted as a black man who often stood up for his rights and challenged the racist views of the world. He’d eventually convert to Islamism and change his name to Muhammad Ali. Kanye feels like he’s in the same situation as Ali, a black man that continues to bring racism to the forefront and encourages blacks to push for independent success.

This could also refer to when Muhammad Ali refused to serve on the (front)lines in the Vietnam War.

Ali’s refusal of the draft and general activism is arguably his true prime (over his boxing career), as it’s much of why he is such an icon — and that is what Kanye is referring to.

Kanye had similar lines on his song “Chain Heavy” that had released a year prior. In the same fashion, he talks about how it’s time for those of color to stand up for themselves, citing various celebrities like Cassius Clay, who he compares himself to in both songs:

How many Cassius' will we see in one lifetime?
That’s why it’s Miles Davis, Kobe, it’s Mike time

line: So I cut the pattern and I sew its seams, and
vault_lines: So I cut the pattern and I sew its seams, and
meaning:
Continuing his metaphor of the sewing machine and what he does with his music:

“Cutting the pattern” refers to the manufacturing of clothes (“sewing of jeans”). Again, Lupe is using this to describe how he takes his lines and uses them to create his own art. Also, the word “cut” is used as a synonym of “eliminate”. In other words, he is “getting rid of the pattern” and doing something different in hip-hop.

“Sewing the seams” is something else seen in clothing manufacturing. A “seam” is a line or junction formed by sewing together two pieces of material along their margins. Similarly, in music, Lupe takes the lines that he uses and connects them with each other.

Additionally, note the homonym, “sew its seams”, with “so it seems” from the opening line.

Also, there is a play on the word “war”, which is a common card game, involving a nearly endless series of “draws” from a deck.

Warhols, of course, are highly in demand and fabulously expensive. A self-portrait sold for $32.6 million in 2010.

On another level Jay-Z is saying that his competitors are too “green” or inexperienced to talk in his hue – they have “too much green” to challenge a veteran like Jay.

Basically, Lupe is warning the listener to not become engrossed by the lure of either the drug game or the mainstream music industry. And shouting out a famous New Yorker who is difficult to “Roc”.

line: Sippin’ on Ooba
vault_lines: Sauce Money, yo, yeah-yeah

The page hasn’t been updated since 2010 and the website, oobabeverage.com, is no longer active, but bottles of the drink can still be found on Amazon and other third-party retail sites.

line: As a youth explosively, clappin’ off the roof Shootin’ guard like Kobe
vault_lines: As a youth explosively, clappin' off the roof
meaning:
This line can be interpreted three different ways, making it a triple-entendre(!).

1) “Shooting guard like Kobe.” Kobe Bryant played the position of shooting guard for the Los Angeles Lakers throughout his NBA career.  Hov hasn’t been known to be an avid hooper, but he did become a part-owner of the New Jersey Nets in 2004, helping relocate the franchise to Brooklyn.

2) “Shooting god like Kobe.” Jay pronounces guard like “god,” as to say his younger self was like a supreme being with his finger on a trigger.

3) “Shooting (at) God like Kobe.” Same pronunciation of “god,” but this interpretation suggests that Jay would shoot his gun at the sky, towards the heavens. This kind of celebratory gunfire is common on American holidays like Independence Day and New Years Eve, but it’s dangerous—falling strays often hit innocent bystanders.

line: Don’t matter what the brand name is I stand behind mine
vault_lines: don't matter what the brand name is
meaning:
This line is inspired by a scene in the American Gangster film which details a time when Frank Lucas found out his competitor Nicky Barnes was chopping down his “Blue Magic” heroin and reducing its quality – but then selling it under the same name.

Hov feels the same way about his personal brand as Lucas felt about “Blue Magic.” The “JAY Z Brand” has become one of the most potent in the world – but it only retains its power if consumers remain convinced that what he is selling genuinely reflects him and his tastes. He declares in this line that anything he creates or endorses can be trusted as a true reflection of his personal taste.

My brands are an extension of me. They’re close to me. It’s not like running GM, where there’s no emotional attachment. My thing is related to who I am as a person. The clothes are an extension of me. The music is an extension of me. All my businesses are part of the culture, so I have to stay true to whatever I’m feeling at the time, whatever direction I’m heading in. And hopefully, everyone follows.

line: As the incense burn And the turntables turn and that Al Green plays I see my mother’s afro As Mama taps her toes, as she rolls her J’s
vault_lines: As the incense burn
meaning:
Jay gets semi-autobiographical here, describing the scene at a house party typical of the ‘70s and '80s eras. He has explained that his childhood home in the Marcy Projects was known the “party house,” where people would come and enjoy themselves:


My Mom and Pop had the party house. We had a makeshift wall unit made out of straight plywood. It was crates of records, then plywood, crates of records, plywood, crates, plywood. Al Green, Prince, Stevie Wonder, the Jacksons, everything.

My mom had early rap records, like Jimmy Spicer. In the middle of the records was a turntable and a receiv­er – I used to scratch records on it – and on top was a reel-to-reel. In front of that wall were more stacks of records. It was either Mom’s record or Pop’s record, and they had their names on each and every one. Ha! Back then, I couldn’t understand why they shared an apartment and kids, but they couldn’t share records.


To set the scene here he claims he saw his mother, Gloria Carter, rolling up marijuana joints for the party-goers:

[They would] smoke J’s, roll ‘em up on the album covers. Back in the day you’d take the Bambu paper, push it up and the seeds would fall out. We wasn’t allowed in the parties, but of course we’d be peeking around corners.

Furthermore, there is the imagery that his mother is “creating” J’s, that is, creating “Jay-Z” and his Soul-influenced love of music.

line: Everything I do, I’m a man behind mine I’m not an angel, I’m sure But every night before I lay, I drop my knees to the floor And I pray
vault_lines: I stand behind mine
meaning:
As Jay said in “Justify My Thug”:

I never asked for nothin I don’t demand of myself
Honesty, loyalty, friends and then wealth
Death before dishonor and I tell you what else
I tighten my belt ‘fore I beg for help

Being a “man”, and all that entails, is a centrepiece to the brand of hustler or gangster you are peddling.

The verse wildly oscillates between justification for his actions, and acknowledgement that they are wrong and illegal. He prays for absolve himself of the sin, but plans to commit it again tomorrow, and the next day.

All you did was motivate me; “Don’t let ‘em hold you back”
What I do? I turned around and I sold you crack
I was a bastard for that, Still I’m drowning in shame

This was a more evolved mindset. Remember, Jay is still “fresh” in the drug game. He’s chasing money, in whatever fashion it comes.

He was birthed in this “Chicken or Egg” conundrum, hence he is “freshly” exposed to the situation, growing up in it, making it harder to step back and observe critically and objectively.

Death is the only certainty. There’s no taxes when you’re a drug dealer. And the average life expectancy of a gang member is just 21 years old…

It’s also a play on the judicial system. Jay is trying to beat a life sentence behind bars.

The line is quoted by Jay-Z  himself in this interview on Jonathan Ross

line: Ahh! Sweet taste of sin Everything I seen made me everything I am

He compares “coke” to the refreshing manner of soda pop. His mind is now so fried from the drugs – selling (which is kinda like using anyway) – that he welcomes the opportunity to break the law, to put another needle in another vein if it means a pay day.

As he said earlier, “when the rules is blurred, what am I to do?”. He’s seen the worst, the corruption and the fiends. He feels railroaded down this path.

line: Now, when the rules is blurred— As they is and were—what am I to do, but pray? Pray the Lord forgive me Pray He guides me by for what I’m ’bout to go through Pray
vault_lines: Now, when the rules is blurred—
meaning:
There’s a different set of rules we abide by here

All of a sudden, right and wrong, as we are taught in school, isn’t applicable. The police are enabling the dealers. This is one of Jay’s main rationalisations as to why he became a drug dealer in the first place. He claims he can’t be held accountable for his actions, when all he see’s around him is corruption and pain. How would you react?

He has progressed from that “D'Evils” mentality though. He prays, seeking repentance for what is about to happen on the album: a technicolour retelling of Jay Z the gangster.

line: He made his way to the trunk, opened it like, “Huh?” A treasure chest was removed Cops said he’ll be back next month What we call corrupt, he calls paying dues

Specifically referencing a scene from the movie American Gangster where Frank is pulled over by detective Trupo, whilst he has drugs in the trunk of his car. The result is, the drugs are taken by the police, and Lucas is now in debt to Trupo, something that would come back to haunt the detective later in the movie.

It runs parallel to the scene during “99 Problems” when Jay was pulled over by the police with work in his car.

In the real life version of this story, the trunk wasn’t raw, it was a compartment in the sunroof that doubled as a stash.

“Dope needles” refer to the explosion of heroin that was portrayed so lyrically in the film. During the explosion in Frank’s business, he takes a trip downtown to observe his money-making in action. People line the streets, fiending for his product “Blue Magic”.

There’s a popular trope in rap music that the only way out of the hood is “shooting hoops or live on the stereo”. What if you’re not athletic and you can’t rap? You sell drugs. You sell drugs to get by, to feed your family, to pay your mom’s light bills.

line: I’m cut from the cloth of the Kennedy’s
vault_lines: I'm cut from the cloth of the Kennedy's
meaning:
Joe Kennedy the patriarch of the Kennedy Clan. Joe was a businessman, investor and government official. It is also purported that Joe had mobster connections such as being associated with Frank Costello (who is said to be one of the most powerful men in American Mafia history).

Jay is saying that he has ties with people from the underworld, though in the public eye he is a philanthropist, music mogul and entrepreneur.

Furthermore, the Kennedy’s came from nothing to something. They began on the street and built a dynasty that is spoken of in hushed tones. Jay did the same, through his troubled upbringing to his creation of Roc-A-Fella records.

line: “Or is there something else you suggest we can do?”
vault_lines: "Or is there something else you suggest we can do?"
meaning:
The cop is suggesting he can be bribed.  Corrupt cops in a song about drug dealing? Whodathunk?

This is yet another reference to the movie American Gangster. There is a scene where the cops catch Frank Lucas with the cocaine in his trunk, and instead of arresting him, the cop takes it away to sell it for himself, and let’s Frank know in no uncertain terms that he now must be paid off in order to maintain his silence.

line: America, meet the gangster Shawn Corey “Hey, Young World,” wanna hear a story? Close your eyes and you can pretend you’re me
vault_lines: America, meet the gangster Shawn Corey
meaning:
There are some nice references in these lines.  Shawn Corey is Jay’s name, but Shawn and Corey are also best friends in the 90’s sitcom, Boy Meets World.  Jay’s inclusion of the words “meet” and “world” confirms the reference.  But it isn’t exactly “boy meets world”, it’s “gangster meets world”.  It’s a nice juxtaposition that highlights the seriousness of Jay’s situation in comparison to the regular people in the sitcom.

Jay also references Slick Rick a couple times here.  “Hey Young World” is a Slick Rick song.  And since Jay is telling the “young world” a story, he is telling a “Children’s Story”, another Slick Rick song.  And Jay takes the momentum of these references one more bar by saying “close your eyes” which is a nod to Slick Rick’s eyepatch.

But first, the age-old question is posed: what came first? The actual act of moving cocaine or the conditions that birthed the unfortunate circumstance in which one has to slang dope for his family to survive, while simultaneously destroying the family lives of others.



Vicious cycle.

line: Leave dudes in the rearview V12 engine, corners spinning Twinkies shinin’, pinky ring
vault_lines: Leave dudes in the rearview
meaning:
Here, ol' “HOV” paints a braggadocious and titillating picture of his romantic endeavors in the context of his sumptuous lifestyle.

In the first line, ol' Jay refers to leaving “dudes in the rearview,” likely referring to ex-boyfriends and sexual “boy toys” that no longer excite him, and are thus left behind as Hova speeds away. But this is no tragedy! JAY-Z describes his reckless driving, taking corners at high speeds…encapsulating his “balls-to-the-wall” lifestyle. HOV does what he wants, leaving the haters (and former male lovers) in the dust. Cars with V12 engines are also known to be highly expensive, cementing the luxury status of Jay’s ride and elevating the self-confidence of this bar…after all, who else but HOV would have the bodacious balls to drive such an expensive car so recklessly? And you already know that ol' Jay’s got the cash to pay for another…the whole song centers around his wealth and pimpishly plentiful playboy personality.



The last bar refers to “Twinkies shinin'” in Jay’s car. The term “twink” refers to a gay man without a lot of body hair. The use of the word “shinin'” likely refers to their freshly waxed bodies, which HOV will later enjoy exploring sexually. At the end of the bar, the mention of Jay’s “pinky ring” evokes images of wealth and criminal activity, as such rings have been worn by famous characters such as Michael Corleone in The Godfather and Saul Goodman in Breaking Bad.

meaning:
Jays first verse was about the enjoyable nature of spending what you’ve earnt, of showing off the money you have made. The next three verses have gone in different directions, but violence has been a centrepiece of all of them. Big Boi ties it all back up at the end, to explain that these are just lyrical barbs.

He utilises a term first penned by E-40, and was a bit of a rage in 2002, “smabbin”, to mean balling out, high rolling.

The final lines are Big Boi’s mission statement. These rappers are not only at the top of their collective games, but at the top of rap as a whole. Popping tags on the rest of the industry.

line: ’Cause the money done slowed down, just a lil bit Dipped, poked out, did some shull-bit Actin’ like a pitfall, bull-pit, dead game is the pulpit

An interesting literary device, Big Boi plays around with the words “bullshit”, “pitbull” and “pulpit” to make a point about the changing desires of a woman faced with the dilemma of a man not earning enough money to satisfy her cravings.

In the end, the “dead game” refers to both the lack of baller status the broke man now has, and also carries on from Killer Mike’s shuddering, violent verse by creating the image of someone who has actually died, and is on the pulpit during their own funeral.

“I could if I would” flips the common saying/idiom “I would if I could” in a way replaces the powerlessness of the original saying with Jay-Z’s complete confidence and control in the situation. meaning:
Here Jay sets the court scene, stepping into the position of authority as the trial’s judge.

Hov’s bars follow a basic trial procedure. After the jury files into their seats the bailiff would announce to the court:

All rise. The Court of [the People] is now in session, the Honorable Judge [Jay-Z] presiding.

Everyone remains standing until the judge enters and is seated. The judge then asks the bailiff to call the day’s calendar, known as the “docket.” Both Jay’s docket number and his mallet is a reference to his weapon of choice at the time, a 9mm handgun—which is also known as a “tool.”

At the time Jay really did have beef with a lot of people. Although his classic beef with Nas was about to be squashed, he was being attacked on all fronts from rappers like The Game, 50 Cent and Dipset.

On top of that, a lot of people wanted Jay to fail after his Presidency at Def Jam. One thing Jay always maintained, though, was that he’d rather be beefing with rappers than drug dealers. His story is legendary, and the things he’s dealt with on the street pale in comparison to what he has to deal with in hip hop.

He plays on the word “iron” to sound like “I am”, perpetually solidifying the message.

line: A journey seldom seen, the American dream
vault_lines: A journey seldom seen, the American dream
meaning:
It’s not possible to foresee the success that Jay has achieved in his life. So many times interviewers and other rappers have claimed he is “living the American dream”, but he is always at pains to explain that the American Dream is individualised. On “Empire State of Mind”, he raps:

8 million stories out there in the naked City
It’s a pity half of y’all won’t make it

The fact that even 4 million people will achieve what they deem to be the American Dream is potent. There’s no one else on the planet living like Jay Z, so to attempt to mirror his success is not possible, especially for other rappers. It sounds like a cold statement, but it’s the truth.

line: But first he brought that crack back like a yo-yo
vault_lines: But first he brought that crack back like a yo-yo
meaning:
There’s multiple layers to this line.

Before becoming a business and hip-hop mogul, Jay was a high level cocaine dealer. He brought crack back to his places of residence from far reaching places, sending it out again in the manner a yo-yo bounces up and down.

He explored the physical action of cooking crack explicitly on 2013’s “Crown”:

You already know what I could do with the coke
Dropped it in the water, made it disappear
I made it reappear, I had that bitch on a rope

That’s the physical act of yo-yo'ing cocaine. He also refers to selling and re-upping the cocaine, similar action to a yo-yo in that you buy, you sell for more, and with that money you invest back in to more cocaine to sell.

If you add that motivation and desire with his fabled intelligence, mogul-status awaits. This record came out after his reign as Def Jam President. His mogul status has only been further confirmed in the ensuing years.

Jay plays on the similarity of “ya” and “a”, with the popular congratulatory message “bundle of joy, a boy” used to show how young and green he was, lost in the “concrete jungle” without a father figure.

line: Aww, whole world’s in awe
vault_lines: Aww, whole world's in awe
meaning:
Awe is an overwhelming feeling of admiration, the whole world admires Hova!

Shock and awe is a military term, meaning rapid dominance. The whole world is in awe because powerful people are always fighting for more power. The dominance could also recall the slavery age and the relationship between whites and blacks.

AWE is also an acronym for some projects like the Australian Worldwide Exploration and the Atomic Weapon Establishment.



Basquiat’s Tuxedo also presents the word Ave various times in it



#DETAILED BREAKDOWN

In Basquiat’s “Tuxedo,” Ave. shows up as an abbreviation for avenue, lingo Jay-Z would have been familiar with as a Brooklyn boy. However, given this rap’s other imagery, one could think of the Latin word Ave (with the “v” often pronounced as a “w”) the greeting Gabriel uses when he appears before the Virgin Mary to announce that she will bear the Son of God. The archangel’s full greeting, “Ave Maria, gratia plena,” means “Hail Mary, full of grace,” which Biggie Smalls quoted in his song “Dead Wrong.”



It should be added that this line from “Dead Wrong” draws a dichotomy between the sacrosanct body of the Virgin and the expendable body of a woman carrying “her Gucci bag and her Northface.” One could link this theme of getting rich through street violence to the themes addressed in “Ocean,” namely, acquiring wealth through violence against an entire race (i.e., slavery)

line: In trouble waters I had to learn how to float

Hov is referring to his rough upbringing in his early years. His childhood home was the Marcy Projects, and as mentioned in the previous line, he was a crack dealer. The Marcy projects are the “trouble water” where he had to sell crack to survive (stay “afloat”). Hov had to turn his life around, culminating in the 1996 release of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt.



Today, Hov is one of the most successful musicians/businessmen in America, with an estimated net worth of $500 million. He has ventured into the world of sports as well as clothing, has a stable family, and has certainly learned “how to float.”



Troubled water recalls John 5:4

For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water: whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in was made whole of whatsoever disease he had.

Jay-Z went through the troubled waters (A metaphor for his drug dealing past) and came out of them clean, able to float, just like Jesus. He’s the God MC after all, isn’t he?

line: Silk and fleeces,
vault_lines: Blessings, blessings, yeah, I see..
meaning:
What appears to be a further reference to Hermes cotton goes much deeper, with a ton of possible references and meanings.



For students of mythology, the word “fleece” will instantly bring to mind the golden fleece. The hero Jason has to retrieve the golden fleece from the claws of an immense dragon in order to regain his rightful place as ruler. In some versions, the goddess Atalanta travels on Jason’s ship, the Argo, as the only female member of the crew. This ties the mythology back to the mention of Atalanta (the “sailing lady” with “ivory”) in the first line of Frank’s hook.

Hov mentions Jesus in the next line, a reference to a Jesus piece, but also to the Christian Lord, who is referred to as the lamb of god because he, like a sacrificial lamb, gave his life for the sins of Christian believers.

Without going into too much depth, there are also a number of secret societies that use the imagery of fleece and wool, including the Order of the Golden Fleece and the Freemasons. Given the many plausible references to secret history in the song…

meaning:
Jean-Michel Basquiat was an American graffiti artist, Neo-expressionist, and Primitivist. He was known especially for his social commentary in relation to race.



Ocean’s fear of dirtying his white tuxedo (a white tuxedo conveying sophistication and class) with his black skin “before the Basquiat show” is an ironic reference to past and present segregation. The whites didn’t want their way of life to be tainted by the negroes (aka Frank Ocean’s black skin dirtying the white tuxedo). To this day the effects of that are seen by the social separation of whites from other races.

The reference to a ‘white tuxedo’ might also be taken as a metaphor for light-skinned people of colour who do not look ‘black’.

Alternatively, the dirty suit metaphor could also refer to Basquiat’s actual suits. JM Basquiat was known to wear expensive designer suits while painting in his studio and would make public appearances while wearing these paint-stained suits.

Tuxedo is also the title of a Basquiat canvas: the work is completely black and white.



There’s also a Basquiat painting called Slave Ships, the main topic of the song. It portrays an African tribesman in regalia, smiling, but in the distance, one can see slave ships approaching…



Some believe that this line makes a connection to earlier  lines of the song. The first line talks about the scandals illegal activity that goes on in the less prosperous Ivory Coast. Here, then, the white tuxedo represents the lavish lifestyle and the black skin refers to what white people expect of people from poor African countries.

He alludes to the 1960 film Ocean’s Eleven which starred Jay-Z’s idol Frank Sinatra. In the film, Danny Ocean gathers a group of his World War II compatriots to pull off the ultimate Las Vegas heist. We all know, of course, how much Jay loves him some Frank Sinatra.

During the filming of its sequel (Ocean’s 12), Clooney would regularly host the cast and crew on a yacht docked near his home in Lake Como, Italy. This was viewed by many as the ultimate in celebrity balling.



To connect this with the song’s overall connotation, look no further than Sammy Davis, a civil rights activist who was also a member of the Rat Pack and one of the main stars of Ocean’s 11. As a Jewish African-American, he faced discrimination from society in the racially-charged 1950s and ‘60s, largely due to his interracial marriage to May Britt.

To suggest another meaning to the lyric, this is the last line before the hook from Frank Ocean. A well known phrase from the movie Spinal Tap is “Turn it up to 11.” Normally, the volume dial only goes to 10, so 11 means he’s over the top, 110%, going hard, going ham. line: The Magna Carta
vault_lines: Blessings, blessings, yeah, I see..
meaning:
#THE MAGNA CARTA

Half the name of Jay-Z’s album Magna Carta Holy Grail. “Carta” is a play on “Carter,” Jay’s surname.

Historically, it’s called the Angevin charter, or  the Magna Carta, one of the first documents forced onto a King of England by a group of his subjects in an attempt to limit his powers by law and protect their privileges. It’s an essential document of history and the development of democracy.



Jay debuted the art for the album next to a page from the real Magna Carta in Salisbury, UK. “We are delighted that Jay Z has chosen Salisbury Cathedral, home to the finest of the four surviving original 1215 Magna Carta, as the location for the global premiere of his artwork for Magna Carta Holy Grail,“ The Dean of Salisbury, the Very Revd June Osborne, said.

We know how important Magna Carta, and all it represents, is to people across the globe. The ideals it embodies are still relevant today. Jay Z, through his album, is creating a huge awareness of this historic document and its modern significance to a huge audience in the run up to its 800th anniversary in 2015. We hope to welcome many of his fans here this summer to see the artwork in the Chapter House alongside our Magna Carta.

Jay also wants to draw attention to some of the deeper meanings of his lyrics through the Magna Carta Holy Grail album art, by drawing an inference to this quote:

I cross out words so you will see them more: the fact that they are obscured makes you want to read them
– JM Basquiat.

Pretty sweet for fans of history and hip-hop.

vault_lines: Elephant tusk on the bow of a sailing lady, docked on the Ivory Coast
meaning:
These lines begin the usage of the white imagery portrayed throughout the song. Ivory is a color that’s an off-white. The image depicted is one in which a boat is docked in Cote d'Ivoire, a country known as the Ivory Coast.

The Ivory Coast has a long history with elephants and ivory  poaching. This country used to be filled with elephants, but currently, the population is under the threat of extinction due to poaching.

Elephants are poached for their ivory tusks, which are very valuable. The tusks being on the bow of a sailing lady (a ship) shows that they’ve already been killed. If you’d like to help stop elephant poaching, check out the Bloody Ivory website.



“Elephant tusks of the bore of a sailing lady docked on the Ivory Coast” might also refer to the slave trade and the money Europeans made off black bodies. The old money that helps them afford their Mercedes in a row, winding down the road…

These lines also bring to mind the Greek goddess Atalanta. Listen to how Frank pronounces “bow” like a bow and arrows, not like the bow of a ship. She has been depicted as carrying her arrows in an ivory quiver, and was, herself, a sailor. Her mythology involved sailing and the ocean. Numerous ships have been named Atalanta over the years, and of course, the city of Atlanta itself.



Another interpretation of these lines portray a reference to the ivory figureheads on slave ships (above), ornately decorated with the trappings of wealth, concealing squalor below deck. The comparison between “clean” white and “dirty” black takes on a new level of irony here, as it really the white slavers who are “dirty” in the figurative sense.

To tie it all back in to elephant poaching, note that these ships held cargo not only of human chattel, but also of ivory. When the wreck of the Dutch slaver Fredenborg was salvaged by divers, they found elephant ivory in the wreck. One can only imagine that the more readily dissolvable bones of slaves might also have been found.

line: On the holiday playin’ “Strange Fruit” If I’ma make it to a billi, I can’t take the same route
vault_lines: On the holiday playin' "Strange Fruit"
meaning:
This is a reference to Billie Holiday’s 1939 rendition of “Strange Fruit.” Famously sampled by Kanye West on 2013’s  “Blood on the Leaves,” the song provides a vivid description of lynching, and how it was rampant in The South. Note Jay’s usage of “holiday” and “billi,” as those words play along with the reference. Also note the homonyms ‘route’ and ‘root’; in “Strange Fruit,” Holiday says:

Southern trees bear a strange fruit
Blood on the leaves and blood at the root



The “holiday” in this line is most likely Independence Day, which also served as the release date for Magna Carta Holy Grail. To take the same route would be to die at the hands of discrimination. This is a continuation of the theme of expanding beyond what Jay has done in the past to accumulate wealth. In the beginning, he and Ty Ty sold drugs to make money; then he used rap to gain wealth; then he became an author, and so on.

Taking another approach at this line, the “route” could be in reference to transatlantic slave trade, a system notorious for the bringing of many slaves to colonial North America. The ships docked at ports in Africa, such as the Ivory Coast, and then went along their route to the colonies. This ties back in with the overall interpretation of the song that was first noted in the beginning of the chorus—that the ocean is symbolic in terms of enslavement, but also looked at as a sign of freedom.

As of 2013, Jay’s net worth was $500,000,000. He still had a long way to go in order to double his net worth. On June 3, 2019—nearly six years following the release of this song—Forbes reported that Jay had doubled his worth and officially become rap’s first billionaire.

The way Jay-Z pronounces “enticing” here employs a heterograph to create multiple meanings. His music is attractive and alluring to the audience with his lexical dexterity and ability to supply strong metaphorical imagery.

Then, the way Jay pronounces “enticing” can also be heard as “Tyson” – that is, Mike Tyson, the American professional boxer who once held the undisputed world heavyweight championship. This boxing reference then connects this line with the previous two about landing blows and knocking sense into the opposition.

Funnily enough in 2013, almost twenty years later, Jay-Z would again use the enticing/Tyson heterograph in reference to the perils of fame – something he was beginning to chase at the time of this record.

As a fellow Brooklynite, Jay noted in an interview that he was so devastated when a then-undefeated Tyson lost his 1990 fight to Buster Douglas in Tokyo he felt “physically hurt” himself.

line: From record sales, to sold-out concerts So, motherfucker, if you want this encore I need you to scream ’til your lungs get sore (Come on)
vault_lines: From record sales, to sold-out concerts
meaning:
Hova uses a translation of the famous Latin phrase “Veni, vidi, vici,” reportedly written by Julius Caesar. This in literature is called an Asyndeton. Caesar used the phrase to describe his military prowess when he conquered all of Europe (other than Scotland). Its basic premise is “Everywhere I have gone, I have fought against everything mankind had to throw at me, and I defeated everything in sight”

Jay uses it in a similar context to show just how dominant he has become in the rap game. He’s travelled the world, dealt with some fucked up shit in his life, and everything he has seen and battled, he has conquered it.

After becoming the most successful rapper ever and one of the best live artists in the history of the rap game, he’s ready for an encore as long as the audience can get loud enough during the interlude that follows these lines.

“45” also refers to a Colt 45 pistol – Jay will come back “packing heat” and won’t be scared to aim a gun at you and pull the trigger, either maiming or killing you. So whatever 45 Jay decides to wear, both insinuate that he’ll “fire shots” at you.

In “It Ain’t Personal” Jay raps:

Normally, one would “crack” a code, not a safe. But Jay followed the G code by not snitching. The safe is simply the safety of the rap game. He was able to crack the safe open (starting Roc-A-Fella with his drug money) and feast on the legal, luscious lifestyle inside.

line: So fuck DeHaven for caving, that’s why we don’t speak Made men ain’t supposed to make statements

meaning:
Dehaven Irby was a hustling associate of Jay’s. He introduced him to the hustling game.

The two had a minor beef around this time. Dehaven claimed Jay wasn’t loyal, and that when he was released from prison Roc Nation “turned their back” on him, almost as if the two had never been close.

The truth? We might ask Memphis Bleek for that. He did an interview in 2014 in which he seemed to explain the situation.

DeHaven is from my projects; we all from the same building. Him and Jay had their hustle ties and things went sour. You want to know the real deal? All you got to do is listen to “A Week Ago” and what’s the joint with R. Kelly where you know your true friends when you both got money. 

The tracks in question, “A Week Ago” and “It Ain’t Personal” are descriptive. “A Week Ago” is the tale of a hustler, incarcerated, who begins to leak information about his associates.

The lawyer I retained you said you leakin some things
All this after a week in the bing

DeHaven had a federal drugs charge around the time the track was released…

“It Ain’t Personal” details the reason for the eventual falling out:

We move through the hood like identical twins
But it just so happen that a nigga made it rappin
You showed your true colors, y'all niggas stay yappin
That don’t stop him, a nigga weigh platinum

Essentially, Jay is saying DeHaven snitched.

In a 2019 interview, Dehaven responded to this bar.

line: Like, Frank Lucas is cool, but I ain’t trying to snitch I’ma follow the rules, no matter how much time I’ma get
vault_lines: Like, Frank Lucas is cool, but I ain't trying to snitch
meaning:
This line uncovers an uncomfortable part of the Frank Lucas story.

Lucas cooperated with authorities in order to reduce his sentence. He “snitched” on his cohorts and business partners, something that is punishable by death in the drug dealing game.

Jay has never been an advocate for snitching, yet his hero was one of the biggest in American history, especially during the movie.

Interestingly, he addressed the very issue of the suitably for movies to mimick real life in his book Decoded, talking about Sacrface:

So many people saw their story in that movie. I’ve always found this a little strange because at the end of the movie, Tony gets shot. He’s wasted. His life is in ruins. His family is destroyed. It seems like the movie ends in some people’s minds about two-thirds of the way through, because it all goes to shit for Tony. And for those two-thirds they are Tony. And after the movie, Tony is still alive in them as an inspiration.

He did go on to qualify this with:

The viewer inhabits the character while the movie runs but when it’s over, the character lives on in the viewer. So instead of passing judgement on Tony, you make a complete empathetic connection to the good and the bad in him.

So Jay cherry picks the parts of Lucas' character that he likes, applies it as inspiration for this record, but discards the aspects he dislikes. The snitching.

As movies are not sold scene by scene, this collection will not be sold as individual singles

This is an experience, a cinematic event, not just the hot new record from the hot rapper.

line: Choices we make, trying to escape, ’scape
vault_lines: Choices we make, trying to escape, 'scape
meaning:
During “Can I Live,” Jay spat the immortal words:

I’d rather die enormous than live dormant, that’s how we on it

His entire first album was dedicated to the choice he made – to be a hustler, and to escape the life that was laid out before him. One of poverty, of hard times.

Even bigger was the decision to relinquish his cocaine empire and make it as a rapper.

On 2003’s The Black Album Jay was autobiographical, rapping:

Till I decided to try this rap shit for a living

It’s a small, almost insignificant line, but it makes all the difference. Jay chased his dream, a dream of being straight and earning real, taxable, legal money. He made the choice to hustle to escape poverty, and he made the choice to rap to escape the underworld.

meaning:
Imagine the pain of Jay’s mother. She’s already lost her husband, Jay’s brother is addicted to crack, and now her youngest is hitting the streets. Couple that with the life expectancy of a young gang member in the US, just 21 years old. It’s no wonder she was terrified.

As Jay said:

Easily explain why we adapt to crime
I’d rather die enormous than live dormant, that’s how we on it

It’s something he condoned from a young age. Bet bit and win, or lose it all and accept your fate. What’s worse: A life spent living on the edge of poverty, of depression and mental illness brought about by ill circumstances. Or a son in a casket at age 21, a son who tried his best to deliver all the riches in the world to his family?

He’s dead either way, so at least take a chance that he might actually make it out.

line: A place to study math at – matter of fact, I learned it all
vault_lines: A place to study math at – matter of fact, I learned it all
meaning:
Studying math in this context is deceiving, it’s not literally studying mathematics. Jay learnt his numbers from dealing crack: budgets, addition and subtraction, multiplication. The streets raised him.

He bends the words “matter of fact” to make it a near homophone of “math at”. Not only did he learn maths in the streets, he learned about life in general. The streets weren’t his second home, they were his first, and they raised him.

“To live and die in N.Y.” might be Jay’s way of combining the West Coast banger from 2Pac “To Live & Die In L.A.” with Nas' East Coast anthem “N.Y. State Of Mind.”

New York City is often represented as a sort of utopia, often associated with themes of finding the “American Dream.” To succeed in New York one must master the art of hustling.

Hov has always presented himself as the ultimate hustler, finding success both illegally and legally. As Jay understatedly said on Kanye’s “Diamonds From Sierra Leone” remix:

I sold kilos of coke, I’m guessin' I could sell CD’s
