These are the set of principles that both Frank Lucas and Hov will abide by throughout their criminality. Hov would continue along this moral compass as he moved from drug-dealing to the legitimate music business:

I’m a man of principles; damn-near invincible

This dialogue is sampled from the album’s inspiration, the film American Gangster. Frank Lucas has just brought his brothers in from North Carolina to help him manage his burgeoning drug empire, and he lays down these tenets as the keys to both his and their success.

Immediately after this, he goes outside and shoots a Harlem business rival, Tango, in the head.

Challah bread is a white, leavened bread that Jews eat during the Sabbath . This connects to the next line in which he states that his lawyer is, in fact, a Jew.



There’s a racial trope that Jewish people make more money than average Americans, the kind of money that can smooth over illegal activities.

Jay’s “Challah bread” is also money, so his Jewish lawyer is doubly happy to receive it.

On the surface, it is either a simple metaphor. You can choose to delve deeper into the meaning. Challah Bread is associated with the Sabbath, so Jay is extending the holiness of the Sabbath to his seemingly unclean drug-earned money to say hustling is his sacred activity. He is, after all, Jay Hova.

This is a remnant from the Dame Dash school of thought. Not quite as extreme, but just as influential.

He would also reference this point on “We Made It Freestyle:”:

I own my own masters
You know I ain’t missin' no royalty statements

This links directly to the movie American Gangster. Denzel’s character Frank Lucas says:

Bumpy was rich, but he wasn’t white man rich, you see he wasn’t wealthy. He didn’t own his own company. He thought he did, but he didn’t. He just managed it. White man owned it so they owned him. Nobody owns me, though. Because I own my company.

Not only did Jay negotiate to have his masters returned to him, he also bought out his last album from Def Jam, freeing him to move on to a deal with Live Nation which spawned Roc Nation. Jay was still his own boss.

keep my movements smooth while manuevering, through all the manure in the sewer that I grew up in

Rolling in the Rolls Royce Corniche

line: Turn nickels to dime, turn dimes to quarters
vault_lines: Turn nickels to dime, turn dimes to quarters
meaning:
Jay loves rapping about the money he accumulated while selling drugs. Usually he shouts out higher denominations, but here he’s emphasizing that he started out from the very bottom – nickels are $5 bags, dimes are $10 bags, and quarters are ¼ ounces. Nickle-and-dime is also an expression of either cheapness – meaning it’s not even worth it – or of small amounts accumulating over time.

Notably, Hova mentions “nickles” and “dime,” in the singular. This could be a reference to one of the greatest punk records of all time, Double Nickles on the Dime by Minutemen (this wouldn’t be his first reference to 20th century rock and roll on this album). The album’s title comes from making fun of a Van Halen song that complains about new driving laws restricting speeds to 55 mph – to mock them, Minutemen made their cover art feature a square-looking guy happily driving 55 mph on Interstate Highway 10 (hence “two nickels on a dime”). Their message was that speeding isn’t all that defiant or badass – instead, they would make an epic album of crazy punk music. Similarly, Jay-Z left the seemingly ‘badass’ drug business where he was dealing nickels, dimes and quarters in order to make truly defiant art.

In his famous final speech before his death, which was given while filming his last movie, Eyes Wide Shut (referenced in the next line), Kubrick compares the late great filmmaker D.W. Griffith to Icarus.



Icarus is the mythical figure that embodies hubris: with his inherited wings of wax and feathers, he flies too high and the sun melts his wings, causing Icarus to fall to his death.

Kubrick, however, reinterprets this classic tale of fatal pride:

I’ve compared Griffith’s career to the Icarus myth, but at the same time I’ve never been certain whether the moral of the Icarus story should only be, as is generally accepted, ‘Don’t try to fly too high,’ or whether it might also be thought of as, ‘Forget the wax and feathers and do a better job on the wings.’

This is Hova’s way of saying that his ambition is not the problem—in fact, it’s his ambition and hard work that’s going to lead him and others to greatness. He gives a similar defense of his ambition in the song “Moment of Clarity”:

If you’re not familiar with J. Ivy, that’s probably because he’s a spoken-word poet, not a rapper. J. Ivy himself explains how he landed on the track:

At 11:00 pm on December 7, 2002, I get a call from Coodie [a mutual friend of mine and Kanye’s]. He said, ‘J, you need to get to L.A. Kanye got this song with him and Jay Z and he wants to put a poet on it. I told him he had to put J. Ivy on it.’ I was like, ’Stop bullshitting.’ He was a comedian, so he was always joking. But they were at Record Plant in Hollywood, and Coodie goes into their studio space and plays the song for me over the phone. I couldn’t really hear the words but he told me what Jay and Kanye were saying in the verse. He was like, ‘J, get out here right now.‘ I said, ‘I’ll find a way,’ and hung up.

He claims God helped him write the song, and then:


I called Coodie and I spit it to him over the phone. He goes in the other room and I hear a bunch of people talking. The music goes down and the people get quiet. He put me on speaker phone, and I spit the piece as if I had done it a million times. When I finished the room exploded. I’m in Bedstuy, broke and by myself. I was like, ‘What’s going on? What’s happening over there?’ I hear Kanye say, ‘Man J, spit it again.’ I did the joint for a half hour, and the piece was only a minute long. So I did it over, over, over and over again. Coodie finally got back on the phone and said, ‘Guess what? Kanye is flying you out here tomorrow.’ I found my way.

[…] On my flight there I was practicing. I perfected it and added one more line. After performing onstage at the Improv†, from there we piled up in a limo, we went to the studio and Kanye was like, ‘You ready?’

[…] “He told me ‘to bring it down just a little bit’ and do it one more time. I did it one more time. Now, I thought I was warmed up and was ready to do it the third time. But he said, ‘That’s it – that was the one.’”

meaning:
“walk softly [and] carry a big clip” is a play on the very famous quote made by Theodore Roosevelt (26th president of the United States) which is “speak softly and carry a big stick”.

Co-founder of Roc-A-Fella Records Damon “Dame” Dash, who would later have a noted falling out with Hov.

Stay hungry, stay foolish

line: When you stop, then you gotta bid it good riddance Goodbye! This is my second major break-up My first was with a pager, with a hoopty, a cook-pot, and the game This one’s with the stu’, with the stage, with the fortune— Well, maybe not the fortune—but certainly the fame

First Jay retired from the drug game, where he’d use a pager to take orders, a hooptie (crappy car) to avoid drawing attention from police, and cookpot to make crack.

Now he’s retiring from the rap game. Note how here he uses “stu'” to mean studio, whereas earlier it referred to his old neighborhood.

In Decoded, Jay calls the way he says “maybe not the fortune” a “bad Prince impersonation.”
In “Adore,” Prince sings:

You could burn up my clothes, smash up my ride
Well, maybe not the ride, but I got to have your face

Jay is a noted Prince fan and listed him as a favorite artist (along with Seal) in a 1996 interview.

line: [Intro: Jay Z]
vault_lines: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder
meaning:
According to producer S1, Jay and Kanye would set up two microphones facing each other, freestyling over beats played by producers in the room. This Jay interlude was taken from his original ad-libs, and he sculpted his verse in only ten minutes:

The way Jay sculpts his ideas and lyrics is so crazy because as soon as I play it, he’s like mumbling and then literally like 10 minutes later, he grabs the engineer, like ‘Yo I’m ready.’ He comes to the mic and just breezes through it. Like he’s writing in his mind as he’s looking around, it’s so brilliant.

line: [Part II: Excellence]
vault_lines: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder
meaning:
The “Excellence” portion of the song (originally titled “Black Excellence”) was produced by Texas native Symbolyc One (S1).



S1 revealed in an interview with Revolt that Kanye and Jay flew him out to London, where they recorded this track:


After I did “Power” I was working with Kanye a lot. So, I would be with him a lot at his sessions … [one day] he told me, ‘Yo me and Jay thinking about doing this collaborative album, we want you to come out and we just gonna go to some random countries and record it.’ He’s so spur of the moment, so I get an email one day like, ‘Fly out to London with me and Jay tonight!’

I remember when I played the “Murder to Excellence” beat, I remember this certain face that Jay gave me. He looked up at me like, ‘Yo, what is this?!’

line: [Verse 1: Jay Z]
vault_lines: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder
meaning:
In a 2011 interview with MTV, Bu Thiam (Def Jam’s Vice-President of A&R) contrasted  Hova’s opulent, materialistic portrayal of himself in this verse with Thiam’s personal experience with Jay Z, the man:

As much as people may think that Jay talks about money and cars, he’s really not that guy. Of course he has it, but his whole mission is to build. He wants to have others join him, he’s trying to build black excellence, like the black youth as the next [generation of] executives.

line: [Produced by S1 and Swizz Beatz]
vault_lines: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder
meaning:
This two-part track consists of “Murder”, produced by Swizz Beatz, and “Excellence” produced by S1.

“Murder” contains a sample of Indiggo Twins’s “La La La,” while “Excellence” samples Quincy Jones’s composition “Katutoka Corrine” from The Color Purple’s soundtrack and “Sorcerer of Isis” by Power of Zeus.

line: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder Bloody murder, murder, murder, murder Bloody murder, murder, murder, murder Bloody murder, murder, murder
vault_lines: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder
meaning: This is a continuation of the end of the last song, “Who Gon Stop Me”, which ends by echoing “black strap, you know what that’s for”. We get our answer here – it is used to commit massive murder. This also foreshadows what the first half of the song will expose – murder in inner cities like Chicago.

line: And said the church ain’t got enough room for all the tombs
vault_lines: And said the church ain't got enough room for all the tombs
meaning: There are so many deaths that there isn’t any room left to place the bodies. This emphasizes the likening of all the murders to genocide, as genocide memorials pay respect to the event as a whole rather than each individual victim.

line: It’s a celebration of Black excellence, black tie, black Maybachs Huh, yeah, uh
vault_lines: It's a celebration of Black excellence, black tie, black Maybachs
meaning: The interlude serves as a transition between the two halves of the song; Murder – Excellence. Jay and Kanye turn from the horror of black-on-black violence to their concerns regarding the under-represenation of blacks among the American elite.

line: Black excellence, truly yours
vault_lines: Black excellence, truly yours
meaning: A double meaning to end the song – “truly yours” could be a final goodbye, as in a letter. Or it could also mean that black excellence could be “truly yours” – as in, it could be something the listener could, and should be a part of. This effort at including and celebrating the listener as opposed to Kanye himself is a notable departure from his usual practice.

line: New crib, watch a movie ‘Cause there ain’t nothin’ on the news but the blues
vault_lines: New crib, watch a movie
meaning:
Yeezy gets the blues due to the widespread media bias that  portrays black folks as perpetrators or victims of crime.

Blues could also refer to the Crips in Chi-town. It’s depressing for Kanye to see all the gang warfare occurring in his hometown. This is very similar to a line Kanye spits on “Gorgeous”.

line: I’ll be a real man, take care of your son Every problem you had before this day is now done
vault_lines: I'll be a real man, take care of your son
meaning:
In Kanye’s opening verse, he says “41 souls murdered in 50 hours”, which is an even more explicit example of his sentiment on his song 2 Words, in which he says “It’s only two places you end up, dead or in jail”.

The act of taking care of a man’s child if he is incarcerated or dies is seen as an essential role, as many people grew up in the ghetto’s of America with no father figure whatsoever, having lost them to death, jail or just the streets. It’s something Jay-Z also explores on “Anything”, and Kanye is showing solidarity with his people, ensuring the future success of the race as a whole by nurturing those who are without a parent.

line: Is it genocide? ’Cause I can still hear his mama cries
vault_lines: 'Cause I can still hear his mama cries
meaning:
Kanye wonders if black-on-black crime (and society’s complicity in it) can be likened to a genocide, which is technically defined as “the deliberate and systematic destruction, in whole or in part, of an ethnic, racial, religious, or national group”.

The historian Ward Churchill reminds us that genocide, by its legal definition, has existed in America since its first settlement by whites – that is, genocide against the native population.  See here for a brief list of historical genocides, including mention of the trans-Atlantic slave trade.

Surely the oppression of blacks in America since the 1600s both institutionally, psychologically, and physically (incidental) is a form of genocide.

line: From parolees that hold G’s, sold keys, low keys We like the promised land of the OG’s In the past if you picture events like a black tie What the last thing you expect to see? Black guys
vault_lines: From parolees that hold G's, sold keys, low keys
meaning:
A powerful four lines. The first reminds folks of the hustling lives led by many young black men – a struggle that has often been more in Jay’s purview than Kanye’s. Even Fox News knows Jay Z sold crack.

The second sets up the duo as a logical end point for black aspirations, noting that the OG’s would recognize the culmination of their street struggles in Jay and Kanye’s massive success and cultural influence.

The final couplet continues this idea, reminding us that not long ago, it would have been literally unthinkable to see blacks in high society.  These lines also continue the album’s motif of black culture, which shows up in lots of different contexts throughout the album, but never as the simplistic “black equals bad” racist formulation so prevalent in pop culture.

line: What’s up to Will? Uh, shout out to O, uh That ain’t enough, we gonna need a million more, uh Kick in the door, uh, Biggie flow
vault_lines: What's up to Will? Uh, shout out to O, uh
meaning:
A key section to the song and album. Jay posits the likes of Will Smith and Oprah as members of the “new black elite”, as mentioned earlier in the song.

Rather than keeping his success for himself, Jay wants young blacks to “kick in the door”  and enter this new elite in humungous numbers. This doubles as a tribute to The Notorious B.I.G., who was shot down by the violence described in this song before he had a chance to kick in the door himself.



This is also a shoutout to Will Smith and Will’s daughter (and Roc Nation artist) Willow Smith.

line: No cheap cologne whenever I “shh-shh” Success never smelled so sweet
vault_lines: No cheap cologne whenever I "shh-shh"
meaning:
Jay uses alliteration and onomatopoeia to express his distaste in cheap cologne. “Shh-shh” mimics the sound of spraying cologne.



Fun fact: In the movie Red Dragon which stars Hannibal Lector (who also appears in Silence of the Lambs) – Hannibal accuses Will Graham (an FBI agent) of smelling like fear under his cheap cologne.

line: In sheepskin coats, I silence the lambs Do you know who I am, Clarice?
vault_lines: In sheepskin coats, I silence the lambs
meaning:
Hov alludes to the film The Silence of the Lambs featuring the cannibal psychopath Hannibal. The film stars Jodie Foster, who plays the protagonist Clarice Starling. Clarice carries early traumatic memories of sheep being slaughtered at her relative’s farm.

The sheep that were slaughtered on Clarice’s farm are the same ones Hov wears on his back.

line: Paper read, “Murder, Black-on-Black murder” Paper read, “Murder, Black-on-Black murder” again (Uh)
vault_lines: Uh, bloody murder, murder, murder
meaning:
Black-on-black violence has been a hot-button issue for quite some time. Whilst some academics claim that its use became a way for the media to argue that “black culture” was “defective (and) aberrant,” the reality is that the gang violence between black communities is higher than ever.

According to the National Gang Center:

In a typical year in the so-called “gang capitals” of Chicago and Los Angeles, around half of all homicides are gang-related; these two cities alone accounted for approximately one in four gang homicides recorded in the NYGS from 2011 to 2012

The issue was brought to more light in 2015 due to the comments of Kendrick Lamar in an interview with Billboard. When asked about the high-profile killings of African-Americans by police in 2014, Kendrick replied:

I wish somebody would look in our neighborhood knowing that it’s already a situation, mentally, where it’s f—ked up. What happened to [Michael Brown] should’ve never happened. Never. But when we don’t have respect for ourselves, how do we expect them to respect us? It starts from within. Don’t start with just a rally, don’t start from looting – it starts from within.

Kanye and Jay use “Murder” to express how sad is to see black men destroying each other when they should do the exact opposite and fight against the real issues that are still around and affect them every single day.

line: Too much enemy fire to catch a friendly Strays from the same shade, nigga, we on the same team Giving you respect, I expect the same thing, uh
vault_lines: Too much enemy fire to catch a friendly
meaning:
Friendly fire is a military term for when someone is shot by their own, or otherwise friendly forces (sometimes called “blue-on-blue”).

Jay points out that black America has more than enough problems with systemic racism and police violence (as per the Danroy Henry case mentioned in the previous line), so the additional threat of what is sometimes called black-on-black crime should be eliminated.

line: I stink of success, the new Black elite
vault_lines: I stink of success, the new Black elite
meaning:
On the surface, this is continuation of the “sweet smell of success” idea above.

On a deeper level, the concept of a new black elite is central to the album’s mantra. Jay and Kanye strive to represent a new black elite, one that represents both high class and hip-hop culture. As Kanye wrote in a XXL story:

I am where art meets commercial.  The sweet spot between the hood and Hollywood.  Having a conversation with Karl Lagerfeld and Jay-Z within the same hour.  When we’re in Paris dressing all crazy at fashion shows, we listening to Jeezy.  Jeezy in Paris, that’s what it is.

The duo not only revels in their status, but consciously try to serve as an inspiration for people to join their ranks.

line: Power to the people, when you see me, see you
vault_lines: Power to the people, when you see me, see you
meaning:
Jigga represents his fans – so when you look at The Throne, you’re looking at yourself.  This is a theme throughout the album, where Jay and Kanye not only celebrate themselves as members of a new black elite, but call on their fans to join its ranks.

Jay also says says “power to the people” in the remix of Kanye’s single “Power”.

line: Sunday morning, praise the Lord You the girl that Jesus had been saving me for So let’s savor this moment and take it to the floor
vault_lines: Sunday morning, praise the Lord
meaning: Kanye continues the theme of blending religion with sex, claiming the only way to thank God for blessing him with a beautiful woman is having kinky sex with her on the bedroom floor.

line: So we won’t take the time out ’til we reach the T-O-P
vault_lines: So we won't take the time out 'til we reach the T-O-P
meaning: Ye and Jay want to stand on the mountain top. Note the “we” is ambiguous – Ye could be alluding to himself and Jay only, or to the entire black race.

line: Real niggas just multiply
vault_lines: Real niggas just multiply
meaning: This line is likely homage to Ice-T – not Jay’s first, incidentally. Thus, Jay is implying that the revolutionary spirit of Fred Hampton was continued through Hov and his work.  See here for another Jay shout-out to a murdered revolutionary.

line: Plus his little brother got shot reppin’ his avenue It’s time for us to stop and redefine Black power
vault_lines: Plus his little brother got shot reppin' his avenue
meaning:
People get in fights for what they “rep” – their hometown, gang, corner, etc. This line alludes to Chi-town incidents in which young teens, and 20-somethings needlessly lose their lives.

Kanye implicitly contrasts this with the civil rights and black power movements, where people were fighting for equality, freedom, and justice.  See the Black Panthers' famous Ten-Point Program for an idea of the goals of the more radical wing of the movement



Yeezy’s own father, not coincidentally, was a member of the Panthers

line: Heard about at least three killings this afternoon Looking at the news like, “Damn, I was just with him after school”
vault_lines: Heard about at least three killings this afternoon
meaning: Ye describes the harshness of living in the hood, and highlights the demographic this affects most – the youth. There’s no telling if you’ll see your friends tomorrow at school..

line: All-black everything, nigga, you know my fresh code I’m out here fighting for you, don’t increase my stress load
vault_lines: All-black everything, nigga, you know my fresh code
meaning:
Just like the original man in black – Jonny Cash, Jay’s dress code in 2011 was an all black look.

Jay Z’s fighting for the black man to progress, but their actions are only making it harder for him.



Jay would mention this again at the start of his guest verse on Justin Timberlake’s “Suit & Tie:”

All black at the white shows

line: Yeah, it’s all messed up when it’s nowhere to go
vault_lines: Yeah, it's all messed up when it's nowhere to go
meaning:
Jay-Z’s previous verse deals exclusively with the upper echelon of black society, the way that he has broken glass ceilings to now chill with royalty and Government.

Kanye takes it back in time slightly, echoing the sentiment from Jay-Z’s classic “Can’t Knock The Hustle”, the idea that even though Kanye was rich during the 2000s, he didn’t have the same social opportunities that comparatively rich white people had.

Country clubs, gala events, fundraisers, these were not associated with rappers at the time, so although Kanye had money, and was dressed up really nice and tight, he basically had the club or a ball game to go to as his options.

line: Know the family traumatized Shots left holes in his face about piranha-sized The old pastor closed the cold casket
vault_lines: Know the family traumatized
meaning: The murder victim in this verse was shot so badly that the funeral had to have a closed casket.  The image of piranha bites is not accidental – the notoriously carnivorous fish with a “sharp appetite for meat” serves as a metaphor for the rapacious and tragic violence of inner-city Chicago.

line: They say my Black Card bear the mark of the beast
vault_lines: They say my Black Card bear the mark of the beast
meaning:
An invitation-only credit card issued by American Express; cardholders reportedly must have spent at least $200K in the calendar or fiscal year to qualify. Otherwise known to Kanye as the “African-American Express”.



Ironically, the Black Card really does bear the mark of the “beast”. Biblical scholars have stated “beast” and “Antichrist” were references to the Roman Empire. As seen above, the American Express logo is the Roman Centurion.

line: Forty-one souls murdered in fifty hours
vault_lines: Forty-one souls murdered in fifty hours
meaning: Between March 31st and April 2nd, 2010, 41 people were shot in Chicago.  Only four of those people died, but what Kanye’s really getting at is the fact that the people who fired the guns have “murdered” their own souls by giving into violence.

line: If you put crabs in a barrel to ensure your survival You gon’ end up pulling down niggas that look just like you What up, Blood? Uh, what up, cuz? Uh, it’s all Black, uh, I love us
vault_lines: If you put crabs in a barrel to ensure your survival
meaning:
The metaphor of crabs in a barrel alludes to how blacks should be uniting in order to elevate themselves, but instead keep tearing each other down so that everyone remains equally miserable.

Jay feels that if you force young black men to compete against each other for territory, money, respect, etc. their entire life, they are going to have less of a problem killing their fellow black man when the situation presents itself. And while they think this is helping them “get ahead”, it ends up holding everyone back because it creates a system where it is encouraged to sabotage the achievers.



Jay uses the 50 Cent line “What up, Blood? What up, cuz?” to demonstrate that he is talking to all young black folks (“Blood” refers to the Bloods gang, and “cuz” is a common Crip salutation).

line: I’m all dressed up with nowhere to go, uh
vault_lines: I'm all dressed up with nowhere to go, uh
meaning: Hov is dressed up in expensive suits, but isn’t surrounded by enough blacks to properly celebrate his success. Likely a reference to a song of the same name.

line: It’s a war going on outside we ain’t safe from
vault_lines: It's a war going on outside we ain't safe from
meaning:
This is a Mobb Deep line off “Survival Of The Fittest”.

Also used by Jay-Z on “Ballad of the Fallen Soldier”, Cam’s opener in “Welcome to New York City” (with Jay-Z) and Brother Ali in “Slippin' Away”.

line: What’s the life expectancy for Black guys? The system’s working effectively, that’s why
vault_lines: What's the life expectancy for Black guys?
meaning:
Black men in America have a much shorter life expectancy than white men.  Yeezy feels this isn’t an aberration or a flaw in an otherwise healthy system, but is the racist way the United States political economy was designed to work. This, rather than black-on-black crime, is arguably the real genocide.

The irony is a system working effectively is usually a good thing – in this case it would be better if it was ineffective.

line: I repeat, my religion is the beat My verse is like church, my Jesus piece
vault_lines: I repeat, my religion is the beat
meaning: Jay isn’t guided by religion, he’s guided by music. His rhymes are the gospel, and he’ll preach to all his listeners. Hov is often oblique about religion in song – see this note for more information.

line: Black excellence, opulence, decadence Tuxes next to the president, I’m present I dress in Dries, and other boutique stores in Paris
vault_lines: Black excellence, opulence, decadence
meaning:
Jay is a black man living the American Dream – he hangs with Obama, travels the globe, and shops at the likes of Dries van Noten.

Hov pronounces “Paris” as “pa-REESE”, like a local Parisian, further indicating how elite he is. This also assists with the rhyme scheme in the next bar.

Note the phrase “black tie” – a concept Kanye plays on later in the song.

line: Hit the mall, pick up some Gucci Now ain’t nothing new but your shoes
vault_lines: Hit the mall, pick up some Gucci
meaning:
You can’t change the world just by changing your shoes.



In the 1978 song “Moving in Stereo” by The Cars. Ric Ocasek sings “Life’s the same I’m moving in stereo, Life’s the same except for my shoes” Kanye expresses the same idea here.

line: I feel the pain in my city wherever I go 314 soldiers died in Iraq, 509 died in Chicago
vault_lines: I feel the pain in my city wherever I go
meaning:
These are 2008 figures: The Associated Press counted at least 314 U.S. soldiers died in Iraq, down from 904 in the previous year, while the Chicago Tribune reported 509 homicides in Chicago (a 15% percent increase compared to 2007).



This isn’t the first time Kanye has referenced the Chicago death count in a song.

line: And they say by 21, I was supposed to die So I’m out here celebrating my post-demise
vault_lines: And they say by 21, I was supposed to die
meaning:
Just like Pusha-T said in “So Appalled”, some people expect African-Americans from the “hood” to be dead by 21. Even with the impact that he made, Fred Hampton also died at this tender age. Jay’s supposed to have been dead since 1990, so he’s just been living it up ever since then.

Contrary to popular belief, the line is “And they say by 21” not “By December 21st”, as proven by the album booklet.

line: I arrived on the day Fred Hampton died, uh
vault_lines: I arrived on the day Fred Hampton died, uh
meaning:
Jay Z was born the same day that Chicago-based Black Panther activist Fred Hampton was shot at point blank in his apartment by Chicago police, in conjunction with the FBI: December 4th, 1969.



This line was supposed to be paying homage to Hampton, but his son, Fred Hampton Jr. took offense to Jay-Z not referring to it as an assassination (though the next line clearly implies this).

line: Now please, domino, domino Only spot a few Blacks the higher I go, uh
vault_lines: Now please, domino, domino
meaning:
Jay uses the rules of dominos to explain class and race hierarchy. In dominos, the black spots are called pips. The person with the fewest number of pips has the HIGHER score – this is how you win.

The higher Hov rises in status and wealth, the fewer blacks he sees until he is almost totally surrounded by white (people).

Domino may also signify “fall back” – long stacks of upright dominos arranged to fall in sequence are called “fall backs”.

line: No shop class, but half the school got a tool And a ”I could die any day”-type attitude
vault_lines: No shop class, but half the school got a tool
meaning:
When a school runs low on funds, potentially useful programs like vocational education are often the first things to go, and kids are left to carry a real gun instead of the glue variety.



People die everyday in the hood, and people live their lives knowing this. This could cause them to act as if their actions have no consequences, since they don’t envision themselves sticking around for too long.

line: This is to the memory of Danroy Henry
vault_lines: This is to the memory of Danroy Henry
meaning:
Danroy Henry was a college football player killed by a police shooting in October 2010. Controversially, the officer who shot him was later given the Officer of the Year award by the police union.

A classmate of Henry’s wrote about the shooting on a Facebook post stating:

DJ followed all the rules, has never been in any type of trouble, yet he was killed in such an inhumane way by the very people that are here to protect us. DJ Henry grew up in a middle/upper class community, and was well known in his community as a quiet, gentle and giving young man. Many were influenced by the way he lived his life.  He was a great young man.

line: And I’m from the murder capital where they murder for capital
vault_lines: And I'm from the murder capital where they murder for capital
meaning:
Even though Jay Z spits this lyric on the intro to “Lucifer”, footage from the studio session shows Kanye freestyle the line first. A “murder for capital” is a murder committed for money.

Kanye’s re-purposing of the line is directed towards his hometown of Chicago, to which he directs this verse and his next. While there is debate as to whether or not Chicago is actually the murder capital, it is the home to the most total murders, despite having a population one-third the size of New York City.

line: Watch it get down, watch it get down Watch it get down, watch it get down

Cole rejects the common cliche phrase of “time is money.” The phrase basically means that if we don’t spend all the time we’re given in life to work and achieve goals in the future, we are–in effect–wasting the profit that we could be making.

line: So fuck what we sellin’, fuck is we makin’? ‘Cause their grass is greener ’cause they always rakin’ in mo’
vault_lines: So fuck what we sellin', fuck is we makin'?
meaning:
The phrase “So fuck what we sellin', fuck is we makin'?” suggests a frustration with the focus on commercial success and materialistic gains in the rap game. It questions the value and significance of what artists are selling and emphasizes the importance of artistic integrity and genuine creativity.

The line “‘Cause their grass is greener 'cause they always rakin’ in mo'” further emphasizes the discontent with the industry. It implies that other artists, who might prioritize profit over artistic expression, appear to be more successful and prosperous. The metaphor of “greener grass” represents their perceived superiority or advantage, indicating that they are consistently earning more money and achieving greater success.

Overall, these lyrics express Jay’s critique of the rap industry, highlighting its tendency towards superficiality, repetitive content, and the allure of monetary gain at the expense of true artistic innovation.

line: And took it to Beverly Hills while we in Calabasas And my head is scratchin’ ’cause that shit is backwards
vault_lines: And took it to Beverly Hills while we in Calabasas
meaning:
The line “And took it to Beverly Hills while we in Calabasas” refers to the trend in the rap game where artists strive for fame, success, and wealth, often associating themselves with luxurious places like Beverly Hills. Calabasas, on the other hand, is a city in California known for its wealthy residents, including several celebrities such as the Kardashians. By contrasting these two affluent locations, Jay highlights the superficiality and materialism that have come to dominate the rap scene.

The following line, “And my head is scratchin' ‘cause that shit is backwards,” expresses Jay’s confusion and frustration with this prevailing mindset. He sees the rap industry moving away from its roots and losing its authenticity. The focus on material possessions and external appearances takes precedence over genuine artistry and meaningful expression, leading to a sense of disillusionment and dissatisfaction for Jay.

In summary, these lyrics in “Moonlight” symbolize Jay’s criticism of the rap game’s current state, where the pursuit of wealth and superficiality has overshadowed the true essence and creativity that the genre once embodied.

line: And y’all niggas is ’posed to be trill?
vault_lines: And y'all niggas is 'posed to be trill?
meaning:
The term “trill” originated in Southern hip-hop culture and refers to being true or real. It signifies an artist’s genuine and genuine character, their adherence to their roots, and their ability to stay true to themselves and their craft. Jay is questioning the credibility of those who claim to be “trill” but, in his view, fall short of embodying those qualities.

By posing this question, Jay suggests that many rappers in the industry have become stale, repetitive, and fake, compromising their authenticity for commercial success or to fit into a particular trend. He implies that these artists lack the genuine qualities that should define the rap game, which ultimately contributes to the perceived decline in originality and substance within the genre.

In essence, Jay’s lyrics express a dissatisfaction with the state of the rap industry and call for a return to the genuine, innovative, and authentic roots that made the genre influential and impactful.

line: I don’t post no threats on the Internet
vault_lines: I don't post no threats on the Internet
meaning:
It suggests that Jay is distancing himself from the current trend in rap music, where artists often resort to using social media platforms to make empty threats or boast about their accomplishments without actually taking real action.

By stating that he doesn’t engage in such behavior, Jay implies that he values authenticity and substance in his music. He may be criticizing the prevalence of online bravado and the lack of genuine content and meaningful messages in contemporary rap. Instead, he aims to focus on delivering music that carries deeper significance and reflects real-life experiences.

line: Glorified seat filler, huh?
vault_lines: Glorified seat filler, huh?
meaning: The lyrics “Glorified seat filler, huh?” in Jay’s “Moonlight” can be interpreted as a criticism of certain individuals in the rap industry who are perceived as lacking genuine talent or originality. The term “seat filler” refers to someone who fills a seat at an event or awards show to maintain the appearance of a full audience. In this context, Jay is suggesting that these individuals are merely occupying space in the rap game without bringing anything substantial or meaningful to the table. It implies that they are more concerned with superficial success and fame rather than creating authentic and innovative music. By using the term “glorified,” Jay emphasizes the inflated perception and recognition these artists receive despite their lack of artistic substance. The overall message of this line is to express Jay’s dissatisfaction with the current state of the rap industry, which he sees as stagnant, repetitive, and lacking artistic integrity.

line: From my Blueprint beginning to that Black Album ending

meaning:
Jay isn’t saying that his career started from The Blueprint – which was in fact his sixth studio album, but rather references the title of the album by playing on the definition of the word ‘blueprint’, which is a “plan, model or template”. This insinuates that from the start of his career, he has set out to always be real.

The Black Album was meant to be his final album, where he would retire after its release – the album cover and its title reference fading into black, almost in a ghostly manner. The final track on the album is titled “My 1st Song”, which further enforces the idea that he has always been the same, legitimate JAY-Z since the beginning.

line: I’m just glad we got to see each other Talk and re-meet each other
vault_lines: I'm just glad we got to see each other
meaning:
In early-2003 Jay reunited with his father, Adnes “AJ” Reeves, at the behest of his mother Gloria. Hov was able to express his feelings to Adnes, and he offered his forgiveness for the act of leaving him and his siblings.

Sadly, just a few weeks after they reunited AJ died of liver failure due to his alcoholism. His passing occurred on the night Hov opened his first 40/40 Club in Manhattan, which was on June 19, 2003. At the time Hov had been in the process of buying him an apartment and furnishing it.

As a gift I would love for our generation and all the people that grew up without their parents, whether you knew them early on or not, is to have that conversation so you could let that anger go. Because that’s the sort of anger that keeps you from love – it makes you put up walls and you don’t let people get close to you, because you don’t ever want to feel that feeling of abandonment or that feeling of hurt again, so you don’t let certain people close to you.

line: So Pop, I forgive you for all the shit that I lived through It wasn’t all your fault, homie – you got caught Into the same game I fought (Ugh) That Uncle Ray lost (Ugh) My big brothers and so many others I saw
vault_lines: So Pop, I forgive you for all the shit that I lived through
meaning:
Jay-Z here forgives his father for all the pain he put him through after abandoning him and his family when he was 11 or 12 years old. He realizes the environment they were living in had a hand in the family’s misfortune.

In 1980, AJ’s brother Ray Reeves was stabbed to death in an altercation at the Sumner Houses in Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn. The death of his baby brother hit Adnes hard, especially as the community knew who had committed the murder but would not speak to law enforcement.

Adnes turned to  heroin and alcohol to numb his pain, and two years later in 1982 he left the family home and never returned. With that disdain in his membrane, Hov couldn’t resist the allure of the crack game and would go on to be a drug dealer at the age of 13. Jay’s friends and brother Eric would also succumb to the evils of the streets, becoming addicted to the same crack cocaine that he was selling.

When I finally did see my father again and we stood face-to-face, it was like looking in a mirror. It made me wonder how someone could abandon a child who looked just like him.

vault_lines: Listen close, you'll hear what I'm about
meaning:
Many people don’t understand Jay Z’s true message, and instead judge him off surface level interpretations of his lyrics.  He later devoted an entire book, Decoded, explaining why his work is so much more meaningful.

Trying to rhyme and be clever and witty and tell a coherent story or talk about a coherent concept and stick to something true about life is difficult.  But it’s that element of truth that makes the songs deeper than just entertainment, that make the music a light that can help people see their way through a hard life.

line: [Produced by Eminem and Luis Resto]
vault_lines: So you can feel my truths
meaning:
Luis Resto told Fader in 2013 about creating the track with Em:

 I worked on the “Moment of Clarity” beat with Marshall. Marshall and I got along. I was classically trained in the piano and always gravitated towards strings. That’s where we got a common ground, that I brought that classical element. When I hear the “Moment of Clarity” lick, I can feel it in my fingers. It’s a pretty sparse track, but that left room for Jay to do his thing and Marshall knew that.



Em spoke in 2007 about how Jay’s rap made the beat better and how it inspired Em to add ad-libs:

I actually met with [Jay-Z] in New York and I played him basically what I had, what I had been working on. He picked that one. We ended up going back to Detroit, he sent it to me. I wasn’t there while he recorded it but he sent it to me pretty much that same week. I don’t know if I was really feeling that beat until he put words to it. Then all of a sudden it became this… Jay-Z has that ability to take things that, you don’t think the beat is good if you just hear the beat. But once he puts words to it it takes on this whole other… He turned the beat incredible. It made me feel exactly what he was saying. There was a couple lines that I even went in the booth and did ad libs on because I felt like the lines were so powerful. So I went in the booth myself and was like “WOO!”

Jay-Z spoke about this session with Interview magazine in 2010:

I never even told him this, but I remember that Eminem came into the studio when we made “Moment of Clarity,” which he produced, on The Black Album. So here’s Eminem. It’s 2003, I think The Eminem Show had come out, and he was like the biggest rapper in the world—he sold like 20 million records worldwide or some ridiculous number. But when he came to the studio, I remember I hugged him, and I could feel that he had on a bulletproof vest. I couldn’t imagine being that successful. I mean, he’s a guy who loves rap and wanted to be successful his whole career. Then he finally gets it, and there’s this dark cloud over him.

And we can assume Hov copped this beat for free since Em raps the following line in his 2003 diss of Jermaine Dupri:

I’ve made beats for Jay-Z for free

Second, “square” is commonly used for middle-class, strait-laced people. These are people who are “normal” in every sense of the word, and not drastically different than anybody else in sense of living.
Therefore “the block where no squares get off” explains that Beanie was living on blocks where no regular person would dare to get out of their car in.

This is about not having fear: “Scars’ll scab” means that even if you injure me, I’ll recover; “I can dodge and jab” means that swinging on me won’t stop me; and even “three shots couldn’t touch me.” The whole point of the “moment of clarity” is  that after I confront my own demons, I’m left with nothing but “my balls and my word,” which makes me untouchable.

Talib Kweli and Common Sense (a.k.a. Common) are socially conscious rappers,  often considered some of the best lyricists in hip hop. However, their commercial presence in comparison to Jay’s is minimal; much like his own in the mid-nineties. He further explained the shout-outs in his book Decoded:

Kweli is a great emcee – as is Common – and they’ve both carved out impressive careers without big records.  They’re great technical MCs, but there is a difference between being a great technician and a great songwriter.  I deeply respect their craft, but even the most dazzling lyrical display won’t translate to a wide audience unless it’s matched with a big song.

Kweli would later respond on “Ghetto Show”. In a Complex article, David Drake commented on these lines:

[…] Completely betraying a back-catalog that we’d defend to the death in the Jay Z vs. Nas wars seemed transparent. Pandering, even, to an audience who only saw value in rap music which would reflect their own progressive values.

Now I know how to make a song so I know when to turn it on and turn it off. I know when to take my foot off the pedal, when I’m gonna lose everyone.

When he simplified his style with a series of averagely received albums for the remainder for the 1990s and early 2000s, he was scorned for doing so by fans and critics alike. Yet simultaneously, the same people condemning Jay still buy those records and go to his shows.

They would also produce tracks on her third album Aaliyah, which was released just weeks before her untimely passing.

In his 2015 memoir, Timbaland revealed that he went through a serious bout of depression after her passing. In 2001 he had explained to MTV:

She was like blood, and I lost blood. Me and her together had this chemistry. I kinda lost half of my creativity to her. It’s hard for me to talk to the fans right now. Beyond the music, she was a brilliant person, the [most special] person I ever met.

Missy Elliott expressed her continued sadness to Entertainment Weekly a decade later in 2011:

What I miss the most about Aaliyah is her laugh and smile. She could light up any room. I miss that from her. I also miss recording with her because she wasn’t ever scared to push boundaries as an artist … If Aaliyah was still with us she would be setting trends as she always did and breaking down barriers. You get the sense that he’s studied every face he’s seen his whole life, looking for the face of his father. And now here it is. It freezes him.

This is even more autobiographical than Jay would like to admit. His father left him when he was eleven. The hardest part about that was, Jay had 11 years with his dad, studying him, learning from him. Throughout Decoded, he is constantly complimentary to his father, and in interviews since he has stressed how close he was to his father.

Imagine having the your father leave, yet knowing he is running the same strip you are. Any day, you could come face to face with him. Jay spent a lot of time out of town, in places like Trenton, trying to grow his brand. Did he also attempt to escape this very scenario?

Romance in the hood is a funny thing. All around the world, women fall for the bad guy, the strong, aggressive one who offers a sense of excitement or danger. It’s a cliche, practically. It’s very difficult to tell someone who is making huge amounts of money to fall back, to take up a safer but more frugal existence. Eventually, as discovered on “Can’t Knock The Hustle”, he gave rap a try. If he wasn’t a successful rapper though, what life would have befallen him?

Back in the days, our parents used to take care of us
Look at em now, they even fucking scared of us
Calling the city for help because they can’t maintain
Damn, shit done changed.

This also happens to be one of Jay’s favourite lines, as he tells in Decoded:

With that line, Big captured the whole transformation in a few words. Guys my age, fed up with watching their moms struggle on a single income, were paying utility bills with money from hustling. So how could those same mothers sit them down about a truant report?

The standard defence for a father scared to take on the responsibility of a child: “that’s not my son, he looks nothing like me. So often we see hood personalities get in to problems through paternity tests. The key seems to be child support. If that didn’t exist, it’s possible many more fathers would claim their children. meaning:
Jay-Z references the Bible in this line, in particular the Book of Matthew chapter 26, verse 52:

Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.

The saying was brought into modern English as “live by the sword, die by the sword,” it would later be co-opted by gunslingers into: “live by the gun, die by the gun”.

“Dead before 38” refers to both the age, and the weapon. You will die in front of the gun, and before you reach the (quite impressive) age of 38.

In place of God, the boy has put his faith in what he deems to be the highest power on the streets: a weapon. “Not even him could save him” takes on a further meaning here, “him” being God, and once you place your faith somewhere other than God you are unable to be saved.

line: Uh, back when ratchet was a ratchet and a vixen was a vixen
vault_lines: Uh, back when ratchet was a ratchet and a vixen was a vixen
meaning:
In the time Jay is referencing (mid to late ‘80s), the word “vixen” was used to describe a gorgeous and classy female, while “ratchet” was the term given to a socket wrench as well as a handgun, specifically a model made by Smith & Wesson.

In 2017, the use of the word “vixen” is uncommon but has become somewhat synonymous with the new slang meaning of “ratchet.” According to The Cut, the term “ratchet” first appeared in a published song in 1999 when Anthony Mandigo released “Do the Ratchet” on Ratchet Fight in the Ghetto. It was later defined in 2004 by producer Earl Williams (aka Phunk Dawg) after he produced a re-released version of the original 1999 song. In the CD liner notes, he wrote:

“Ratchet” n., pron., v, adv., 1. To be ghetto, real, gutter, nasty. 2. It’s whatever, bout it, etc.

line: Assume a virtue if you have not Or better yet here’s a verse from Hamlet ”Lord, we know who we are Yet we know not what we may be” So maybe I’m the one or maybe I’m crazy
vault_lines: Assume a virtue if you have not
meaning:
Hamlet is a play William Shakespeare wrote at the turn of the 17th century. It’s considered one of the most important literary works of all time. The excerpt JAY-Z quotes comes from the 44th line of Act 4, Scene 5, and means that it’s only possible to know who we are in the present moment.

“Assume a virtue if you have not” is also a Hamlet quote, but from Act 3, Scene 4. It means, even if you don’t believe you have a certain desirable quality, at least pretend to have it—in other words, “fake it ‘til you make it.” In JAY-Z’s case, this meant acting like the greatest rapper even when his environment made him feel like it was an unachievable goal.

In a 2013 interview with Elliott Wilson, JAY-Z said of Shakespeare:

Shakespeare was a man who wrote poetry. I’m a man who writes poetry. Why not compare yourself to the best?

line: Reek of coca leaf in my past Came through the bushes smellin’ like roses I need a trophy just for that
vault_lines: reek of coca leaf in my past
meaning:
JAY-Z juxtaposes the coca leaf with a bush full of roses. The coca leaf represents the hustling Jay had to do as a drug dealer pushing cocaine, while a bush full of roses represents his success. To “come up smelling like roses” describes a situation where someone endures hardship and still emerges in a favourable position.

The hardships/success juxtaposition may be a nod to the infidelity Jay admitted to earlier in the record.

This line is also another example of Hov’s next-level, multi-layered lyricism, which often goes unnoticed. It is likely a reference to the 2006 Rose Bowl college football national championship game, in which the Texas Longhorns beat the USC Trojans, led by Heisman Trophy winner Reggie Bush.

The game was won on a game-winning fourth-down touchdown run by Texas quarterback Vince Young. Vince Young was the runner-up in Heisman Trophy voting that season, coming second only to Reggie Bush. The Heisman Trophy is awarded annually to the most outstanding player in college football in the United States. Reggie Bush would later be forced to forfeit his Heisman Trophy for violating NCAA rules. Thus, Vince Young can be seen to have won in the Rose Bowl the trophy he literally deserved–and he did it by going through Reggie Bush and the Trojans.



Pictured: Vince Young and Reggie Bush with the Heisman Trophy before Bush was awarded the honor.

line: (Como hás nome, cavaleiro?)
vault_lines: Gave birth to my verbal imagination
meaning:

What is your name, knight?
My name is Everybody
And my time […]

This was sampled from the Portuguese song “Todo o Mundo e Ninguém”, by Quarteto 1111, a group which included José Cid and Tozé Brito. It was inspired by Gil Vicente’s Auto da Lusitânia, a 16th century play where Nobody is a peasant that lives a morally correct life and Everyone is a rich knight who lives an immoral life.

About the sample, Tozé Brito said:


I was amazed when I knew they wanted to use the theme. I still don’t understand how they, in New York, discovered a song released here as a single in 1970.

I think this is the first time a sample of ours is used on this level. JAY-Z is famous worldwide. The request got here at SPA [Sociedade Portuguesa de Autores] about six weeks ago, and we authorized right away, we negotiated an… appealing percentage. And we got a symbolic sum.


José Cid said:

Time goes by and Quarteto 1111’s work is ignored. [Being sampled by JAY-Z] is a way of making justice.

line: When Slick Rick made “Mona Lisa”
vault_lines: When Slick Rick made "Mona Lisa"
meaning:
A reference to Slick Rick’s 1989 classic “Mona Lisa” off of The Great Adventures of Slick Rick.

Jay wrote of his admiration for Slick Rick in his 2010 book, Decoded:

Slick Rick also wrote some of the first rap songs that were genuinely sad — which sounds like a strange thing to say. … Slick Rick was too much of an artist to come out with straight-up tearjerkers, but like all great comics he knew how to hide deeper emotions between the punch lines, emotions like regret and loss, the kind of feelings that could make you pause even while you were speeding down the New Jersey turnpike on the way to your hustling spot. … Slick Rick taught me that not only can rap be emotionally expressive, it can even express those feelings that you can’t really name — which was important for me, and for lots of kids like me, who couldn’t always find the language to make sense of our feelings.

Slick Rick’s influence has been essential to Jay’s craft. On Jay’s 2000 album, The Blueprint, he named the introduction track after Slick Rick’s 1988 song “The Ruler’s Back”. He also sampled Slick Rick’s 1985 hit “La Di Da Di” on his 2004 song, “The Return.”

line: When Denzel was blottin’ carpet, I’ll pack a nine millimeter
vault_lines: When Denzel was blottin' carpet, I'll pack a nine millimeter
meaning:
In the 2007 film American Gangster, Denzel Washington played Frank Lucas, the right-hand man of real-life Harlem mob boss Ellsworth “Bumpy” Johnson. During one scene, a gangster shoots another in the leg and gets blood all over a white alpaca-fur carpet. Afterwards, Denzel scolds the people cleaning the blood out of the rug for rubbing it rather than blotting it:

Don’t rub on that! You blot that. You understand? That’s alpaca. That’s $25,000 alpaca. You blot that shit, you don’t rub it.

JAY-Z raps “I’ll pack a” so it’s a homophone of “alpaca.” An alpaca looks like a small llama, and Llama Firearms is a Spanish arms company that manufactured nine millimeter handguns throughout the 20th century. Back when JAY-Z was young in the 1980s and 1990s, possibly carrying a pistol like that, Denzel was first becoming a big movie star.

During the filming of American Gangster, Denzel urged producer Brian Grazer to have JAY-Z write the score, but Grazer said he “just didn’t think there’d be enough” for JAY-Z to do. A month after the movie debuted, JAY-Z released his concept album American Gangster anyways, and matched the songs to specific scenes from the film. He spoke about the project to The New York Times a month prior to the movie’s release:

It was like I was watching the film, and putting it on pause, and giving a back story to the story. It immediately clicked with me. Like Scarface or any one of those films, you take the good out of it, and you can see it as an inspiring film.

line: I’m a Sufi to goofies, I could prolly speak Farsi That’s poetry,

meaning:
The oldest surviving poetry is from ancient Mesopotamia, the region of modern day Iraq and Iran. Jalal al-Din Rumi, a 13th century Persian and pioneer of modern poetry, wrote most of his works in Farsi. Iranian culture values poetry very highly. In fact, linguistically, modern Farsi was molded heavily by the proliferation of poetry throughout Iranian history. Sufism, a branch of Sunni Islam focuses on mysticism. It is a religious sect that many poets, including Rumi himself, belong to.

Jay compares himself to Rumi, by proclaiming his lyrics are mystical similarly to how Rumi’s poetry is captivating to the many. The line also nods to the name of one of JAY-Z and Beyoncé’s twins. Shortly after the twins were born in 2017, it was reported that the couple filed trademarks for “Rumi Carter” and “Sir Carter.”

The two first couples of the civil rights movement (and of black America as a whole), Martin Luther King, Jr. and his wife Coretta Scott King; and Malcolm X and his wife Betty Shabazz are set up as icons.  Jay and Kanye position themselves here as inheritors of their legacy, and also thank them for establishing the groundwork that allowed the two rappers to become the new black elite.



Additionally, these heroes are given just as much thanks for our protagonists' success as Jesus' mother and father, as well as Christ Himself.



As a final note, notice the titles used for the two civil rights leaders. While “King Martin” is an obvious pun on his name, “Brother Malcolm” is the usual way of addressing fellow members of the Nation of Islam (and his later splinter groups).

Any damage done is seen as important to the piece’s history, rather than something needing to be thrown-away or disguised.



Like Beyoncé did in “Sandcastles”—in the video both a kintsugi bowl and Jay appear—he pledges to repair their relationship following the philosophy of kintsugi: instead of hiding the damage or running away, Jay is revealing his mistakes publically while trying to make amends to his wife. line: I hate all girls with ulterior motives That’s why I’m 20 plus years old, no sons, no daughters
vault_lines: I hate all girls with ulterior motives
meaning:
Jay expresses his deep distrust towards women who approach him with ulterior motives, such as exploiting his wealth and fame rather than forming a genuine connection. This distrust stems from his awareness that many people are inherently attracted to money and fame. In Western society, famous individuals are often seen as high status. From an evolutionary perspective, status and resources, which are often acquired through wealth, are linked to better survival prospects—an essential human need. This inherently makes these traits attractive, but it may also attract superficial mates who don’t love Hov for who he truly is.

This wariness has led him to avoid deep, committed relationships, as reflected in his admission of having no children despite being in his twenties. This line underscores a recurring theme in Jay’s music: the challenges and loneliness that accompany fame and success. It also hints at his desire for genuine connections, which he finds difficult to achieve due to his celebrity status.

However, three years later, Jay met the love of his life: Beyoncé. The couple began dating and eventually got married on April 4, 2008. They have since welcomed three children into their family. Their first daughter, Blue Ivy Carter, was born on January 7, 2012. On June 13, 2017, Beyoncé gave birth to twins, a daughter named Rumi and a son named Sir. Their relationship and family life mark a significant turn from the isolation and distrust Jay once felt, highlighting his journey towards finding genuine love and connection despite his fame.

vault_lines: Oww, hoes turn they heads like owls
meaning:
The first bar has four possible meanings that Jay may have intended to count towards his “triple entendre”.


“Oww” is a way to call attention to pain. Girls turn their heads so quickly as Jay walks past they suffer pain.
Owls can turn their heads 270 degrees, so Jay implies women watch him wherever he goes.
Drake’s OVO Sound crew uses an owl as a logo.

Jay may be setting up an extended metaphor based around being in the sky, or higher than his competition. This begins with “owl” and ends with the line “caught the Mayweather fight cause the satellite was crispy”.



“Man of the hour” merely means Jay is the centre of attention, hence the following bars, “trillion watt lightbulb when I’m in the nightclub”.

It’s not certain that these interpretations are enough to be a triple entendre.  An English professor once went through some of Jay’s most famous lines that are considered multi-entendres, and came to the conclusion that only about 10/50 of Hov’s best “entendres” actually qualified as double-entendres.

True double entendres rely upon more than just dual references; they require two parallel levels of meaning, one explicit and one coded. Traditionally, that coded meaning was usually of a sexual nature. Jay-Z uses a lot of puns—where the humor derives from a similar sounding words and/or that word’s multiple meanings. Jay-Z also uses a lot of similes, and metaphors. Excellent lines like “I was moving birds like an Oriole fitted” and “I’m on the block like I’m 8 feet tall” do convey the sense of two distinct images, but as mentioned before, the meaning is clear, not coded.

Note that Jay may also be nodding to James Robert “Radio” Kennedy, the “intellectually challenged” lead character played by Cuba Gooding, Jr. in the 2003 movie Radio



It’s worth reading Jay’s very insightful comments on radio play below, from his 2010 book Decoded:

It’s a recurring story in hip-hop, the tension between art and commerce. Hip-hop is too important as a tool of expression to just be reduced to a commercial product. But what some people call “commercializing” really means is that lots of people buy and listen to your records. That was always the point, to me. After my first record got on the radio and on BET, it was wild being at home, feeding my fish, and suddenly seeing myself on TV. But it was satisfying. Hearing it on the radio was even better. There may be some artists who don’t believe in radio, especially now, because the radio business is such a shady racket, but radio love puts you in the hood for real. I care if regular people— sisters on their way to work, dudes rolling around in their cars— hear my shit. I’m a music head, so I listen to everything. People around me are passionate about music. We study music, seek it out. I know there are a million music blogs out there and people who are willing to put in the work finding new music on them. But I like to reach people who get their music from clubs and the radio and television, too. I want my music to play where those people live. While there’s something intensely personal about what I rap about, I also make choices in technique and style to make sure that it can touch as many people as possible without it losing its basic integrity.

meaning:
Although JAY-Z is still rapping about himself, these lines establish that he’s also beginning to address Kanye West. “You dropped outta school” references Kanye’s 2004 album The College Dropout. There’s also a play on words with “principles” and “principals”—dropping out of school might show a lack of principles, and you would literally no longer have a principal.

“Saint Pablo” is a song that appeared on Kanye’s 2016 album The Life of Pablo and “Saint” is also his son’s first name.

“‘Ye” is an abbreviated version of Kanye’s name, which Jay fuses with “Kumbaya,” the title of a classic campfire spiritual recorded in the 1920s. It’s meant to inspire peace and merriment, which clearly doesn’t fall in line with a “fuck everybody” attitude.

While many listeners thought the lyric was about Jay’s mother, Gloria, he told VIBE Magazine:

When I said that, I meant [it as] a metaphor for, like, the mothers of our nation.

On 2013’s “Holy Grail,” Jay also rapped about how addictive fame can be—like boosting his ego and feeling invincible, as if he were on drugs.

In 2014, JAY-Z and Solange Knowles (Beyoncé’s sister), were involved in an altercation in an elevator at the Met Gala. Rumors swirled that the fight had something to do with Jay’s infidelity, but neither party addressed it at the time. Here, Jay makes a play on “egg” to not only fit in the with the breakfast theme but also suggest he was responsible for instigating the conflict in the first place.

This is also a nod to a lyric Jay spit on “Public Service Announcement” from 2003’s The Black Album:

On January 22, 2019, Future stopped by Atlanta radio station Hot 107.9 to promote his album, Future Hndrxx Presents: The WIZRD. During this interview with The Durrty Boyz, DJ Kash asked Future about this line, prompting Future to express the following statement after claiming JAY-Z was apologetic:

line: Crazy how life works You got a knot in your chest, imagine how a knife hurts You stabbed Un over some records Your excuse was “He was talkin’ too reckless!”

meaning:
On December 2, 1999, Jay made an appearance at a release party in New York City for Q-Tip’s debut album Amplified. Also in attendance was Lance “Un” Rivera, a record producer and close friend of The Notorious B.I.G.

At the time, Jay was preparing to release his fourth studio album, Vol. 3… Life and Times of S. Carter, on December 28th. Allegations that Lance Rivera helped bootleg Jay’s unreleased album a month before its release date were circulating all throughout the hip-hop world.

When Jay and his crew discovered one of the supposed bootleggers was at the same nightclub, a physical altercation ensued, which resulted in a stabbing that sent Lance Rivera to the hospital. The following day, Jay admitted to being the perpetrator and turned himself in. He was facing 15 years in prison for the alleged stabbing, but was instead given three years of probation.



These lines are very different from the way Jay has rapped about the stabbing incident in the past. For example, on “Dear Summer” Jay rapped:

I don’t talk shit, I just flip it Un ya
Sorry Lance, I’m just trying to advance my quotes

line: And you know better, nigga, I know you do But you gotta do better, boy, you owe it to Blue You had no father, you had the armor But you got a daughter, gotta get softer
vault_lines: And you know better, nigga, I know you do
meaning:
JAY-Z grew up in the Marcy Houses in Brooklyn with his mom Gloria and his three siblings—his father Adnis “AJ” Reeves left them when Jay was 11 or 12. He spoke about the hazardous effects it had on his childhood in an interview:

My father, I looked just like him. As a kid, you look at your father—that’s like your superhero. No one can beat your dad, right? To have that person that I looked up to most in the world, removed out of your life–it’s like a traumatic experience, y'know?

JAY-Z uses “armor” as a metaphor for the emotional resilience he had to build up in lieu of his father’s love. But now that he has a daughter of his own, he has to break down those emotional walls to show her love. Just 10 days after Blue was born, Jay released the heart-warming “Glory,” where he meets fatherhood with anticipation of spontaneous unconditional love.

line: Which is why I ain’t never played myself
vault_lines: Which is why I ain't never played myself
meaning:
The creation of Roc-a-fella Records was necessary because when Jay decided to throw himself in to the music industry, around 1994, no major labels wanted to sign him. Reasonable Doubt originally came out via a simple distribution deal with Priority Records. When Jay says he “wasn’t felt”, he doesn’t mean as a rapper, because his buzz at the time was legendary. He means by major labels and industry insiders, who didn’t think he was a bankable star.

It’s also a reference to a pivotal time in Jay’s career. Whilst touring with Big Daddy Kane during the mid to late 80s, Jay heard his line, on a freestyle, “So put a quarter in your ass, cause ya played yourself”, which sparked a creative spurt in him. From Decoded:

“I couldn’t get Kane’s freestyle out of my head. I remember one punchline in Kane’s verse: put a quarter in your ass / cuz you played yourself. “Played yourself” wasn’t even a phrase back then. He made it up right there on that tape. Impressive.

It’s also a shot at the fact that rappers blow up too quickly, before they have honed their craft, before they have put the work in. During the early 2000s, pop-rap was beginning to explode, and some artists were gaining huge hype that was translating in to recording contracts, only to burn out by their second or third album. Jay never had that problem, so he never “played” himself.

line: You understand I am chasin’ my breath I am narrowly escapin’ my death,
vault_lines: You understand I am chasin' my breath
meaning:
On Jay-Z’s “Can I Live” from Reasonable Doubt, he says, “I’d rather die enormous than live dormant.” In several of his songs, Jay alludes to people being “dead” despite the fact that they’re actually alive (as in, their heart’s aren’t beating). They’re “dead” because they aren’t chasing their dreams or going after what they want. To Jay, accomplishing dreams is the essence of “life.”

When he says “I am chasin my breath” he is stretching the racing metaphor present in several lines on this verse to say he is chasing the essence of life itself – getting everything he wants. In going after his dreams- “life” – he is simultaneously fighting the forces of “death” (boredom, apathy, stagnation, addiction, laziness, etc.). He likens this to “narrowly escapin his death.”

It gets deeper. The entire second verse is about the struggle one encounters once he has accomplished so much. He likens this struggle to a race. Hence Michael Schumacher metaphor in the following line as well as his admission that one day even he, the great Jay-Z, will have to deal with engine burnout.

line: Don’t have me relapsin’ Relaxin’s what I’m about,

He doesn’t want to use force because he’s accomplished so much and would rather sit back in a beach chair on Turks & Caicos, thus “relaxin’s what I’m about.”

Many of the associates and artists that were in Jay-Z’s Roc-A-Fella circle around 2003 are no longer around today. Rap fans were disappointed that Hovito didn’t keep artists like Freeway and Young Chris in the fold and fell out with Beanie Sigel so bad that the two would spend the latter five years trading jabs on record. Yet, he received the most sideeyes when he received full ownership of Roc-A-Fella Records––after he and co-owners Damon “Dame” Dash and Kareem “Biggs” Burke sold it to Def Jam––and exed his partners out.

vault_lines: They say, "An eye for an eye, we both lose our sight"
meaning:
Jay-Z is questioning the common retort to the Biblical saying “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” and the famous Gandhi quote “an eye for an eye makes the whole world blind” and the related saying “two wrongs don’t make a right”.  He wants to know how much he must be wronged before it is OK to fight back and retaliate.

Hov thus attempts to ‘justify his thug’ by referring to the crushing poverty as the first wrong and the ruthlessness of the drug and rap game as the second wrong. His question is when does one stop following the rules that are only going to continue the poverty cycle and fight against the system by taking control of their own wealth and destiny?

The rest of this verse describes the war between society and the impoverished individual.

He will literally raise hell, in the sense of elevating it until it’s up in the skies, and thus; heaven.

Here Jay-Z makes a reference to the is a 1993 gangster film “A Bronx Tale” – and it isn’t the first time he’s done it. A Bronx Tale details the life of a young boy named Calogero (also known as C). This boy grows up in the tough borrough of the Bronx, the majority of the film deals with the struggle of C being torn between his father’s good intentions and a fascinating gangster named Sonny.

Unfortunately, Calogero begins to resent his father and follows in Sonny’s footsteps, eventually leading to racial violence, his friend’s being killed by Molotov Cocktails and almost losing his his life, as well as his lover. Eventually, however, C makes amends with his father and the story ends in a rather happy light.

Sadly, reality and movies are not similar. In the film Bronx Tale the main character suffers significantly but eventually reaches a happy ending. In reality, leading a life such as this, especially in an area such as the Bronx, is extremely dangerous. During 2014, the year this song was recorded, murder rates went up 28.5% in the Bronx, there are nearly 26 crimes per every 1,000 residents.

In the film, the poorer areas of Rio were filled with corruption, mostly within the law enforcement system. This, along with the gang activity, made it difficult and dangerous for Rocket (the main character) to achieve his goals in the photography field.

The current situation in Brasil is highly similar – there is still poverty and corruption that holds citizens back from achieving their goals, such as becoming a futbol (soccer) star. These futbol-related lines link to the 2014 World Cup, which is currently being held in the country.

In 2008, Jay may seem as far removed from the street life as he’s going to get. He reaffirms his hood credentials, strengthened by his continued ties with day one “thugs and gangsters” like Memphis Bleek and Emory Jones.

Jay walked out “playing” the opening riff of “Wonderwall,”  and singing the opening lines, before launching into a rock version of “99 Problems.”

This could also be a triple entendre, which would make it the fifth-millionth one Hov has built off of the ambiguities of ‘rock/Rock/Roc’.


Rock star = Jay is likening himself to Rock star status, on par with Oasis.
Rock star = Rock being slang for crack rock; a reference to his drug-dealing past.
Roc star = the face of the R-O-C (Roc-a-Fella Records).

The “crooked officer” is likely racially profiling Jay, as occurred in “99 Problems.” He’s grown up from that incident, but is still facing unfair police attention because of his penchant for flashy items.

line: I rock with Obama but I ain’t no politician

Jay-Z was a vocal proponent of Obama during the campaign, holding free shows to encourage people to vote and performing in front of Obama photos during his “Heart of the City” tour with Mary J. Blige.

It’s just one of many future Hov/Obama references, as their flourishing friendship became the darling story for multiple publications.

Could be a reaction to Noel Gallagher’s comments on Jay’s headlining slot at 2008’s Glastonbury Festival. He references it later in the track, and during the performance he “owns” the Glastonbury stage, earning rave reviews.

In the Book of Isaiah Immanuel (meaning “God with us”) was ‘called from the womb’ by God and significantly named prior to his birth because of his divine destiny. Three years later on his track December 4th, Jay’s mother Gloria Carter would utter sentiments similar to these. Jay-Z, whose friends nicknamed him Jayhovah on account of his God-like talents, believes the ‘writing is on the wall’ and his ‘fate has been sealed’ as the greatest rapper of all time.

There has been speculation rife for years that Jay took Chris' flow. Chris was interviewed about it in 2011 and said

“"Yeah I hear [speculation],” he told Meet Tha Dealer. “I don’t really indulge in it but I hear it though. We were all around each other [in the studio] so that shit rubs off on each other. We took from everybody. Everybody took from each other. I always say steel sharpens steel and that’s what I mean [and] that’s what defines that.”"

Peedi Crakk who was also part of the State Property collective said:

“"I want to clarify that [Jay] doesn’t steal anyone’s songs,” Peedi said. “He steals swag, ideas, concepts… Jay doesn’t just straight up jack you for a song, he’s smooth with it. You ever listen to Young Chris rap and then go back and listen to Jay? You almost start to scratch your head. The old Jay-Z never rapped like that… Jay has no swag of his own.”"

Chris went on to say:

“"I don’t really get into that. [Jay’s] my man. People say I took his shit. A few weeks back they was saying I sound like Jay-Z, but years down the line they’re like, ‘Oh hold on, maybe [Jay-Z] took his shit!’”"

As a huge fan of both Chris and Jay, it’s difficult to say if Jay borrowed from Chris or if it was vice versa, but Jay Z has one of the most diverse flows in hip hop, and in my opinion it is unmatched, so certainly he may have borrowed for a track or two, but to say he jacked the kids entire style is way off base.

meaning:
The idea is that major labels sign bad artists as tax write-offs. By spending a huge amount of money signing and artist that they then drop, they make a net profit from the venture. If they, saypend $500,000 signing an artist, that money helps them avoid entering an even larger income tax bracket, which would cost them more than the $500,000 they initially spent, hence making a net profit from the venture.

As we can case here though, this isn’t a sound business model and, despite widespread belief that it occurs in the industry, isn’t a common occurrence.
