Hov is alluding to himself being the cancer of The Hamptons, that is, he has invaded the usually white-dominated seaside community and spread his new black wealth throughout the exclusive resort. The Hamptons features some of the most expensive and luxurious residential properties in the United States, and is a favorite Summer holiday destination for the most affluent New Yorkers.

In classic Jay-Z wordplay, he employs a homograph in cancer/Cancer. Someone who is born between June 21 and July 22 is given the astrological sign of Cancer. In the United States this month-long period occurs in the middle of the Summer – the time when Jay-Z would be holidaying in the Hamptons. Since 1997 Jay-Z and the Roc-A-Fella Records family had been renting mansions (which often came with a $30,000-a-week rent tag) and hosting Summer long parties for their family and friends. The festivities would culminate in a massive Independence Day soirée. In 1998 his Fourth of July party was attended by over 800 people – hence the noise pollution!



In an interview with New York magazine in 1999 (the same year this song was released) one of the town’s property owners, who was renting out a mansion neighboring the mansion the Roc-A-Fella crew would be staying that Summer, explained that one client backed out upon hearing of the arrival of a rap brigade for reasons he “would not like to characterize.” What’s the bet the people who pulled out were “uppity white folks” who stereotyped Jay-Z and his group and didn’t approve of their lifestyle?

However, the actress Sandra Bullock wasn’t worried at the prospect of rap neighbors, and ended up renting the neighboring house for the Summer. She even attended Hov’s Fourth of July party and hung out with Puff Daddy – who had left his much smaller Hamptons property to join the Roc’s festivities.

Dame Dash had this to say in the New York magazine article:

We know people are expecting us to cut up and bug out, but we got no wilder than anyone else. There’s an expectation that we’re gonna come in there and fuck shit up, but nothing bad happened. It was a big time, it was ill."

When you miss an important shot your character is tested and questioned; and if someone is put in that situation they will often lose all of their playing confidence. But if you do make the shot, you’re automatically a hero among your team-mates and fans. A few inches to the left or right is the only difference between “They’re a superstar!” or “They’re a selfish player!”

NBA professional basketball player Paul Pierce can explain the feeling best:

The entire arena is filled with nervous energy. With seconds left on the clock, everyone is watching you, waiting to see when you’ll make your move and whether it will be good enough to win the game. You step back, put up your best shot and… it rims out. The other team starts celebrating; you’re crushed. Part of the appeal of taking the big shot is experiencing a wide range of emotions, from potential euphoria to complete distress. Making the big shot wouldn’t feel so good if missing it didn’t feel so awful.

line: Heaven or Hell, the cards we been dealt Are the cards that we play, play, play

meaning:
An allusion to predestination: the philosophical and metaphysical idea that we’re travelling the path planned for us. A common reference in religion, at least as interpreted popularly in phrases like “everything happens for a reason,” “God works in mysterious ways,” and so on.

Jay is saying, whether you’re a villain, a hero, a pragmatist, or some combination of the three, you’re doing what you can with what you have. It’s not to excuse anyone’s actions, but rather an extension of empathy to others' stories, probably with a nod to his own past, and his own complex niche in pop culture.

And I can’t shake the feeling that it alludes to the phrase, “Better servants in Heaven than kings in Hell.” We know that Jay has paid homage to (or, calling a spade a spade, ripped off) Jedi Mind Tricks before.

line: Die for what you believe, only one god recedes When the shots spray, spray, spray
vault_lines: Die for what you believe, only one god recedes
meaning:
Death for a higher power is equivalent to death for any cause, maybe for a country, an organization, or a belief: in any case, people are willing to lay their life on the line for abstract concepts. Like the Christian post-hardcore band Thrice said in their song “Like Moths to Flame.”

I nod but don’t know what to say
But I know you
And I believe you’re who you say you are so
I will follow you, lay down my life
I would die for you, this very night

Here, there are two possible meanings.

When Jay says, “Only one God recedes when the shots spray” (bullets fire), he could be referring to himself, the “god in the flesh,” JayHova. He is more pragmatic, rather than idealistic; as the partition in an earlier lyric implies, he keeps a respectful distance from whatever belief system he subscribes to. He isn’t willing to take a bullet for an abstract concept, the archetypal “survivor.”

On the other hands, he might be saying that your god will recede when the shots spray, in your final moments of life. You might reconsider offering up your life to that higher power that was apparently unable to save you when you needed it/Him most.

Another idea is that he’s referring to money. Money is a god to many, and it’s the only god that becomes less important when the shots spray (in the face of death). You can’t take it with you. Belief (knowledge, wisdom, freedom, and understanding) is what you should try to amass before death, and Jay alludes to that in the opening lines of the song.

line: And God is my chauffeur,
vault_lines: And God is my chauffeur,
meaning:
Jay is referencing the prior two lines. He is basically saying that differences in religious ideologies are insulting to god; and make about as much sense as if he were in his Maybach (divided by a partition) and God is playing the role of a chauffeur.

There’s some serious double meaning here. On the one hand, Jay says that God is his chauffeur, his driver, so God is taking him where he goes, he is nothing more than a tool to get Hova to where he wants to go. But with the partition, he alludes to separation from God. A problem all religious believers deal with. He could also be suggesting that he controls his own fate, telling God where he wants to go, but at the end of the day, his life is still in God’s hand, and He can make a left turn at any moment even if Jay wanted to go right…

Although not always, apparently, God is somehow always in control. Duality or…?

A chauffeur is someone that is paid to drive a vehicle.  In other words, is God on Jay’s payroll too?

#A HINDU INTERPRETATION



One really cool interpretation of these lines references the Mahabharata, an Indian Epic on family feuds, and a book within that epic, the Bhagavad Gita, the main holy book for Hindus, and an important text for spiritual seekers of all stripes. Jay’s well-read, and in all likelihood has read the text.

The Bhagavad Gita contains a conversation between Pandava prince Arjuna and his guide Lord Krishna on a variety of theological and philosophical issues.

Krishna is the charioteer (the ancient version Maybach Chauffeur perhaps?) and imparts wisdom and guides Arjun towards action. Krishna’s essential message was that one must follow his dharma or duty according to his natural turn, abilities and capacities.

Arjun was in a dilemma because he was set against his cousins who he felt attached and did not want to fight them but Krishna persuaded by telling him that he had a duty to fight and that is what is important. Krishna’s conduct also was questionable since he used unfair methods to win the war and eventually once he died was not allowed re-entry to heaven because he was not ‘good’. However the essence of the message is that, you must do what you can with what you have (the cards we been dealt, etc.).

The second part of this line refers to the Lamborghini Murcielago. The “angel wings” refers to the way in which the doors open and close, resembling the wings of an angel. See Lupe’s “Lamborghini Angels” for more on this comparison.



How do we know it’s a Murcielago? In the preceding line, Jay says “Have mercy.” Kanye West’s song “Mercy,” also features this play on words.



In this context it sounds as if Jay is saying that they symbolize how he’s starting to think of fame and celebrity as our culture’s new “God.”

According to the Koran, angels that turned on God are called djinn, and their wings are taken from them. The term djinn is pronounced similar to ‘ghini, so this could easily be a reference to Islam. Additionally, in Islamic tradition, Judas turned into a djinn. Have mercy on the djinn that betrayed God, by giving him his wings back.

And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several was of one pearl

Moreover, pearly gates are the entrance to the Kingdom of God, and in the other verses of Revelation 21, the entire Kingdom is described as composed in twelves. Jay-Z means to contrast this Christian 12 with the earlier NGE 12.

line: [Produced By: Mark the 45 King]
vault_lines: Take the bass line out
meaning:
The track production here is definitely influenced by theatre, more specifically, the play Annie song from the 1982 film version of the musical Annie, “It’s The Hard-Knock Life.”

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-0bOH8ABpco

In a 1998 interview with Blues & Soul magazine, Jay explained why he chose to sample the musical Annie:

What happened was I was on tour and Kid Capri played me the track. Mark ‘45’ King had produced it, and at the time it was just beats and the sampled hook. You know, Mark’s known for making famous hip hop beats like “900 Number”’ with no rap on them. So, once I heard it, I was like ‘I gotta have that’ – and I tracked Mark down. At first he was like ‘Nah man, it’s for my compilation album,‘ but he eventually let me have it. You know, I knew how people in the ghetto would relate to words like, ‘Instead of treated we get tricked’ and ‘Instead of kisses we get kicked’… It’s like when we watch movies we’re always rooting for the villain or the underdog because that’s who we feel we are. It’s us against society. And, to me, the way the kids in the chorus are singing ‘It’s a hard-knock life’ is more like they’re rejoicing about it. Like they’re too strong to let it bring them down. And so that’s also the reason why I call it the ‘Ghetto Anthem.’

When Jay Z recorded the song in 1998 he had to clear the sample with the Annie creators. After his request was turned down, he wrote the company a letter, saying that when he was in the seventh grade, his teacher ran an essay contest with the winner receiving tickets to the Annie musical.

This was, as he writes in Decoded, “A lie… I wrote that from the moment the curtain came up I felt like I understood honey’s story.” The company bought the story and cleared the sample.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xgC6uS_AA0A

Dame Dash claims he paid Mark the 45 King 10 grand in cash for the beat in The Rise of Jay-Z documentary.

In the music business it worked in the opposite way for Jay; he created a classic with Reasonable Doubt but not everyone appreciated it due to complex wordplays and obscure references (Obscure before Rap Genius came along!).

In the following records (One each year from ‘96 to '03) he dumbed down to sell more copies, deleting everyone else’s name from the board and leaving him alone at the top.



This is also a subliminal diss at Nas, at a time when Jay Z and Nas was throwing jabs each other way. Meaning he came out on top over Nas. Nas confirms this on HuffPostLive At 28 minutes in.

The “School of Hard Knocks” is an idiom equating a painful or difficult upbringing with a normal school education. Jay learnt from a young age his turf was sacred, and he had to defend it to the death.

line: I’m calling “guts” every time,
vault_lines: I'm calling "guts" every time,
meaning:
Guts is a street version of poker in which everybody gets dealt three cards. In the most common variant, each player has to put a certain amount of money in the pot. Once you’ve been dealt your hand, the dealer says “one, two, three, drop” Everyone can either hold their cards up or, if they’re not going to stay in, drop them. If you’ve got guts, if you feel you can win, you hold your cards up to see if you have the best hand and can win the pot

Calling guts every time is always staying in to the end; while this is tough and shows resilience, it’s not necessarily always the best strategy

He also disses Sisqó in the song “Shorty”:

Said I wouldn’t mention Sisqó, fuck it, he’s a bum

And in the song “Stop” from his and Jay-Z’s next album Unfinished Business:

Keke yellin' “stop”, Sisqó’s album flopped

Sisqó along with King Of The Hill responded to R. Kelly’s disses with their diss track “This Is A Heart” from DJ Kay Slay’s mixtape Renegades Part 8 Betrayal.

In his 2010 interview with Vibe, Sisqó was asked if he still had beef with R. Kelly to which Sisqó said:

I don’t have any beef with anybody. I remember that. And it was weird because R Kelly had took a shot at me on a record that he had done, I think with Jay-Z, and that was weird because I had just saw him a couple of months before that and I was wondering what did I do for him to start taking shots at me. It was ironic because the album that he was taking shots at me on stopped selling because of the scandal that went down. Whatever he said, I just retaliated on a [Kay Slay] mixtape. It was crazy because I wasn’t gonna say anything but I just wanted them to know⎯as a matter of fact⎯MTV reported on it and they quoted something that said something like, “If you mess with a rattle snake, you’re bound to get bitten” [laughs]. And it was crazy because I learned how to write songs studying R Kelly in middle school. So when he took a shot at me I was hurt. Like, here’s somebody I look up to who took a shot at me over nothing. I didn’t do nothing to him. But then we squashed it. This was around the time that the scandal happened. I went on the radio and said I ain’t have no beef with R Kelly and I respect him. I felt like he was like a Marvin Gaye of our time with his song writing ability. He’s incredible. And then he turned around and put the same song on the last album and ironically, here’s the crazy part, his album got shut down in the exact same time period that he got shut down before. So karma is a motherfucker. Don’t mess with a child of God.

Hov reveals here that his wife Beyoncé was pregnant before she carried Blue Ivy to term. Unfortunately, the early stages of pregnancy can be fraught with risks, and she suffered a miscarriage. In her Life is But A Dream documentary in 2013 she discussed the tragic event:

About two years ago, I was pregnant for the first time. And I heard the heartbeat, which was the most beautiful music I ever heard in my life … I picked out names, I envisioned what my child would look like. I was feeling very maternal … I flew back to New York to get my check-up – and no heartbeat. Literally the week before I went to the doctor, everything was fine, but there was no heartbeat.

The concept of being “destiny’s child” is found in the Bible, in a passage in the Book of Isaiah; and can be explained as someone who is very honorable and has a pre-determined destiny bestowed upon them by God. In the Book of Isaiah, Immanuel (meaning “God with us”) was “called from the womb” by God and significantly named prior to his birth because of his divine destiny. Hov bestows the same value on his daughter, who he has waited many years for.

On his 2003 track December 4th, Jay’s mother Gloria Carter would utter sentiments similar to his lines here, saying she knew he was a special child and would have a bright future.

line: These ain’t songs, these is hymns ’cause I’m him It’s the Psalm 151, this New Testament The book of Hov (The book of Hov) Jesus turned water to wine, for Hov, it just took a stove
vault_lines: These ain't songs, these is hymns 'cause I'm him
meaning:
Psalms is a book containing lyrics to ancient Hebrew religious hymns included as part of the Christian Old Testament as well as the Jewish Tanakh. In Christian and Jewish tradition, there are only 150 Psalms – hence Hov (also a religious reference – Jay-hova / “Jehovah”, a name for the Abrahamic God) is writing the 151st, his own hymn to his miraculous success. He then escalates this to a new New Testament and picks out a title for the new Bible book about him.

The New Testament of the Christian Bible is concerned with the teachings of Jesus Christ, who, as the second person in the Trinity, is God – God can be referred to as “Him” or “He”, which is the sense in which Jay uses it in “hymns ‘cause I’m Him”. Hov’s comparing himself to Jesus, who turned water to wine at a party in the way Hov miraculously turned cooking crack on the stove into a business empire.

A real “Psalm 151” does exist in the Septuagint, an early Greek translation of the Old Testament that includes parts later excised. The Psalm is written from the point of view of David, celebrating his victory over Goliath, and praising God for choosing him to become a great leader over his tall, better-looking brothers – thematically similar to the story Jay is recounting in “GOD DID”.

God anointed me with holy oil;
God made me leader for his people,
ruler over the children
of his covenant.

line: Some new niggas out of pocket, talkin’ exotic You barely been to the Baham— (Haha) that’s another topic
vault_lines: Some new niggas out of pocket, talkin' exotic
meaning:
The line starts out with some wordplay – out of pocket is a phase that means either losing money in a transaction, or behaving inappropriately. Hov suggests his poor enemies/obnoxious haters are so far out of the pocket that they’re exotic, then plays that association into the exotic holiday destination of the Bahamas – while most people would be happy to spend a week in a hotel there, the Carters have their own island. Exotic is also slang for marijuana, transitioning from the weed theme of the previous bars.

Hov then playfully cuts off his association because he remembers the Bahamas are a tax haven. Citizens of the Bahamas do not pay tax on income or capital gains and foreign businesses can be incorporated there. This has made the Bahamas the third richest country in the Americas, after the USA and Canada.

While tax avoidance is legal, it’s an exploitation of loopholes that goes against what taxation is supposed to achieve – to keep money in the local economy and pay for infrastructure that businesses use to achieve their fortunes in the first place. Hov’s change of topic is a joking attempt to correct bringing up a dirty secret. Topic may be a pun on tropics.

The Bahamas were also a popular place for sourcing illicit drugs, though Jay-Z’s own connect was in St. Thomas.

Monogram is the name of Jay-Z’s luxury medicinal marijuana brand. On the red carpet, stars usually dress up in suits and tuxedos. It’s not uncommon for a gentleman to have a pocket square with his initials monogrammed on them.

Giggs is from the roads, a London term meaning he comes from the streets and street life. So when Jay mentions “niggas on the road”, it’s referring to hustlers in Britain recognising him as one of their own – and, as Hov sees himself in Giggs, he recognises them as like minds in return.

line: All this pain from the outside, inspired all this growth within So new planes gettin’ broken in Highest elevation of the self They done fucked around and gave the right niggas wealth

An extremely dense passage of double-meanings and wordplay.

1) Plane refers to Jay’s private plane, an emblem of his wealth. His new planes are broken in (when he takes them for a ride for the first time), he reaches his highest elevation (physically in the sky), and he makes a playful pun that he and his associates are the “right niggas” (“Wright niggas”, referring to the Wright Brothers who pioneered flight.)

2) Jay-Z owns the Paper Planes clothing brand. “[N]ew Planes getting broken in” refers to the process of wearing a new piece of clothing until it becomes more comfortable.

3) Jay is also undergoing a spiritual ascension, in preparation for becoming God in the following lines: “new planes” refers to the concept of the astral plane, an esoteric concept of a higher form of existence beyond mortality and the physical. The growth to his highest spiritual elevation is an ascent to Godhood.

4) Jay’s getting high on weed – see “growth within” and “highest elevation”. A paper plane is slang for a joint made out of rolling paper like the Monogram No.03.

line: I left the dope game with my record clean, huh
vault_lines: I left the dope game with my record clean, huh
meaning:
Here, Jay boasts about never being caught for selling drugs. His criminal record is clean. Leaving the dope game with a “clean” record is such a rare feat that Jay-Z acknowledges it here. Record can also be a reference to the “paperwork” people get when they turn informant.

Record is a double entendre for recorded music, sometimes pressed onto vinyl records. While commercial-quality vinyl recordings are pressed from molten plastic, ‘clean’ records do exist as raw material for a record cutting process called lathing. The imagery is of a blank slate onto which Jay can write his recording career.

Note also the juxtaposition between “dope” (drugs) and “clean” (a word which refers to someone who is abstinent from drugs). Hov is perhaps presenting his choice to quit selling drugs as analogous to quitting using.

line: Nobody touched the billi’ until Hov did
vault_lines: Nobody touched the billi' until Hov did
meaning:
Triple entendre.

1) Jay-Z was named the first rapper to become a billionaire in 2019. However, this is somewhat semantic – Dr. Dre claimed to be the “first billionaire in hip-hop” in 2014, but does not consider himself a rapper as he does not write his own lyrics. It’s possible Dre was exaggerating – he was worth “only” $800 million after the sale of Beats, making Hov the first to hit the billion.

After he achieved this, the next rapper to achieve billionaire status was Kanye West in 2020, who has boasted about being richer than Hov despite evidence to the contrary.

2) Jay-Z is also stating in this line that nobody touched G.O.A.T status until he did (the term “billy” referencing a male goat).

3) Bill Gates reached out to Jay in 2008 to help him with a video short for his keynote speech to Microsoft. In the video he contemplates becoming a rapper and raps a version of Jay-Z’s “Big Pimpin” while Jay-Z records him and directs him in the studio. In this way, Jay was the first rapper to touch (impact) the “Billy” Gates – who also happened to be a billionaire.

Jay also might have been the first to impact and have a relationship with famed billionaire Warren Buffet as they linked in 2010 and provided an interview to Forbes.

line: Breezy what the business is We pushin’ Fenty like fentanyl, the shit is all legitimate (Woo)
vault_lines: Breezy what the business is
meaning:
“Breezy” is the nickname of Jay-Z’s business partner, Jay Brown, who is the manager of Rihanna. Hov has previously referenced Brown by this nickname in the 2007 song “Success”:

“I got these niggas, Breezy, don’t worry about it”

As Jay-Z’s entertainment company Roc Nation manages Rihanna, they’re instrumental in putting together the deals for her Fenty brand, which sells makeup and lingerie – a long way from the illegal business of selling drugs.



Fitting the drug-dealing theme, Fentanyl is a notoriously potent opioid that is favoured by dealers for its low cost compared to heroin, and therefore commonly used to press cheap illegitimate opioids. Jay plays on that by saying “this shit is all legitimate”. America’s love affair with Fentanyl came about due to drugs companies irresponsibly pushing opioid painkillers in order to make profit – all legitimately.

A more famous Breezy is Chris Brown, who is known for his attempt to push Robyn Rihanna Fenty out of his moving Lamborghini in 2009. Considering Jay’s classy tone throughout the rest of the song, is it an intentional sick joke?

meaning:
This is an evolution from a line Jay raps on Drake’s 2013 song “Pound Cake”:

I’ve done made more millionaires than the lotto did
Dame made millions, Biggs made millions
Ye made millions, Just made millions
Lyor made millions, Cam made millions

Jay mentored many people who became millionaires, but in “GOD DID” he considers that his investments in others have created billionaires. It demonstrates that even in the last 10 years Jay’s wealth and influence has grown exponentially.

The musician billionaires listed in this lyric are Jay-Z himself, Kanye West (a signee of Jay’s Roc-A-Fella Records in 2002) and Rihanna (who Jay arranged to get signed to Def Jam in 2005). The fourth billionaire is LeBron James, the legendary basketball player, who is Roc La Familia due to his close ties with Jay-Z since the early 2000s – he can be seen with Jay on this magazine cover:



Jay-Z uses a flutter of poetic devices on the topic of basketball here. Lebron James has… 4 rings.  A technical is a type of foul in basketball.  A rock is also slang for basketball.

The “Hov crib” line is a double entendre – it also refers to Jay-Z himself and the fact that not many billionaires could come from Marcy Projects.

“Crib” also sounds like “rib,” a reference to Adam giving up one of his ribs to allow God to create Eve. Like Adam, Hov had to give up parts of himself to create the billionaires he spawned.

meaning:
The farm animal wordplay on “G.O.A.T.” and “donkey” is almost too trivial to mention.

“Donkey” is an insult referring to a stubborn idiot who won’t accept Jay is the G.O.A.T. / Greatest Of All Time (hence Jay’s apology for getting too passionate in the following lines), but Mark 11:1-11 of the Gospels states that Jesus rode a donkey into Jerusalem – the first event in what would be the final days of Jesus’s mortal life, a story known as the Passion of Christ. When Hov jokes “that’s my Passion”, he’s therefore imagining himself as Jesus triumphantly riding into the city on his haters and doubters.

In one memorable exchange from a 1996 “60 Minutes” interview with Mike Wallace, Nation of Islam Minister Louis Farrakhan responds to Mr. Wallace’s suggestion that Nigeria is the “most corrupt nation in the world” by pointing out the USA’s own corruption, emphasizing that the USA should not consider itself to be in a position of moral superiority and “should keep quiet” before it seeks to condemn other nations. At the end of the clip, Minister Farrakhan takes a conciliatory tone with Mr. Wallace, stating, “I didn’t mean to be so fiery. That’s my passion.”

line: Come money dance with the good fellas

meaning:
A “money dance” is an Italian wedding tradition used to help offset the cost of the lavish celebrations. As guests arrive they slip an envelope of cash into a purse the bride carries on her wrist. Every male guest is expected to dance with the bride and contribute their share. In 2012 Chicago rapper Lil Mouse popularized

Jay’s inviting y'all to come celebrate life (cent'anni!) with his goodfellas – a term used in the Mafia to determine a trustworthy person. Presumably Hov’s goodfellas include members of the Roc-A-Fella Records and Roc Nation crews he has kept around him throughout his career.



Beginning the verse’s Mafia references, this line also alludes to the infamous organized crime movie GoodFellas. Often regarded as one of the greatest films of all time, it starred Hov’s friend Robert De Niro – which cleverly links this line to the dinero wordplay in the next two.

line: Hov just landed in Rome, nigga All hail, Caesar’s home, niggas

meaning:
When Jay lands in exotic vacation spots like Rome, he walks around like he owns the place, even referring to himself in third person, much like a ruler would.

The reference to Julius Caesar, head of the Roman Empire, is an allusion he has used before:

You can call me Caesar / In a dark Czar



Interestingly enough, Caesar often referred to himself in the third person in his writing (see The Gallic Wars). Rather than say “I just landed…”, perhaps Jay is using his nickname (Hov) as a reference to the stylistic device (called Illeism: It is the act of referring to oneself in the third person instead of the more appropriate first person..) that Caesar employed in his work.

This verse was recorded earlier in 2013 (presumably in March, when he instagrammed his studio session with Hov) while Ross was still endorsed by Reebok. However, the song was released in July, a few months after he had been dropped from his Reebok endorsement for his now infamous molly raps.

Despite being dropped from Reebok, Ross maintains a good relationship with them. After this song dropped in late July, Ross reiterated his good relationship with Reebok, saying that he would “make an announcement when the time is right”. Ross' good relations with Reebok is perhaps why Ross left these lyrics unchanged. Rumors surfaced that Ross had re-signed with Reebok after being pictured with their CEO.

In professional sports, a free agent is a player who is eligible to sign with any club or franchise, i.e. not under contract to any specific team. The term is also used in reference to a player who is under contract at present, but who is allowed to solicit offers from other teams. In some circumstances, the free agent’s options are limited by league rules.

The term came into wider use after sports leagues stopped using the “reserve clause”, which allowed a repetitive option by the club to renew the contract for one (or more years) but did not allow the player to terminate it.

However, while Ross discusses contracts, he is likely referring to the philosophy of Plato:

In sociology and philosophy, agency is the capacity of an agent (a person or other entity, human or any living being in general, or soul-consciousness in religion) to act in a world. The capacity to act does not at first imply a specific moral dimension to the ability to make the choice to act, and moral agency is therefore a distinct concept. In sociology, an agent is an individual engaging with the social structure. Notably, though, the primacy of social structure vs. individual capacity with regard to persons' actions is debated within sociology. This debate concerns, at least partly, the level of reflexivity an agent may possess.

Agency may either be classified as unconscious, involuntary behavior, or purposeful, goal directed activity (intentional action). An agent typically has some sort of immediate awareness of their physical activity and the goals that the activity is aimed at realizing. In ‘goal directed action’ an agent implements a kind of direct control or guidance over their own behavior.

In short, Ross is restricted by neither contracts or social structures.

line: The spook that spoke sterling silver and pearls twirled, tumbled out my nappy coils
vault_lines: The spook that spoke sterling silver and pearls twirled, tumbled out my nappy coils
meaning:
This line plays on identity, code-switching, and shedding imposed personas. “Spook” carries a double meaning, it can refer to a ghost (something hidden or intangible) but is also a historically racist term for Black people. By pairing it with “spoke sterling silver and pearls,” the lyric suggests a version of the self that speaks in a polished, refined, Eurocentric way—symbolizing assimilation into elite or white-dominated standards.

“Twirled, tumbled out my nappy coils” flips that image. “Nappy coils” refers to natural Black hair, often stigmatized but here reclaimed as a symbol of authenticity. The movement (“twirled, tumbled”) suggests that this artificial, assimilated persona is unraveling or being cast off.

Overall, the line reflects the tension between performative refinement and authentic Black identity, showing the speaker rejecting imposed standards and returning to their natural self.

Jay Elec claims that Louis Farrakhan saved him from ruining his life and running towards his demise.

The Sunnah literally translates to mean “The Way” and is regularly referred to with regards to the Prophet Muhammad PBUH: The Sunnah of the Prophet – the way of the Prophet. Here, Jay Elec says that Farrakhan pointed him towards the Sunnah, meaning that he pointed him towards the right path in life.

As opposed to the adlibs on the first two lines of this verse, he says “Mash'Allah” this time, which translates to “What Allah has willed”. line: I send duaa’s up from the belly of the Dunya (Subhanallah) Duaa’s up for my umi in the ummah (Subhanallah) Duaa’s up for the honorable Louis Farrakhan
vault_lines: I send duaa's up from the belly of the Dunya (Subhanallah)
meaning:
The word “Duaa'” (transliterated from its Arabic original) literally means invocation. It means to call out, or to supplicate and is generally used when Muslims are making dua, i.e they are calling upon Allah or supplicating towards Him.

The Dunya means the world. The Arabic word for world is Dunya.

Umi is the word for “my mother” in Arabic. As many Hip-Hop fans and scholars will know it became popular in the hood vernacular after Mos Def (now addressed as Yasiin Bey) released his famous track “Umi says” on his 1999 “Black on Both Sides”.

JAY-Z also uses the word “Umi” in his 2018 BLACK EFFECT when he says (referring to Mos Def’s Umi Says):

Shining my light on the world just
 like Umi says

The word Ummah means “Nation”. It comes from the root word “Umm” which is also the root word for “Umi”. It seems that Jay Elec has studied the languages and understands these connections because in the next line he sends his duaa’s up for Louis Farrakhan who is the current leader of the Nation of Islam.

The word “subhanAllah” means “How perfect is Allah” and is used as a supplication for when something is surprising, or someone makes shocking allegations among other uses.

meaning:
This line has several meanings.

Jay could be alluding to the time he pled guilty to a misdemeanor assault charge in the connection of the 1999 stabbing of record executive Lance “Un” Rivera in the back. As in, the “old Jay” was willing to stab his rivals.

The homonym he creates with “old Jay” and “O'Jay, so Jay could also be referencing The O'Jays 1972 soul classic “Back Stabbers.” On the track, the group sung about disingenuous friends who smile in your face, but are really envious. The song peaked at Number 3 on Billboard’s Hot 100.

It’s possible that Jay is also making a thinly veiled reference to OJ Simpson, who famously was on trial for the 1994 stabbing and murder of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman.

Hov uses the line to illustrate how much he’s changed. He’s now a billionaire, who runs several successful entertainment businesses (Roc Nation/ TIDAL), sports (Roc Nation Sports) and alcohol suppliers (Armand de Brignac, D'USSÉ). But Jay also suggests that he quickly can revert back to the mentality he had as a hustler in the streets of Brooklyn and New Jersey, where he was much more ruthless.

line: But I evolve with the flow
vault_lines: But I evolve with the flow
meaning:
In 2011, while on a promotional run for his memoir Decoded, Hov explained how he has mastered many types of flows over his career:

When I first started writing raps, I was a kid. I started when I was nine-years-old, so I didn’t have real life experiences. The thing I drew off of was being creative. It was more about the technique than what I was saying. I was trying to say things in different ways – doing faster flows and triplet styles. It was more of a technical thing.”

Jay added that as he collected more real life experiences, he focused more on subject matter and less on the technical aspects of his rhymes:

It became more about the words, more about what I was saying and more about this emotion and this truth. But I still had the technical side because I was writing for so many years.”

In turn this increase in his emotional delivery has resulted in the silky smooth flow we hear on most of his songs today, where he manages to find the pocket in almost any beat.

The “crossover dribble” is when a player moves the ball from hand to hand to change direction quickly and confuse the defender. A slam dunk is when a player scores with both feet off the ground and one or both hands touching the rim.

He locks it all together with a reference to the infamous Rucker Park in Harlem, which is one of New York’s most hallowed streetball courts. Many famous NBA players honed their skills at the park growing up, including Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Wilt Chamberlain, Julius “Dr. J” Erving, Kobe Bryant, Stephon Marbury, Metta World Peace, Kyrie Irving, and Harlem Globetrotters legend Jumpin' Jackie Jackson.

The year before this track’s release, in the Summer of 2003, Hov had formed a S. Carter team to battle for streetball supremacy in the Rucker Park “Entertainers Basketball Classic.”

Ironically, after buying the Ace of Spades Champagne along with Armand De Brignac, Jay called for a boycott on Cristal, ceasing from mentioning its name in his raps. Cristal is wine brand created in 1876 for Alexander II.

line: It’s just once in a blue when there’s nothing to do When the tension gets too thick for my sober mind to cut through
vault_lines: It's just once in a blue when there's nothing to do
meaning:
Hov employs the idiom “one in a blue moon” here to describe how he rarely smokes marijuana. He explains he is using the weed as a calming influence as the tensions of the streets overrun his brain.

His protégé J. Cole riffs on these lines in “How High:”

No I don’t smoke, maybe once in a blue
When the tension gets thick then there’s nothing to do

line: No doubt, they can vouch my life is real as shit ’95 South
vault_lines: No doubt, they can vouch my life is real as shit
meaning:
Before he became a full-time rapper Jay used to drug-run along the I-95. The legendary DJ Clark Kent can do the vouching for Hov here:

Last night, my man Jay-Z killed the B-Sides show. There were plenty of great moments. But, for us, nothing was better than seeing this sign on stage. Probably didn’t mean much to many, but, there were a group of us that loved this one feature. Before I could search, find, and convince Jay to get to the music, this was the way, the road, the route to the paper. It was the main reason Jay didn’t want to rap. But, once I talked enough, we started to work. One of the first songs was named ‘95 South..’ It quickly became our unofficial theme song. It was so important to us, we made a second version. As soon as I saw the sign on stage, I could hear every one of the six verses. Might not have meant to much to those of you that saw the show but to us it was everything. Just look at how far you can go. You killed it Homie.

line: I’m in the rain doing a buck 40, hydroplaning, what, shorty?
vault_lines: I'm in the rain doing a buck 40, hydroplaning, what, shorty?
meaning:
Despite a rainy forecast, Jigga has one of his whips out for a drive. The roads are wet and slippery, but this doesn’t stop him from doing 140 miles-per-hour, eventually causing him to “hydroplane.” Hydroplaning occurs when a car’s wheels lose grip with the road as a result of water building between the tires and surface or the road.



Going 140 mph is probably not the safest thing to do while its raining, but Jay-Z pretty much does what he wants.

line: I keep it tight for all the nights my momma prayed I’d stop Said she had dreams that sniper hit me with a fatal shot, those nightmares, ma Them dreams that you say you got
vault_lines: I keep it tight for all the nights my momma prayed I'd stop
meaning:
Jay would elaborate more on this during “Regrets”:

My mom’s crying because her insides are dying
Her son trying her patience, keep her heart racing

During interviews he hasn’t been too open about the way his mother must have felt, to lose another of her family to the streets. He’s been very vocal on tracks though:

Til you heard the cries of my mama, me givin her drama
Told her I ain’t promised tomorrow, gotta live for the day
And before she could say Jay…
I was out the door, pouch full of raw, a outlaw mentality

The “sniper” in this instance most likely refers to the Feds, whom Jay was slightly paranoid about at the time:

 you gotta know
It always crossed my mind that Feds be tappin the lines like Gregory Hines

By this point Jay was out of the game for good, so he can look back on it with a more calm frame of mind.

line: The Cristals they keep me wet like Baywatch
vault_lines: The Cristals they keep me wet like Baywatch
meaning:
Baywatch was still incredibly popular during the mid 90s, a TV show about surf-lifesavers and their complex personal lives. Cristal is wet, but it’s a double entendre. To be “wet” also means to be with women, so not only does Cristal quench Jay’s thirst, it makes him seem more appealing to women due to his wealth.

Now he just uses cash.

line: (Where you disappear to, son?) Maintaining Putting myself in a position most of these rappers ain’t in, I’m living
vault_lines: (Where you disappear to, son?) Maintaining
meaning:
This is a direct call back to his hustling days. During Decoded Jay recalled times when he would disappear for months on end to hustle out of state:

When I’d leave Brooklyn for long stretches and come back a hundred years later, Clark would find me and say, ‘Let’s do this music.’… I was so skeptical about the business that I would also get annoyed.

Jay also explained that the feeling on the street was “these rappers are hoes,” being pimped out by the major record labels. And after his mentor Jaz-O was handled poorly by EMI, it further showed Jay he had to create his own situation, and not rely on corporate people to keep their word.

line: We paid the price to circle us, success, they turned my mic up I’m ’bout to hit these niggas with some shit that’ll light your life up
vault_lines: We paid the price to circle us, success, they turned my mic up
meaning:
This was a major theme on Reasonable Doubt, the idea that Jay had paid his dues, living “a whole bunch of life” in order to craft these stories.

To “light ya life up” means to give hope or meaning where there was none before. Again, this proved to be prophetic, because Jay gave another version of the stereotypical Black American narrative (you either play ball or sell drugs). Now, a kid from the streets could attain wealth and power merely through strength of will.

line: Since diapers, had nothing to live for like them lifers but Making sure every nigga stay rich within my cipher
vault_lines: Since diapers, had nothing to live for like them lifers but
meaning:
A huge theme during Reasonable Doubt was the idea that hustlers are pre-determined to be hustlers, via the harsh conditions they face and the lack of opportunities. A “lifer” is someone imprisoned for life, Jay feels rail-roaded into a certain existence as if he’s already serving a life sentence.

On that note, now that he’s achieved a little bit of success he wants to ensure he shares it with those around him. This line was incredibly prophetic. In subsequent years he’s “made more millionaires than the Lotto did,” with people like Memphis Bleek, Dame Dash, Cam'ron, Beanie Sigel, Emory Jones, and even Lyor Cohen profiting off his incredible run. This isn’t an exhaustive list by any means.

line: Bone crushers I keep real close, I got the skill for this On my back the flyest clothes, looking ill as shit
vault_lines: Bone crushers I keep real close, I got the skill for this
meaning:
The opening of the verse is spoken directly to a female companion, as Jay displays his trademark cockiness but manages to back it up, with a whole bunch of Cristal, and incredible clothing, which at the time might have seen like a boast, until his Iceberg Slim persona rocking Iceberg clothing, and his eventual creation of a Rocawear empire.

“Bone crusher” was mentioned in “Can’t Get With That,” in similar circumstances. It may mean his lyrical skill, or it may simply mean something like brass knuckles.

line: I’m feeling it, feel the high that you get from the lye
vault_lines: I'm feeling it, feel the high that you get from the lye
meaning:
Back in the day Jay did occasionally indulge in marijuana, although he basically swore it off in the years that ensued. In Decoded Jay recalls a scene where he was with The Notorious B.I.G. and got completely smoked out.

Weed plays a huge role in this track, with Jay riding the feeling that the game has given him down whatever road it takes him. In this instance, it takes him towards getting high and enjoying himself.

An “L” is a blunt.

line: [Chorus: Mecca]
vault_lines: Ha ha, ha ha
meaning:
Per Village Voice, Mecca was just 17 when Ski flew her from Virginia to NYC to sing this hook.

As Mecca tells it:

I was there with Ski, and he and I created the melody together, and then Ski came up with the lyrics.

Or as Ski tells it:

[Mecca] got paid for singing, obviously. But I wrote the hook for the song. I guess the people that she was dealing with got in her ear and made her think she wrote the song and that she deserved all the publishing and that burned the bridge for what we was doing. They definitely wanted to work with her but it never got that far.

And that explains why you don’t see Mecca on any other Jay-Z songs.

line: [Produced by Ski Beatz]
vault_lines: Ha ha, ha ha
meaning:
The sample for this track is Ahmad Jamal’s jazzy-toned “Pastures.”

Skip to 1:09 for the sample

https://soundcloud.com/docdrilla/ahmad-jamal-pastures#t=1:09

Ski Beatz had this to say when asked about his role in the song:


That was my song! It was a song I was working on for my album at the time. It was me and Suede from Camp Lo rapping on it. I was happy about the song so I ran up in Dame’s house and Jay was there. I played it for them and they got the mad frown face, bopping they head, like, ‘This is dope!’

Then Jay was like, ‘You know you gotta give me that song right?’ I was like, ‘What do you mean? I just did this song!’ He was like, ‘Come on B, I need that for my album. You know we’re working on this album. Give me that beat, I want that hook too.’ He took the beat, the hook, and the flow too! Which was cool, it wasn’t like he didn’t ask me for it. He didn’t jack it. He told me he was going to do it.

The thing with Mecca [was] she sung the hook. She got paid for singing, obviously. But I wrote the hook for the song. I guess the people that she was dealing with got in her ear and made her think she wrote the song and that she deserved all the publishing and that burned the bridge for what we was doing. They definitely wanted to work with her but it never got that far.

line: But at the same time these dimes keep me feeling tight
vault_lines: But at the same time these dimes keep me feeling tight
meaning:
Dimes refers to dime bags, which keep him feeling tight because being a drug dealer causes you to feel trapped, always having to watch for police or cats that wanna kill you.

The line could also refer to dimes as in beautiful women (10 out of 10=dime) because they compliment him now that he’s paid, which makes him feel good (“tight”).

line: Give me the chills but these mills, well, they make me hot
vault_lines: Give me the chills but these mills, well, they make me hot
meaning: The nightmares that he might get shot cause him anxiety, nerves. During “Regrets” he admits to being scared, but on “Can I Live” he’s defiant, saying “I’d rather die enormous than live dormant.” These lines are somewhere between the two extremes. He’s almost detached, saying her fears scare him too, but it’s a small price to pay for the money he’s making.

line: And all the towns like Cambridge that I killed with shit
vault_lines: And all the towns like Cambridge that I killed with shit
meaning: Hov’s close friend Emory “Vegas” Jones grew up in Cambridge, Maryland. Hov would stay with Vegas when he was drug-running along the I-95, stopping to cook crack at his house on Robbins Street.

line: Y’all don’t feel me Enough to stop the illing right?
vault_lines: , y'all don't feel me
meaning:
“‘Illin’”  is referencing the ‘illegitimate’ transactions he must do to get by.

It’s used the same way in “Can I Live”:

Illin' for revenue/Rayful Edmonds like"

Is the money he’s made enough to get him out of the game permanently? It’s a gamble either way. If he stays, he’s gambling with his life. If he leaves, he’s gambling his future and income.

line: And Papi on the Hill and shit
vault_lines: and Papi on the Hill and shit
meaning:
Jay-Z often mentions a “Papi” as his early drug connect, along with “Spanish Jose” and other intentionally unverifiable names, like “sure, I used to sell drugs! Who was my connect? Papi…you know…Papi, Papi Chulo, the one on the Hill.”

“The Hill” is a historic black neighborhood on Maryland’s Eastern Shore in a town called Easton where Jay Z used to sell drugs. Easton is a neighboring town to Cambridge, in which he refers in the following bar.

line: I’m so confused Okay I’m getting weeded now I know I contradicted myself, look, I don’t need that now
vault_lines: , I'm so confused
meaning:
Jay is confused from the weed smoke, and doesn’t “need” your input on his consistency. He’s self commenting on how weed disorients your train of thought.

He’s confused whether or not to get out of the game.  His mom is scared of him getting killed, and he has already made millions.  But the attention from the girls the pecks that come with the drug-dealing life make this a hard decision.

The verse flows in a probing fashion. Jay is painting a picture of an inner struggle to quit the game of drug dealing as well as the burden of knowing his loved ones(mom most pointedly) are worried about how this is going to end for him. His confusion is with all these choices and decisions he has to make and then it gets so bad, he succumbs to smoking weed, something he’s been against just to show the listener how vulnerable he’s feeling by the end of this verse. He’s aware of the contradiction and he doesn’t need you to add any further chastising to his already tormented/confused state of mind.. Just let him be…

line: The Ill Street Blues got you hunger paining
vault_lines: The Ill Street Blues got you hunger paining
meaning:
A play on the title of the T.V. show Hill Street Blues, Jay-Z’s streets are “ill” (sick); the denizens are hungry for sustenance

 Also a reference to this Kool G Rap classic.

line: If every nigga in your clique is rich, your clique is rugged Nobody will fall ’cause everyone will be each others crutches
vault_lines: If every nigga in your clique is rich, your clique is rugged
meaning:
There’s a theme in rap of successful artists coming back and putting their friends on. Eminem did it with D12, Nelly did it with St. Lunatics, and Jay did it with Roc-A-Fella.

This is another way of diversifying your income stream. If each member of an entourage has their own identity, and their own way of making money, if one of them falls the others can pick them up. Jay’s basically laying out the blueprint for how he would run Roc-A-Fella, although it didn’t quite work out that way.

Essentially, Jay remained the key piece of the money-making puzzle. If he ever fell off, his friends would too, which was exemplified by the split of The Roc and Dame Dash and Kareem Burke’s subsequent financial failures.

Even Memphis Bleek, who achieved Gold success more than once on the label, is still reliant on Jay’s name, although he works incredibly hard himself.

line: Transactions illegitimate ’cause life is still a bitch And then you die but for now, life, close your eyes and feel this dick
vault_lines: Transactions illegitimate 'cause life is still a bitch
meaning:
This is a reference to AZ’s existentialist hook on “Life’s A Bitch” by Nas:

Life’s a bitch and then you die

Jay takes the personification of life even further by fucking her, enjoying her while he can.

line: (Ha-ya) Ha-ya, ha-ya, ha-ya, ha-ya (Ha-ya) Ha-ya, ha-ya, ha-ya (Ha-ya) Ha-ya, ha-ya, ha-ya Ha-ya-ya-ya Ha-ya, ha-ya Love me like, love Yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah Like, yeah, yeah, yeah
vault_lines: (Ha-ya) Ha-ya, ha-ya, ha-ya, ha-ya
meaning: This samples “Ha-Ya” by The Clark Sisters. “Ha-Ya” is a Hebrew tongue that means life.

line: Can I get “Amen” from the congregation? Amen, amen (Ha-ya) Can I get a “Amen” from the congregation? Amen, amen (Ha-ya) Ha-ya-ya-ya
vault_lines: Can I get "Amen" from the congregation?
meaning: “Amen” is a Hebrew word meaning it is so or indeed/truly. Amen is used in predominately Christian cultures to end prayer or to express agreement. Jay Z asking for an Amen is similar to how Christian preachers will ask for the congregation to follow what’s he/she is saying. Jay Z is asking his listeners if they agree with what he is “preaching”.

line: Fuck rap, crack cocaine
vault_lines: Fuck rap, crack cocaine
meaning:
To many old heads, “rap” has been the cause of the deterioration of the hood and young black men. To many who have grown up in drug-plagued communities me it’s hard to tell them that “rap” has been more detrimental to their lives and community than ‘the glass pipe’.

Furthermore, there’s a far bigger world out there of options that they haven’t explored, which would allow them to further support the Black community if they start entering new territories. The more ways there are to keep money within the Black community, the more they win.

line: Hahahaha (Ha-ya) I would say I’m the realest nigga rappin’ (Ha-ya) But that ain’t even a statement (Ha-ya) That’s like sayin’ I’m the tallest midget (Ha-ya) Wait, that ain’t politically correct, forget it (Ha-ya)
vault_lines: I would say I'm the realest nigga rappin' (Ha-ya)
meaning:
Jay uses a term used for an extremely short person, often one afflicted with dwarfism. The tallest midget is therefore something a bit oxymoronic – “midgets” themselves are extremely short, so the tallest of midgets is still shorter than the average person. Out of all rappers, Jay’s labeling himself the best; it’s a bit of a weak label, though, because all rappers these days aren’t very good in the first place.

With the rise of a more “politically correct” culture, people have highlighted that “midget” is a hateful, insensitive term. Jay fits into a growing number of critics of “PC” culture, pushing concerns about sensitivity to the side after briefly acknowledgment.

line: Ain’t no such thing as an ugly billionaire, I’m cute (Mmm, mmm) Pretty much If anybody gettin’ handsome checks, it should be us
vault_lines: Ain't no such thing as an ugly billionaire, I'm cute
meaning:
Here, Jay pokes fun at the negative comments made online about his looks — for example, the Joe Camel look-alike meme. In relationships, looks are known to sometimes be cast to the wayside when money comes into the picture, so he points out the fact that to those people, it should be irrelevant with his almost-billionaire status.

The last two lines also contain wordplay on appearances – “Pretty much” and “handsome checks.”

This isn’t the first time Hov has used these appearance verbs in his rhymes. This, from 2008’s “Jockin' Jay-Z (Dopeboy Fresh)”:

I ain’t no pretty boy, I got a gorgeous wrist
Cut handsome checks and my flow’s pretty, sick

line: Nobody wins when the family feuds
vault_lines: Nobody wins when the family feuds
meaning:
JAY-Z’s use of “family” encompasses both his own family and the black community as a whole. 4:44 is largely driven by the value of black capitalism—here, he’s expressing the need for black people to support black-owned business, since it’s already at a disadvantage.

Ironically, a feud of sorts was already happening behind the scenes. Kanye West, who was originally a co-owner of TIDAL, ceased his contract with the streaming service about a month before the release of 4:44. He claimed that the company owed him money, and TIDAL threatened to sue if he were to move to another service. News of the situation broke two days after the album dropped.

line: New niggas is the reason I stopped drinkin’ Dos Equis
vault_lines: New niggas is the reason I stopped drinkin' Dos Equis
meaning:
Dos Equis is a beer brand famous for its “Most Interesting Man in The World” advertising campaign. The original Most Interesting Man was Jonathan Goldsmith, who was the face of the brand for years, but in 2016, the brand retired Goldsmith and introduced a new Most Interesting Man—actor Augustin Legrand. The replacement was generally not well received by fans of the brand. Similarly, JAY-Z has stopped listening to new, popular hip-hop because he doesn’t like the up-and-coming generation of rappers.

This may also be a subliminal shot at hip-hop magazine XXL, since “Dos Equis” translates to “two Xs.” XXL’s 2016 Freshman Class included newer rappers like Lil Uzi Vert, 21 Savage, Lil Yachty, and Kodak Black, but Hov was the cover star on the first ever XXL magazine back in 1997. He may be suggesting the magazine’s decline.

line: How is him or Pill Cosby s’posed to help me? Old niggas never accepted me
vault_lines: How is him or Pill Cosby s'posed to help me?
meaning: Bill Cosby is also part of the older generation that has their fair share to say about the younger generation. He is also known to disparage the black community and advocate “respectability politics” as a cure for racism. However, with the recent allegations of his sexual assault of multiple women, how much room does he actually have? To further assert his point, Jay also changes up his name to Pill Cosby, due to claims of Bill drugging the women.

line: Y’all think small, I think Biggie
vault_lines: Y'all think small, I think Biggie
meaning:
To “think small” is to have short-term or easily-achievable goals, but Jay adds a little twist, referencing The Notorious B.I.G., also known as “Biggie Smalls.” JAY-Z does this not only to state that he “thinks big”, meaning he has long-term and difficult-to-attain goals, but he also wants to leave behind a legacy similar to Biggie Smalls', whom he’s carried the New York torch for since Biggie’s death in 1997.

Biggie and Jay were close before Biggie’s death, collaborating on “Brooklyn’s Finest” from Jay’s 1996 debut album Reasonable Doubt, and “I Love the Dough” from Biggie’s 1997 sophomore album Life After Death.

line: Super Bowl goals
vault_lines: (Ha-ya) My nigga got on
meaning: Jay’s wife Beyoncé has played the Superbowl Halftime Show on two occasions. In 2013, during Super Bowl XLVII, Bey was the headliner. She also joined headliner Coldplay in 2016 during Superbowl 50 and stole the show performing her song “Formation.”

line: Hovi’s home, all these phonies come to a halt
vault_lines: Hovi's home, all these phonies come to a halt
meaning:
Jay, no stranger to the the art of the grand re-introduction, announces his much talked about return to rap game, noting as he does a distinct lack of activity in his presence from those who may have tried to occupy his spot in his absence.

The release of 4:44 comes almost a full four years after the similarly quick-strike release of his last record, 2013’s Magna Carta… Holy Grail, making it the longest gap between album’s of his career, with even his short-lived, post Black Album retirement resulting in a shorter hiatus.

He underscores the magnitude of his re-emergence by invoking one of his most self-aggrandising nicknames, Hovi being a short for Jay-Hova, itself a riff on the Jehovah, which is a Hebrew name for God.

This is not the first time that Hov has announced his arrival in this exact fashion, perhaps most notably declaring that “Hovi’s home!” over the opening strains of the stellar, M.O.P. featuring remix to his track “U Don’t Know”, way back on his 2002 album The Blueprint 2: The Gift & The Curse.

line: I cooked up more chicken when the kitchen closed
vault_lines: I cooked up more chicken when the kitchen closed
meaning:
“Chicken” is slang for a kilogram of cocaine, by extension of the slang term “bird” which means the same. Jay’s moved on from that life—he “closed the kitchen”—but he’s still making more money now with music than he would’ve by selling drugs.

Jay also literally cooked up chicken at Crown Fried Chicken in Brooklyn before his music career.

line: My wife in the crib feedin’ the kids liquid gold We in a whole different mode
vault_lines: My wife in the crib feedin' the kids liquid gold
meaning: Colostrum, the first stage of breast milk, is sometimes referred to as “liquid gold” for its gold-ish color as well as its high nutritional content and antibodies. It can also be sold for $1 to $3 per ounce. It seems Beyoncé is breastfeeding her and JAY-Z’s children. The family life is quite different from Jay’s rocky past.

line: Uh, we gon’ reach a billi’ first
vault_lines: Uh, we gon' reach a billi' first
meaning:
The race is coming to a close! Rap moguls JAY-Z, Diddy, and Dr. Dre are in an unofficial competition to become hip-hop’s first self-made billionaire.

As of January 2017, Diddy currently sits in first place with an estimated net-worth of $820 million. Jay is only $10 million behind on $810 million; and Dre trails behind them at $740 million. Jay has got it set in mind that the TIDAL/Sprint deal and touring this album will push him to a billion by 2018.

line: Al Sharpton in the mirror takin’ selfies
vault_lines: Al Sharpton in the mirror takin' selfies
meaning:
A reference to an Al Sharpton Instagram post from June 18, 2017, which instantly became a viral meme sensation:

https://www.instagram.com/p/BVec_JAgpah/

Mentioning such a recent event suggests that Jay was recording the album up until just a few days before it was released, which was confirmed in an interview with producer No I.D.:

We did that maybe Monday? Maybe Tuesday. I finished it Thursday morning.

Al tweeted a response of sorts in the afternoon on release day:

https://twitter.com/TheRevAl/status/880924266740547586

Jay first called out the pastor in 2007 on “Say Hello” after he led a march to various record labels calling for more decency in hip-hop lyrics:

And if Al Sharpton is speaking for me
Somebody give him the word and tell him I don’t approve
Tell him I remove the curses
If you tell me our schools gon' be perfect
When Jena Six don’t exist
Tell him that’s when I’ll stop saying bitch

line: All this old talk left me confused You’d rather be old rich me or new you?
vault_lines: All this old talk left me confused
meaning:
Most likely a “friendly” shot at Drake with whom Jay has traded jabs a few times in the past.

On “Summer Sixteen” Drake rapped :

I used to wanna be on Roc-A-Fella then I turned into Jay

And more recently on Portland :

Fuck bein' rich when I’m forty, man, I’m tryna make it now

Which many took as a shot at Jay, who now says that he and whoever else is coming for him needs to decide rather they want to be him or themselves.

line: (Ha-ya) My nigga got on (Ha-ya) My nigga got on all white, no socks (Ha-ya, ha-ya) My nigga got that cocaina on today That’s how he feel, turn my vocal up (Ha-ya) That’s how you feel, Emory? (Ha-ya) Turn my vocal up some more
vault_lines: (Ha-ya) My nigga got on
meaning:
Hov is referencing his close friend and former-drug-dealing partner Emory “Vegas” Jones. In January 2000 he went down for 16 years on a cocaine trafficking charge—but he never snitched on Jay. He served thirteen years in prison and was released in 2010.

“Cocaina” is the Spanish term for cocaine. Like cocaine, Emory’s outfit is all white.

Give me one shot, one pot
I’ll show up in all white, wearing no socks

line: I told my wife the spiritual shit really work Alhamdulillah, I run through ’em all
vault_lines: I told my wife the spiritual shit really work
meaning:
It seems that as Jay’s success level rises, he believes that his past prayers towards such have been answered and has a newfound love for religion. If one worked, others must, right? He states he’ll “run through ‘em all,” even throwing out the Arabic “Alhamdulillah,” meaning “Praise be to God,” normally used within the Muslim community.

Though different in meaning, Jay also has a 2016 song called “spiritual,” which has a related line:

(All this work can pay off)
I just want all this work to pay off
(Just don’t calculate us)
Don’t calculate us

Jay may also reference the self-study book A Course In Miracles. His wife, Beyoncé, first linked to it on her song “All Night” and Jay later mentioned it in his verse on Pusha T’s “Drug Dealers Anonymous”:

I’m a course of miracles with this shit
Nothing real can be threatened, nothing unreal exists
Therein lies the piece of God

line: The kid that used to pitch bricks can’t be pigeonholed
vault_lines: The kid that used to pitch bricks can't be pigeonholed
meaning:
Jay has always been open about his drug dealing past. As a kid, Jay used to convince people to buy bricks from him. But he has since built a reputation for himself and can no longer be “pigeonholed” by the term drug dealer because he has become much more than a drug dealer. Jay speaks directly to his success in a large variety of fields and the many titles he has gained; specifically, he points to how difficult it is to define him with just one title.

Along with bricks, a “bird” is also another term for cocaine, presenting more wordplay connecting to “pigeonholed.”

line: And old niggas, y’all stop actin’ brand new Like 2Pac ain’t have a nose ring too, huh
vault_lines: And old niggas, y'all stop actin' brand new
meaning:
JAY-Z calls out the hypocrisy of hip-hop’s older generation for criticizing new wave rappers' fashion forward style choices.

While “hip-hop purists” crucify the likes of Young Thug and Lil Uzi Vert for rocking nose rings, dresses, blouses, and other clothes that express femininity, they seem to forget that 2Pac, who many hip-hop fans consider to be one of the greatest rappers of all time, also pushed boundaries, often wearing a nose ring, too.



The day after 4:44 was released, Young Thug posted a screenshot of the previous version of this Genius annotation on his Instagram account with the comment “Thanks JAY…”.

line: Turn my vocal up, Guru! (Ha-ya) Turn the music up too

Jay wants to help upcoming artists make it in the game. He offers up some wordplay…

1) on tools, surrounding the word with “screwed” and “fix.”

2) on referees, or officials, and the stripes that make up their standard uniform. “No stripes” refers to no experience and not being signed to any labels, and could in turn refer to the stripes of the JAY-Z owned record label Roc Nation.



Jay continues this sports theme in the next lines. In touch football, the quarterback can have 10 seconds in the Mississippi countdown – “1 Mississippi, 2 Mississippi…” – to attempt a pass before the opposition can move in to intervene (at “10 Mississippi”). When Jay gets “big thoughts,” his competition in the rap game is in danger.

line: And we merrily merrily eatin’ off these streams
vault_lines: And we merrily merrily eatin' off these streams
meaning:
This is a play on the classic “Row, Row, Row Your Boat" nursery rhyme:

Row, row, row your boat
Gently down the stream
Merrily, merrily, merrily, merrily
Life is but a dream

JAY-Z is rowing his own boat by being an owner of the music streaming service TIDAL. On these, a song’s total “streams” is the number of times it’s been played. TIDAL’s name itself also relates to the rhyme as tides and streams are both water-related, which is where you row boats.

Life is definitely dream-worthy for Jay with the amount of money coming in from his song streams. TIDAL reportedly pays artists royalties over three times the amount that Spotify pays per stream. Jay debuted 4:44 exclusively on TIDAL, and there was a lot of promotional push to drive up streams beforehand. Sprint even had a deal that prevented anyone but Sprint customers from signing up for TIDAL after 12AM EST on the night of its release.

line: Nobody wins when the family feuds But my stash can’t fit into Steve Harvey’s suit
vault_lines: Nobody wins when the family feuds
meaning:
Steve Harvey is the current host of the television game show Family Feud. Jay again refers to his almost-billionaire status and how he has too much money—or too big of a ‘stache, as a play on Steve’s recognizable mustache—to be hidden in one of Harvey’s suits. Whether that being a suit from Steve’s clothing line or a reference to the fact that he is known for wearing oversized suits, the point still stands.



Hov wants the rap game to model themselves after the premise of the game show, by working together as a family rather than infighting. He doesn’t want to see the “old school” beefing with the “new school"—this only causes tension in the genre and changes the way outsiders look at the artists.

Drug dealers also used to hide their supply and money in the lining of suits, which could tie these lines into Jay’s past experience in the business.

The two have an established relationship, with them meeting through Bad Boy Records rapper Biggie in 1996 and supporting each others projects ever since.



Moreover, regardless of who the actual billionaires are, Jay wants everyone within the culture, or black people in general, to succeed in their lives.

line: I’ll be damned if I drink some Belvedere while Puff got CÎROC
vault_lines: I'll be damned if I drink some Belvedere while Puff got CÎROC
meaning:
As heard throughout the song, Jay is clearly a proponent of supporting black-owned business, and it’s common thought that Diddy owns CÎROC, which is apparently not the case.

CÎROC is actually owned by the liquor company Diageo, but Puff does have a brand ambassador deal, getting 50% of proceeds from the company. The company’s current CEO and chairman are Indian-born and Spanish, respectively, and past representatives include those of English, British, and Swiss-Austrian backgrounds — but none of a black lineage. Diddy receiving half of the profit could be grounds for an argument of ownership, but in all technicality, it’s not there.

In the end, Jay could just be applauding a fellow black man’s business game. Before Diddy signed the deal in 2007, CÎROC was selling about 60,000 cases. For the year of 2009, that number rose to 400,000. As of 2015, he was bringing in double-digit millions per year, with the liquor being the bulk of the income.

Jay showed support for the liquor previously on another No I.D. produced song, “Primetime”:

I hit the club, ordered some Grey Goose
Switched it for CÎROC to give Puff’s stocks a boost

In 2014, Jay acquired the Armand de Brignac champagne brand, also known as “Ace of Spades” because of the bottles' golden spade logo. Perrier-Jouët is also a brand of champagne, but it’s a primarily white-owned company.

Armand de Brignac consistently beat out Perrier-Jouët in total number of searches on Wine Searcher until December 2015 when it trailed behind Perrier-Jouët by a margin of nearly a thousand. Ace of Spades' total search numbers have continued to decline since, which speaks to the thesis of the song. If Jay can’t influence you to buy in to black-owned businesses, then how does the black community change the narrative?

Fans of the Beyhive assumed “Becky” to be designer Rachel Roy, who posted a photo with the caption “good hair, don’t care” on Instagram shortly after the release of Lemonade. Roy later debunked the idea that “Becky” referred to her.

Jay references this lyric from “Sorry” and warns Becky, whoever that may be, to leave him alone because if given the opportunity, he might fuck up a good thing (his marriage with Beyoncé) again.

There’s a bit of wordplay active with “alone” as well, which also can translate as an economic loan — given the song’s overarching discussion of wealth, it fits right in.

My mom’s advice – ‘What you put in is what you get out’ – worked for me and against me. Sometimes I took it too literally – since the rhymes came so easily to me, since I wrote them so fast, I thought they weren’t worth anything. line: And I need you to remember one thing (One thing) I came, I saw, I conquered From record sales to sold-out concerts So, motherfucker, if you want this encore I need you to scream ’til your lungs get sore
vault_lines: Thank you, thank you, thank you!
meaning:
Hova uses a translation of the famous Latin phrase “Veni, vidi, vici,” reportedly written by Julius Caesar. This in literature is called an Asyndeton. Caesar used the phrase to describe his military prowess when he conquered all of Europe (other than Scotland). Its basic premise is “Everywhere I have gone, I have fought against everything mankind had to throw at me, and I defeated everything in sight”

Jay uses it in a similar context to show just how dominant he has become in the rap game. He’s travelled the world, dealt with some fucked up shit in his life, and everything he has seen and battled, he has conquered it.

After becoming the most successful rapper ever and one of the best live artists in the history of the rap game, he’s ready for an encore as long as the audience can get loud enough during the interlude that follows these lines.

line: Soon you gonna see you can’t replace him With cheap imitations–for these generations!
vault_lines: Soon you gonna see you can't replace him
meaning:
At the time of this song, Jay was threatening retirement. This is him reminding the rap world that finding rappers to take his place would be very difficult

The West Indian lilt Jay gives to the words “this generation” is a reference to the 1982 Musical Youth song “Pass the Dutchie”.  Jay may also know it from its being sampled by Public Enemy in their 1990 song “Revolutionary Generation”

line: Who you gon’ find doper than him? With no pen, just draw off inspiration?
vault_lines: With no pen, just draw off inspiration?
meaning:
Jay Z loves to brag that he doesn’t actually write his raps down: he goes into the studio, listens to the beat, and composes the rap in his head. Gee Roberson, who worked with Hova on The Black Album, was impressed by this skill:

I’ve always been amazed with Jay writing in his head. Like, what in the world’s going on there? Him hearing a track and mumbling, and those mumbles becoming verses that he could recite and remember as if he wrote them down on a piece of paper or a Blackberry or something. It was like watching magic. I’m just completely in awe of that. It’s an incredible gift.

Additionally, ‘draw’ is a term used to refer to marijuana, which plays into Jay being ‘doper’ than anyone out.

line: Golfer above par like I putted
vault_lines: Golfer above par like I putted
meaning:
A par is the minimum number of hits you have to make in a golf hole to not go negative. Jay has done more than the necessary and became one of the greatest ever. A putt is a golf shot you make from inside the green, which is usually really easy, just like it was easy for Hova to become the best in the game.



Bragging about being above par though? “Obviously, you’re not a golfer”

line: The rest of y’all know where I’m lyrically at Can’t none of y’all mirror me back Yeah, hearin’ me rap is like hearin’ G Rap in his prime
vault_lines: Can't none of y'all mirror me back
meaning: Hova compares the buzz he generates to the one Kool G. Rap generated in his prime, everybody wanted to hear his latest track and go to his concerts.

line: So this here is the victory lap Then I’m leavin’, that’s how you get me back
vault_lines: So this here is the victory lap
meaning:
The victory lap is a term used in races that indicates the last lap of a race in which the first one has a big lead and receives the cheers of the crowd while he drives around.

In the following lines, Jay explains how to get him to start rapping again; with hindsight, we know Jay Z would come back on his own.

Also, the way Jay pronouncing the word “leaving” is a shout-out to John Denver’s famous song “Leaving on a Jet Plane”.

Furthermore, note how he initiates his last verse using the same rhyme he started the first verse with: “victory lap” and “riddle me that”.

Jay also samples the line “then I’m leavin'” from A Tribe Called Quest’s “Rap Promoter”.

line: When I come back like Jordan Wearin’ the 4-5, it ain’t to play games with you It’s to aim at you, probably maim you If I owe you, I’m blowin’ you to smithereens
vault_lines: Wearin' the 4-5, it ain't to play games with you
meaning:
Jay-Z’s fellow Brooklyn native Michael Jordan (he was born there and stayed for about his first five years, when his family moved to North Carolina) briefly came out of retirement after abruptly retiring in response to his father’s death, wearing the number 45 in place of his original, trademark 23™

The Black Album – on which this song appeared – was billed as Jay-Z’s “retirement album”, although hints like this make it fairly obvious that Jay was fibbing all along.



“45” also refers to a Colt 45 pistol – Jay will come back “packing heat” and won’t be scared to aim a gun at you and pull the trigger, either maiming or killing you. So whatever 45 Jay decides to wear, both insinuate that he’ll “fire shots” at you.

meaning:
The “bomb” is the crack rock, and the sock is an interesting hiding place. Maybe the smell of his feet masks the aroma of cocaine, so the dogs aren’t able to sniff it out?

A “Colgate smile” implies Jay’s incredibly happy with his current situation, despite the bleak appearance. He’s selling drugs, and his clothes aren’t fly (indicating again he’s still very low level), yet he’s independent, and making his own money.

In Decoded he says:

This song is about the true nature of the work. You get up early. You wear the same clothes.
