vault_lines: Yeah, I wake up, hit my shoebox, I snatch out a few rocks
meaning:
During Decoded Jay wrote:

The shoe box tells us from the first line that this is a low level hustler.

He revisited the famous shoe box on “Roc Boys (And The Winner Is…)”

Thanks to the duffle bag, the brown paper bag
The Nike shoe box for holding all this cash

He’s graduated from simply moving 8’s (an eighth of an ounce), a rock is usually a little more than an “8”, and Jay’s obviously got enough stashed for a couple of days of work.

line: Fiends swarm I’m gettin’ rid of this bomb, as I
vault_lines: I'm gettin' rid of this bomb, as I
meaning:
From Jay Z’s autobiography Decoded:

This is the best of times and worst of times, but it’s also the best and worst of who we are and what we can be. The narrator is caught up in a crazy system, one that treats addicts like criminals and forces the young and ambitious into a life that might end with him shot up or locked up. To me, there’s something moving about the kid who goes to sleep dreaming about plans to make money, wakes up early with a Colgate smile, buries his work in the dirt, and fills his small pocket with crack rocks (pockets full of hope). When he’s swarmed by fiends, lost souls driven by addiction, it’s hard to know if we should be happy for him because he’s unloading his work, getting closer to his dream, or if we should feel fucked up because we know the shit is so hopeless. I like leaving the listener without an easy answer.

line: Same routine: I’m runnin’ game to fiends Exchangin’ cash for crack rocks, back and forth to my stash box Hundred dollars a week
vault_lines: Same routine: I'm runnin' game to fiends
meaning:
From Jay Z’s autobiography Decoded:

“Hundred dollars a week” is not a lot of money for a cat waking up early in the morning, working all day dealing drugs to “fiends”. The narrator here is still dreaming of big money, not making it. This is the reality of the low rungs of the drug game. But the ambition is still clear, not just in the scheming but in the work he’s doing to get what he wants, waking up early, throwing on yesterday’s clothes, and hitting the block hard.

line: I got loads of capers to come up with this paper I got money schemes that come to me in my dreams
vault_lines: I got loads of capers to come up with this paper
meaning:
A “caper” is “an illicit or ridiculous activity,” meaning Jay’s got all kinds of schemes and plots to make money. This is something he’s carried into his post-dealing life. He copyrighted a colour, he bought a streaming site, and he even invested in Carol’s Daughter.

From Jay Z’s autobiography Decoded:

You obsess over making money. The work doesn’t have a social value. It’s not like you can motivate yourself by thinking about all the good you’re doing for the world. You start off doing it for all kinds of dumb reasons – because it’s cool, because you get to hang out with your friends all day – but the only thing you get out of it is money. And the money becomes your obsession.

line: Hit the block like a veteran Fiends need they medicine, I’m the relief pitcher Their clean up hitters

meaning:
Despite only having a shoe box of work, he acts like a veteran, displaying a confidence that immediately puts his opposition on the back foot.

A relief pitcher comes on when the main pitcher is injured or fatigued. Jay utilises this metaphor to describe the way he hooks up the needy (his team) with work (pitching) when they’re desperate for it.

From  Decoded:

They came to us suffering for more of that shit. We relieved them and then cleaned up whatever money they had. This line is meant somewhat ironically in the song, but the truth is that drug addicts have a disease. It only takes a short time in the streets to realise that out-of-control addiction is a medical problem, not a form of recreational or criminal behaviour. And the more society treats drug addiction as a crime, the more money drug dealers will make “relieving” the sufferings of the addicts.

meaning:
“Break bread” in this usage means that Jay socializes with and learns from the older gangsters. But it also has other connotations.

It could be an allusion to The Last Supper, where Jesus broke bread right before he died. Jay could be contrasting the purity of Jesus breaking bread to the corruption of meeting up with other gangsters and discussing how to make it to the top. Same general idea as the God/Gotti line.

This is a play on the phrase “for the love of God”. But this song documents the transition to loving money more than God. Because of that, he is willing to shoot up rival gangs (“give lead showers”) to protect his money.

Also plays on weather vocabulary, since it could be heard as

For the love of money, sun
I’m giving lead showers (as in rain)

Just another example of Jay mixing in some wordplay to strengthen the lyricism of the song.

vault_lines: That's right, it's wicked – that's life, I live it

Sinning got him to where he was, and is, now. And he fully accepts that and wants to continue the pursuit of money.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying,

“The narrator isn’t thinking about redemption or turning back – he’s totally focused on making money, "ends.”

meaning: The game is double-edged; it will give you things you wish for but what you wish for might not necessarily be what a person should be seeking for in the first place.  Lupe Fiasco took this further on his album, “The Cool”.

line: Liquor’s invaded my kidneys
vault_lines: Liquor's invaded my kidneys
meaning: Drinking too much alcohol can cause kidney failure (over time). This follows up the Remy line, since he is now drinking so much Remy Martin that it is starting to damage his health. This indicates that things have gotten even worse for the narrator. He is probably living with PTSD after gunning down his childhood friend, and trying to drink away the pain.

line: Whoever said illegal was the easy way out Couldn’t understand the mechanics And the workings of the underworld, granted
vault_lines: Whoever said illegal was the easy way out
meaning:
Most people view drug dealing and hustling as easy money, and working a corporate desk job as hard earned money. But there is a lot more at risk when you’re hustling compared to working in a cubicle. Drug dealers are often depicted as ballers who drive nice cars without a care in the world, and regular employees are often depicted as hard-working citizens with a lot of pressure on them. But a drug dealer always has to think about getting shot down by rival dealers and such, while the worst thing that can happen to a 9 to 5 worker is getting fired and having to find a new job. So someone in Jay-Z’s profession has a lot more on their mind than it seems.

“The ‘mechanics’ here aren’t about the technical details of the business, but the psychological and emotional machinery that’s always working under the surface.”

                           -Jay-Z, Decoded


Note the play on “underworld” and “granted.” “Granted” sounds like granite – a type of rock that is found within continental crust.

line: Nine-to-five is how you survive, I ain’t tryna survive I’m tryna live it to the limit and love it a lot
vault_lines: Nine-to-five is how you survive, I ain't tryna survive
meaning:
References to these lofty ambitions pervade Reasonable Doubt.  See this line on “Dead Presidents,”, this line on “Regrets” and essentially the album’s mission statement on “Can I Live”

I’d rather die enormous than live dormant,
That’s how we on it

Jay is saying that getting a job (or other mainstream means of making ends meet) is safe and he could do that and survive, but he doesn’t want to just survive. He is willing to put his life on the line to get the most out of his life that he can. Go big or go home!



Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying,

“The first defence of a lot of people who take the criminal route is that they had no choice, which is almost true. Most of us had choices, but the choices were bleak. The street life was tough and morally compromised and sometimes ugly, but a dead-end nine-to-five job at permanent entry level wasn’t all that attractive, either. The righteous seed in a hustler’s mentality was this: He wanted something more for himself.”

line: But now this higher learning got the Remy in me
vault_lines: But now this higher learning got the Remy in me
meaning:
A play on Remy Martin…Remy was also a character in the 1995 movie Higher Learning. He starts off as a shy, lonely white guy, who gets into a couple run-ins with black classmates. He turns to a white supremacist group to combat feeling powerless, eventually shooting up a multi-ethnic peace rally and then killing himself. Jay compares his decision to jump into the drug trade to Remy joining the group, as they both end up corrupting.



Also, Remy Martin is a brand of cognac. So Jay is also saying that all of his knowledge about the ugly world of drug dealers leads him to drinking to try and forget it.

line: This shit is wicked on these mean streets
vault_lines: This shit is wicked on these mean streets
meaning:
Reference to the Martin Scorcese mafia film, the first of several mafia references in this verse.

Reasonable Doubt is filled with the imagery of Italian gangsters, a stylistic and attitudinal inspiration for many black crack dealers-turned rappers, including Jay’s boy Biggie Smalls (his fashion sense, his crew’s name of ‘Junior M.A.F.I.A.’) – the cover art even shows Jay-Z dressed like one

line: “Dear God, I wonder, can you save me?” “Illuminati want my mind, soul and my body”
vault_lines: "Dear God, I wonder, can you save me?"
meaning:
Sets up the struggle between God and doing the right thing and the dark forces of capitalism that defines Jay-Z’s life and ghetto life in general. This line led to thousands of YouTube videos claiming this line confirms Jay-Z sold his soul to the mysterious Illuminati in exchange for fortune and fame. But what Jay-Z is trying to get across is that the struggle for money corrupts completely (mind, soul, and body). Jay is acknowledging that he is starting to fall prey to the pursuit of money, and asks for “God” (in some capacity) to save him.



The Snoop Dogg sample is taken from his song “Murder Was The Case”, which in turn samples an earlier Snoop & Dre song “Lil Ghetto Boy”.

The “Illuminati want my mind, soul, and my body” part of the hook is a Prodigy (from Mobb Deep) sample from his verse in the LL Cool J song “I Shot Ya (Remix)”.

line: We used to fight for building blocks Now we fight for blocks with buildings that make a killin’
vault_lines: We used to fight for building blocks
meaning:
The “building blocks” here have multiple meanings here.

First off, when the narrator and his friend were only kids, they used to just play games with stacking blocks.



Then as they both became heavy in the drug game, they started to search for the “building blocks” with which to build their empires on. This would include where they set up, how much money they had to invest, and of course the drugs themselves.

This progressed to literally “building blocks” meaning city blocks. He has gone from trying to build up his wealth to literally controlling buildings. But this creates conflict with his former friend, who also wants to set up at these buildings, to make a “killing”. Since the building block being controlled is so profitable it leads to many turf wars over control.

As a whole, this line frames the rest of Verse 2. It describes the origins of his relationship with a friend that he grew up with in the drug game that eventually becomes a bitter enemy of his. It also serves as a metaphor for Jay’s rise in the rap game from Hawaiian Sophie to Reasonable Doubt.



In a Reasonable Doubt documentary, Jay describes this line, saying:

“When we was young fighting for those little building blocks, now we fighting for blocks with buildings. Like “I own that block”, you know? And the irony in that, you know, we grew up together so we learnt things together we learnt about our first jump shot, and our first time we rode a bike,  and the first time we learned how to use a condom”

It’s here: go to 27:45. http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IXfgKbp9ncQ

line: “Secret society, tryna keep they eye on me”
vault_lines: "Secret society, tryna keep they eye on me"
meaning:
The Illuminati’s seal (which is featured, according to a certain kind of person, on the back of the $1 bill) features an all-seeing eye

This is a sample from a Prodigy (of Mobb Deep) verse on LL Cool J’s “I Shot Ya Remix”. Prodigy has been outspoken against the Illuminati.

line: And even if Jehovah witness, bet he’ll never testify D’evils
vault_lines: And even if Jehovah witness, bet he'll never testify
meaning:
This refers to the practice of killing a witness to a crime before that witness can testify against you. Jay claims that even if a god like Yahweh, who is supposed to have the highest morality in the universe witnessed this crime, Jay-Z would be able to intimidate Him into silence (note the play on the name of the Jehovah’s Witness religion).

Since one of Jay’s nicknames is Jayhova, this could be him referring to himself in the third person and claiming that even if he saw someone else commit a crime, he would never snitch.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying:

The song ends with a dizzying carousel of conversations: First the narrator address his mother, then his girl (“boo), and finally a last victim. The narrator is completely lost to the "D'Evils.” He taunts his victims, defends himself, brags about how low he gets down, invites niggas to try to come get him like George Bush saying “bring ‘em on” to the terrorists. The final two lines, contrasting the demons in his head with a God he thinks is powerless, show how deeply he’s fallen into a moral vacuum. The song isn’t about literal demonic possession, of course, even if some sloppy listeners claim that it is; the truth is you don’t need some external demon to take control of you to turn you into a raging, money-obesessed sociopath, you only need to let loose the demons you already have inside of you.

line: Stop screamin’, you know the demon said it’s best to die
vault_lines: Stop screamin', you know the demon said it's best to die
meaning:
No point in protesting your impending murder. Jay-Z cites Satan’s suggestion that death be embraced (from the Book of Genesis: “In that day ye eat of that fruit ye shall die”) and in so doing shows that he accepts the “devil’s” authority.

Additionally Jay-Z is referring to the practice of selling one’s soul “for the love of money” and in turn receiving eternity in hell. If you go through with this, your fate is sealed no matter what, so you might as well enjoy your time on Earth instead of fearing your inevitable death the whole time. In the sense of this song, he is referring to how there is no turning back after the awful deeds he has done (kidnapping the girl, killing his friend, shooting at rival gangs, etc.), so it better have been worth it.

line: Was thought to be a pleasant guy all my fuckin’ life So now I’m down for whatever, ain’t nothin’ nice
vault_lines: Was thought to be a pleasant guy all my fuckin' life
meaning:
Nice guys live decent lives, but usually aren’t cut out to make it to the top. They work the 9-to-5 jobs that Jay said don’t interest him in the first verse. So in order to make it to the top, the narrator has to resort to crime and corrupt himself. Similar to Breaking Bad’s Walter White.

Also a reference to “Down 4 Whateva,” a song from an early 90’s group called Nuttin' Nyce.

line: The Exorcist got me doin’ sticks Like, ”Homie, you don’t know me But the whole world owe me, strip!”
vault_lines: The Exorcist got me doin' sticks
meaning:
Killing his childhood friend set a dangerous precedent for the narrator. Now that emotion doesn’t factor into his decisions, he is willing to stick up anyone. But there is still some residual guilt, so even though he acts like he isn’t afraid to kill, he still blames his actions on others right before he takes out the victim.

Notice the excesses/exorcist homophone, which ties in with material possessions being connected with the devil.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying,

Another quick scene: Possessed by material lust, the narrator sticks up random people. The quick line of dialogue is meant to show someone completely blinded by desire, reckless and aggressive, but also haunted, the kind of character who talks to his vics as he’s robbing them, making jokes and justifying himself by saying the whole world has done him wrong, so now everyone owes him. This could be the same character from the opening verses; driven over the edge by killing off his best childhood friend, now he’s just a raging psychopath.

line: In time I’ll take away your miseries and make it mine D’evils
vault_lines: In time I'll take away your miseries and make it mine
meaning:
Ending the verse with a semi-Biblical touch as he promises redemption for the girl by taking on her pain and sorrow.

Right now, Jay-Z is feeling good. He got the location of the man like he needed, and is ready to take things in his own hands. But he knows that “in time” the pain and suffering he caused to both the girl and his old friend will come back to haunt him. Pain, like matter and energy in the universe, never goes away, it merely gets transferred or rearranged.  Therefore, Jay absorbs the pain of all those he has wronged and has to carry it for the rest of his life.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying

In the end, I get her to do what I want, but it’s a grim victory. Not only will blood be shed based on the information she’s given me- hers and his- but the last vision of her, tears like a veil over her eyes, begging for both of their lives, is going to haunt me. Her miseries became mine.

line: Who could ever foresee? We used to stay up all night at slumber parties Now I’m tryna rock his bitch to sleep All the years we were real close Now I see his fears through her tears Know she’s wishin’ we were still close
vault_lines: Who could ever foresee?
meaning:
The narrator never would have thought when they were little going to slumber parties that he would grow up and try to “rock this bitch to sleep” (kill one of his best friends). But he is not completely cold hearted to the friend, he just feels the need to kill him is a business move (“it’s not personal, it’s strictly business”). Since our narrator is suffering from the same issues as his friend he sympathizes with him, and would still like to be friends with him if they weren’t rivals.

Alternatively, the “bitch” that Jay has to rock to sleep could be the baby’s mama he kidnapped in the previous lines. He is either killing her to send a message, or trying to lull her into a false sense of security (“rock her to sleep”) so she is more willing to hand over the information he needs.

line: She said the taste of dollars was shitty, so I fed her fifties About his whereabouts I wasn’t convinced I kept feedin’ her money ’til her shit started to make sense
vault_lines: She said the taste of dollars was shitty, so I fed her fifties
meaning:
Jay is trying to find this friend-turned-enemy so he keeps paying her. This finishes off the extended metaphor of feeding money: she doesn’t like the “taste” of the first cheese because it was a smaller amount, so he changes the cuisine and gives her bigger bills until she “shits out” the information he needs.

“Shit started to make sense” is a play on words, it can be interpreted as what she was saying started to make sense as in she was telling the truth. But it also can be as she has been eating so much of his money that she started shitting out cents as in money.

A deeper meaning that Jay probably wasn’t actually referring to (but is still interesting food for thought) is that the money the girl is fed appears in her shit, so it wasn’t completely absorbed. So it could be viewed as a commentary of man’s essential inability to ‘digest’ money.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying

Extending the money-as-food metaphor, I keep feeding her larger bills till she shits out some information, the dollars breaking down to cents/sense as she digests them.

line: My hand around her collar, feedin’ her cheese
vault_lines: My hand around her collar, feedin' her cheese
meaning:
Jay-Z choking the woman to intimidate her into cooperation and then beginning to bribe her (cheese = money) into giving him information about the friend with whom he’s had a falling out.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line

The “cheese: is money, which I’m feeding her to try to get her to rat out the location of her man.

line: Thinkin’ back when we first learned to use rubbers He never learned, so in turn I’m kidnappin’ his baby’s mother
vault_lines: Thinkin' back when we first learned to use rubbers
meaning:
In Decoded, Jay-Z’s book breaking down his rap lyrics, Jay singled out this couplet as one of his favorite lines from his work

Jay reminisces about an earlier, more innocent age when he and his friend were first learning to use condoms, and then connects it back to his current predicament. Since his friend never actually got the lesson and never used condoms, he impregnated a woman. Now Jay-Z is kidnapping that woman to gather information on his old friend’s whereabouts. This plays on the theme of the impossibility of innocence in the ghetto – having a kid, rather than being a joy, is a vulnerability.

Jay-Z in Decoded explains this line saying,

I tried to convey a lot of information in one line: that we were friends so close that we learned basic sex ed at the same time; that he ‘never learned’, which sets him up as someone sloppier, less calculating and cunning than me; that he had a child as a result, and "a baby’s mother”; and that I kidnapped her, which shows how profoundly “blackhearted” I had become, violently exploiting any opening – even the innocent mother of his child. Ike is struggling to stay relevant and Tina is beginning a professional ascent that, more or less, never stops.

This double use of the word project opens up an entire discourse on the American public housing system, race relations, politics and capitalism.

Projects like Marcy, says Jay, were a project by the government, an experiment. The problem for the elite was where to put the growing population of citizens (mostly African American) who were left by the wayside by 20th century capitalism and the racism still endemic to the United States. In his autobiography, Jay says this about the projects:

Housing projects are a great metaphor for the government’s relationship to poor folks: these huge islands built mostly in the middle of nowhere, designed to warehouse lives.

meaning:
In the original song, this acts as the chorus rather than the bridge.

  


Jay is well-versed in “feeling like a pimp”, as evidenced by tracks like “Parking Lot Pimpin'” and “Big Pimpin'”.

To “get that dirt off your shoulder” has different meanings to different people-some people identify it as a pimp move, like barber Jay Perry:

He’s sayin' if you’re a pimp, go on, brush your shoulders off. You can be a pimp in your job. You can be a pimp when it comes to relationships – ladies are pimps, too. If you’re feelin' that way, go on and brush your shoulders off. You floss a lot, you got a nice ride, you spend money around town, you’re a big-timer, so you brush your shoulders off, dig? He’s not talkin' about dandruff, I’m pretty sure.

Others, such as housewife Barbie Besse-Morris, think it’s about getting women off your back:

There’s probably a hidden meaning to that song, and I’m not sure I even want to go there. It could be a woman that he’s trying to get off his back, and he’s calling [her] ‘dirt.’ That’s usually what men are talking about anyway when they do that kind of song.

Palace Guard Academy trainee Tom Augustino thinks he’s brushing the haters off:

It’s about being envied. You pull up in a nice car, they see you with a nice girl, and they start talkin' shit about you and that’s what you need to brush off your shoulders. There’s no reason to talk bad about anybody, no reason to care about what other people think. All that’s important is what you think about yourself.

No matter what your interpretation is, what really matters is that Obama did it while campaigning in response to attacks from Hillary Clinton.



We miss you, 44.

At this time, The Black Album was his sixth consecutive #1 album on the Billboard charts and he won three Grammy Awards — two for his appearance on Beyoncé’s “Crazy in Love” and a Best Rap Album award for Vol.2…Hard Knock Life.

line: If you feelin’ like a pimp, nigga, go on—brush your shoulders off Ladies is pimps, too; go on—brush your shoulders off Niggas is crazy, baby; don’t forget that boy told you Get that dirt off your shoulder
vault_lines: You gotta get (Get) that (That) dirt off your shoulder
meaning:
Jay is well-versed in “feeling like a pimp”, as evidenced by tracks like “Parking Lot Pimpin'” and “Big Pimpin'”.

To “get that dirt off your shoulder” has different meanings to different people-some people identify it as a pimp move, like barber Jay Perry:

He’s sayin' if you’re a pimp, go on, brush your shoulders off. You can be a pimp in your job. You can be a pimp when it comes to relationships – ladies are pimps, too. If you’re feelin' that way, go on and brush your shoulders off. You floss a lot, you got a nice ride, you spend money around town, you’re a big-timer, so you brush your shoulders off, dig? He’s not talkin' about dandruff, I’m pretty sure.

Others, such as housewife Barbie Besse-Morris, think it’s about getting women off your back:

There’s probably a hidden meaning to that song, and I’m not sure I even want to go there. It could be a woman that he’s trying to get off his back, and he’s calling [her] ‘dirt.’ That’s usually what men are talking about anyway when they do that kind of song.

Palace Guard Academy trainee Tom Augustino thinks he’s brushing the haters off:

It’s about being envied. You pull up in a nice car, they see you with a nice girl, and they start talkin' shit about you and that’s what you need to brush off your shoulders. There’s no reason to talk bad about anybody, no reason to care about what other people think. All that’s important is what you think about yourself.

No matter what your interpretation is, what really matters is that Obama did it while campaigning in response to attacks from Hillary Clinton.

Now he’s got 52 bars of rap for his audiences, 52 cars with removable ceilings, and 52 broads for you to be jealous of. That’s a come-up.

line: Tryna stretch out the coca, like a wrestler, yessir

Jay’s trying to “stretch out” (dilute) the cocaine to sell more of it.  Weight is slang for drugs, and wrestlers frequently cut weight in order to make a lower weight class.

Wrestlers stretch people (chiropractors do, too). Also, a wrestler’s fluctuation in weight leads to stretch marks, which cocoa butter is used to remove.

line: Like a running back — get it, man? I’m straight off the block
vault_lines: Like a running back — get it, man? I'm straight off the block
meaning:
JAY: We get it! and we’ll explain it to those who don’t.

Depending on the emphasis of some words, this is a triple entendre.

1) The literal meaning is that Jay is comparing himself to a running back in football, who uses the blocks from his teammates to get free and run up field.

2) The figurative meaning of “straight off the block” is that Jay came directly from selling crack on the corner of his block and immediately became a household name as a rapper.

3) Finally, when you emphasize the word straight in terms of its colloquial/slang meaning, Jay is saying that he is “straight”, as in financially secure, off of all the work he did selling crack on his block.

line: Came from the bottom of the bottom to the “Top of the Pops”

Jay-Z appeared on the show in 1999, performing his hit single “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)”. The day before the show Hov contacted the play’s writer and director Martin Charnin and asked if the current cast would join him in his performance of the Annie-sampling track.

Checkers is a much simpler game than Chess. Chess requires combatants to plan their strategy well ahead, whilst Checkers requires on the spot moves.

In the end, Jay made stupid money out of the decline of Rocafella, while Dame made a little, and Burke made barely anything. By 2006, there was no game. The legal wranglings had been completed, Jay had pocketed his money, and Dame has split with Def Jam to create his own, ultimately unsuccessful imprint.

Being “in the hole” means you either owe money, or you’re in a much worse situation than when you started. In the context of the song, Jay allowed his enemies to dig their own grave’s, mafia style, and all he did was push them in.

His first solo record after the deal went sour, Killa Season, didn’t fare well enough to have first week sales even reported on. Some reports claim it hasn’t even sold 200k, a meagre amount during the heyday of the mid 2000s (even Memphis Bleek went gold).

Cam certainly received his world famous Roc chain. What’s become of it now is anyone’s guess.

A wise man told me don’t argue with fools
Cause people from a distance can’t tell who is who

Jay carved out a path for African Americans to create their own businesses through hard work and perseverance. On a holistic level, he brought in to being the positive energy needed to spur others to action.

On a much simpler level, he allowed Dame Dash and his young Harlem crew, most particularly Cam'ron, to achieve success in hip hop. Dash helped create Rocafella, which wouldn’t exist without Jay’s influence and ridiculous talent.

Furthermore, Cam'Ron’s only platinum record Come Home With Me was masterminded by Rocafella and propelled by their marketing campaigns.

How do you diss the hand that fed you?

The way he pronounces “ol' boy” sounds suspiciously like “Oh Boy”, one of Cam'ron’s biggest hits. He was also part of the collective Dipset, with whom Jay had beef with as well after the Rocafella split and their siding with Dame.

Mister Gepetto is a fictional character who controlled the puppet Pinocchio. The claim is that his targets are just puppets for those higher than them. Cam'Ron and his crew are the puppets, and Dame Dash is the main man…

line: I’m like air, lil’ shots go through me Won’t tear one tissue, no tears, no tissue, not an issue Don’t cry for me

meaning:
If Jay actually responded, or was injured, by every shot thrown at him, he’d be dead ten times over.

Over his career he’s had issues with Beanie Sigel, Drake, Big Punisher, Birdman, Lil Wayne, Cam'ron, Nas, Mobb Deep, Cassidy, Dame Dash, DMX, 2Pac, The Game, Jaz-O, Jim Jones, Joe Budden, LL Cool J, MC Hammer, R. Kelly, Sean Paul, Jadakiss, 50 Cent…

Not to mention all of the non-rappers, like De-Haven, and entities like Cristal.

Everyone is gunning for the throne. Jay’s higher than that. The shot’s go through him like air, and he waves as they pass by. He only really responds to those he considers in the same ballpark as him lyrically. For everyone else, his usual response is to dismiss them. This line is, in a way, a similar message.

Jay came, saw, and conquered. As of 2006, he is president of one of the largest hip hop labels of all time, and easily in the top 5 worldwide sellers in hip hop. Musically, there was little left for Jay to accomplish at this point in his career.

Jay is bossing up on Cam'ron and Beanie Sigel, as well as Dame Dash. Dash is obsessed with “bosses”, something that would become even more apparent in years to come.

Jay’s invitation that he has dresses for his enemies is likely a nod back to his famous “Takeover” diss of Prodigy wearing a ballerina’s outfit.

It’s ominous. That diss track was widely regarded as one of the finest in hip hop history.

“H.O.” refers to Jay, as H.O.V.A.

meaning:
A common theme on this record is Jay’s perceived absence from hip hop, and how that has influenced other rappers, giving them courage where they had none before.

Again, Jay falls back on his tried and tested technique of positioning himself as more grown than his opponent.

Either Cam & co will be orphaned when they lose Dame or the simultaneous meaning is Jay will make orphans of Cam & Co’s kids.. take it how you want it.. paow!

The Disciples were Jesus' personal followers. They were unwavering in their support.

Cam has spoken on his time at Rocafella, claiming that Jay was “cool” towards him, and that it was mainly Dame who was pulling strings for him and his group.

The claim from Jay is that Dame gassed up Cam'Ron to diss Jay, and that Jay was his “Idol”. No interview with Cam has he ever professed such strong feelings towards Jay.

He is gonna give them a history lesson on how they got here.

It’s no secret that jay constantly draws parallels between himself and Christ or the rap game and religion …

Here Jay is simply saying that, he wasn’t gonna waste time killing the puppets every time they popped up with a new diss ie Cam'ron, Jim Jones and all the lil rappers throwing shade at him at the time.

The main culprits were Dame and Biggs so he’ll rather wait till all his foes including their generals can be killed in one shot. He expends less energy and resources and wins more glory .. Jay is an efficient Commander if you will

He is patient enough to let his foes tire off continuously digging their own grave so he’ll have the easy task of just destroying them with their own handiwork.

Here Jay is using an allegory to simply say; his enemies will bring about their own downfall. This song was released at the height of tensions after he parted ways with his former business partners and label mates ie. Damon ‘Dame’ Dash & Kareem ‘Biggs’ Burke and Cam'ron.

When he engages with his enemy, he wants to finish him off completely. Even if it means being patient for months, he’ll only strike at the moment where it will be fatal to his enemy. This is all literal but if you study how he has handled confrontation and challenges throughout his career, this is typical Jay strategy.

This loaded line resonates to the line on Streets Is Watching, “You Only A Customer” where he raps: “To make a nigga die bleeding is nothing / You make a motherfucker die breathing then you saying som'n, beeaatch!!”

line: Hov gon’ get you, I ain’t forget your lil’ disrespect
vault_lines: Hov gon' get you, I ain’t forget your lil' disrespect
meaning:
The disrespect referred to is the removal of Jay’s verse on “Oh Boy”.

Cam hadn’t been particularly happy with the cold welcome he had received at The Roc.

I just know when [Dipset] first got [to Roc-A-Fella], we just tried to be cool. And it’s only so long you can try and be cool when somebody giving you they ass to kiss, pardon my language

So, when Young Guru greets the Dipset lads with news of a Hov verse on “Oh Boy” one day, Cam was less than impressed.

So we walk up into the studio room, and we’re like, ‘What’s the surprise?’ and [Young] Guru pulls up ‘Oh Boy,’ with a Jay-Z verse. On top of the Jay-Z verse, he’s dissing Nas!

Guru would later go on to say during a Combat Jack episode that the verse still exists in some realm, but Cam was adamant that Jay wouldn’t be on the track.

line: Don’t look at Hov like he done something wrong to ‘em ’Cause he’s on to ’em He just took what belonged to him
vault_lines: Don’t look at Hov like he done something wrong to ‘em
meaning:
When Jay took on leadership of Def Jam and the Roc fell apart, Jay was seen as the villain for taking the Roc-a-Fella trademark, effectively ending Dash’s career.

The split occurred when Dash, Jay and Burke sold their stake in Rocafella to Def Jam. Their share was $10 million.

Part of Jay’s deal with Def Jam was that, after a certain period of time with him at the helm, he’d retain the rights to his masters. He also retained control of the brand name Rocafella records, though this was not without a fight.

Jay offered Dame and Burke full control of the Rocafella name in exchange for exclusive rights to the masters of Reasonable Doubt, which the trio co-owned. His offer was rejected. “I was like, let me try to figure out some way where everyone can be happy. Let me get Reasonable Doubt and I will give up Rocafella. I thought it was more than fair…. And when that was turned down, I had to make a choice.

To stain the relationship even further, Dame sold his stake in Rocawear clothing for $22 million to Jay. He went on to sell the company 3 years later for $204 million…

Some claim Jay took what belonged to all three of them. Both Dame and Burke are struggling for money (Burke is actually incarcerated), whilst Jay goes from strength to strength.

line: It’s nothing but a hobby to him Simple as a serve in volley to him

line: So I’m prayin’ that it spills outside of the booth That’s when ya’ll niggas outside of your truth Outside of your league, that’s not what you do Niggas throwin’ Roc signs outside of your Coupe
vault_lines: So I’m prayin' that it spills outside of the booth

When Cam'Ron was shot in an attempted car jacking in 2005, he claimed the shooter “Threw up the Roc sign” before shooting him.

He addressed it on the Jay diss track “You Gotta Love It”, and he also spoke about it on The Breakfast Club.

For Jay’s part, he never claimed responsibility for the shooting, and this is the only time on wax that he has mentioned it.

It’s also hard to blame Cam on this occasion. He was shot driving his Lamborghini, and managed to drive himself to the hospital, where he refused to incriminate anyone via his no snitching policy.

Then again, Jay is a big fish. If he wants someone shot, chances are they’re going to get shot.

He’s claiming that these diss tracks are just rappers committing lyrical and career suicide. They tie the knot themselves and slip the noose around their own neck, all he has to do is kick the chair away to finish the job.

line: Little was known of Sierra Leone And how it connect to the diamonds we own
vault_lines: Little was known of Sierra Leone
meaning: Diamonds mined in Sierra Leone and other countries at war during the 20th-21st century are called blood diamonds, conflict diamonds, and other names because the diamonds are mined in war zones. Sierra Leone had a civil war from 1991-2002, hence its diamonds being labeled blood diamonds. Sierra Leone is a country with many diamonds in its quarries and mines, and many of these diamonds that are mined there are sent over to the United States and many other countries. Kanye is referencing how the diamonds he owns and wears come from Sierra Leone (and probably other African countries at war), but since Sierra Leone is a small, poor, African country, its problems are rarely spoken about.

line: (Throw your diamonds in the sky if you feel the vibe)

Throwing up a diamond is a sign of affiliation with Roc-A-Fella records, a record label Ye used to be signed to. Throwing up this sign was commonly done at concerts to express the vibe of Roc-A-Fella’s artist’s performances.



Videotaped: Ye and Jay-Z at Downey, California during the shoot of their song “Otis.”

line: Good night!
vault_lines: (And ever) Ever, ever? Ever, ever?
meaning:

Here is a classic Jay-Z triple entendre, in which he employs a homophone to lock it all together. Hov’s lyrics are often a combination of socio-cultural consciousness and elite word-play. In African-American culture the pronunciation of “for” is often said as “fuh.” Therefore, with his pronunciation, Hov leaves this line open to interpretation – “blast for me” or “blasphemy.” His awareness of how language is a construct of culture allows him to incorporate this lexical ambiguity.

1. Hov is referencing the allegiance his fans have to him – they will fight for the uplifting of his name like a religious person would for their God. Further than that, he is implying that these fans will shoot any naysayers.
2. Jay has many up-and-coming rappers that take unwarranted shots (“blast”) at him in their songs.
3. Jay’s rapid enunciation of “blast for me” can be heard as “blasphemy.” One of Jay-Z’s infamous nicknames is Jayhovah – which is a play on Jehovah, the Hebrew word for God. His friends gave him this nickname when they witnessed his God-level rapping talents. Some believe when his fans call him Jayhovah it is blasphemy against God.

line: [Produced by Just Blaze]
vault_lines: Dear Summer, I know you gon' miss me
meaning:
As one of Just Blaze’s many classics, this track originally started off as a track for Memphis Bleek to rap on. Jay Z at the time was retired, but when the beat was played for him, he freestyled over it – literally over the whole beat. Bleek ended up placing it on his album anyway, even though he didn’t have any recorded vocals on the track.

As far as the beat goes, the sample is the soulful Weldon Irvine’s “Morning Sunrise.” Just Blaze sped it up, added drums, and most likely double tracked the sample, one track without any effects and the other with a low pass fileter, to bring out the original bassline.

line: I pick the gun up Niggas back up; they know I’m not no fronter I don’t talk SHIT, I just flip it Un ya Sorry Lance, I’m just trying to advance my quotes I ain’t making you the butt of my jokes
vault_lines: I pick the gun up
meaning:
Jay-Z is not just bark; he also bites.  He’ll “flip it on you,” or retaliate.  He pronounces “on” “Un” to add credibility to his threat by alluding to the incident in which he stabbed Lance “Un” Rivera and almost went to jail for it.

Jay Z referenced the incident several times in his career. Once on the hook of The Blueprint single “I.Z.Z.O.” produced by Kanye West:

“Not guilty, ya’ll got to feel me”

And again on the single “Guilty Until Proven Innocent” which appeared on the Rocafella compilation “The Dynasty: Roc La Familia.”

Jay-Z was heated off the premature leak of Vol 3: Life and Times of S. Carter. Rumors were that Lance “Un” Rivera was behind the leak. Jay Z talked about the incident in his book Decoded:

“Before I even realized what I was doing, I headed back over to him, but this time I was blacking out with anger. The next thing I knew, all hell had broken loose in the club.”

Cam'Ron, fellow Rocafella label mate, also discussed this incident in an interview with DJ Whoo Kid. He stated the Jay Z and Un Rivera beef was over Charli Baltimore:

“I’m not going to get into the details of what happened and why, but it’s just a lot of where Jay liked Charli at one time and that was Biggie’s girl. Un felt that that was the artist and Jay was teaching her the business. Un and Jay sh**, they can say a song leaked or whatever but it was all over Charli Baltimore.”

On Reasonable Doubt Jay speaks a lot about spending time (and money) in Las Vegas, which is  the most populated city in the state of Nevada. Assuming the role of a “Big Willie” in Vegas is a sign of the vast wealth he had acquired in the drug game.

vault_lines: I want these bitch motherfuckers to try to flip so I can fill up this clip
meaning:
To “flip” is a synonym for snitching to the cops. Microphone Nut wants his enemies to flip so he can have an excuse to kill them.

The clever wordplay here, though, is that when someone doesn’t want to snitch to the cops, they’ll “plead the fifth,” i.e., the fifth amendment, which allows those who are arrested or who testify in court to “remain silent” without it being held against them. In other words, pleading the fifth means to keep your mouth shut.

Since people who are snitching are not, by definition, keeping their mouths shut–they’re acting as informants to police to avoid being incarcerated–Microphone Nut is basically saying he’ll literally shut these snitches mouths by sticking his .45 caliber pistol in their mouths–i.e., his “four-fifth”.

The snitches in question could’ve pleaded the fifth, but because they talked to the cops, now they’ll be smoking the four-fifth–I.E., they will be killed with his pistol.

This whole line is an homage to “You’re Nobody (Till Somebody Kills You)”, the last song on Disc Two of The Notorious B.I.G.’s Life After Death:

Here’s a tissue, stop your blood clot crying
The kids, the dog, everybody dying, no lying

This bar is quite a popular one. 50 Cent uses it in his song, Stop Crying from his 2011 album, The Big 10.

This line could be a shot a multiple big names in the industry. “Blood clot crying” could be a shot at Game who was apparently caught on camera crying, he also happens to be a Blood. The metanarrative around The Blueprint 3 release has often invoked a parallel between Sinatra’s and Hova’s respective comebacks. The idea seems to have cemented itself in the public consciousness after Kanye West’s infamous May 20, 2009 blog post on the music industry A-list in which Ye wrote “JAY IS SINATRA.”

And of course, Jay-Z straight up says “I am the new Sinatra” in “Empire State of Mind”

The lyrics were alluding to the infamous music video for Tha Dogg Pound’s track “New York, New York” featuring Snoop Dogg, in which Snoop is seen kicking down buildings in New York. In response to this track, East-coast based Duo Capone-N-Noreaga collaborated with Mobb Deep & Tragedy Khadafi, and released a response track called “L.A., L.A.”.



Prodigy spared no time addressing his distaste for Jay’s lines in an interview with The Source:

Jay was nowhere to be found when that drama popped off between Mobb Deep, Dogg Pound, Pac, and Biggie, That was our little personal beef, not a coastal war… so Jay Z is a bitch-ass nigga for making that quote in his lyrics.

In an special report with MTV called A day with Jay'—recorded after Vol. 2… Hard Knock Life dropped in 1998—Jay told the reporter during the recording that he decided Vol. 2 was gonna be his last album.



Jay was frustrated with the sales of Reasonable Doubt and Vol.1  and he wanted to retire after Vol.2 and switch to handling business aspects, but after Vol.2 blew up he changed his mind and decided to pursue his legendary career.

line: Yo, the summer’s ’bout to get hot Niggas home from jail and they plottin’ Heard about the watch, the Bentley hard-top The Continental T, got ‘em resentin’ me
vault_lines: COME AND GET ME!
meaning:
In keeping with the theme of this song, which serves largely to recount his Marcy upbringing and air out his grievances with what he seems to perceive as an undercurrent of jealousy and hatred directed towards him from certain parties in his old hood, Jay speculates that things might be about to heat up.

Although Hov often makes reference to the summer in his music, it’s usually concerning his ability to run things musically during the season. The heat he is referring to here, however, is more likely to be relation to the violence he feels is likely to erupt, fuelled by the jealousy his material wealth has provoked in others.

He makes specific mention of his car collection as a point of envy, with his Bentley Continental in particular taking centre stage.



Jay famously posed, in typically nonchalant fashion, alongside a Bentley on the cover of his previous album, the multi-platinum Vol. 2… Hard Knock Life.

vault_lines: I made it so, you could say Marcy and it was all good
meaning:
Reasonable Doubt, Jay’s debut album, sold, in his own words, like “30,000 copies first week.” He was still able to walk in grocery stores untouched.

It wasn’t until “Hard Knock Life” dropped and Vol. 2 sold 5 million copies that Jay was catapulted to the forefront of hip hop and pop culture. MTV was falling over itself to feature the artist, even commissioning one of their famous Making the Video episodes for the single “Girl’s Best Friend.” One look at the video for “Hard Knock Life”, which got heavy airplay on all music video stations, is proof of his ability to bring the hood to the suburbs.



That’s Jay’s angle. He didn’t sell out, he didn’t change his sound for radio airplay. He made it cool for suburbanites to act gangster.  Iceberg clothing sold markedly more product after Jay shouted them out early in his career, and by 2001 his prophecy had come true, featured in New York Travel magazine for a romp in the Hamptons.

meaning:
“Come and Get Me” is directed towards Jay-Z’s public detractors and the other rappers in the game challenging his throne. The hook solidifies this theme, challenging anyone and everyone to come at him.

Similar themes can be heard on Nas’ “Come Get Me,” with the subliminal shots sent back and forth adding to the brewing issues between them. Hov is telling Nas that he does in fact have the crown, and if he wants it, he’ll have to come and take it. Furthermore, if he comes, Jay-Z will be ready with the “fifth”, otherwise known as a .45 caliber pistol.

This hook may also be a subliminal reply to 50 Cent and the shots he sent at Hov on his “How to Rob” track. On the track 50 threatened to rob and/or shoot high-profile rappers, Jigga included.

The first portion of this verse deals with a slightly self-conscious Jay-Z trying to come to terms with exactly why people don’t like him. Then he remembers that when people hate, he puts in his best work. The ambivalence fuelled him to become one of the most successful recording artists of all time.

line: I wear more bling to The Source and Soul Trains More chains than rings, niggas won’t do a thing
vault_lines: I wear more bling to The Source and Soul Trains
meaning:
Jay references award shows “The Source Awards” and the “Soul Train Music Awards.” Both of these award shows have an infamous reputation of descending into violence and rappers getting jacked for their jewelry. Headlining Hov is braggadocio here, declaring that he will wear more chains than rings (10 fingers = 10+ chains!) because no one would dare steal from him.

These lines kicked off a mini-beef between Hov and his Def Jam label-mate Jayo Felony. As a Crip gang member Jayo felt these cocky lines were disrespectful to his gang, who had claimed responsibility for some of these robberies. Jayo released a non-subliminal diss record called “True’d Up (Crip Anthem);” which he would claim Hov tried to block the release of by talking to label head Lyor Cohen.

Hov recruited Crips members Daz Dillinger and Kurupt for the track’s remix to prove he didn’t take any of Jayo’s words to heart and had superior Crips connections.

Yeah, what happened was, I wrote so much in this book, I would sit at my table for hours and hours till my mother made me go to bed. And it was like this obsession with words and with writing. And as I got further away from that notebook – now as I was on the street and these ideas would come, I would run into the corner store, the bodega, and grab, like, a paper bag or just buy a juice, anything just to get a paper bag. And then I’d write the words on the paper bag and stuff these ideas in my pocket till I got back. And then I would transfer them into the notebook. And as I got further and further away from home and from the notebook, I had to memorize these rhymes longer and longer and longer. And, like, with any exercise, you know, once you train your brain to do that, it becomes a natural occurrence. So you know, by the time I got to record my first album, which was – I was 26, I didn’t need pen to paper. My memory had been trained, you know, just to, you know, listen to a song, think of the words and then just lay them to tape.

Solipsism is the belief that the only thing that’s actually real is one’s own experiences and thoughts.  It comes from the Latin Solus Ipse, roughly “alone self.” From a solipsistic perspective, reality would be something like a dream that the observer is having.



Solipsism has a long history as a philosophical problem; it seems absurd to common sense, but is remarkably difficult to come up with purely logical arguments against. It’s also a psychological experience described by people with mental illness or serious neurological damage. He felt he didn’t have full artistic control as he and the label argued over the direction of his music. Prince was also not happy with the financial aspects of his contract, including the fact that the label owned the masters of his music, meaning the record label controlled the sounds in the master recordings and could collect royalties as they license Prince’s music to third parties—even without his permission.



His frustration with the music business inspired him to write the word “slave” on his cheek and change his name to an unpronounceable “love symbol” in protest, leading him to be referred to as “The Artist Formerly Known as Prince"—or simply just "The Artist"—and releasing his music through his own NPG Records label. In a 1996 interview with Rolling Stone, he discussed his thought process on the situation:

People think I’m a crazy fool for writing ‘slave’ on my face. But if I can’t do what I want to do, what am I? When you stop a man from dreaming, he becomes a slave. That’s where I was. I don’t own Prince’s music. If you don’t own your masters, your master owns you.

Prince went back to using his name in 2000, and after a long battle, he was able to gain control of the masters for his back catalog from Warner Bros. in 2014. Based on the other lines in this verse, Jay seems to be suggesting that Prince’s estate—his family and his attorney L. Londell McMillan—are essentially selling him out to the highest bidder. Despite the fact that Jay “sat down with Prince, eye to eye” to discuss how he wanted his music handled going forward—such as only having his music streamed through the artist-owned TIDAL service—Jay feels Prince’s estate has their own money-making agenda. line: My confederation, dead a nation Explode on detonation, overload the mind of the said patient
vault_lines: My confederation, dead a nation
meaning:
On the surface, Jay merely comments on a dream that his drug crew is going to rise to the highest echelon of money in America, basically overthrowing the establishment and the stigma that black people don’t amount to anything.

However, when you look deeper, “confederation” alludes to the “Confederacy” in the Civil War, which like Jay’s crew tried to “dead a nation,” i.e. secede from the Union thus breaking up the country (incidentally, the Confederate States of America is a dead nation).  But the Confederacy was ultimately beaten by the Union.  And what’s more, it stood for a morally disgusting cause simply because it sustained the southern economy.

The Confederacy and Jay’s confederation are thus directly compared, forcing us to ask ourselves how similar or different they really are/were.

“explode!/On detonation” can also apply to the nation Jay’s crew is trying to overthrow, or to Jay’s mind which earlier in the verse is depicted as “infested with sick thoughts” and is “dual levels.”

Also note the world play on the homophonic ‘dead-a-nation’ and ‘detonation’, and also Jay’s masterful use of internal rhyme: ‘confederation’, ‘dead a nation’, ‘detonation’, ‘said patient’.

Biggie started selling crack at age 12, and, at the age of 17, he dropped out of high school just to continue dealing drugs. The two Brooklyn natives have referenced their crack-dealing days in their songs before; in the beginning of the second verse in Biggie’s “Machine Gun Funk,” he raps:

Now I pack gats to stop all the snitches

meaning:
It is widely known that Jay-Z does not write his rhymes down on paper, but instead develops them in his mind and memorizes them. In an interview with NPR, Jay spoke on how this habit came about:

Yeah, what happened was, I wrote so much in this book, I would sit at my table for hours and hours till my mother made me go to bed. And it was like this obsession with words and with writing. And as I got further away from that notebook – now as I was on the street and these ideas would come, I would run into the corner store, the bodega, and grab, like, a paper bag or just buy a juice, anything just to get a paper bag. And then I’d write the words on the paper bag and stuff these ideas in my pocket till I got back. And then I would transfer them into the notebook. And as I got further and further away from home and from the notebook, I had to memorize these rhymes longer and longer and longer. And, like, with any exercise, you know, once you train your brain to do that, it becomes a natural occurrence. So you know, by the time I got to record my first album, which was – I was 26, I didn’t need pen to paper. My memory had been trained, you know, just to, you know, listen to a song, think of the words and then just lay them to tape."
