This record was as much a display of technical skill as it was lyrical acrobatics. On “Hovi Baby” he experimented with a thumping Just Blaze beat and a number of different flows, and he uttered the line on “What They Gonna Do Part II”:

In some places they say this, I am God with the flow
Like my office, but they’re biased, too involved with the flow

So often he has had to defend his use of the term “God” or “Hov”. He explained to NPR that he didn’t anoint himself God, rather it was an impressed onlooker.

line: I’m back before you had a chance to miss me My mama can’t save you this time, niggas is history
vault_lines: I'm back before you had a chance to miss me
meaning:
Jay was releasing an album every year at this time. His previous album, The Blueprint, was released in September 2001 and his follow up, The Blueprint² The Gift & The Curse, was released in November 2002, so the year didn’t end without word from Jay.

In between “Ether” in December of 2001, and this track the following November, Jay dropped “Supa Ugly,” a graphically personal track that many deemed to go too far.

I came in your Bentley backseat, skeeted in your Jeep
Left condoms on your baby seat

Jay dropped the track on Hot 97 and the day after returned with hat in hand to apologize for the lyrical content, claiming his mother Gloria Carter had called him in tears after hearing the song.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mAlktQAgLf8

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hM18fB4GphA&t=20s

He’s less compassionate this time around, saying even his mother won’t be able to control what he says. The next day Jay-Z returned to Hot 97 where he apologized in a interview with Angie Martinez.

This was viewed as a big loss and a move that Dame Dash said made Jay “look crazy.” In a December 2001 interview with Funkmaster Flex on Hot 97, Nas and his younger brother Jungle commented on this. Nas said he respected Jay-Z’s mother stepping in while Jungle said it’s not something that is supposed to be admitted or known.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=76iPb3b1h8A&t=75s

line: These dudes is all politics, depositin’ checks They put in they pocket, all you get in return is a lot of lip
vault_lines: These dudes is all politics, depositin' checks
meaning:
An issue he would later revisit explicitly on “Minority Report” in the wake of Hurricane Katrina.

Sure, I ponied up a mil' but I didn’t give my time
So in reality I didn’t give a dime
Or a damn, I just put my monies in the hands
Of the same people that left my people stranded.

The problem is, the money he was donating wasn’t going to the right people. Instead it was lacing the pockets of those in charge, not helping the needy.

The same can be said of the music industry. Rappers earning exorbitant amounts of money, placing it straight in their bank accounts with no thought of helping those around them.

line: They call me this misogynist But they don’t call me the dude to take his dollars to give gifts at the projects
vault_lines: They call me this misogynist
meaning:
Jay is not defending his misogynistic lyrics in this line, in fact in subsequent years he has blasted himself for the way he treated women on wax.

Some [lyrics] become really profound when you see them in writing. Not “Big Pimpin.” That’s the exception. It was like, I can’t believe I said that. And kept saying it. What kind of animal would say this sort of thing? Reading it is really harsh.

His relationship with fame, exemplified beautifully in the “Gift & The Curse” title, is tortured. Articles such as this consign his contributions to a tiny little box, and place him up against heavy hitters such as Madonna, who earned significantly more money during this period.

The generosity rarely recieves the big money headline that the misogyny does. During the early 2000s Jay initiated a number of projects aimed at giving back to the Projects that raised him, yet these were scarcely reported on, except to highlight star power or mention his assault case.

line: Ain’t I supposed to be absorbed in myself? Every time there’s a tragedy, I’m the first one to help
vault_lines: Ain't I supposed to be absorbed in myself?
meaning:
One of the most prevalent criticism’s of Jay around this time, and enduring to this day, was his hyper-capitalism and an embrace of the “bling” culture.

In his book Mo Meta Blues Questlove said:

Admiring him was one thing — but collaborating with him? That seemed like it could be a real train-wreck of cultural signifiers: his big-money, above-the-title hip-hop, our legit indie reputation.

The belief, even by some in the industry, was a man consumed by money. During Decoded he related the story of the famous MTV Unplugged show, where he was wearing a Che Guevera shirt, and was called out by journalist Elizabeth Mendez for wearing it.

“You don’t feel funny?” I was like, Huh?, because I knew she meant funny as in weird, and I was thinking, Actually, I feel real comfortable; this is one of the best albums of my career… . But then she said it again: “You don’t feel funny? You’re wearing that Che T-shirt and you have–” she gestured dramatically at the chain around my neck. “I couldn’t even concentrate on the music,” she said. “All I could think of is that big chain bouncing off of Che’s forehead.”

People believed him to be completely consumed by wealth and his status, there are countless editorial pieces on the subject. Yet it’s apparent from his philanthropic gestures that this is not the case.

line: The Blueprint 2, baby, on the way
vault_lines: The Blueprint 2, baby, on the way
meaning:
The standard call out for when a record is in the works. Jay now grows his hair when he is in album mode, but his tendency during the early 2000s was to shout out the name of his record on every feature or release.

Jay predicted many fans would have the opportunity to cop the album before it’s release date, as he was experiencing tedious leaks at this point in his career.

line: Nah, nah, don’t be afraid Y’all and your articles hock spit at Jay Y’all, from afar, threw darts my way What you thought, I would not have nothin’ to say? Nope
vault_lines: Nah, nah, don't be afraid
meaning:
In 2001 Jay’s various enemies weren’t shy about expressing their dislike for the star. Prodigy was particularly vocal in the press about his relationship with Jay. His claim was that Jay stole the idea of talking about the Marcy and Brooklyn with such depth from Nas, a point he reiterated in his book.

The result was what Jay perceived to be a “bitch” move from his competition: remaining at arm’s length, instead preferring to “hock spit” (spitting long distances) rather than coming in close for hand to hand combat.

It must also be remembered during the same period Jay copped a lot of criticism in the press for the brutality of his “Supa Ugly” diss.

line: H-O-V-A
vault_lines: "JAY-Z this," "JAY-Z that" ("JAY-Z won't hold my hand no more")
meaning:
Jay’s most common moniker, since the explosion of “Izzo (H.O.V.A.)”.

It’s also a subtle diss to former mentor Jaz-O. Jaz dropped the track “Ova” earlier in the year, a clear diss to Jay:

I be in it till its (ova)
Look at your name, same as the letters of your god
People put it together.

Jay pauses after he says the H, to highlight the fact he is about to drop a response.

line: Let’s do this thing (Let’s do it right this time) Come on
vault_lines: Let's do this thing (Let's do it right this time)
meaning:
There’s no denying that Nas came hard on “Ether”, yet Jay and his Roc-A-Fella crew, admitting it was a hard track, failed to see how it was better than “Takeover”.

Memphis Bleek:

Anybody that listens to facts would. ‘Ether’… I’m not going to say it was a bad record. It was dope, but all that shit was just fake shit, he didn’t say no facts in that song. That’s why I can’t hold it up there against ‘Takeover.’ ‘Takeover’ was factual.

The criticism of “Takeover” was a lack of emotion from Jay. The criticism of “Supa Ugly” was too much emotion. This track is meant to walk the line between the two.

line: I won’t rest ’til you on one knee
vault_lines: I won't rest 'til you on one knee
meaning:
Getting on one knee in front of your opponent symbolizes admitting defeat. Jay-Z won’t rest until his rivals or opponents give up or admit defeat.

Jay would eventually sign Nas during his stint at the head of Def Jam, which can be read as a victory for either Nas or Jay, depending on one’s perspective.

“Taking a knee” is also a way of taking a rest, usually used in sport when the coach or an authority figure has an announcement to make. Once again Jay places himself above Nas in the hip-hop stakes.

line: You street dreamin’, all y’all niggas livin’ through me I gave you life when niggas was forgettin’ you emcee
vault_lines: You street dreamin', all y'all niggas livin' through me
meaning:
These lines, (and the line before it) refer to not only Nas but also the non-mentioned recipients of Jay’s venom (i.e. Prodigy of Mobb Deep and Ja Rule)

“Street Dreams” was a single from Nas' 1996 It Was Written. The song’s video (which was a play on the movie Casino) and the album as a whole saw Nas take a different direction in his style and persona, entering a mafioso genre that had been mined heavily by Jay on Reasonable Doubt.



The reference to “Street Dreams” was another opportunity for Jay to re-iterate that he doesn’t believe Nas lives the life he rhymes about.

There’s an argument going around that the beef with Jay saved Nas' career. Despite strong sales during the time between his debut album in 1994 and Stillmatic in 2001, the sentiments on “Takeover” were ringing true:

1 was “nah,” the other was Illmatic
That’s a one-hot-album-every-10-year average
And that’s so (lame)

line: I get the spoils ’cause the victor is me (Me, nigga) You’re an actor, you’re not who you’re depicted to be
vault_lines: I get the spoils 'cause the victor is me (Me, nigga)
meaning:
From the old saying “To the victor goes the spoils”.. i.e. winnings, credit. Also, ‘the spoils of war’ is the bounty or rewards after you win in combat. Jay is getting the lion-share of the spoils of this ‘war’ with Nas i.e. – media exposure, financial gain, love of his fans etc etc, at least in Jay’s opinion …

He is saying Nas puts on a front similar to an actor, referencing Nas' role in the 1998 Hype Williams film Belly.



In 2015, most agree that Jay won the war, but lost the battle. Yet Jay makes a potent point. Despite commentators claiming he “lost” the battle, Blueprint sold more than Stillmatic, and Blueprint 2 sold significantly more than Nas' 2002 album God’s Son. It depends on how you define success…

line: But I will not lose, for even in defeat There’s a valuable lesson learned, so it evens up for me
vault_lines: But I will not lose, for even in defeat
meaning:
Jay is referencing a very famous proverb:

We learn wisdom from failure much more than from success
-Samuel Smiles

Nas was declared the winner during the Hot 97 playoff between “Ether” and “Supa Ugly”. The lesson learned was to toe the line between facts and emotion, which is the intention of this track.

Jay continued to admit the power of the song in subsequent years, in 2006 rapping:

The Joneses can’t keep up
Maybe my n— Nas, but I got stronger after Ether

line: And now, you’s can’t leave You opened the door, God, I’m at you annually
vault_lines: And now, you's can't leave
meaning:
“I’m at you annually” refers to Jay’s consistent album releases – every year from Reasonable Doubt to his ‘retirement’ with The Black Album (1996-2003).

He also references the movie A Bronx Tale. In the movie the line “Now you’s can’t leave” is delivered to a group of bikers who enter a bar and decide to stir up trouble. It was a trap, and once they were stuck inside they saw the folly of their situation.

line: Let’s get to the proceedings preceding this evening
vault_lines: Let's get to the proceedings preceding this evening
meaning: This is a pun on Roberts Rules of Order. Jay is setting the theme of the song up to imply that he’s about to clarify issues like you would in an official meeting.

line: And the little homie Jungle is a garden to me
vault_lines: And the little homie Jungle is a garden to me
meaning:
Jungle is Nas’s younger brother and a member of the Bravehearts. Jay plays on his name by calling him a garden, something much smaller and far less threatening than a jungle.

Jungle responded in Bravehearts song “Bravehearted”:

Jungle’ll live by the morals of the street
Not like snitch C.J. or bitch Jay-Z
In beef them niggas only play defense
Guns never sparkin', afraid of my offense
Too rusty, I put they body in the garbage
Ya’ll niggas pussy, we bravehearted

In a December 2001 interview with Angie Martinez on Hot97, Jay-Z talked when he saw Jungle at McDonald’s and they talked and Jungle told him that they were gonna come back at him after he had dissed Nas at Summer Jam and Jungle also told him that he enjoys his music and then they gave each other a dap.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2iEMkpIu5Js&t=131s

Jungle also talked about this in Nas’s December 2001 interview with Funkmaster Flex on Hot97 where he said that Jay-Z was lying as he never told nobody he loves their music except Nas.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A3jq1gRtHzk&t=221s

line: I’m Big Dog, Glenn Rob, listen, God, you a flea
vault_lines: I'm Big Dog, Glenn Rob, listen, God, you a flea
meaning:
That’s basketball player Glenn “Big Dog” Robinson



God’s Son is Jesus, and Jesus is God, so Jay makes sure there are no mistakes when interpreting this line. Directed at Nas, he continues to debase his role in hip-hop, claiming he is a bit-part player.

line: And I’ma let karma catch up to Jaz-O, whoa
vault_lines: And I'ma let karma catch up to Jaz-O, whoa
meaning:
Jaz-O’s diss track “Ova” never recieved a response from Jay. Their beef is filled with emotion, and it continued well past the early 2000’s.

There were rumours that Jaz provided Nas with material for “Ether”, but there was no real incentive for Jay to devote anything more than subliminal shots to that. Jaz, by this time, hadn’t put out a studio album since 1991, and his production credits had dried up dramatically. Karma ran its course if the rumours were true.

line: When the grass is cut, the snakes will show I gotta thank the little homie Nas for that, though (Haha) Savin’ me the hassle of speakin’ to half of these assholes
vault_lines: When the grass is cut, the snakes will show
meaning:
Jay thanks Nas for the beef since it has brought out the true colors of people, making them choose sides, thus allowing Jay to identify the “snakes.”

Furthermore, by dissing Nas and holding his own in the subsequent exchange of disses, Jigga never had to expand past his final bars from “Takeover”:

And all you other cats throwing shots at Jigga
You only get half a bar – fuck y'all niggas

“Cutting the grass” is an idiom but Jay Z lends the common phrase some extra heft by giving it some additional interpretations: it may be referring to cutting off money (both grass and money being green) – which reveals the freeloaders – the rappers who hide behind or underneath others; and it’s a huge shot at Jaz-O, whose money was significantly reduced when he parted ways with Jay.

This line later became quite popular among NBA Players.

https://twitter.com/carmeloanthony/status/40993105960239104

line: I’ve been real all my life, they confuse it with conceit Since I will not lose, they try to help him cheat
vault_lines: I've been real all my life, they confuse it with conceit
meaning:
“I will not lose” is one of Jay-Z’s credo’s, originally on “Change the Game,” and later on “U Don’t Know.” Nas later mocked the phrase on “Ether.”

Rapping has always been an art of exaggeration and bravado, and conceit fits in to this, with some entertainers exaggerating their lavish lifestyle to appear more successful than they are. Jay, however, has really lived this life. These accusations are particularly tailored towards Nas, who Jay-Z claimed was a fake.

Jay is also implying that he’s been consistent in his rap and in his message. As Jay-Z explains earlier in the song; Nas is inconsistent. Nas received criticism for his inability to choose an identity, going from the optimistic street kid on Illmatic, to the gangster rapper on It Was Written…, to philosopher on Nastradamus. Jay-Z has always been Jay-Z.

line: Is it Oochie Wally Wally or is it One Mic? Is it Black Girl Lost or shorty owe you for ice?
vault_lines: Is it Oochie Wally Wally or is it One Mic?
meaning:
Jay Z is asking for the “real” Nas:  is it the “One Mic” Nas or the “Oochie Wally (Remix)” Nas? Hov ridiculed Nas for “Oochie Wally (Remix)” on “Takeover”:

To your bodyguard’s “Oochie Wally”’s verse better than yours
Matter of fact you had the worst flow on the whole fucking song
But I know: the sun don’t shine, then son don’t shine

With songs like “Black Girl Lost,” he expresses pity for how black women are demoralizing themselves in the streets, yet in “You Owe Me,” he discusses a girl owing him a blow job because he let her hold his diamonds.

line: And y’all buy the shit, caught up in the hype ’Cause the nigga wear a kufi, it don’t mean that he bright ’Cause you don’t understand him, it don’t mean that he nice It just means you don’t understand all the bullshit that he write
vault_lines: And y'all buy the shit, caught up in the hype
meaning:
A kufi is a Muslim headdress, associated with the Nation of Islam. One influential manifestation of the Nation of Islam was the Five Percent Nation, an offshoot, which talked a great deal about bringing enlightenment, kicking knowledge, etc. As Five Percent Doctrine became increasingly influential in rap in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the kufi became associated with rappers who cast themselves as “conscious”, “prophetic”, “political”, etc.

Nas was never Five Percent, but incorporated much of its terminology and became friends with its most influential promoters in rap, the Wu-Tang Clan. Here Jay is using the kufi as a metonym for the “conscious” rap tradition that Nas supposedly belongs to, pointing out that not everyone who has the superficial trappings of a sage is actually smart or interesting.

The accusation is that Nas is putting on the kufi as a kind of “costume” to establish his credibility, setting up the next lines about Nas' chameleonic persona.

line: When the Twin Towers dropped, I was the first in line (It’s real) Donatin’ proceeds off every ticket sold When I was out on the road, that’s how you judge Hov, no?
vault_lines: When the Twin Towers dropped, I was the first in line (It's real)
meaning:
Jay’s album The Blueprint was released on September 11th, 2001, the same day as the attacks on the World Trade Center. On his album tour, he donated $1 from every ticket sold to the relief effort.

Years later, shortly after the release of The Blueprint 3, he held a 9/11 benefit concert at Madison Square Garden.



Unfortunately, most are quick to judge Jay based on his lyrical content. As he was at pains to explain in Decoded, rappers are entertainers. What they say on the record and what they do in real life are sometimes separate entities, and Jay is dismayed that he is judged by lyrics rather than actions.

It’s part of his criticism of Nas, who sounds wonderful on record, but in reality isn’t doing anything to help or move the genre and culture forward.

line: I put dollars on mine, ask Columbine
vault_lines: I put dollars on mine, ask Columbine
meaning: Jay-Z had a concert in Denver right after Columbine and he and DMX both donated all their proceeds to support the families.

line: Won’t break you a crumb of the little bit that he makes And this is with whom you want to place your faith?
vault_lines: Won't break you a crumb of the little bit that he makes
meaning:
Jay has been a bit of a philanthropist for years without taking credit for it. He’s calling Nas out for never giving anything back to the community he comes from.

“Little bit that he makes” points out that Nas doesn’t make much money to begin with. Clever.

Jay draws on the Parable Of The Talents in the Bible, since he’s on this whole ‘false prophet’ accusation at Nas to basically say; Nas is a waste to the hip-hop community. He makes money but doesn’t share it. He has the microphone and the ability to influence opinion and behaviour, but he doesn’t use it effectively.

line: Can’t y’all see that he’s fake, the rap version of T.D. Jakes Prophesizin’ on your CD’s and tapes
vault_lines: Can't y'all see that he's fake, the rap version of T.D. Jakes
meaning:
A direct reference to Nas being a prophet on his CD and a reply to “Stillmatic”, where Nas calls Jay the rapping version of Sisqo.

T.D. Jakes is a televangelist who leads a megachurch called The Potter’s House. His sermons are shown on several TV stations including BET.



Why the comparison with Nas? Because TV evangelists, while being widely popular with their flock, are generally not seen as having much credibility. Most people consider them hypocrites and fakes.

line: And I’m sorry, Ms. Rosie Perez I call a spade a spade, it just is what it is But you can’t give cred to anything dude says Same dude to give you ice and you owe him some head Shorty, it’s time to wake up the dead You sound a little naïve in them articles that I read
vault_lines: And I'm sorry, Ms. Rosie Perez
meaning:
Actress Rosie Perez said in XXL Magazine that she didn’t appreciate Jay’s frequent use of the word ‘bitch’ and applauded Nas' support of women of color.

Jay offers a half-apology for the language, but basically says that he calls it as he sees it (the NWA defense). He goes on to question her allegiance to Nas, pointing out what he feels is Nas' hypocrisy on the subject.

Nas received acclaim for his song “Black Girl Lost” which spoke up for women of color and warned against using their bodies for material gain. But in “You Owe Me” he suggested women trade sexual favors for ‘ice’ (jewelry).

Shorty, say what’s your price
Just to back it up, you can hold my ice
Now let’s say you owe me something

He says the word “shorty” to further strengthen the tie to the Nas song.

He is effectively calling Rosie Perez and those of like-mind brain dead. He attempts to bring life into their minds by educating them throughout the remainder of the song. “Waking up the dead” is to bring up ignored/hidden/forgotten truths. A cleverly hidden gem of a shot at the casual listener. Jay says don’t skim through his music.

line: Y’all fell into the booby trap I set the trap just to see dude react, and now
vault_lines: Y'all fell into the booby trap
meaning: The way Jay allowed the beef with Nas to play out revealed the true nature of other rappers in the game, and their true feelings towards him. By posturing it as a “King of New York” rivalry, compounded by the fact he stopped saying “Nas” at the end of “Where I’m From,” he almost forced artists to take sides. “Supa Ugly” was so graphic it tested the loyalty of fence-sitters, and the result was a laundry list of personalities and rappers who came out against him.

line: What, y’all niggas get front-page articles? Y’all mention JAY-Z name? (This thing on?) JAY-Z, JAY-Z “In JAY-Z news” (Check) I understand what y’all tryna do
vault_lines: Get off JAY-Z' dick
meaning:
Jay accuses those who frequently mention him in the media for using his name to gain exposure.

This was a particular stab at Prodigy, who did an interview with The Source {wrong link?}. Unprovoked, he mentioned Jay claimed the song “Where I’m From” was based off of Nas’s life, and not Jay’s own. Jay constantly hounded him {where?} for wasting his interview on him.

line: “JAY-Z this,” ”JAY-Z that” (”JAY-Z won’t hold my hand no more”) “JAY-Z this,” ”JAY-Z that” “JAY-Z that,” ”JAY-Z this” (”JAY-Z won’t give me no money”) Get off JAY-Z’ dick
vault_lines: "JAY-Z this," "JAY-Z that" ("JAY-Z won't hold my hand no more")
meaning:
The rhyme scheme follows Big L’s Let ‘Em Have It “L”:

You sayin', ‘L’s this’ and ‘L’s that’;
Get off L' dick

The intro sets the tone for the song: everyone – from other rappers to the media – has some beef to pick with Jay, and he’s fed up.

line: [Outro: Denzel Washington from American Gangster] “’Blue Magic’—that’s a brand name. Like ’Pepsi’—that’s a brand name. I stand behind it. I guarantee it. They know that, even if they don’t know me any more than they know the— the Chairman of General Mills. My man...”
vault_lines: I'ma stand as a man
meaning:
This sample is taken from a scene in the American Gangster film which details a time when Frank Lucas found out his competitor Nicky Barnes was chopping down his “Blue Magic” heroin and reducing its quality – but then selling it under the same name.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FFJo3KhcZw4
Hov feels a similar way about his own personal brand.

line: So let the champagne pop I partied for a while – now, I’m back to the block
vault_lines: So let the champagne pop
meaning: Hov makes a toast in honor of his success and the way he has stayed true to his values. For Hov the party continues in the streets, not in a club. This demonstrates where his values lie, both personally and when making music. American Gangster was a rejection of the current rap market, which was based around selling singles with catchy hooks.

line: I’ma stand as a man Never dying on my knees, last of a dying breed
vault_lines: I'ma stand as a man
meaning:
Similar to 1996’s “Can I Live,” Hov announces he will never back down in the face of adversity. The idiom “last of a dying breed” paints a portrait someone who can do things that very few people can do – in this track he is referring to successfully manufacturing and distributing crack cocaine without getting caught.

Jay interpolates a famous quote (“I’d rather die on my feet, than live on my knees”) by Emiliano Zapata Salazar, a leading figure in last century’s Mexican Revolution.

Jay’s unique flow throws off the listener, who is waiting for Jay to finish the rhyme for “Siamese,” but before he raps “knees” he throws in the quick rhymes of twin/end and stand/man.

line: North Beach leathers
vault_lines: The imperial Skateboard P
meaning: North Beach Leathers was a high-end leather clothing company that created the iconic “8-Ball Jacket” in the late 80s early 90s. The jacket, which included a picture of an 8 Ball — a common slang term for an 8th ounce of cocaine — was highly sought after by hustlers due to the expensive price tag and implied drug dealer connotation.

line: No pain, no profit
vault_lines: No pain, no profit
meaning:
Jay plays off the idiom “no pain no gain,” which refers to the way humans physically and mentally become stronger by going through pain. Jay replaces “gain” with “profit” since money — or the lack of it — was the source of his pain and the motivating factor that drove him to succeed. Jay was able to channel the pain of growing up poor and hustling to survive, into songs that made millions of dollars.

Tracks like “Can I Live,” and especially “Regrets” highlight the turmoil he’s gone through as a hustler to get to his current position. And his classic lines on the original “Dead Presidents”:

I’m here to tell niggas it ain’t all swell
There’s heaven, and then there’s hell niggas
One day you’re cruising in your 7, next day you’re sweating, forgetting your lies
Alibis ain’t matching up, bullshit catching up
Hit with the RICO, they repo your vehicle
Everything was all good just a week ago
‘Bout to start bitching ain’t you? Ready to start snitching ain’t you?
I’ll forgive your weak ass; hustling just ain’t you

line: Niggas wanna bring the ’80s back That’s okay with me, that’s where they made me at Except I don’t write on the wall I write my name in the history books, hustlin’ in the hall
vault_lines: Niggas wanna bring the '80s back
meaning:
In the 1980s graffiti artists tagged their names all over the city in an attempt to become legends through their art. In contrast, drug dealers gained legendary status by making a substantial amount of money. At the time Jay chose not to focus on his art and instead hustled crack in the hallways of Marcy Housing Projects.

The idiom “writing my name in history” is a play off the fact that graffiti artists wrote their names on walls as a status symbol. In truth, Jay Z never actually made history selling drugs. Instead, he channelled that experience to enter the history books as one of the greatest artists (similar to heroes like Banksy)  In the book “Decoded,” Jay Z states:

…I literally “hustled in the halls” of buildings, even though I never made history — for better or worse.

line: I got Creole C.O. bitches for my niggas Who slipped, became prisoners, treats taped to the visitors
vault_lines: I got Creole C.O. bitches for my niggas
meaning:
Jay recycles a line  from close friend Biggie’s “You’re Nobody (Til Somebody Kills You)” to reference correctional officers who supervise inmates at prisons and jails.

Commissary, the prison system’s method of selling extras to inmates, is unnecessary for Hov’s crew because he has connections, “C.O. bitches,” who will bring them whatever they need – including contraband.

line: If it wasn’t for the crime that I was in But I wouldn’t be the guy who rhymes it is that I’m in (that I’m in)
vault_lines: If it wasn't for the crime that I was in
meaning: As East Cost rap took on a more gangster persona in the early 90s, Jay was able to use his hustler reputation to his advantage. Jay Z’s unique rhyme schemes and real street credibility propelled him to the top of the rap game. Jay makes the best of his checkered past by bragging about how authentic it makes his rhymes.

line: D.A. wanna indict me
vault_lines: D.A. wanna indict me

line: Can’t turn my back on the hood

meaning:
Two quotes from Republican politicians and operators sum up ways that being a Black Republican might be perceived as turning your back on the community you came from.

““You understand what I’m saying? We knew we couldn’t make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin. And then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities. We could arrest their leaders. raid their homes, break up their meetings, and vilify them night after night on the evening news. Did we know we were lying about the drugs? Of course we did.” Jon Ehrlichman, a domestic policy chief unde Richard Nixon.

Lee Atwater, RNC Chair and adviser of Ronald Reagan pioneered the strategy of using economic language to replace Republican strategy directly targeting the black community as a way to appeal to the Southern White supremacist voting block that Barry Goldwater and George Wallace appealed to, without openly courting white supremacy.

“You start out in 1954 by saying, “Nigger, nigger, nigger.” By 1968 you can’t say “nigger”—that hurts you, backfires. So you say stuff like, uh, forced busing, states’ rights, and all that stuff, and you’re getting so abstract. Now, you’re talking about cutting taxes, and all these things you’re talking about are totally economic things and a byproduct of them is, blacks get hurt worse than whites.… “We want to cut this,” is much more abstract than even the busing thing, uh, and a hell of a lot more abstract than “Nigger, nigger.” – Lee Atwater from his 1981 interview with the Nation.

Republican’s campaign against women’s rights also tied into this strategy, following the Supreme Court case Runyon v. McReary outlawing de jure segregated Christian schools, a coalition formed between segregationists Protestants and right wing Catholics with the goal of creating a judiciary that would openly  engage in activism against abortion rights, while at the same time deciding court decisions that were detrimental to the voting power of the black community (ex. Holder v Shelby County, Citizens United, )

Clarence Thomas (inspiration for Samuel L Jackson’s character in Django Unchained, and often treated as an archetypical Black Republican.) and other right wing Supreme Court Justices have made statements questioning the legality of seminal cases such as Brown v. Board of Education and Loving v. Virginia.

Instead he and Irby chose to spend their days hustling crack cocaine on the streets. They became successful quickly, expanding their operation to Maryland and Virginia.

The relationship became sour when Irby was arrested and sent to jail for five years on a federal drug-conspiracy charge – the same case that took down Emory “Vegas” Jones. vault_lines: Bitch, don't kill my vibe, bitch, don't kill my vibe
meaning:
Kendrick is trying to chill – he doesn’t mind if you are around, just don’t fuck up his mood.

But to further this conjecture, this song hook is a complex revelation of Kendrick’s true psychology and the chorus is actually a declaration of his attitude towards the world.

Kendrick is a diverse person, and there are many layers to his personality. He is spiritual, accepting and thoughtful, but he also comes from a city of violence, drugs, crime, etc. Kendrick is an incredibly empathic person; he sees things from all points of view and thus does not fall into any specific classification but rather covers the entire spectrum of humanity. Because of his debilitating empathy, there is a slight distance between himself and his peers. He lives in his own kind of world, observing the behavior and the nature of everything and everyone around him and contemplating it to himself. He is sincere and stable and his ultimate quest is to spread peace.

However, a common tendency for people of this personality-type is to shy away from complex, inexplicable situations where no fair and amicable solution is apparent. When such scenarios occur they may try to retreat into their metaphysical bubble and escape the paradoxical anxieties of life. This is exactly what Kendrick demonstrates in this song (either consciously or subconsciously), and the phrase “Bitch Don’t Kill My Vibe” is a solemn declaration of his desire to attain peace when things cannot be resolved easily.

But what I do know, is that He’s real and He lives forever
So the next time you feel like your world’s about to end
I hope you studied because He’s testing your faith again

Kendrick’s “hat” covered in thorns is a reference to the Crown of Thorns that Roman soldiers forced Jesus to wear during his crucifixion in John 19:2. The soldiers mocked Jesus, calling him the “King of the Jews”—Kendrick may be comparing this to the mockery he receives for his own musical sensibilities.

Frank off-roading in the BDC zine 

His ‘four wheel’ could also be describing a car. Ocean is an avid fan of cars and has made multiple references to them on almost all of his albums. He was even spotted drag racing on the streets with Tyler a while back.

The thrill that off-roading and racing provides exceeds the joy he experiences on his simple two-wheeled bike. The line creates a sense of maturity and evolution, and could be seen as a metaphor for his growth as an artist.

No temptation has taken hold of you except what is common to mankind. But God is faithful—He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can handle. But with the temptation He will also provide a way of escape, so you will be able to endure it.

meaning:
Continuing on the topic of marriage and love, Frank is contemplating the possibility that romantic love is only a temporary phenomenon.

Frank is strongly considering having a child, a “clone.” Frank’s father (who Frank referred to as a “weak individual” in a deleted tweet) abandoned his family when Frank was 5 years old. It’s safe to assume Frank understands the importance of a father being there for his child, and that Frank looks forward to fulfilling that role.

The line “Me and my baby can’t do on our own” can refer to both Frank and his partner longing for a child together. He and his companion may feel lonely or like something is missing. Another interpretation may have to do with the fact that if his partner is male, it is impossible for them to have a child that is biologically theirs– they can’t do it on their own and have to use a surrogate or adopt.



Frank also sang about a fictional child of his on “Sierra Leone”:

Tonight I’ll lay her in the cradle if it’s time for go to sleep

Continuing with the theme of riding bikes, Frank doesn’t get tired or “weak in the knees” when riding. However, this is also a metaphor about embracing life.

Regarding life, in “Dust,”Frank sings:

There’s no erasing and the best advice I got
Was keep writing, and keep living, and keep loving

Frank’s had his up’s and down’s, and documents them in his music. That being said, he’s not as naive or nervous like he was earlier in his life. Now, he embraces his sexuality and finally became an independent artist,  making money doing what he loves.

“Hundreds spread out like a fan” refers to the popular way to display all your cash which resembles a handheld folding fan.

line: On my lapel, at the table, I’m givin’ a toast (Givin’ it, clink) The first weddin’ that I’ve been in my twenties Thinkin’ maybe someone is not somethin’ to own Maybe the government got nothin’ to do with it
vault_lines: On my lapel, at the table, I'm givin' a toast (Givin' it, clink)
meaning:
Frank is at the beginning of the phase in his life where all the friends around him are getting married. This is not the first time Frank has made a comment on the nature of weddings. On “American Wedding” from his debut mixtape, nostaliga, ULTRA, Frank attacked the institution of marriage in the USA:

It’s just an American wedding
They don’t mean too much, they don’t last enough
We had an American wedding
Now what’s mine is yours, American divorce

Here he reflects on similar views. He sees two issues with marriage, firstly the interference of the government; he believes the state should have nothing to do with love. This could be as a result of his sexuality, since it was illegal for two men to marry in the US until June of 2015. He sings on “We All Try”:

I believe that marriage isn’t
Between a man and woman but between love and love

Although gay marriage is now legal, his sentiments against institutionalized love still remain. He talked more about this in the poem “Boyfriend” from his Boys Don’t Cry magazine:

I could say that I’m happy
They let me and my boyfriend become married
I could say that I’m happy
But cross my heart I didn’t notice

His second problem with marriage seems to be about its permanence. He believes someone shouldn’t be “owned” by another person.

There is also a reference to the contraction of “Mrs.” While now it is pronounced “misses” it was once pronounced “Mister’s”, indicating the ownership of a man.

“The Shaw” is short for Crenshaw Boulevard, a popular and historic street in Los Angeles. Biking from Coldwater to Crenshaw is about a nine mile ride.

Somnambulism, more commonly called sleepwalking, is a behavior disorder that causes people to perform complex behaviors while in deep sleep. Most cases of sleepwalking disappear after a short period of time, but treatment administered by trained professionals is necessary for people who deal with it persistently.

Like a sleepwalker, Frank doesn’t have control over his problems, and he isn’t able to ask for help because he’s unaware of the problems while they’re happening.

line: I’m fuckin’ with Addy, I’m watchin’ my dose 24 hours like they never close
vault_lines: I'm fuckin' with Addy, I'm watchin' my dose
meaning:
“Addy” is short for Adderall, a drug that helps people focus (“watchin'”). It’s most commonly used to subdue the effects of ADHD or narcolepsy, but Frank uses it to focus on his music career 24/7.

Substance abuse is a common theme in Frank’s music, dating back to “Novacane,” from his 2011 album nostalgia, ULTRA, where he used the numbing agent Novocain as a metaphor for his apathy.

line: God gave you what you could handle Gave you what you could handle I got the grip like a handle And I’m bikin’
vault_lines: God gave you what you could handle
meaning:
Frank literally holds tight to the “handles” on his bike, but he also plays on the word “handle” to reference dealing with personal hardships. He believes God wouldn’t have given him the troubles he’s faced if he didn’t think Frank could “handle” them. This seems to be a reference to the Bible verse 1 Corinthians 10:13 (TLV):

No temptation has taken hold of you except what is common to mankind. But God is faithful—He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can handle. But with the temptation He will also provide a way of escape, so you will be able to endure it.

line: That’s a full cab and a backflip, uh
vault_lines: That's a full cab and a backflip, uh
meaning:
“Full cab” and “back flip” are both BMX tricks.
A full cab is where the rider starts out riding in reverse, then performs a horizontal 360 degree jump, landing backwards, originally a skateboarding trick named after pro skater Steve Caballero.



To perform a backflip on a bike the rider has to get significant airtime, then pull straight back on the bike and rotate it vertically 360 degrees.

line: I’m Roger Rabbit in the air I don’t care,
vault_lines: I'm Roger Rabbit in the air
meaning:
Who Framed Roger Rabbit is a 1988 neo-noir comedy film that utilizes both live-action and animated styles. In 2016, the film was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry for being “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.”

Tyler could be referring to the specific scene where the main character is captured falling in the sky alongside Micky Mouse and Bugs Bunny. The two characters are from rivaling animation studios so it’s rare to see them together.

He may also be alluding to the “bunny hop,” a bike trick where the rider launches their bike into the air.

line: I’m bikin’ uphill, and it’s burnin’ my quads (Obstacles) I’m bikin’ downhill, and it sound like a fishin’ rod
vault_lines: I'm bikin' uphill, and it's burnin' my quads (Obstacles)
meaning:
As Frank bikes uphill it puts a strain on his lower leg muscles, his quads, but that all changes when he gets over the hill. As he travels downhill he doesn’t need to pedal and lets gravity do the work. When you don’t pedal on a bike you are just left with the sound of the ratchet mechanism moving within the gear set, which sounds like a fishing rod reeling in.

This could be a wider representation of his life and career. He’s faced struggles to get to the top, like his conflict with Def Jam but now he has made it in the music world and is independent he can just relax and make the music he wants to.

line: 12 o’clock, boy, silly nice, huh
vault_lines: 12 o'clock, boy, silly nice, huh
meaning:
This line transitions between Hov’s time motif and the the track’s bike theme. The “12 O'Clock Boys” are a Baltimore-based group who ride dirt-bikes and quads. In a 2013 documentary film that brought the group national attention, a pre-teen hustler named Pug described the origin of the group’s name:

They call them the 12 o'clock boys because they drop the bike straight back, like the hands on a clock. If you get to 12 o'clock, you’re the shit.

“Silly nice” is Hov’s way of saying how good his timepiece collecting and rapping skills are.

line: Wristwatch got a Russian face like a oligarch, ah
vault_lines: Wristwatch got a Russian face like a oligarch, ah
meaning:
While an oligarchy is a small group of people who control the majority of a country’s wealth, the term “Russian oligarch” refers to a wealthy Russian businessman. Jay’s watch face looks so expensive, he compares it to that of a Russian billionaire.

Jay previously worked alongside Mikhail Prokhorov, a Russian billionaire who owns the Brooklyn Nets. In 2012, Nets minority owner Bruce Ratner brought Jay Z on board as a fellow minority owner during his campaign to build an arena for the team in Brooklyn. Jay and Prokhorov were then pictured side-by-side in billboard ads. In 2013, Forbes described Prokhorov as an oligarch.

line: Shammgod with the AND1 moves Throw that shit ’round your neck, right quick
vault_lines: Shammgod with the AND1 moves
meaning:
God Shammgod played basketball for the Washington Wizards from 1997-1999. AND1 is a clothing company that used videos of streetball moves called AND1 mixtapes to market their shoes and clothes, which influenced the wider use of “and one” to mean a foul.

God Shammgod was known for his incredible crossovers, a flashy move favored by street ballers. Jay is likely referring to his own baller behavior, flashing his incredibly expensive watches when on the streets (“Willie in traffic”).

line: Audemars before all of y’all’s
vault_lines: Audemars before all of y'all's
meaning:
An avid watch collector, Jay told WatchTime Magazine in 2005 that he first fell in love with watch maker Audemars Piguet in 1997:

…it wasn’t until the American President of Audemars Piguet, François Bennahmias, brought me into the private vault at their New York headquarters that I really got serious about wristwatches. It was in 1997, so that’s when it got in my bones, right there.

Jay has since collaborated with the brand numerous times, most notably in 2005 on a three-piece “Royal Oak Offshore” collection. To celebrate his tenth anniversary in the music industry, the timepieces were packaged with an engraved iPod containing his entire discography.

Evidently, Jay was before his time. He first mentioned Audemars in hip-hop on his 2002 song “Show You How”:

Audemars Piguet with the alligator strap

After Jay’s association with the brand in 2005, usage of the term spiked dramatically:

line: Arms stretch a tee like I nailed it
vault_lines: Arms stretch a tee like I nailed it
meaning:
After Frank “nails” the BMX tricks Jay mentions at the end of his verse, he stretches his arms out perpendicular to his torso so his body’s shaped like the letter “T.” This is also a reference to Jesus Christ’s crucifixion—the cross is shaped like a lower case “t.”

Frank Ocean, a Christian himself, has addressed religion before, notably on 2012’s “Bad Religion” and a Tumblr post following the Orlando shootings. His father sued him over the post, accusing him of defamation.

line: E.T. on the handles, uh
vault_lines: E.T. on the handles, uh
meaning:
E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial is a 1982 American science-fiction film. A famous shot from the film shows E.T. hidden in a basket attached to the handlebars of Elliott’s bike.



Ironically, E.T. is one of Hov’s least favorite films. In 2011 Aziz Ansari explained on the Juan Epstein podcast why this is:

One time I had seen E.T. recently and I was like ‘Man, E.T. is like amazing!’ … and Jay Z was there and he was like ‘I don’t fuck with E.T.’ He was like ‘I don’t like E.T., but you know what’s dope? Johnny 5, Short Circuit’ … He said he didn’t like the effects in E.T., that it didn’t look right.

During the interview, host Cipha Sounds texted Hov about the movie, and his response was, “Fuck E.T. You watch it. Shit is horrible.”

Tattoos are often linked to criminal activity, more specifically gang culture, so Frank having them may make him seem more like a criminal to those that are quick to judge, a theme he commented on in “Chanel”:

line: Big Willie style, yeah Nigga, one wheel, one wheel, one wheel (Nigga, one) Nigga, one wheel, I fishtail downhill, yeah (One wheel, woo) I rose my rate, brand new brakes Why I name it Slater? Ask my date
vault_lines: Big Willie style, yeah
meaning:
Tyler featured Frank on “Slater,” a track about riding bikes from his 2013 album Wolf. In a tweet from that same year, Tyler explained that Slater is the name of his favorite bicycle. “Slater” is a homophone of “slayed her,” which insinuates that he and his date had sex.

This is also a reference to Jay’s earlier “Big Willie” line. Tyler pronounces “Willie” like “wheelie,” just as Jay did. Big Willie Style was the title of Will Smith’s 1997 debut album.

“Fishtailing” is a BMX trick where the back wheel of the bike moves laterally while the bike is simultaneously moving forward. Willie D of the Aggro Alliance Trick Team demonstrates this trick in a 2013 YouTube video.




https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TXkTA9eawcg




“Fishtailing” also refers to a handling problem when the rear wheel(s) lose traction and move side to side, resulting in oversteer. Tyler’s use of the term connects back to Frank’s line about his bike sounding like a fishing rod when he rides it downhill.

line: Uh, turn
vault_lines: So 'fore it goes down, nigga, get you some icicles
meaning:
“What goes around comes around” is an idiom meaning a person who initiates events will eventually feel their effects. Bike wheels literally go around when put into motion.

“Icicles” is another form of “ice,” which is slang for diamond jewelry. Jay Z is no stranger to jewelry, but rather than flaunting it, he’s suggesting fame and success are only temporary, so rappers should enjoy their wealth before it disappears.

He also pronounces “icicles” in a similar manner to “cycles,” following the track’s bike motif.

line: I’m bikin’, I’m bikin’, I’m bikin’ these blocks, yeah Since Ben Baller sold all his ice up at Slauson (Oh)
vault_lines: I'm bikin', I'm bikin', I'm bikin' these blocks, yeah
meaning:
Ben Baller is one of hip-hop’s go-to jewelers. Back in the 1990s, Baller was a record executive, with over 20 platinum records to his name—he even worked with Jay Z while he was employed at Priority Records, shortly before he and Roc-A-Fella Records jumped ship to Def Jam Recordings.

He got his start as a jeweler selling out of the Slauson Supermall in Los Angeles in 2005, which happens to be the same year Frank moved from New Orleans to LA to focus on his music career.

Baller has completed custom orders for Kanye West, Drake, Lil Uzi Vert, Nas, and Pusha T. He also lent a few diamond chains to Frank back in 2011.

line: Alcoholic, way I handle the bar
vault_lines: Alcoholic, way I handle the bar
meaning:
“Bars” has three meanings here: the part of the bicycle used for steering, establishments that serve alcohol, and lines of lyrics.

Tyler compares his bike-riding and rapping skills to an alcoholic’s tolerance for liquor. He doesn’t actually drink, though—he has tweeted about being “straight edge,” and in his 2013 appearance on the Arsenio Hall show, he said drugs and alcohol “aren’t for everyone.”

This line is also a callback to Jay Z’s earlier lyric:

Handlebars like a Xanax

line: Handlebars like a Xanax
vault_lines: Handlebars like a Xanax
meaning:
Xanax is a highly-addictive anxiety-relieving prescription drug that’s manufactured in the form of rectangular tablets, or “bars.”

Handlebars are a bicycle’s steering mechanism, but Jay’s playing on the word to brag about how deftly he handles his rap lyrics—his “bars.” He also owns the 40/40 Club, a chain of sports bars located in New York City and Atlanta.

line: Willie in traffic, I’m Philly nice, uh
vault_lines: Willie in traffic, I’m Philly nice, uh
meaning:
This is a callback to one of Hov’s infamous lines on 1996’s “Can’t Knock The Hustle”:

Chilly with enough bail money to free a Big Willie
High stakes, I got more at stake than Philly

“Willie,” short for “Big Willie,” is a 1990s hustler term for a big shot. Jay also pronounces “willie” so it sounds like “wheelie” to paint a picture of him pulling wheelies on his motorcycle in traffic—a stunt which isn’t farfetched considering he said he’s been doing it since he was six years old on 2000’s “Best of Me Pt. II:”

Used to wheelie bicycles since I was six

The “bike life” is a large part of Philadelphia culture, and gangs of urban dirt bike riders will sometimes ride through the streets. This is also an allusion to Jay’s friend Will Smith, who was born and raised in West Philly; his 1997 debut studio album was titled Big Willie Style.

This could also be a reference to William Penn’s statue on top of City Hall in Philadelphia, which is one of the highest points in the city. It’s located in the middle of Broad Street and is visible when a driver is stuck in traffic.

I keep em looking good, pretty and all that, but no dough.” These lines have been referred to a lot in hip hop, but it’s not meant to endorse actual pimping, that was never my thing. line: [Verse 3: Pimp C, Bun B]
vault_lines: But I don't fuckin' feed 'em
meaning:
When ranking his own albums through 2013, Jay-Z specifically cited this verse as one of Vol. 3’s high points (along with “So Ghetto”).

But Pimp C was hardly eager to hop on this track! He feared fans wouldn’t like him working with a mainstream rapper and he even hated the beat at first, saying, “This got a lotta flutes man, I don’t know about them flutes, man.”

Bun B and Jay-Z eventually talked him into recording, but Pimp C agreed only on the condition that he would rap just eight bars. But what a memorable eight bars they were, with elements of this verse eventually used by:



Kenrick Lamar on “Blow My High (Members Only”) (2011)

Timbaland on “Triple Threat” (2012)

Isaiah Rashad on “Free Lunch” (2016)

Pimp C himself on “Pourin’ Up” (2006)

Keeping with the general theme of this verse, namely his own influence on, and dominance over, the Hip-Hop landscape, Jay claims to possess the necessary authority to line the entire rap game up behind him with nothing more than a simple gesture of his hand.

It’s very possible, given his reference earlier in this verse to Nat Turner, who famously led a 1831 slave rebellion in Virginia, that Hov is continuing his black-power rhetoric here with a nod to Malcolm X, one of the most famous civil rights activists in history.



In 1957, in one of his more well-documented stand-off’s with the authorities, Malcolm mobilised the Nation of Islam in response to one of their number, a man named Reese Poe, being beaten and held, without medical attention, by the NYPD.

Their initial march on the police precinct where Poe was being detained was enough to prompt his transportation to a local hospital for medical attention, followed again by Malcolm and his group of well-disciplined followers.

The event was dramatised in one of the more memorable scenes from Spike Lee’s 1992 biopic in which Malcolm, after getting his desired outcome, famously moves his Nation of Islam colleagues on with a single wave of his finger, in a silent and measured show of both authority and force that intimidates the police chief with whom he is dealing.

meaning:
There’s mixed messages again from Jay. This is the culmination of the track, and it can be seen as a summing up of his career.

His original verse on “Dead Presidents” is a precursor to this. In it, he details the exact struggles and insecurities all hustlers face, ones he wishes he’d had the insight to avoid.

Watch how I’m walking cause even the thoroughest niggas be narkin'
Tryin' to strike a bargain hoping that they might get pardoned
Shit I’m involved with got me pins and needles
And my cerebral breeds the wickedest evil thoughts that this sport’ll feed you

Essentially, what he said on “Beach Chair” to his unborn daughter is being rephrased to appeal to hustlers.

A blueprint for you to print
A map for you to get back
A guide for your eyes, and so you won’t lose scent

What is the American Dream after all? Does success in hustling define it for African Americans?

Jay himself has redefined the game, giving hope and heart to millions of drug dealers who saw no way out other than to peddle drugs.

Jay has to pause for a second, he’s caught up in the American Dream that he has concocted for himself.

line: I open the door for them, what else can I do These niggas want me to walk for them Somebody talk to them before I go off on them
vault_lines: I open the door for them, what else can I do
meaning:
Jay uses “opening the door” as a metaphor for giving other artists opportunities, access, and a path forward. His frustration is that some people apparently expect more than the opportunity itself—they expect him to carry them through it as well. “These niggas want me to walk for them” extends the metaphor: Jay can open the door, but he cannot do another person’s walking for them.

That interpretation closely matches how Jay has described his philosophy toward artists later in life. In a 2026 GQ interview, he explained that with J. Cole, he wanted to give him the tools and opportunity to reach a larger audience while ultimately allowing Cole to “find his journey” and determine his own direction. Jay contrasted this with his much more hands-on relationship with Memphis Bleek, whom he described as his “little brother.”

Bleek’s own comments reinforce the distinction. Despite Jay famously promising to look after him financially, Bleek said in a 2025 Club Shay Shay interview, “I still got to work… He ain’t give it to me now. I still got to earn it.” Bleek has also described how Jay repeatedly advised and guided his career, including giving direct feedback on records and helping shape releases.

Taken together, the lines read less like Jay refusing to help people and more like frustration with people who confuse access with entitlement: he can create the opportunity, provide guidance, and open the door, but the person receiving that opportunity still has to walk through it themselves. “Somebody talk to them before I go off on them” closes the thought with Jay’s patience with that expectation wearing thin.

line: I’m like a Russian mobster, drinking distilled vodka
vault_lines: I'm like a Russian mobster, drinking distilled vodka
meaning:
He’s painting a vivid image of power, luxury, and his calculated approach to life and business.

Russian mobsters are often depicted in pop culture as ruthless, disciplined, and powerful—running highly organized, strategic operations. By comparing himself to them, Jay aligns his own success and hustle with their image of control, influence, and fearlessness.

Distilled vodka is associated with purity and quality, particularly in Russia, where vodka is culturally significant. This emphasizes Jay’s refined tastes, his status, and his ability to enjoy the finer things in life.

Together, the line highlights HOV’s persona:
• He’s a boss who moves smart, like a mob leader.
• He enjoys the highest quality things in life, a testament to his success.
    • The “allure” of that lifestyle—dangerous yet luxurious—is something he can’t resist, which ties back to the song’s theme of being drawn to the hustler lifestyle despite its risks.

It’s a masterful line that blends imagery of power, sophistication, and Hov’s street origins.

line: I never felt more alive than riding shotgun In Klein’s green 5', until the cops pulled guns
vault_lines: I never felt more alive than riding shotgun
meaning:
A reference to Calvin “Klein” Bacote, a Brooklyn stick-up kid turned drug kingpin as pat of the Marcy Posse. Klein and a young Shawn Carter ran together in the ‘80s selling crack cocaine. The line is referring to when Hov and Klein were arrested together while driving in the Brooklyn Don’s green BMW E34 sedan.



In 1989 they were at a house party in Maryland when a fight broke out between their crew and the hosts. They were arrested and charged with attempted murder, attempted murder to maim, battery assault, and possession of a deadly weapon.

Klein paid the victim $50,000 in return for him dropping the charges on one of the two. Klein already had prior attempted murder convictions, so Jay offered to take the charges and stand trial in his place. Luckily for us, Klein recognized Hov’s rap potential and took the weight of the case. Hov was acquitted and released. He would later testify on Klein’s behalf and help his 40-year sentence be reduced to four years.



After being released on drug convictions in 2004 Klein claimed that Hov embellished his past in his raps:

I give him 10% of his life that he talked about. He is from Brooklyn, he lived in Marcy Projects, his name is Shawn Carter, he got that right. Calvin Klein, a Brooklyn Don, my legacy speaks for itself. Jay had to take parts of that in order to be who he is.

Later, in a 2014 interview with Complex, Klein recanted on his earlier statements:

You have to kind of look at his history. How many times have you caught him in a lie? You have to give him the benefit of the doubt … Was Jay-Z a good hustler? I’m a hell of a hustler too, but he’s a hell of a hustler. You gotta give it to him. He took nothing and turned it into something.

line: When I blast the pump, I leave you relaxed In the hospital, lookin’ at M*A*S*H for months
vault_lines: When I blast the pump, I leave you relaxed
meaning:
Jay let’s any potential adversaries know the consequences of going against him. It’s going to involve a close encounter with his shotgun, followed by a lengthly period of convalescence at the local hospital.

He underscores his point here by making a clever reference to the long-running sitcom M*A*S*H, in a line that could be interpreted one of three different ways;

Firstly, and perhaps most straight-forwardly, the setting for M*A*S*H was a Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean war. Hov is simply reiterating his point that fucking with him will land you in the hospital.

Secondly, and again tying into the hospital theme, it works as a reference to stereotypically bad food one is served during a hospital stay, mashed potatoes being a particular staple!

And, finally, given that M*A*S*H is amongst the highest-rated and most watched television shows in US history it is, as a result of syndication, regularly subject to re-runs. Jay is informing would-be challengers to his throne that they will have plenty of time to catch up with the adventures of Hawkeye and the gang whilst they’re laid-up, recovering from the injuries he’s inflicted.

line: I guess I got my swagger back
vault_lines: I guess I got my swagger back
meaning:
Jay-Z recites this line in the song “Otis” to evidence his claim that he invented swag.

“Swagger” had been used as a noun to mean “braggadocio” for many, many years – Shakespeare used the term in his play A Midsummer Night’s Dream, circa-1590. But Jay Z was the first known rapper to use the term on wax, back in 2001 on this track. He uses the shortened version (‘swag’) on The Black Album’s tracks “Public Service Announcement” (“Check out my swag' yo, I walk like a ballplayer”) and “December 4” (“My self-esteem went through the roof, man. I got my swag”). Nowadays it is one of the most popular terms used in the rap game today to express the supreme way someone presents themselves – I guess he really did invent swag.

line: We used to hustle in the hood, for all to see Problems—I called on him, he called on me We wasn’t quite partners, I hit him off my P
vault_lines: We used to hustle in the hood, for all to see
meaning:
Shawn and DeHaven Irby’s friendship flourished after moving to Trenton, New Jersey in the late ‘80s. They would develop a sprawling drug dealing operation, eventually transitioning from powder cocaine to the cheaper and more addictive crack nuggets. As Irby explained in 2011, they were very close and supported each other financially:

We were like brothers. Whatever I was doing, he was doing. He picked it up quick.

At the end of the last line here, and in the next, Hov claims that the partnership wasn’t exactly equal – he sometimes had to support Irby financially, that is, give him a cut of his “P” (package).

Jay was more efficient. I would overpay the runners so they would be happy and not steal, and he would pay exactly what they were worth. I kept 15 runners and he had two people and was doing pretty much the same numbers … A lot of people thought of him as stingy. If the product was $10, you couldn’t get it for $9.

DeHaven is from my projects; we all from the same building. Him and Jay had their hustle ties and things went sour … You want to know the real deal? All you got to do is listen to ‘A Week Ago’ and the joint with R. Kelly where you know your true friends when you both got money.

meaning:
The Jay Z and Prodigy beef started when Jay said on “Money, Cash, Hoes”

It’s like New York’s been soft
Ever since Snoop came through and crushed the buildings

This was referring the the track “New York, New York” by Tha Dogg Pound and Snoop Dogg. In the music video for the track, Snoop was showed kicking down buildings in New York City. Mobb Deep, Capone-N-Noreaga, and Tragedy Khadafi would return with the track L.A., L.A..

Prodigy took offense to Jay’s statement, saying that Jay wasn’t involved in the ‘East/West’ feud:

[Jay Z] should have just shut the fuck up and minded his business. We went after him after that. Like, I fucking hit you in the head. I took it upon myself like, ‘You know what? This fucking bitch ass nigga popping shit about some shit that he wasn’t even around and his name was involved.’ Tupac was going at him. His name was all in that and he didn’t have nothing to say at that time.

Jay Z responded by dissing Nas and Prodigy in his track “Takeover” in which he says,

I don’t care if you Mobb Deep, I hold triggers to crews
You little fuck, I got money stacks bigger than you
When I was pushin' weight back in ‘88
You was a ballerina, I got the pictures, I seen ya
Then you dropped “Shook Ones,” switched your demeanour
Well, we don’t believe you, you need more people

Jay Z also put up a picture of Prodigy at P’s grandmother’s dance school when he was young on the 2001 Summer Jam screen (as mentioned in the next line).

Prodigy said that he didn’t take offense to the picture, but later found Jay Z at a restaurant, and wanted to fight Jay, along with one of Prodigy’s mans who wanted to shoot him. Instead, Jay Z went to shake Prodigy’s hand and didn’t fight him, saying it was just music.

Here, Jay is saying that Prodigy took the beef too far by wanting to take an argument in music to real life, in which someone could have gotten beat up, stabbed, shot, or killed.

line: [Verse 4: J. Cole]
vault_lines: Every day a star is born (And you say New York City! Yeah, yeah)
meaning:
Making an appearance on The Blueprint 3 was exciting, but at the same time very pressuring. A few days after the project released, Cole sat with Complex to speak about the process for writing his verse:

Complex: How long did it take you to write the verse?

Probably about an hour. It felt like forever, because I was so nervous. But in actuality it was only like an hour, if that. 45 minutes, maybe.

Complex: Did you feel any pressure to follow the model Jay laid down with his verses?

All I felt was the necessity to, cause the beat is fast, so a sixteen on that kind of beat don’t really last that long. So i was like okay, if I only got 16 bars, I want to tell as much of my story as possible. So I definitely wanted to shout out the ‘Ville and let people know that i came up. — I wanted to give them my story if I could.

At the time Cole had only released two mixtapes, so therefore landing this verse (and given the symbolism of the song title) was a major coup.

This was one of the last vehicles purchased by 2Pac before his untimely passing in September 1996. He also featured a Humvee in the video for his 1995 single “California Love,” which had an apocalyptic war and Mad Max-esque theme.



The freedom Hov speaks of is the then-recent formation of his new entertainment company Roc Nation. Prior to forming the label he was serving as President of Def Jam Recordings. He paid $5 million to leave that position owning all of his master recordings, and was clearly happy to be moving on and beginning a new [completely independent] chapter with Roc Nation:

I can honestly say, working with [Universal Music Group CEO] Doug Morris and [Def Jam chairman] L.A. Reid has been a unique and fulfilling experience and I respect them immensely. I’ve been in the family for almost my entire career. I thank [Morris] for allowing me to be a completely independent artist. Not every artist can say they own or are given the opportunity to own all of their music.

Since its introduction the company has gone from strength to strength; including the formation of a boutique sports agency, a boxing promotion division, various entertainment and fashion partnerships, and a venture fund.

On “Takeover” in 2001 he claimed that the Nation’s spiritual predecessor Roc-A-Fella Records was “the army, better yet the navy.”

Jay is trying to figure out if he actually spoke with the late great Biggie Smalls or simply had a dream featuring the rap icon. Thus, “was it all a dream?” (a play off of Biggie’s most famous line, ‘it was all a dream’) is repeated over and over as her continuously asks himself the question “did this actually happen?” over and over again.

This is why the line is repeated multiple times  as Jay-Z repeatedly asks himself this question.

meaning:
This is setting the scene for what BIG said to Jay in this dream of his. His head was racing around and he was trying to figure out what was going on as he was so incredibly confused by his visit from this unreal being. He questions whether it was a dream with “it was all a dream” then contradicts the statement with “it felt so real to me”.

This back and forth battle in his head both plays off of the famous Biggie Smalls line “it was all a dream” from “Juicy” as he does multiple times in this song and shows the struggle within Biggie’s head as he thinks about all that is wrong with the scenario he is faced with and why it may or may not have actually been the ghost of Biggie Smalls visiting him.

line: “Careful what you wish for, you might receive it,” he said “I see,” I said, “jealousy” I said “Got the whole industry mad at me,” I said Then B.I. said,

meaning:
Biggie says that his death came about not because of his roots on the street but by the trappings of fame and fortune and the jealousy they inspire. Jay interprets this as being a warning; if Jay wishes for the same wealth and notoriety Biggie had, then he may be inadvertently be wishing for a similar death as well.

We already know how Jay feels about jealousy, but this line is very indicative of the bitterness that Jay still held towards an industry that outwardly rejected him.

During Decoded he expressed his view that the “industry shady and need to be taken over,” and how he saw Jaz-O get taken advantage of by major labels and left for dead. It left a bad taste in his mouth, and his success as an independent artist was karma, in his mind, for the way major’s were treating artists.

line: It—It—It was all a dream
vault_lines: It—It—It was all a dream
meaning:
From “Juicy” by The Notorious B.I.G.

Jay’s reenactments give the line two different meanings. The first, exclaimed, conserves the original reminiscent quality. It is a quotation of Biggie’s most well-known line and illustrates that Jay-Z is thinking back at how much this one dream affected him.

The second meaning, less assertively delivered, conveys doubt. As insightful as Biggie’s advice to Hova is and as realistic as the dream felt to Jay-Z, it was still just a dream… Right? This meaning is a theme throughout the song.

line: “I agree,” I said, “my one of a kind self” Getting stoned every day like Jesus did

meaning:
Jay-Z agreed with what was said, for he knew he was one of a kind. Jay also uses a play on words, getting “stoned” as in high, smoking weed. Where as in the bible, there are many references to people getting “stoned” as in getting rocks thrown at them and bludgeoned to death. In John 10:30-33 Jesus says: “I showed you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you stoning Me?”

It’s also a way for Jay to distance himself from the “Jay-Hova” line. He has been at pains to explain throughout his career that he is not calling himself “God”, or comparing himself, but rather than amongst rappers he see’s himself as the pinnacle, and that God works through him.

In Fade To Black, he says “I don’t know how it works man. They say you put the right artist, with the right beat, leave the door open and let God in”.

Big’s original reference was to the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center, but since this track came out just a year after the devastating September 11 attacks it was edited out of respect.

The split-screen is reapplied, as we’re asked to view a hustler on the corner risking their life next to a soldier literally ending lives. Both the hustler and the soldier are killers for a living. It’s only their methods that differ.

meaning:
Quadruple Entendre:

-In the military if you transgress an order or step out of line, your punishment is that you will be sent to be confined by yourself for a certain amount of time.

-Drug dealing on the streets could lead to prison and being sent to “the hole”, which is a very dark and lonely place in prison where you stay by yourself.

-Drug dealing could also lead to being killed and locked in a casket in a 6 foot deep hole where your body would never see the light of day again.

-Drug dealing is a gamble. You purchase drugs and hope to sell them at a higher price. If you are robbed or arrested and lose your stash, you find yourself in a “hole”. When Jay was first arrested as a teenager in Trenton, his work was confiscated.

The damage was done – they confiscated the work I was holding. That combined with a series of other setbacks, and suddenly we were in a hole.

Many high school graduates see the army as a viable career option. It is a stable if not outstanding income, with travel/board/food paid for. In some families it is even a rite of passage to serve your country, part of becoming an adult.

Bleek is aiming his barrel at the sky to celebrate the success, and it serves as a motivational statement to the rest of the family, to aim for the sky because nothing is unachievable.

It was Rocawear that would be the most successful, but Jay used all of this to build his own empire, one that now takes in sports, nightclubs, music,  and even beauty products.

Too many ladies give these niggas too many chances
Too many brothers wannabe lovers don’t know what romance is
Too many bitches stuck up from too many sexual advances
No question; Jay-Z got too many answers

All four of these lines are connected. The first two lines answer questions that the third line might pose, before they arise. “Too many bitches stuck up from too many sexual advances” answers the question as to why there are a lot of stuck up females in the world. “Too many brothers wanna be lovers don’t know what romance is” answers the question as to why so many sexual advances are made towards woman. “Too many ladies give these niggas too many chances” answers the question as to why they get “too many sexual advances” and men don’t just stop after the first rejection. This line also refers to women that stick with their men (giving them another chance) after they do them wrong by cheating on them. We know that Jay-Z is referring to men cheating on their women because of the next line “Too many brothers wanna be lovers don’t know what romance is” giving this line more then one meaning.

The final line in this set, “No question; Jay-Z got too many answers” is highlighting how he just explained the last three lines in a way that built up to the final explanation, leaving no room for any questions on the subject. It also speaks towards Jay just being knowledgeable in general which he starts to expand on with the next line “I been around this block too many times” and goes on a bit about it after that.

This of course isn’t the format I’d use explaining these lines but there is a lot more going on in this verse (and whole song) then what’s on the surface.

Jay even emulates Jordan in some regards. For example, Jay retired in 2003 only to return to the rap game shortly after. Similarly, Jordan’s 1993 retirement was short lived. Jay’s return to the game was no surprise especially since he spoke about doing so on, what was said to be his last album, The Black Album.

When I come back like Jordan wearing the 45…

Jay also uses wordplay to illustrate the connection between “His Airness” and HOV. When Jordan was in the NBA, he wore a wristband on his forearm to keep sweat off his hands. Jay has also worn a wristband on his forearm in past performances, however, he is likely referring to the band of his watch or bracelet.
